s: Paracelsus's De natura rerum book IV ('Of the life of naturall things'; c. 1537, in John French's English of 1650) opens: no one can deny that air gives life to all things generated of the earth, and defines the life of each thing as 'nothing else then a spirituall essence', invisible and impalpable; no bodily thing lacks a hidden spirit and life.

src.l: Paracelsus, Sendivogius, Michael, 1650, A New Light of Alchymie ... also Nine Books of the Nature of Things, written by Paracelsus (trans. John French), London: Cotes for Williams
src.q: NO man can deny that Aire gives life to all things, bodies, and substances, that are produced, and generated of the Earth.

src.l: Paracelsus, Sendivogius, Michael, 1650, A New Light of Alchymie ... also Nine Books of the Nature of Things, written by Paracelsus (trans. John French), London: Cotes for Williams
src.q: it is nothing else then a spirituall essence, a

s: Glauber (Teutschlands Wohlfahrt IV, 1659) says air is not pure life but life is invisibly dispersed in it like a little salt in much water; in the same way life is distributed in human and animal bodies and dwells invisibly in the blood, without which the body is dead and motionless.

src.l: Glauber, Johann Rudolph, 1659, Des Teutschlandts Wohlfart, part 4 (Germany's Prosperity)
src.q: All air is not pure life, but life is invisibly dispersed within it, like a little salt in much water; one sees the water, but not the salt.
src.qo: Alle Lufft ist nicht lauter Leben / sondern das Leben ist unsichtbahr darin zerspreit / wie ein wenig Salß in vielem Wasser

src.l: Glauber, Johann Rudolph, 1659, Des Teutschlandts Wohlfart, part 4 (Germany's Prosperity)
src.q: Alle Lufft ist nicht lauter Leben / sondern das Leben ist unsichtbahr darin zerspreit / wie ein wenig Salß in vielem Wasser

s: Digby (Discourse on the Powder of Sympathy, 1658; 1664 English) cites the Cosmopolite (Sendivogius): 'There is a hidden food of life in the air', and offers as evidence small vipers fed only on air that grew to a foot long within a year, and vitriol and saltpetre that increase 'onely by attraction of air'.

src.l: Digby, Kenelm, 1664, A Late Discourse ... Touching the Cure of Wounds by the Powder of Sympathy, London
src.q: Hence it came that the Cosmopo- lite had reason to say, Est in aere occul- tus vitæ cibus ; There is a hidden food of life in the air.

s: Fludd (Answer to Foster, 1631), defending the weapon-salve, calls the volatile salt spread everywhere in the open air 'the purest essence of and in the ayre, in which the graine of life is', and quotes the same dictum 'Est in aëre occultus vitæ cibus'.

src.l: Fludd, Robert, 1631, Dr. Fludds Answer to M. Foster or, the squesing of parson Fosters sponge
src.q: it is the volatile salt, which is euery where expansed in the open ayre, and it is the purest essence of and in the ayre, in which the graine of life is

s: Planis Campy (L'Hydre morbifique, 1628) says rain's fertility comes from 'the life that it has acquired while passing through the Air', a life that joins with the Salt Nitre of the earth, for 'Salt Nitre was Air itself'.

src.l: Planis Campy, David de, 1628, L'Hydre morbifique exterminée par l'Hercule chymique, Paris: Du Mesnil
src.q: This impregnation and fertility occur by means of the life that it [the water] has acquired while passing through the Air. This life joins with the Salt Nitre of the Earth
src.qo: Laquelle impregnation & fer- tilité se fait par le moyẽ de la vie qu'el- le a acquife en passant par l'Air.

s: The German Turba / Book of the Golden Art (1613) quotes Arnold's Rosarium: putrefaction is necessary in the work, for nothing is born or grows, nor has a soul and life, except after putrefaction; this putrefaction is not stinking but a mingling of water and earth in their smallest parts.

src.l: Anonymous, 1613, Turba philosophorum, das ist, das Buch von der güldenen Kunst (The Assembly of the Philosophers and the Book of the Golden Art)
src.q: for nothing is ever born or grows, nor does anything possess a soul and life, except after putrefaction.
src.qo: dann es wird niemals etwas geboren/ oder wächset/ es hat auch nichts ein Seele vnd leben/ dann nach der putrefaction.

src.l: Anonymous, 1613, Turba philosophorum, das ist, das Buch von der güldenen Kunst (The Assembly of the Philosophers and the Book of the Golden Art)
src.q: dann es wird niemals etwas geboren/ oder wächset/ es hat auch nichts ein Seele vnd leben/ dann nach der putrefaction.

s: Paracelsus (De natura rerum I, Huser's German ed. 1589) glosses putrefaction as 'a reversal and the death of all things', a destruction of the first essence, from which comes rebirth and new birth 'with thousandfold improvement'; putrefaction is the first degree of generation.

src.l: Paracelsus, 1589, Erster [- zehender] Theil der Bücher und Schrifften des edlen, hochgelehrten und bewehrten philosophi und medici Philippi Theophrasti Bombast von Hohenheim ...
src.loc: De natura rerum I, p. 259; scan 1926
src.q: is a reversal and the death of all things/ and a destruction of the first essence/ of all natural things/ from which comes to us the rebirth/ and new birth/ with thousandfold improvement.
src.qo: Die Putrefaction ist ein vmbkehrung vn der Todt aller dingen/ vnd ein zerstörung deß ersten Wesens

src.l: Paracelsus, 1589, Erster [- zehender] Theil der Bücher und Schrifften des edlen, hochgelehrten und bewehrten philosophi und medici Philippi Theophrasti Bombast von Hohenheim ...
src.loc: De natura rerum I, p. 259; scan 1926
src.q: Die Putrefaction ist ein vmbkehrung vn der Todt aller dingen/ vnd ein zerstörung deß ersten Wesens

s: Crollius redivivus (Hermetischer Wunderbaum, 1647) praises the power of putrefaction, 'how it kills and makes alive again', turning earth to water, water to air, air to fire, and making the body spiritual and the spiritual heavenly.

src.l: Anonymous, 1647, D.O.M.A. Crollius redivivus: Hermetischer Wunderbaum, Frankfurt: Weiss
src.q: the power and might of putrefaction , how it kills and makes alive again
src.qo: die Macht vnd Gewalt der putrefaction, wie sie tödtet/ vnd wider lebendig machet

src.l: Anonymous, 1647, D.O.M.A. Crollius redivivus: Hermetischer Wunderbaum, Frankfurt: Weiss
src.q: die Macht vnd Gewalt der putrefaction, wie sie tödtet/ vnd wider lebendig machet

s: Stoltzius's emblem verse 'Putrefactio' (Viridarium chymicum, 1624): the seed must first putrefy and die so that it may rise; without this path nothing grows; while pale death kills the lovers, Vulcan (the fire) gives new threads of life.

src.l: Stoltzius von Stoltzenberg, Daniel, 1624, Viridarium chymicum figuris cupro incisis adornatum
src.q: The seed must first putrefy and die together, So that it may arise to higher riches.
src.qo: Putrefcat primùm, fimul emoriatur oportet Semen, ut ad fuperas exoriatur opes.

src.l: Stoltzius von Stoltzenberg, Daniel, 1624, Viridarium chymicum figuris cupro incisis adornatum
src.q: Putrefcat primùm, fimul emoriatur oportet Semen, ut ad fuperas exoriatur opes.

s: Paracelsus's De natura rerum ('De morte rerum', Huser ed.) speaks of 'the killing of metals, of their destruction and the removal of their life', and lists kinds of killed metal: rust of iron is dead, every crocus Martis is a killed iron, and so are vitriol and verdigris.

src.l: Paracelsus (1493-1541), 1589, Erster [- zehender] Theil der Bücher und Schrifften des edlen, hochgelehrten und bewehrten philosophi und medici Philippi Theophrasti Bombast von Hohenheim ... / [Erster bis sechster Theil.]
src.q: As you have now heard of the killing of metals, of their destruction and the removal of their life, you should also know that there are still many kinds of killed metals.
src.qo: Vnd also wie jhr nun gehört haben von dem tödten der Metallen / von jhrer Zerstörung vnnd hinnemmung jhres Lebens: solt jhr auch wissen / daß jhr noch vilerley tödtet Metallen sind.

s: Leo Suavius's Compendium of Paracelsus (1567) says there is a spirit in metals that arises as in germinating things, from the Platonic mind that moves the universe, citing Ficino's De vita ('spirit lies hidden in stones and metals, oppressed by the mass of matter'), and reads the 'vivum' of argentum vivum as the life that is vegetation.

src.l: Suavius, Leo (Jacques Gohory), Paracelsus, 1567, Theophrasti Paracelsi philosophiae et medicinae utriusque universae compendium, Paris: Rovillius
src.q: For there is also a spirit within metals, from the Platonic mind which moves this mass of the universe, and mixes itself with the great body
src.qo: Hic videt in verbo argẽti viui, vitã quæ vegetatio eſt

src.l: Suavius, Leo (Jacques Gohory), Paracelsus, 1567, Theophrasti Paracelsi philosophiae et medicinae utriusque universae compendium, Paris: Rovillius
src.q: Hic videt in verbo argẽti viui, vitã quæ vegetatio eſt

s: Basil Valentine's Last Will (1671 English) defines a 'living metal' operationally: take a metal that attracts breath; when the exhalation is stronger, 'then is it a living metal', for breathing things are alive; such a metal grows like a child, ten years by ten years, to its perfect body.

src.l: Basilius Valentinus, 1671, Basil Valentine his Last Will and Testament, London: Brewster
src.q: then is it a living metal, because a lively quality is in it : for breathing things are alive, and breathing is compared unto life

s: Jacques Aubert (De metallorum ortu et causis, 1575), against the Paracelsians, calls Cardano's claim that metals live 'a delirium and the dream of a fanatic' needing hellebore: imperfectly mixed bodies do not live, for they lack the organs of life and soul and have only similar (homoeomerous) parts; metals are such bodies.

src.l: Aubert, Jacques, 1575, De metallorum ortu & causis, Lyon: Berion
src.q: For bodies that are imperfectly mixed do not live. They lack the organs of life and the soul.
src.qo: Corpora enim imperfectè mista non viuunt: nam carent vitæ & animæ organis

src.l: Aubert, Jacques, 1575, De metallorum ortu & causis, Lyon: Berion
src.q: Corpora enim imperfectè mista non viuunt: nam carent vitæ & animæ organis

s: Jugel (Berg-, Schmelz- und Figier-Kunst, 1766) concludes that fixed metals are not dead in themselves but still living creatures at rest, carrying their life and motion, shown by their fluidity in fire, locked in their centre; dead things are those from which the spirit of life has gone.

src.l: Jugel, Johann Gottfried, 1766, Natürliche Berg-, Schmelz- und Figier-Kunst
src.q: they are not dead in themselves, but are still living creatures that remain in their state of rest.
src.qo: daß dieselben zwar an sich selbst nicht todte sondern an- noch lebende Creaturen sind, die in ihrer Ruhe stehen

src.l: Jugel, Johann Gottfried, 1766, Natürliche Berg-, Schmelz- und Figier-Kunst
src.q: daß dieselben zwar an sich selbst nicht todte sondern an- noch lebende Creaturen sind, die in ihrer Ruhe stehen

s: Becher's Physica subterranea (1669; 1738 ed.) structures its mineral section on the animal and plant model (comparison of seeds, nutrition, excrement, perfect bodies of both sexes, zoophytes and phytominerals) and opens: it is certain that animals and plants have sperm and seeds, 'we see this also in the mineral kingdom'.

src.l: Becher, Johann Joachim, 1738, Subterranean Physics
src.q: First, it is certain that sperm and seeds are provided in animals and vegetables; we see this also in the mineral kingdom
src.qo: Primo, in animalibus & vegetabilibus spermata & semina dari, certum est; quod & in minerali regno

src.l: Becher, Johann Joachim, 1738, Subterranean Physics
src.q: Primo, in animalibus & vegetabilibus spermata & semina dari, certum est; quod & in minerali regno

s: A chapter 'Of the Seed of Gold' in the German Select Chemical Treatises attributed to Starkey (1748) argues that the Creator implanted a seed in every species to preserve and propagate it, that the seed is each thing's perfection and what lacks seed is imperfect, so a metallic seed must exist; metals were not all made in the six days but have multiplied and grown.

src.l: Starkey, George (attrib.), 1748, Auserlesene chymische Tractätlein (Select Chemical Treatises), Vienna: Krauss
src.loc: Book of Metals ch. IV, p. 231; scan 249
src.q: And the seed is the perfection of every thing, and whatever lacks a seed is rightly to be judged as imperfect. Thus, there is also no doubt that a metallic seed exists.
src.qo: Und der Same ist eines jedweden Dinges Vollkommenheit, und welches keinen Samen hat, ist billich vor unvollkommen zu schätzen.

src.l: Starkey, George (attrib.), 1748, Auserlesene chymische Tractätlein (Select Chemical Treatises), Vienna: Krauss
src.loc: Book of Metals ch. IV, p. 231; scan 249
src.q: Und der Same ist eines jedweden Dinges Vollkommenheit, und welches keinen Samen hat, ist billich vor unvollkommen zu schätzen.

s: Steinbergen's Metallischer Baumgarten (1741) asks who can doubt that God gave minerals and metals their own seed, place and order, like every other kind, and answers the objection that metals have no seed and do not keep growing because God made them all at creation.

src.l: Steinbergen, Christian Friedrich von, 1741, Metallischer Baumgarten (The Metallic Orchard), Frankfurt and Leipzig: Fleischer
src.q: oh, who then can doubt that GOD should not also have given the minerals and metals their own seed, place, position, and order, as well as His blessing?
src.qo: Ey wer kan denn zweifeln, daß GOTT denen Mineralien und Metallen, nicht auch seinen Saamen, Ort, Stelle und Ordnung, auch seinen Seegen gegeben haben solte.

src.l: Steinbergen, Christian Friedrich von, 1741, Metallischer Baumgarten (The Metallic Orchard), Frankfurt and Leipzig: Fleischer
src.q: Ey wer kan denn zweifeln, daß GOTT denen Mineralien und Metallen, nicht auch seinen Saamen, Ort, Stelle und Ordnung, auch seinen Seegen gegeben haben solte.

s: Pruggmayr (Scrutinium philosophicum de vero elixire vitae, 1687) argues that metals produced without seed could not be made perfect, since everything without seed is imperfect; whoever doubts this 'is not worthy to scrutinize the secrets of nature: for nothing is born in the world which is devoid of seed.'

src.l: Pruggmayr, Martin Maximilian, 1687, Scrutinium philosophicum de vero elixire vitae (Philosophical Scrutiny of the True Elixir of Life), Salzburg: Mayr
src.q: for nothing is born in the world which is devoid of seed.
src.qo: nihil enim in orbe nascitur, quod femine destituatur.

src.l: Pruggmayr, Martin Maximilian, 1687, Scrutinium philosophicum de vero elixire vitae (Philosophical Scrutiny of the True Elixir of Life), Salzburg: Mayr
src.q: nihil enim in orbe nascitur, quod femine destituatur.

s: Glauber (Furni novi philosophici, Latin ed. 1651) compares sowing perfect metals into imperfect ones, where they putrefy and attract their like for growth, to fennel and onion seeds drawing their own from the soil; but gold is only 'the habitation of that metallic seed, and not the seed itself'.

src.l: Glauber, Johann Rudolph, 1651, Furni novi philosophici (New Philosophical Furnaces), Latin ed., Amsterdam: Janssonius
src.loc: Appendix to Part V, p. 55; scan 487
src.q: for gold is merely the habitation of that metallic seed, and not the seed itself in its entire substance.
src.qo: Hoc etiam accidit in regno mine- rali metallico, dum perfecta seminantur in im- perfecta, ubi putrescunt, suumque pro incre- mento attahunt simile.

src.l: Glauber, Johann Rudolph, 1651, Furni novi philosophici (New Philosophical Furnaces), Latin ed., Amsterdam: Janssonius
src.loc: Appendix to Part V, p. 55; scan 487
src.q: Hoc etiam accidit in regno mine- rali metallico, dum perfecta seminantur in im- perfecta, ubi putrescunt, suumque pro incre- mento attahunt simile.

s: Sennert (De chymicorum cum Aristotelicis consensu, 1619 ed.) reports the Chymists' view that the seeds and species of minerals flourish in the seminal reasons of matter, kept 'in that Night of Orpheus', in Hippocrates' Orcus and Paracelsus' Iliaster, awaiting their appointed time.

src.l: Daniel Sennert, 1619, On the Consensus and Dissensus of Chemists with Aristotelian and Galenic Scholars, Book I
src.loc: De generatione et mistione, p. 223; scan 396
src.q: their seeds and species flourish in the seminal reasons of matter, and are preserved in that Night of Orpheus
src.qo: semina eorum & species in feminalibus materiæ rationibus vi- gere

src.l: Daniel Sennert, 1619, On the Consensus and Dissensus of Chemists with Aristotelian and Galenic Scholars, Book I
src.loc: De generatione et mistione, p. 223; scan 396
src.q: semina eorum & species in feminalibus materiæ rationibus vi- gere

s: A Theatrum chemicum treatise (1659 ed.) calls the element of water 'the mother, seed, and root of all minerals', with an Archeus in it that orders each thing to its ultimate natural matter, which is man's first artificial matter: 'where nature ends, there the art of man begins'.

src.l: Anonymous (ed.), 1659, Theatrum chemicum, praecipuos selectorum auctorum tractatus ... continens (1659 ed.)
src.q: The element of water is, therefore, the mother, seed, and root of all minerals
src.qo: Est itaque elementum aquae mater, ſemen, & radix mineralium omnium, & Archeus in ipsa est is qui singula disponit ordine quodam

src.l: Anonymous (ed.), 1659, Theatrum chemicum, praecipuos selectorum auctorum tractatus ... continens (1659 ed.)
src.q: Est itaque elementum aquae mater, ſemen, & radix mineralium omnium, & Archeus in ipsa est is qui singula disponit ordine quodam

s: Boyle (Observations about the Growth of Metals, 1670) turns the life of metals into a question of evidence: he asked an old mine-owner whether he could prove, 'otherwise than upon the Conjectures of vulgar Tradition', that minerals grow even after the veins have been dug, and records his affirmative answer and proofs.

src.l: Boyle, Robert, 1670, Tracts ... about the Cosmicall Qualities of Things ... (Hidden Qualities of the Air), with Observations about the Growth of Metals, London
src.q: Whether he could, otherwise than upon the Conjectures of vulgar Tradition, prove, that Minerals grow even after the Veins have been dug?

s: Ruland's Lexicon alchemiae (1612) defines Elixir as 'the ferment, leaven, yeast, sourdough', made from water, 'for Yxir is Water': a coloured water mixed with bodies, also the white stone, the treasure and the prima materia.

src.l: Ruland sr., Martin, 1612, Lexicon Alchemiae Sive Dictionarium Alchemisticum: Containing a Clear Explanation of Obscure Words and Hermetic Matters, as well as Theophrastus-Paracelsian Phrases, by Martin Ruland, Doctor of Philosophy and Medicine, and Person of His Imperial Majesty
src.q: For Yxir is Water; it is a colored water mixed with bodies.
src.qo: Elixir ist das ferment, Urheb / Beyffend / Sawrteig

src.l: Ruland sr., Martin, 1612, Lexicon Alchemiae Sive Dictionarium Alchemisticum: Containing a Clear Explanation of Obscure Words and Hermetic Matters, as well as Theophrastus-Paracelsian Phrases, by Martin Ruland, Doctor of Philosophy and Medicine, and Person of His Imperial Majesty
src.q: Elixir ist das ferment, Urheb / Beyffend / Sawrteig

s: Donato d'Eremita (Dell'elixir vitae, 1624) says ELIXIR VITAE means nothing other than 'renovatio vitae' and derives elixir 'ab elixando', from cooking: an aqueous body in which the spirits digest and cook, so that it makes food cook in the stomach by warming it.

src.l: Donato d'Eremita, 1624, Dell'elixir vitae, Naples: Roncagliolo
src.loc: Book I ch. IV, p. 5; scan 29
src.q: thus it makes the food in our stomach cook, warming it by causing the digestion
src.qo: altro egli non vuol dire, che renouatio vitæ Elixir ab elixando, cioè, dal cuocere

src.l: Donato d'Eremita, 1624, Dell'elixir vitae, Naples: Roncagliolo
src.loc: Book I ch. IV, p. 5; scan 29
src.q: altro egli non vuol dire, che renouatio vitæ Elixir ab elixando, cioè, dal cuocere

s: Rupescissa (De consideratione quintae essentiae, c. 1351; Heidelberg MS) says flesh put into the quintessence does not corrupt but stays 'more enlivened', and that it preserves the whole human body from all corruption: it is 'the heaven of the human being', preserving the body's qualities as heaven preserves the universe.

src.l: Johannes de Rupescissa, n.d., De consideratione quintae essentiae (manuscript, Universitätsbibliothek Heidelberg)
src.q: This is the quintessence, the heaven of the human being, which alchemists strive for, for the preservation of all qualities of the human body, just as the heaven is for the preservation of the whole universe
src.qo: Quod autẽ incorruptibilis et cõseruat

src.l: Johannes de Rupescissa, n.d., De consideratione quintae essentiae (manuscript, Universitätsbibliothek Heidelberg)
src.q: Quod autẽ incorruptibilis et cõseruat

s: The pseudo-Lullian De secretis naturae seu de quinta essentia (14th c.; 1541 ed.) says no medicine but 'our celestial, animal, and vegetable menstruum', the fifth essence, can do this: it preserves flesh from corruption, strengthens the elemental nature, restores original youth and vivifies the spirit.

src.l: pseudo-Raymond Lull, 1541, Raimundi Lulli de secretis naturae sive quinta essentia libri duo
src.q: For it preserves flesh from corruption, strengthens the elemental nature, restores original youth, vivifies the spirit
src.qo: na carnes a corruptione conseruat, elementatiua confortat, iuuentus pristina per ipsam restaurat, spiritum viuificat

src.l: pseudo-Raymond Lull, 1541, Raimundi Lulli de secretis naturae sive quinta essentia libri duo
src.q: na carnes a corruptione conseruat, elementatiua confortat, iuuentus pristina per ipsam restaurat, spiritum viuificat

s: Drebbel's treatise on the fifth essence (1608; Latin 1628) defines it as 'a thing eternal, immutable, and incombustible, like the invincible heavens', perfect in all elements and abounding in heat, extractable from minerals, metals, plants and animals.

src.l: Drebbel, Cornelis, Laurenberg, Peter (trans.), 1628, Tractatus duo: de natura elementorum, de quinta essentia, Geneva: de Tournes
src.q: is a thing eternal, immutable, and incombustible, like the invincible heavens
src.qo: est res æterna, immutabilis, incombustibilis, vt cœlum inuincibile,

s: The epistle to Paracelsus's De vita longa (1566 ed.) divides medicine in two, one to preserve the body and one to restore what has been lost, and practice likewise in two, the physical and that 'of long life'.

src.l: Paracelsus, Gerhard Dorn (ed.), 1566, Libri V de vita longa
src.q: Twofold medicine must be applied to it: one, so that it may be preserved; the other, so that what has been lost may be restored.
src.qo: Duplex medicina ipſi adhibenda, altera, ut cõſeruet̃

src.l: Paracelsus, Gerhard Dorn (ed.), 1566, Libri V de vita longa
src.q: Duplex medicina ipſi adhibenda, altera, ut cõſeruet̃

s: De vita longa III (1566 ed.) says whatever the tincture tinges 'contributes greatly to a long life', the more as it is refined, and dismisses 'the fables of Rupiscissa', who wrote rashly about gold and Mercurial things in the tincture of the body.

src.l: Paracelsus, Gerhard Dorn (ed.), 1566, Libri V de vita longa
src.q: it contributes greatly to a long life
src.qo: Quicquid ergo tin- ctura illa tingit, longæ vitæ plurimū in- seruit

src.l: Paracelsus, Gerhard Dorn (ed.), 1566, Libri V de vita longa
src.q: Quicquid ergo tin- ctura illa tingit, longæ vitæ plurimū in- seruit

s: A gloss in the 1566 De vita longa defines 'liquor of mummia' as 'a water that, after digestion, breaks forth by distillation from human flesh', set before a general cure for gout, apoplexy and paralysis that considers only 'the power of nature'.

src.l: Paracelsus, Gerhard Dorn (ed.), 1566, Libri V de vita longa
src.q: The liquor of mummia is a water that, after digestion, breaks forth by distillation from human flesh.
src.qo: Liquor ex mummia est aqua, quæ post digestio- nem destillando erumpit ex carne hominis.

src.l: Paracelsus, Gerhard Dorn (ed.), 1566, Libri V de vita longa
src.q: Liquor ex mummia est aqua, quæ post digestio- nem destillando erumpit ex carne hominis.

s: In a Paracelsian treatise on human generation (Huser ed. 1589, 'Der Ander Tractat' ch. II), the Liquor Vitae is a liquor distributed through the whole body, holding the nature and properties of every limb and spirit; it is kindled by the imagination's 'speculatio' and becomes seed, in men and women alike.

src.l: Paracelsus, 1589, Erster [- zehender] Theil der Bücher und Schrifften des edlen, hochgelehrten und bewehrten philosophi und medici Philippi Theophrasti Bombast von Hohenheim ...
src.q: but it becomes a seed for the reason that it lies distributed throughout the entire body.
src.qo: Als dan entzünde fich der Liquor Vitæ von der Speculatio

src.l: Paracelsus, 1589, Erster [- zehender] Theil der Bücher und Schrifften des edlen, hochgelehrten und bewehrten philosophi und medici Philippi Theophrasti Bombast von Hohenheim ...
src.q: Als dan entzünde fich der Liquor Vitæ von der Speculatio

s: Croll's Praefatio to the Basilica chymica (1609; 1658 ed.) names the same thing 'Radical Moisture, Vital Balsam, and the most precious Nectar of our Life', since the strengthening force of the human and animal body proceeds from the spirit of life; while it keeps its quantity, disease is not felt.

src.l: Croll, Oswald, 1658, Basilica chymica (Geneva: Chouët ed.)
src.q: Moisture, Vital Balsam, and the most precious Nectar of our Life
src.qo: Humor, Balsamus Vitalis, & Vitæ nostræ Nectar pretiosissimū

src.l: Croll, Oswald, 1658, Basilica chymica (Geneva: Chouët ed.)
src.q: Humor, Balsamus Vitalis, & Vitæ nostræ Nectar pretiosissimū

s: Thomas Browne (Religio Medici, 1642) says that in burning the forms of things are not perished but withdrawn into their combustible part, 'This I make good by experience, and can from the ashes of a plant revive the plant', and argues from it to the resurrection of the body.

s: Against treating 'the life of metals' as one alchemical doctrine: on SL's pages it is at least four different things. A metaphysical doctrine (Suavius 1567: a Ficinian spirit in metals); an operational term with a test (Basil Valentine: a metal that draws breath is 'living'); a laboratory idiom for calcination ('killing' metals, De natura rerum); and a contested empirical claim that Aristotelians denied outright (Aubert 1575: no organs, no life) and Boyle (1670) re-asked as a question of miners' evidence. Seed claims that 'alchemists held metals to be alive' flatten this.

src.l: Aubert, Jacques, 1575, De metallorum ortu & causis, Lyon: Berion
src.q: For bodies that are imperfectly mixed do not live. They lack the organs of life and the soul.
src.qo: Corpora enim imperfectè mista non viuunt: nam carent vitæ & animæ organis,

src.l: Basilius Valentinus, 1671, Basil Valentine his Last Will and Testament, London: Brewster
src.q: then is it a living metal, because a lively quality is in it

s: Against reading the elixir and quintessence as medicines that ADD life: the earliest texts on SL define them by incorruptibility, not vitality. Rupescissa's quintessence keeps meat from rotting and is 'the heaven of the human being'; pseudo-Lull's first effect is 'preserves flesh from corruption'; Drebbel's fifth essence is 'eternal, immutable, and incombustible'. Prolongation here is embalming. This sits in tension with the same tradition's other maxim, that nothing has soul and life except after putrefaction: the elixir is made through rot, and works against it.

src.l: Johannes de Rupescissa, n.d., De consideratione quintae essentiae (manuscript, Universitätsbibliothek Heidelberg)
src.q: it will preserve the entire human body from all corruption
src.qo: et omi corpore hūanũ ab oĩm corrũpt̃oẽ s̃uabit

src.l: Anonymous, 1613, Turba philosophorum, das ist, das Buch von der güldenen Kunst (The Assembly of the Philosophers and the Book of the Golden Art)
src.q: nor does anything possess a soul and life, except after putrefaction.
src.qo: es hat auch nichts ein Seele vnd leben/ dann nach der putrefaction.

s: Aristotle (De anima II.1, 412a) defines life (ζωή) not as a thing a body has but as its own nutrition, growth and decay: 'by life we mean self-nourishment, growth and decay'.

src.l: Aristotle, 1831, Aristotelis Opera (Complete Works)
src.q: Of natural things, some possess life, while others do not; and by life we mean self-sustained nutrition, growth, and decay.
src.qo: τῶν δὲ φυσικῶν τὰ μὲν ἔχει ζωήν, τὰ δ’ οὐκ ἔχει· ζωὴν δὲ λέγομεν τὴν δι’ αὑτοῦ τροφήν τε καὶ αὔξησιν καὶ φθίσιν.

s: Aristotle (De anima II.2, 413a) says the ensouled is distinguished from the soulless by living (τῷ ζῆν), and that 'living' is said in many ways: mind, sensation, local motion, and the motion of nutrition, decay and growth; SL's English turns the verb into 'the presence of life'.

src.l: Aristotle, 1831, Aristotelis Opera (Complete Works)
src.q: we must start our inquiry by distinguishing the ensouled from the unsouled by the presence of life. Since "living" is said in many ways, if even one of these exists, we say the thing is alive: such as intellect, sensation, local movement and rest, and furthermore the movement regarding nutrition, decay, and growth.
src.qo: διωρίσθαι τὸ ἔμψυχον τοῦ ἀψύχου τῷ ζῆν. πλεοναχῶς δὲ τοῦ ζῆν λεγομένου, κἂν ἕν τι τούτων ἐνυπάρχῃ μόνον, ζῆν αὐτό φαμεν, οἷον νοῦς, αἴσθησις, κίνησις καὶ στάσις ἡ κατὰ τόπον, ἔτι κίνησις ἡ κατὰ τροφὴν καὶ φθίσις τε καὶ αὔξησις.

src.q: διωρίσθαι τὸ ἔμψυχον τοῦ ἀψύχου τῷ ζῆν. πλεοναχῶς δὲ τοῦ ζῆν λεγομένου, κἂν ἕν τι τούτων ἐνυπάρχῃ μόνον, ζῆν αὐτό φαμεν, οἷον νοῦς, αἴσθησις, κίνησις καὶ στάσις ἡ κατὰ τόπον, ἔτι κίνησις ἡ κατὰ τροφὴν καὶ φθίσις τε καὶ αὔξησις.

s: Aristotle (De anima II.2, 413a25–30) counts all plants as living because they have in themselves a power and principle (δύναμις, ἀρχή) of growth and decay in opposite directions.

src.l: Aristotle, 1831, Aristotelis Opera (Complete Works)
src.q: For this reason, all growing things are thought to live; for they clearly possess a power and a principle by which they receive growth and decay in opposite directions.

s: Aristotle (De anima II.4, 415a) calls the nutritive soul the first and most common power of soul, 'according to which life belongs to all' living things; its works are generating and using food.

src.l: Aristotle, 1831, Aristotelis Opera (Complete Works)
src.q: for the nutritive soul belongs to other beings as well, and it is the first and most common faculty of the soul, according to which life belongs to all. Its works are to generate and to use food;

s: Aristotle (De anima II.4, 416b) argues that nothing is nourished that does not partake of life, so food is food only for an ensouled body as ensouled.

src.l: Aristotle, 1831, Aristotelis Opera (Complete Works)
src.q: Since nothing is nourished unless it partakes of life, the ensouled body is that which is nourished, in so far as it is ensouled, so that food is toward the ensouled and not by accident.

s: The pseudo-Aristotelian De spiritu opens by asking how the innate pneuma (τὸ σύμφυτον πνεῦμα) lasts and grows, observing that it grows greater and stronger with age and bodily condition; SL glosses the Greek as 'vital spirit/breath'.

src.q: What is the duration of the innate spirit pneuma [vital spirit/breath], and what is its growth? We see that it becomes greater and stronger both according to changes in age and the condition of the body.
src.qo: τὸ δὲ πνεῦμα δι’ ὅλου τὸ σύμφυτον.

src.q: τὸ δὲ πνεῦμα δι’ ὅλου τὸ σύμφυτον.

s: Plato's Timaeus (30b) concludes that the cosmos came to be a living creature (ζῷον) with soul and intelligence, because the god put intelligence in soul and soul in body.

src.l: Plato, 1902, Platonis Opera (Republic, Timaeus, Critias)

s: Thomas Taylor's 1793 English renders Timaeus 30b as 'it is necessary to call the world an animal, endued with intellect', dropping 'ensouled' (ἔμψυχον) and turning ζῷον into 'animal'.

s: Thomas Erastus (1572) quotes the Hippocratic Regimen I (c. 400 BCE) as saying the soul, having a blend of fire and water (σύγκρησις πυρὸς καὶ ὕδατος), creeps into man, and attacks the view that 'the soul is nothing else than fire and water' entering bodies from without.

src.loc: Disputationes, on Hippocrates' Regimen I; scan 502

s: Aristotle (De generatione animalium II.3, 736b33–737a1; Gaza's Latin, 1476) says what makes seeds fertile is the so-called heat, which is not fire but the pneuma (spiritus) enclosed in the seed's foam, and the nature in that pneuma is analogous to the element of the stars.

src.l: Aristotle, Theodore Gaza (trans.), 1476, De animalibus (Gaza's Latin of HA, PA, GA)
src.q: For there is present in the seed of all things that which makes the seeds fertile, namely, that which is called heat, and that is not fire, nor any such faculty, but a spirit, which is contained in the seed and the foamy body, and the nature which is in that spirit corresponds in proportion to the element of the stars.

s: Aristotle (GA III.11, 762a18–21) explains spontaneous generation: animals and plants arise in earth and moisture because there is water in earth, pneuma in water and soul-heat (θερμότης ψυχική) in everything, 'so that in a way all things are full of soul'.

src.l: Aristotle, Theodore Gaza (trans.), 1476, De animalibus (Gaza's Latin of HA, PA, GA)
src.q: since moisture is in the earth, spirit is in the moisture, and animal heat is present in the universe, so that in a way all things are full of soul

s: Aristotle (Historia animalium V.1, 539a, c. 340 BCE; Thompson's English) says some animals come from parents of their kind while others grow spontaneously, some from putrefying earth or vegetable matter, as many insects, others inside animals from the secretions of their organs.

src.l: Aristotle, D'Arcy Wentworth Thompson (trans.), 1910, Historia Animalium
src.q: others grow spontaneously and not from kindred stock; and of these instances of spontaneous generation some come from putrefying earth or vegetable matter,¹ as is the case with a number of insects

s: Aristotle (De motu animalium 10, 703a9–16) says all animals appear to have connate pneuma (πνεῦμα σύμφυτον) and to have strength through it; it relates to the soul's origin in the heart as the hinge-point does in a joint, both moved and moving.

src.l: Aristotle, 1495, Aristotelis Opera, Vol. 3 (Aldine: De anima, Parva naturalia, De motu animalium)
src.q: All animals appear to possess connate … and to have strength through it. What the work of this connate pneuma is has been stated in other works.

s: Clement (Stromata II, in SVF II.714) reports the Stoic ladder: stones have hexis (cohesion), plants physis (nature), irrational animals have both plus impulse and representation, and the rational power is proper to the human soul; plants are counted 'inanimate'.

src.l: Hans von Arnim (ed.), 1964, Stoicorum Veterum Fragmenta, vol. 2: Chrysippus
src.q: Thus, stones possess … plants possess … and irrational animals share in these two and also in impulse and representation

s: Galen (SVF II.715) reports that the Stoics call what governs plants 'nature' and what governs animals 'soul', yet hold the substance of both to be a connate pneuma differing in quality: the pneuma of soul is drier, that of nature moister, and both need food and air to persist.

src.l: Hans von Arnim (ed.), 1964, Stoicorum Veterum Fragmenta, vol. 2: Chrysippus
src.q: For the … of the soul is drier, while that of nature is moister; both need not only food but also air for their persistence.
src.qo: ξηρότερον μὲν γὰρ πνεῦμα τὸ τῆς ψυχῆς, ὑγρότερον δὲ τὸ τῆς φύσεως εἶναι, δεῖσθαι δ’ ἄμφω πρὸς διαμονὴν οὐ τροφῆς μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἀέρος

s: The pseudo-Galenic Introductio (SVF II.716) says the ancients held two pneumata, psychic and natural, and the Stoics added a third, the hektikon ('holding'), which they call hexis: the hektic pneuma holds stones together, the natural nourishes animals and plants.

src.l: Hans von Arnim (ed.), 1964, Stoicorum Veterum Fragmenta, vol. 2: Chrysippus
src.q: According to the ancients, there are two spirits: the psychic and the natural. But the Stoics introduce a third
src.qo: πνεύματα δὲ κατὰ τοὺς παλαιοὺς δύο ἐστί, τό τε ψυχικὸν καὶ τὸ φυσικόν. οἱ δὲ Στωϊκοὶ καὶ τρίτον εἰσάγουσι τὸ ἑκτικόν, ὃ καλοῦσιν ἕξιν.

s: Cicero's Stoic Balbus (De natura deorum II.31–32, 45 BCE) argues that the world's heat (ardor) moves of itself, that what moves of itself must be a soul (animus), 'ex quo efficitur, animantem esse mundum', and that the world, being better than any part, must be wise.

src.l: Marcus Tullius Cicero, 1541, De philosophia vol. 2: De natura deorum etc.
src.q: It is therefore absurd to say, when men and beasts are held by this heat, and on account of it move and have sense, that the world is without sense
src.qo: quoniam ex mundi ardore motus omnis oritur, is autem ardor non alieno impulsu, sed sua sponte mouetur: animus sit necesse est. ex quo efficitur, animantem esse mundum.

src.l: Marcus Tullius Cicero, 1541, De philosophia vol. 2: De natura deorum etc.
src.q: quoniam ex mundi ardore motus omnis oritur, is autem ardor non alieno impulsu, sed sua sponte mouetur: animus sit necesse est. ex quo efficitur, animantem esse mundum.

s: Cicero's Latin Timaeus (De universitate, c. 45 BCE) renders Timaeus 30b as 'hunc mundum animal esse, idque intelligens': the Greek ζῷον becomes Latin animal, the word through which the living world-animal passed into Latin.

src.l: Marcus Tullius Cicero, 1546, De philosophia vol. 2 (incl. De universitate, Cicero's Latin Timaeus)
src.q: we must not hesitate to profess, if only something can be investigated by conjecture, that this world is a living being
src.qo: hunc mundum animal esse, idque intelligens, et diuina prouidentia constitutum

s: Seneca (Epistle 41.1–2, c. 64 CE) writes that God is near you, with you, within you: 'a sacred spirit (sacer spiritus) dwells within us', the observer and guardian of our goods and evils, who treats us as we treat it.

src.l: Seneca, 1512, Epistulae morales, vol. 1 (Letters 1–40)
src.q: God is near you, he is with you, he is within you. 2 I mean this, Lucilius: a sacred spirit dwells within us, the observer and guardian of our evils and our goods.
src.qo: prope est a te deus, tecum est, intus est. 2 Ita dico, Lucili : sacer intra nos spiritus sedet, malorum bonorumque nostrorum observator et custos.

src.l: Seneca, 1512, Epistulae morales, vol. 1 (Letters 1–40)
src.q: prope est a te deus, tecum est, intus est. 2 Ita dico, Lucili : sacer intra nos spiritus sedet, malorum bonorumque nostrorum observator et custos.

s: Lucretius (De rerum natura III.136–144, c. 55 BCE) says the mind (animus) and the soul (anima) are joined and form one nature; the animus, the counsel, rules from the middle of the chest, and the rest of the anima, spread through the whole body, obeys it.

src.l: Lucretius, Andrea Navagero (ed.), 1515, Lucretius (De rerum natura)
src.q: Now I say that the mind and the soul are held joined together and form one nature from themselves.
src.qo: Nunc animum, atque animam dico coniuncta teneri Inter se: atque unam naturam conficere ex se.

src.l: Lucretius, Andrea Navagero (ed.), 1515, Lucretius (De rerum natura)
src.q: Nunc animum, atque animam dico coniuncta teneri Inter se: atque unam naturam conficere ex se.

s: Lucretius (DRN III.830–831) concludes 'Nil igitur mors est ad nos', death is nothing to us, since the nature of the mind is mortal: life ends with the scattering of the atoms of animus and anima, and nothing survives to feel it.

src.l: Lucretius, Andrea Navagero (ed.), 1515, Lucretius (De rerum natura)
src.q: Therefore, death is nothing, and it pertains to us not at all, since the nature of the mind is considered mortal
src.qo: Nil igitur mors est: ad nos neque pertinet hilum: Quandoquidem natura animi mortalis habetur

src.l: Lucretius, Andrea Navagero (ed.), 1515, Lucretius (De rerum natura)
src.q: Nil igitur mors est: ad nos neque pertinet hilum: Quandoquidem natura animi mortalis habetur

s: Lucretius (DRN V.122–131) says the earth, sun and sky are far from divine and are rather an example of what lacks vital motion and sense ('vitali motu sensuque remotum'); mind cannot exist in just any body, as there are no trees in the ether or fish in the fields.

src.l: Lucretius, Andrea Navagero (ed.), 1515, Lucretius (De rerum natura)
src.q: Of what is removed from vital motion and sense. For indeed it is not with just any body, that the nature of the mind Is thought to be able to be, and counsel.
src.qo: Quid sit uitali motu, sensuque remotum.

src.l: Lucretius, Andrea Navagero (ed.), 1515, Lucretius (De rerum natura)
src.q: Quid sit uitali motu, sensuque remotum.

s: Galen (On the Natural Faculties I.1, c. 180 CE) says sensation and voluntary motion are proper to animals and are works of the soul, while growth and nutrition, shared with plants, are works of nature (φύσις): animals are governed by soul and nature together, plants by nature alone.

src.l: Galen, 1916, On the Natural Faculties
src.q: We say that animals are governed at once by their soul and by their nature, and plants by their nature alone, and that growth and nutrition are the effects of nature, not of soul.

src.l: Galen, 1300, Galen, Medical Writings (Cambridge, Gonville and Caius College, MS 360/587)
src.loc: Nat. Fac. I.1, Greek MS; scan 87

s: In Galen's Natural Faculties (III.5) Brock's English says only that for Erasistratus the pneuma driven through the arteries into the stomach helps digestion, but SL's version inserts a gloss calling this pneuma 'the "vital spirit" or "breath of life"'.

src.l: Galen, 1916, On the Natural Faculties
src.q: according to Erasistratus, the pneuma, which is propelled through the arteries and into the alimentary canal, is of great service in digestion

src.l: Galen, 1916, On the Natural Faculties
src.q: the "vital spirit" or "breath of life," thought to be a refined substance carried in the arteries

s: Plutarch (Why the Oracles Cease 48–50, c. 100 CE; Goodwin's English) explains prophecy by giving it for subject the soul of man and for instrument an 'enthusiastic exhalation' from the earth, which is not always the same, sometimes slack and sometimes strong.

src.l: Plutarch, William W. Goodwin (ed.), 1878, Plutarch's Morals, Vol. 4 (incl. Why the Oracles Cease)
src.q: we allow it for its subject the soul of man, and for its instrument an enthusiastic exhalation

src.l: Plutarch, William W. Goodwin (ed.), 1878, Plutarch's Morals, Vol. 4 (incl. Why the Oracles Cease)
src.q: I believe the exhalation itself which comes out of the ground is not always of the same kind, being at one time slack, and at another strong and vigorous

s: Philo (Quod deterius 80–84, c. 40 CE) says 'soul' is said in two ways, the whole and its ruling part, and that for the lawgiver the soul's substance is double: blood for the whole, divine pneuma (πνεῦμα θεῖον) for the ruling part, citing 'the soul of all flesh is blood' and Gen. 2:7.

src.l: Philo of Alexandria, 1828, Philonis Judaei Opera Omnia (Vol. 3)
src.q: it seemed to the lawgiver that the substance of the soul is also double, blood being that of the whole, and divine spirit that of the most ruling part.

s: Corpus Hermeticum XII.15–16 (2nd–3rd c. CE) says the whole cosmos, the great god and image of the greater, is the fullness of all life (πλήρωμα τῆς πάσης ζωῆς), and that nothing in it, whole or part, has been, is or will be dead; what men call death is change.

src.l: Hermes Trismegistus (attrib.), 1535, Corpus Hermeticum (Greek manuscript)
src.q: πλήρωμα ἐστὶ τῆς πάσης ζωῆς

src.l: G. R. S. Mead, 1906, Thrice-Greatest Hermes, Vol. II
src.q: For not a single thing that’s dead, hath been, or is, or shall be in [this] Cosmos.

src.l: Hermes Trismegistus (attrib.), 1535, Corpus Hermeticum (Greek manuscript)
src.q: it is the … of all life. And there is nothing in this [cosmos] throughout the whole of … —neither of the whole nor of the parts—which does not live.
src.qo: πλήρωμα ἐστὶ τῆς πάσης ζωῆς

s: Plotinus (Ennead III.8.8, c. 250 CE; Ficino's Latin, 1580) says every life is a kind of thought (omnis vita est intelligentia quaedam), one fainter than another as life is: there is a vegetative, a sensitive and a psychic intellection, and the first and clearest life is the first intellect.

src.l: Plotinus, Marsilio Ficino (trans.), 1580, Plotini Enneades
src.q: sed hæc quidem vegetalis intelligentia, hæc autem sensualis, alia deniq; animalis. Quo igitur mo- do intelligentiæ sunt? Quia videlicet sunt ra- D tiones, & omnis vitā est intelligentia quædam, sed alia tenuior alia, ficut & vita.

s: Proclus (In Timaeum III, on Tim. 36e, c. 440 CE) reads the world soul's being 'woven through' the body as a community of life, continuity and life-generation (ζωογονία) proceeding from the demiurge and returning to him: an ensouling (ψύχωσις) that runs through all things.

src.l: Proclus, Ernst Diehl (ed.), 1903, In Platonis Timaeum commentaria
src.loc: In Tim. III (Diehl II p. 286), on 36e; scan 295
src.q: of life and continuity and life-generation, proceeding from the demiurge and turning back again to him
src.qo: ζωῆς καὶ συνέχεια καὶ ζωογονία προϊοῦσά τε ἀπὸ τοῦ δημιουργοῦ καὶ ἐπιστρέφουσα πάλιν πρὸς αὐτόν

s: Diego López de Zúñiga (1519), defending the Vulgate against Lefèvre, says Latin has one name for life where Greek has two: ζωή is properly the life by which we, like other animals, live and breathe; βίος is the rational life only, the lifetime, sustenance and means.

src.l: Diego López de Zúñiga, 1519, Annotationes contra Iacobum Fabrum Stapulensem
src.q: For the single name "life" that the Latins have, two are found among the Greeks
src.qo: At vero ζωή eam proprie vitam significat qua ut cetera animalia & vivimus & respiramus. βίος vero & rationalem solum vitam & vite tempus & victum ac substantiam id est facultates sonat.

src.l: Diego López de Zúñiga, 1519, Annotationes contra Iacobum Fabrum Stapulensem
src.q: At vero ζωή eam proprie vitam significat qua ut cetera animalia & vivimus & respiramus. βίος vero & rationalem solum vitam & vite tempus & victum ac substantiam id est facultates sonat.

s: Grynaeus's theses on life (1580) collect ancient definitions: life is the union of soul and body, 'vita est ἐνέργεια intelligendi', Aristotle's 'βίος ἐστὶ λογικὴ ζωή' (bios is rational zōē), and Galen's 'the action of the soul is life, which respiration greatly aids'.

src.l: Johann Jakob Grynaeus, 1580, Thesium de vita aeterna et eius haeredibus decades X
src.q: Vita hominis eſt unio animæ & corporis, quæ fini tio materialis eſt. Vita eſt ἐνέργεια intelligendi. Et illud Ariftotelis, βίος ἐστὶ λογικὴ ζωή.

src.l: Johann Jakob Grynaeus, 1580, Thesium de vita aeterna et eius haeredibus decades X
src.q: The action of the soul is life, which is greatly aided by respiration
src.qo: Vita hominis eſt unio animæ & corporis, quæ fini tio materialis eſt. Vita eſt ἐνέργεια intelligendi. Et illud Ariftotelis, βίος ἐστὶ λογικὴ ζωή.

s: Against citing 'Thales held the magnet has a soul' or 'all things are full of gods' as Thales' doctrine of a living world: both reach us through Aristotle, who hedges each ('to judge from what is recorded', 'perhaps'), and through a doxography six centuries later; the hylozoist Thales is Aristotle's reading in his own vocabulary of soul and motion.

src.l: Aristotle, 1931, The Works of Aristotle, Vol. 3 (De mundo, De anima, Parva naturalia; Oxford translation)
src.q: it is perhaps for that reason that Thales came to the opinion that all things are full of gods

src.l: Aristotle, 1931, The Works of Aristotle, Vol. 3 (De mundo, De anima, Parva naturalia; Oxford translation)
src.q: to judge from what is recorded about him

s: Against presenting 'the ancients' as holding a living cosmos: the Epicureans denied it outright (Lucretius: sun, earth and sky lack vital motion and sense), Aristotle objected that soul spread through air or fire makes no animal, and the Stoics themselves called plants 'inanimate'; the world-animal was one party in an ancient debate.

src.l: Lucretius, Andrea Navagero (ed.), 1515, Lucretius (De rerum natura)
src.q: Of what is removed from vital motion and sense.

src.l: Hans von Arnim (ed.), 1964, Stoicorum Veterum Fragmenta, vol. 2: Chrysippus
src.q: if one grants that plants are inanimate

s: Aristotle (De longitudine et brevitate vitae 5, 466a18–22, c. 350 BCE) says an animal is by nature moist and warm, 'and to live is to be of such a constitution', while old age is dry and cold, and so is a corpse: living is a state of the body's qualities, and ageing is drying.

src.l: Aristotle, 1931, The Works of Aristotle, Vol. 3 (De mundo, De anima, Parva naturalia; Oxford translation)
src.q: animal is by nature humid and warm, and to live is to be of such a constitution, while old age is dry and cold, and so is a corpse.

s: Tylor (Primitive Culture, 1871) proposes 'as a minimum definition of Religion, the belief in Spiritual Beings', rejecting narrower definitions (supreme deity, judgment after death) as tied to particular developments.

src.l: Edward Burnett Tylor, 1871, Primitive Culture: Researches into the Development of Mythology, Philosophy, Religion, Art, and Custom, Vol. I
src.q: It seems best to fall back at once on this essential source, and simply to claim, as a minimum definition of Religion, the belief in Spiritual Beings.

s: Tylor (1871) gives the name Animism to 'the general doctrine of spiritual beings', avoiding 'Spiritualism' because it had become the name of a modern sect.

src.l: Edward Burnett Tylor, 1871, Primitive Culture: Researches into the Development of Mythology, Philosophy, Religion, Art, and Custom, Vol. I
src.q: The sense of Spiritualism in its wider acceptation, the general doctrine of spiritual beings, is here given to Animism.

s: Tylor (1871): 'Animism, in its full development, includes the belief in controlling deities and subordinate spirits, in souls, and in a future state', issuing in worship; the verbatim form of the seed's paraphrase.

src.l: Edward Burnett Tylor, 1871, Primitive Culture: Researches into the Development of Mythology, Philosophy, Religion, Art, and Custom, Vol. I
src.q: Thus Animism, in its full development, includes the belief in controlling deities and subordinate spirits, in souls, and in a future state, these doctrines practically resulting in some kind of active worship.

s: Tylor (1871) derives the soul from 'two groups of biological problems': what makes the difference between a living body and a dead one, and what the human shapes seen in dreams and visions are; 'savage philosophers' answered both with one ghost-soul.

src.l: Edward Burnett Tylor, 1871, Primitive Culture: Researches into the Development of Mythology, Philosophy, Religion, Art, and Custom, Vol. I
src.q: thinking men, as yet at a low level of culture, were deeply impressed by two groups of biological problems. In the first place, what is it that makes the difference between a living body and a dead one; what causes waking, sleep, trance, disease, death?

s: Tylor (1871) defines the 'lower races'' soul as a thin unsubstantial human image, 'a sort of vapour, film, or shadow', the cause of life and thought in what it animates, able to leave the body and to enter other men, animals and things.

src.l: Edward Burnett Tylor, 1871, Primitive Culture: Researches into the Development of Mythology, Philosophy, Religion, Art, and Custom, Vol. I
src.q: It is a thin unsubstantial human image, in its nature a sort of vapour, film, or shadow; the cause of life and thought in the individual it animates

s: Tylor (1871) reports that the Salish of Oregon distinguish the spirit from the vital principle: the spirit can leave the body unnoticed but must be restored soon, and the medicine-man replaces it down through the patient's head.

src.l: Edward Burnett Tylor, 1871, Primitive Culture: Researches into the Development of Mythology, Philosophy, Religion, Art, and Custom, Vol. I
src.q: The Salish Indians of Oregon regard the spirit as distinct from the vital principle, and capable of quitting the body for a short time without the patient being conscious of its absence

s: Tylor (1871, vol. II) says that in tree-worship it is often hard to tell whether the tree is 'inhabited, like a man, by its own proper life or soul' or possessed, like a fetish, by another spirit using it as a body.

src.l: Edward Burnett Tylor, 1871, Primitive Culture, Vol. II
src.q: Whether such a tree is looked on as inhabited, like a man, by its own proper life or soul, or as possessed, like a fetish, by some other spirit which has entered it and uses it for a body, is often hard to determine.

s: Tylor (1871, vol. II) says Lafitau's account shows 'the transformation of native animistic conceptions under missionary influence': general terms for spiritual beings such as 'oki' or 'manitu' became for him names of one supreme being.

src.l: Edward Burnett Tylor, 1871, Primitive Culture, Vol. II
src.q: Such general terms for spiritual beings as ‘oki’ or ‘manitu’ had become to him individual names of one supreme being.

s: Codrington (The Melanesians, 1891, in a quoted passage set as a note) defines mana as 'a power or influence, not physical, and in a way supernatural' that shows itself in physical force or any excellence, is fixed in nothing, and originates with personal beings.

src.l: Robert Henry Codrington, 1891, The Melanesians
src.q: It is a power or influence, not physical, and in a way supernatural; but it shews itself in physical force, or in any kind of power or excellence which a man possesses. This Mana is not fixed in anything, and can be conveyed in almost anything

s: Codrington (1891): mana is beyond the ordinary power of men and outside the common processes of nature; 'it is present in the atmosphere of life', attaches to persons and things, and is known only by results; the verbatim form of the seed paraphrase.

src.l: Robert Henry Codrington, 1891, The Melanesians
src.q: beyond the ordinary power of men, outside the common processes of nature; it is present in the atmosphere of life, attaches itself to persons and to things, and is manifested by results which can only be ascribed to its operation

s: Codrington (1891, ch. Magic) calls mana the invisible power thought to cause whatever transcends the regular course of nature, residing in spiritual beings and imparted to names and things, and 'the active force in all they do and believe to be done in magic'.

src.l: Robert Henry Codrington, 1891, The Melanesians
src.q: is that generally known as mana. Without some understanding of this it is impossible to understand the religious beliefs and practices of the Melanesians; and this again is the active force in all they do and believe to be done in magic, white or black.

s: Frazer (Golden Bough, 1890) says the savage, unable to conceive life abstractly as a 'permanent possibility of sensation' or a 'continuous adjustment of internal arrangements to external relations', thinks of it as a concrete material thing that can be kept in a box or jar, apart from the body.

src.l: James George Frazer, 1890, The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion, Vol. II
src.q: Unable to conceive of life abstractly as a “permanent possibility of sensation” or a “continuous adjustment of internal arrangements to external relations,” the savage thinks of it as a concrete material thing of a definite bulk, capable of being seen and handled, kept in a box or jar

s: Frazer (1890): the life so conceived need not be in the man; it may be absent and 'still continue to animate him, by virtue of a sort of sympathy'; while the object called his life or soul is unharmed he is well, and if it is destroyed he dies.

src.l: James George Frazer, 1890, The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion, Vol. II
src.q: It is not needful that the life, so conceived, should be in the man ; it may be absent from his body and still con- tinue to animate him, by virtue of a sort of sympathy or “action at a distance.”

s: Frazer (1890) reads the effigies of spring and midsummer fires as representatives of 'the fertilising tree-spirit or spirit of vegetation', clearest when the effigy is an unthreshed sheaf or covered with flowers.

src.l: James George Frazer, 1890, The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion, Vol. II
src.q: effigy over which the bride must leap is a repre- sentative of the fertilising tree-spirit or spirit of vegetation.

s: Hewitt (Iroquoian Cosmology, 1903) says beasts, plants, rocks and streams with human or other attributes 'in a paramount measure' were taken as controllers of those attributes, available 'by orenda or magic power'; the Iroquois word rendered 'god' means 'disposer' or 'controller'.

src.l: J. N. B. Hewitt, 1903, Iroquoian Cosmology, in Twenty-first Annual Report of the Bureau of American Ethnology, 1899-1900
src.q: were naturally regarded as the controllers of those attributes or properties, which could be made available by orenda or magic power. And thus began the reign of the beast gods, plant gods, tree gods, and their kind.

s: Parker (Seneca Myths and Folk Tales, 1923): 'There is such a thing as orenda or magical power', which makes its possessor master over the natural order; it may be an attribute of the individual or inhere in a charm, and there is good and evil orenda.

src.l: Arthur C. Parker, 1923, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales
src.q: There is such a thing as orenda or magical power. Such power makes its possessor the master over the natural order of things. This orenda may be acquired in various ways. It may be residual, and therefore an attribute of the individual, or it may be inherent in some charm or fetish.

s: Parker (1923) states as a Seneca principle that 'Everything in the Seneca philosophy lives and is conscious', each thing a being in communication with other parts of nature that can be spoken to and hear.

src.l: Arthur C. Parker, 1923, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales
src.q: All nature is conscious. Everything in the Seneca philosophy lives and is conscious. It is a being and in communication with other parts of nature. Anything in nature may be spoken to and it will hear what one has said.

s: Doutté (1908) calls the magician's projected desire 'cette force' that can exteriorize itself and attach to objects, says Hubert and Mauss showed it is the mana of the Malays, the orenda of the Hurons and the manitou of the Algonquins, and adds Ibn Khaldūn's nefs and rouh', 'esprit, souffle'.

src.l: Edmond Doutté, 1908, Magie et religion dans l’Afrique du Nord
src.q: It is this force—which can exteriorize itself, attach itself to objects, and even pre-exist within them—which is the magical essence par excellence (3). Hubert and Mauss have shown that this is the same as the mana  of the Malays, the orenda of the Hurons, the manitou of the Algonquins (4)
src.qo: C'est cette force qui peut s'extérioriser, s'attacher aux objets, préexister même en eux, qui est le magique par excellence (3). Hubert et Mauss ont montré que c'est là le mana des Malais, l'orenda des Hurons, le manitou des Algonquins (4), etc... : c'est aussi le nefs et le rouh' (deux mots qui veulent dire esprit, souffle)

src.l: Edmond Doutté, 1908, Magie et religion dans l’Afrique du Nord
src.q: C'est cette force qui peut s'extérioriser, s'attacher aux objets, préexister même en eux, qui est le magique par excellence (3). Hubert et Mauss ont montré que c'est là le mana des Malais, l'orenda des Hurons, le manitou des Algonquins (4), etc... : c'est aussi le nefs et le rouh' (deux mots qui veulent dire esprit, souffle)

s: Doutté (1908) concludes that the first man who threw water while looking at the sky in order to see rain fall 'was the ancestor of the metaphysicians': 'le mana est une hypothèse métaphysique'; magic is at origin a collective creation of the clan (after Hubert and Mauss).

src.l: Edmond Doutté, 1908, Magie et religion dans l’Afrique du Nord
src.q: était l'ancêtre des métaphysiciens ; le mana est une hypothèse métaphysique.

src.l: Edmond Doutté, 1908, Magie et religion dans l’Afrique du Nord
src.q: was the ancestor of the metaphysicians; mana  is a metaphysical hypothesis.
src.qo: était l'ancêtre des métaphysiciens ; le mana est une hypothèse métaphysique.

s: Brinton (1897) says that through the Pacific 'the impersonal Divine' was expressed by one term, mana: the natives believed in departed souls and in spirits (vui), but the supernatural power through which both acted was mana.

src.l: Daniel G. Brinton, 1897, Religions of Primitive Peoples
src.q: Turning to the island world of the Pacific we find through its countless groups of sunny isles the impersonal Divine expressed by one general term, mana.

s: Brinton (1897) glosses mana as 'that which is within one', later intelligence or mind, 'whence power or might, as the expressions of Will applied to the concept of universal life and motion', and insists such words carry no idea of personality.

src.l: Daniel G. Brinton, 1897, Religions of Primitive Peoples
src.q: mana appears to be “that which is within one,” and, later, the intelligence on mind, whence power or might, as the expressions of Will applied to the concept of universal life and motion.

s: Brinton (1897) says the Dakota wakan, also found in Quichua and Aymara, applies to everything extraordinary, out of the course of nature, sacred or divine: 'It was not a deity, but expressed the deific power'.

src.l: Daniel G. Brinton, 1897, Religions of Primitive Peoples
src.q: It is there applied to every-thing which is extraordinary or immense, out of the course of nature, and especially to everything sacred or divine. It was not a deity, but expressed the deific power

s: Westermarck (Ritual and Belief in Morocco, 1926) says words like manitou, wakan or wakanda, mana, kalou, atua and ndriamanitra 'are used to denote a mysterious force or something wonderful or divine', testifying to a felt difference between the ordinary and the awe-inspiring.

src.l: Edward Westermarck, 1908, Ritual and Belief in Morocco, Vol. 1
src.q: Words like the Algonkin manitou, the Dacotah wakan or wakanda, the Melanesian mana, the Fijian kalou, the Maori atua, the Malagasy ndriamanitra, are used to denote a mysterious force or something wonderful or divine.

s: Crooke (1926) uses 'Animatism or Pre-animism' (the latter less apt, since it implies priority in time) for Indian belief 'based on the feeling of awe in the presence of some unknown force', the reverence paid to 'the unaccountable Thing'.

src.l: William Crooke, 1926, Religion and Folklore of Northern India
src.q: He is thus led to adopt the doctrine of Animatism or Pre-animism—the latter a less appropriate term as it seems to imply that in order of time it is antecedent to the more general form of belief known as Animism. Animatism is based on the feeling of awe in the presence of some unknown force

s: Clodd (Occultism, 1922): with 'The non-living and the living being alike credited with Mana', there follows the tendency to project personality on the forces of nature, 'Hence the origin of Animism'; mana is put before animism in time.

src.l: Edward Clodd, 1922, Occultism: two lectures delivered in the Royal Institution
src.q: The non-living and the living being alike credited with Mana, there follows the tendency of the primitive mind to project its own personality on the forces of nature. Hence the origin of Animism, or belief in indwelling spirits everywhere.

s: Aston (Shinto, 1905) says Kami, the commonest Japanese word for deity, probably means 'above, superior' (kami = hair of the head, upper waters); gods are Kami because they dwell in heaven, men because of rank.

src.l: W. G. Aston, 1905, Shinto: The Way of the Gods
src.q: Kami.—The most common and comprehensive word for deity in the Japanese language is Kami. It is probably connected with kaburu, to cover, and has the general meaning of "above," "superior."

s: Wissowa (Religion und Kultus der Römer, 1912) derives Genius from gen-, gignere (to beget): only men have a Genius (women a Juno), born with the person and originally dying with him; his place is the marriage bed, the lectus genialis.

src.l: Georg Wissowa, 1902, Religion and Cult of the Romans
src.q: Not often does the etymology of a god's name speak as clearly as here: the connection with the root gen, gignere
src.qo: Nicht oft spricht die Etymologie eines Götternamens so deutlich wie hier:

src.l: Georg Wissowa, 1902, Religion and Cult of the Romans
src.q: Every person has their own Genius, or their Juno, who are born with them, remain inseparable from them throughout their entire life, and according to the original conception, also die with them
src.qo: Jeder Mensch hat seinen Genius, bezw. seine Juno, die mit ihm geboren werden, während seines ganzen Lebens von ihm unzertrennlich sind ^3) und nach der ursprünglichen Vorstellung auch mit ihm sterben;

s: Tregear (The Maori Race, 1904): mana 'was shown when a man undertook to do an unusual and almost impossible thing and yet succeeded'; defeat after success meant some observance was neglected, and a slave's child could rise to have mana.

src.l: Edward Tregear, 1904, The Maori Race
src.q: Mana was shown when a man undertook to do an unusual and almost impossible thing and yet succeeded. If, after a course of happy issues, defeat should follow, it was because some religious observance had been disregarded.

s: Farrow (1926) says mana is not the same as 'magic', since it is attributed to inanimate objects: a stone resembling a yam is buried among the yams and a good harvest is credited to its mana; any power or skill beyond the average counts.

src.l: Stephen Septimus Farrow, 1926, Faith, Fancies and Fetich, or Yoruba Paganism
src.q: It is not the same as "magic," for it is sometimes attributed to inanimate objects, such as a stone of unusual form. Should one be found resembling a yam, it may be buried where yams are cultivated, and if a good harvest results this is attributed to the mana possessed by the said stone.

s: Jung (Psychological Types, 1923) names the suppression of individuality Rousseau describes 'that primitive collective mentality which Lévy-Bruhl has aptly termed "participation mystique"', a residue of an archaic time without individuality.

src.l: C. G. Jung, 1923, Psychological Types
src.q: For what Rousseau depicts is nothing but that primitive collective mentality which Lévy-Bruhl has aptly termed “participation mystique”.

s: Lang (The Making of Religion, 1898) says that by animism 'Tylor does not mean the alleged early theory' that all things are animated personalities, though early man may half-consciously have extended his own sense of animated existence to all nature.

src.l: Andrew Lang, 1898, The Making of Religion
src.q: Tylor does not mean the alleged early theory, implicitly if not explicitly and consciously held, that all things whatsoever are animated and are personalities.

s: Against Tylor's minimum definition: Aston (1905) objects that '"Spiritual being" is insufficiently comprehensive as an equivalent for God', since the Sun, the Wind, the Moon and the Lama of Tibet are gods without being spirits.

src.l: W. G. Aston, 1905, Shinto: The Way of the Gods
src.q: "Spiritual being" is insufficiently comprehensive as an equivalent for God.—The Lama of Tibet is a God; but he is not a spiritual being. Neither is the Wind nor the Moon. The assumption that Gods are always spirits has been the source of much confusion.

s: Zhuangzi, 'Zhi bei you' (ch. 22, 4th–3rd c. BCE; 1699 printing): human life is the gathering of qi; gathered it is life, dispersed it is death, so life and death are companions; SL's English adds the gloss 'vital energy' to qi.

src.l: 莊周 Zhuang Zhou, commentator of the 莊子旁注, 1699, 莊子旁注 (Zhuangzi with Commentary), Vol. 3
src.q: Human life is the gathering of qi vital energy. When it gathers, there is life; when it disperses, there is death.
src.qo: 人之生氣之聚也聚則爲生

src.l: 莊周 Zhuang Zhou, commentator of the 莊子旁注, 1699, 莊子旁注 (Zhuangzi with Commentary), Vol. 3
src.q: 人之生氣之聚也聚則爲生

s: Zhuangzi, 'Zhi bei you': 'what they find beautiful is the marvellous, what they hate is the putrid; the putrid changes back into the marvellous … so it is said, all under heaven is one qi'; SL glosses this qi too as 'vital energy'.

src.l: 莊周 Zhuang Zhou, commentator of the 莊子旁注, 1699, 莊子旁注 (Zhuangzi with Commentary), Vol. 3
src.q: It is but one qi vital energy. Therefore, the Sage values this "One."
src.qo: 下一氣耳聖人故貴一

src.l: 莊周 Zhuang Zhou, commentator of the 莊子旁注, 1699, 莊子旁注 (Zhuangzi with Commentary), Vol. 3
src.loc: scan 141 (original; the sentence begins 故曰通天 on scan 140)
src.q: 下一氣耳聖人故貴一

s: The 1699 Zhuangzi pangzhu commentary on 'Gengsang Chu' (ch. 23) explains 'there is birth' as qi gathering to make life (氣聚而生), and death and life as the gathering and scattering of qi, which people cannot know; SL renders 氣 here as 'energy'.

src.l: 莊周 Zhuang Zhou, commentator of the 莊子旁注, 1699, 莊子旁注 (Zhuangzi with Commentary), Vol. 4
src.q: This means energy gathers and produces, like the formation of a birthmark.
src.qo: 謂 氣聚而生。如黶閽成靨

src.l: 莊周 Zhuang Zhou, commentator of the 莊子旁注, 1699, 莊子旁注 (Zhuangzi with Commentary), Vol. 4
src.q: 謂 氣聚而生。如黶閽成靨

s: Mencius 2A2 (4th c. BCE; Legge 1861): the 浩然之氣 is exceedingly great and strong; nourished by rectitude and unharmed it fills all between heaven and earth; it is produced by accumulated righteous deeds. Legge renders 氣 'passion-nature', neither breath nor force.

src.l: 孟子 Mencius, James Legge (tr.), 1861, 孟子 (Mencius): The Chinese Classics Vol. 2
src.q: This is the passion-nature:—It is exceedingly great, and exceedingly strong. Being nourished by rectitude, and sustaining no injury, it fills up all between heaven and earth.

src.l: 孟子 Mencius, James Legge (tr.), 1861, 孟子 (Mencius): The Chinese Classics Vol. 2
src.q: 其為氣也至大至剛以直養而無害則塞于天地之間

s: Mencius 2A2: 'the will is the commander of qi; qi is what fills the body' (夫志氣之帥也氣體之充也); in Legge (1861) 'the passion-nature pervades and animates the body', with the will first and qi second.

src.l: 孟子 Mencius, James Legge (tr.), 1861, 孟子 (Mencius): The Chinese Classics Vol. 2
src.q: The will is the leader of the passion-nature. The passion-nature pervades and animates the body.

src.l: 孟子 Mencius, James Legge (tr.), 1861, 孟子 (Mencius): The Chinese Classics Vol. 2
src.q: 夫志氣 之帥也氣體之充也

s: Mencius 2A2 gives the method of cultivating qi as constant practice without forcing: 'let not the mind forget, but do not help it grow' (勿忘勿助長), illustrated by the man of Song who pulled up his sprouts to help them grow.

src.l: 孟子 Mencius, James Legge (tr.), 1861, 孟子 (Mencius): The Chinese Classics Vol. 2
src.q: Let not the mind forget its work, but let there be no assisting the growth of that nature. Let us not be like the man of Sung.

src.l: 孟子 Mencius, James Legge (tr.), 1861, 孟子 (Mencius): The Chinese Classics Vol. 2
src.q: 勿忘勿助長也無若宋人

s: Ge Hong, Baopuzi neipian 'Jindan' (c. 320; 1778 Siku copy): the golden elixir grows more wondrous the longer it is fired, and gold never decays; eaten, these two 'refine the human body' so one neither ages nor dies, 'borrowing external substances to strengthen oneself', like verdigris that keeps feet from rotting.

src.l: Ge Hong, 1778, Baopuzi: Inner Chapters
src.q: When one consumes these two medicines , they refine the human body, and can thus cause a person never to age and never to die. This is indeed borrowing external substances to strengthen oneself
src.qo: 服此二藥鍊人身體故能 令人不老不死此盖假求於外物以自堅固

src.l: Ge Hong, 1778, Baopuzi: Inner Chapters
src.q: 服此二藥鍊人身體故能 令人不老不死此盖假求於外物以自堅固

s: In SL's English of Ge Hong's Baopuzi (1778 copy), the term note on 導引 daoyin calls it 'an ancient precursor to Qigong … to circulate vital energy (Qi)'; the note imports a 20th-century practice name and 'vital energy' into a text that says neither.

src.l: Ge Hong, 1778, Baopuzi: Inner Chapters
src.q: an ancient precursor to Qigong involving breath control and physical movements to circulate vital energy (Qi).

s: Caraka Saṃhitā, Sūtrasthāna 1 (early centuries CE; 1819 ed.): āyus is defined as the union (saṃyoga) of body, senses, mind and self, and its synonyms are dhāri, jīvita, nityaga and anubandha; SL's English turns the four synonyms into predicates ('as is that which maintains, which is eternally flowing…').

src.l: Charaka, 1819, चरकसंहिता (Caraka Saṃhitā)
src.loc: scan 82 (Sū. 1.42 in the vulgate; v. 16 here)
src.q: The combination of the body, senses, mind, and soul is called life , as is that which maintains, which is eternally flowing, and which is an extension.
src.qo: शरीरेन्द्रियसत्त्वात्मसंयोगो धारि जीवितम् । नित्यगश्चानुबन्धश्च पर्यायैरायुरुच्यते

src.l: Charaka, 1819, चरकसंहिता (Caraka Saṃhitā)
src.q: शरीरेन्द्रियसत्त्वात्मसंयोगो धारि जीवितम् । नित्यगश्चानुबन्धश्च पर्यायैरायुरुच्यते

s: Kunja Lal Bhishagratna, introducing his English Suśruta (early 20th c.), reads Punarvasu's (Caraka's) definition of āyus as 'the continuous adjustment of molecules, their successive breaking down and building up within an organised living body', and calls Hindu biology 'molecular in every sense'.

src.l: Suśruta, Kunja Lal Bhishagratna (tr.), n.d. (early 20th c.), Sushruta Samhita Vol. 2 (English Translation from Sanskrit)
src.q: Molecular in every sense is the Biology of the Hindus. Virtually speaking, Ayurveda is our Science of Life, and we will presently shew that Life and Ayus are identical. The continuous adjustment of molecules, their successive breaking down and building up within an organised living body

s: Haṭhayogapradīpikā 2.3 (15th c.; 1867 ed.): 'as long as vāyu stays in the body, that is called life (jīvana); its departure is death; therefore restrain vāyu': life is defined as the breath's residence in the body.

src.l: Svatmarama, 1867, Hathayogapradipika (Sanskrit, 1867)
src.q: As long as the breath remains in the body, it is called life. Its departure is death. Therefore, one should restrain the breath.
src.qo: यावद्वायुः स्थितो देहे तावज्जीवनमुच्यते ॥ मरणं तस्य निष्क्रांतिस्ततो वायुं निरोधयेत्

src.l: Svatmarama, 1867, Hathayogapradipika (Sanskrit, 1867)
src.q: यावद्वायुः स्थितो देहे तावज्जीवनमुच्यते ॥ मरणं तस्य निष्क्रांतिस्ततो वायुं निरोधयेत्

s: Haṭhayogapradīpikā 2.2: 'when the wind moves, the mind moves; when it is still, the mind is still; the yogi becomes immovable as a post', so breath is restrained to still the mind.

src.l: Svatmarama, 1867, Hathayogapradipika (Sanskrit, 1867)
src.q: When the breath moves, the mind moves. When the breath is still, the mind becomes still.
src.qo: चले वाते चलं चित्तं निश्चले निश्चलं भवेत्

src.l: Svatmarama, 1867, Hathayogapradipika (Sanskrit, 1867)
src.q: चले वाते चलं चित्तं निश्चले निश्चलं भवेत्

s: Haṭhayogapradīpikā 2.73–75: when 'absolute' retention (kevala kumbhaka), without exhalation or inhalation, is perfected, nothing in the three worlds is hard to obtain, because one can hold the wind at will; from kumbhaka the kuṇḍalī awakens.

src.l: Svatmarama, 1867, Hathayogapradipika (Sanskrit, 1867)
src.q: Nothing in the three worlds is difficult for him to obtain. Because he is capable of holding the breath as he desires through absolute retention
src.qo: न तस्य दुर्लभं किंचित्रिषु लोकेषु विद्यते ॥ शक्तः केवलकुंभेन यथेष्टं वायुधारणात्

src.l: Svatmarama, 1867, Hathayogapradipika (Sanskrit, 1867)
src.q: न तस्य दुर्लभं किंचित्रिषु लोकेषु विद्यते ॥ शक्तः केवलकुंभेन यथेष्टं वायुधारणात्

s: Haṭhayogapradīpikā 3 (śakticālana, 1867 ed. p. 122): moving the kuṇḍalī, the yogi has no fear of death 'even in death's mouth'; in the next verse the Sanskrit says only 'she' (asau, the kuṇḍalī) rises in the suṣumṇā, but SL's English writes 'the energy' and glosses suṣumṇā as 'the central energy channel'.

src.l: Svatmarama, 1867, Hathayogapradipika (Sanskrit, 1867)
src.q: Even if one has entered the mouth of death, why should there be any fear of death? || 16 || By moving the energy fearlessly for the duration of two muhurtas approximately 96 minutes , it is drawn slightly upward, having arisen in the Sushumna the central energy channel

src.l: Svatmarama, 1867, Hathayogapradipika (Sanskrit, 1867)

s: Chāndogya Upaniṣad V.1.1 (Müller 1879): 'Breath indeed is the oldest and the best'; the chapter then sets breath against speech, eye, ear and mind as the faculty without which the body cannot live.

src.l: F. Max Müller (tr.), 1879, The Upanishads, Part 1 (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 1)
src.q: He who knows the oldest and the best becomes himself the oldest and the best. Breath indeed is the oldest and the best.

s: Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad II.1 (Müller 1879): 'Prâna (breath) is Brahman, thus says Kaushîtaki'; mind is its messenger, speech its housekeeper, eye its guard, ear its informant: breath is the ruler and the faculties its household.

src.l: F. Max Müller (tr.), 1879, The Upanishads, Part 1 (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 1)
src.q: Prâna (breath) is Brahman, thus says Kaushîtaki. Of this prâna, which is Brahman, the mind (manas) is the messenger, speech the housekeeper, the eye the guard, the ear the informant.

s: Praśna Upaniṣad II.3–4 (Hume 1921): prāṇa, 'the chiefest', tells the other faculties that it, dividing itself fivefold, supports the body; when it rises they all rise, as bees follow the king bee.

src.l: Robert Ernest Hume (tr.), 1921, The Thirteen Principal Upanishads
src.q: To them Life (prāṇa, the life-breath), the chiefest, said: “Fall not into delusion! I indeed, dividing myself (ātmānam) fivefold, support and sustain this body!”

s: Praśna Upaniṣad III.3–4 (Hume 1921): prāṇa is born from the ātman as a shadow is cast by a person, enters the body by the mind's action, and commands the other breaths as an overlord his village overseers.

src.l: Robert Ernest Hume (tr.), 1921, The Thirteen Principal Upanishads
src.q: This life (prāṇa) is born from the Spirit (Ātman, Self). [b] Its embodiment As in the case of a person there is this shadow extended, so it is in this case.

s: Yogi Ramacharaka (W. W. Atkinson), Science of Breath (1905, Chicago): 'Prana' is 'the Sanskrit term meaning "Absolute Energy"', and occultists teach it is the universal principle of all energy or force: the English 'energy' reading of prāṇa, in print, with no Sanskrit text behind it.

src.l: Yogi Ramacharaka (William Walker Atkinson), 1905, Science of Breath
src.loc: scan 21 (ch. IV, The Esoteric Theory of Breath)
src.q: we, in this work, will speak of the principle as “Prana,” this word being the Sanskrit term meaning “Absolute Energy.”

s: rGyud bzhi (12th c. trad.; 1888 print), on internal wind disorders: for the 'life-holding' wind (srog 'dzin rlung) massage with sesame oil, give mild nasal medicine and warm the wind points: rlung is one of five winds, treated with oil and heat.

s: Against reading qi or prāṇa as 'the stuff of life': the definitions the texts themselves give are positional or relational: life is qi GATHERED (Zhuangzi, Zhu Xi), vāyu STAYING in the body (HYP 2.3), the UNION of body, senses, mind and self (Caraka); death is dispersal, departure, separation, not the loss of a substance.
