s: Hobbes (Leviathan, Introduction, 1651; Latin 1668) defines life as 'but a motion of Limbs, the beginning whereof is in some principall part within', and asks why all automata that move themselves by springs and wheels, as a watch does, may not be said to have an artificial life.

src.l: Thomas Hobbes, 1651, Leviathan (1651 first edition)
src.q: For seeing life is but a motion of Limbs, the beginning whereof is in some principall part within; why may we not say, that all Automata (Engines that move themselves by springs and wheeles as doth a watch) have an artificiall life?

src.l: Thomas Hobbes, 1668, Leviathan (Latin version)
src.q: Cum enim vita nihil aliud sit quam artuum motus, cujus principium est internum in parte aliqua Corporis principali

s: Hobbes (Leviathan I.6, 1651) distinguishes in animals a 'Vitall' motion, begun in generation and continued without interruption through the whole life (the course of the blood, the pulse, breathing, concoction, nutrition, excretion), needing no imagination, from voluntary 'Animal' motion.

src.l: Thomas Hobbes, 1651, Leviathan (1651 first edition)
src.q: One called Vitall; begun in generation, and continued without interruption through their whole life; such as are the course of the Bloud, the Pulse, the Breathing, the Concoction, Nutrition, Excretion, &c; to which Motions there needs no help of Imagination

s: Boyle (Free Inquiry into the Vulgar Notion of Nature, 1686; Shaw's abridged English, 1725) says the commonest sense of 'nature' is 'a semi-deity, or other strange kind of Being', the notion his book examines, and spells it out as a most wise being that does nothing in vain and, as in the human frame, cures diseases.

src.q: Sometimes, too, and that most commonly, we would express by the word nature, a semi-deity, or other strange kind of Being; which is the notion we here examine.

src.q: Nature is a moſt wiſe being, that acts nothing in vain, never miſſes of her ends, but always does what is beſt

s: Boyle (Free Inquiry, 1686; Shaw 1725) calls the human body 'an incomparable engine' framed to last many years, and attributes the crises of diseases not to a watchful nature but to God's providence 'exerting itself by the mechanism of that great machine, the world'.

src.l: Robert Boyle, Peter Shaw (abridger), 1725, The Philosophical Works of Robert Boyle, abridged by Peter Shaw, Vol. 2
src.q: But the body of a man is an incomparable engine, which the most wise author of things has so skilfully framed, for lasting many years

src.l: Robert Boyle, Peter Shaw (abridger), 1725, The Philosophical Works of Robert Boyle, abridged by Peter Shaw, Vol. 2
src.q: I, on the other side, attribute crises to the wisdom and ordinary providence of God, exerting itself by the mechanism of that great machine, the world

s: Boyle (Final Causes of Natural Things, 1688; Shaw 1725) says there is infinitely more art in the structure of a dog's foot than in the famous clock at Strasbourg, and that he never saw an inanimate production of nature whose contrivance compared with the meanest limb of the most despicable animal.

src.l: Robert Boyle, Peter Shaw (abridger), 1725, The Philosophical Works of Robert Boyle, abridged by Peter Shaw, Vol. 2
src.q: there is infinitely more art express'd in the structure of a dog's foot, than in that of the famous clock at Strasburg

s: Leibniz (Monadology §64, 1714; Latta's English 1898) calls the organic body of each living being a divine machine or natural automaton, and says the machines of nature, living bodies, are still machines in their smallest parts ad infinitum, whereas a human machine is not a machine in each of its parts.

src.l: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, Robert Latta, 1898, The Monadology and Other Philosophical Writings (Latta)
src.q: But the machines of nature, namely, living bodies, are still machines in their smallest parts ad infinitum

src.l: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, Heinrich Köhler (tr.), 1740, Kleinere philosophische Schriften (German, incl. Köhler's Monadology translation)
src.q: Demnach ist ein iedweder organischer Körper eines lebendigen Wesens eine Art von den Göttlichen Machinen oder natürlichen automatibus

s: Leibniz (Monadology §66-67, 1714) holds that in the smallest particle of matter there is a world of creatures, living beings, animals, entelechies, souls, and that each portion of matter is like a garden full of plants and a pond full of fishes, each branch, member and drop again such a garden or pond.

src.l: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, Robert Latta, 1898, The Monadology and Other Philosophical Writings (Latta)
src.q: Whence it appears that in the smallest particle of matter there is a world of creatures, living beings, animals, entelechies, souls.  67. Each portion of matter may be conceived as like a garden full of plants and like a pond full of fishes.

src.l: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, Heinrich Köhler (tr.), 1740, Kleinere philosophische Schriften (German, incl. Köhler's Monadology translation)
src.q: Ein iedwedes Stück von der Materie kan als ein Garten voller Pflanzen und Bäume, und als ein Teich voller Fische von uns angesehen werden.

s: Anne Conway (Principia, 1690) argues that as God did not make death, so he made no dead thing: no creature could receive from infinite life and love an essence so vile that it shares nothing of life or perception and could never aspire to it.

src.l: Anne Conway, 1690, Principia philosophiae antiquissimae et recentissimae
src.q: It has been truly said by a certain person  that God did not make death; and it is equally true that he made no dead thing.
src.qo: Vere dictum est à quodam, Deum non fecisse mortem: verumque pa- riter, quod nullam rem fecerit mortuam

src.l: Anne Conway, 1690, Principia philosophiae antiquissimae et recentissimae
src.q: Vere dictum est à quodam, Deum non fecisse mortem: verumque pa- riter, quod nullam rem fecerit mortuam

s: Conway (Principia, 1690) asks what progress in goodness 'dead matter' (materia mortua) could make: after infinite changes of motion and figure it must stay as dead as before, so if motion and shape contribute nothing toward receiving life such matter never becomes better.

src.l: Anne Conway, 1690, Principia philosophiae antiquissimae et recentissimae
src.q: for what further progress in goodness or perfection does dead matter  have? Because after it has undergone infinite changes of motion and figure , it is always compelled to remain exactly as it was before: dead.
src.qo: enim progressum ulteriorem in bonitate vel perfectione habet materia mortua ? Quia postquam infinitas subiit mutationes , mo- tionis & figuræ, semper permanere cogitur, ut antehac , mortua

src.l: Anne Conway, 1690, Principia philosophiae antiquissimae et recentissimae
src.q: enim progressum ulteriorem in bonitate vel perfectione habet materia mortua ? Quia postquam infinitas subiit mutationes , mo- tionis & figuræ, semper permanere cogitur, ut antehac , mortua

s: Conway (Principia, 1690) asks whether spirit and body are of one nature and substance and so mutually convertible, and cites as evidence that the soul loves the body and leaves it unwillingly, some souls lingering over their bodies after death until these decayed to dust.

src.l: Anne Conway, 1690, Principia philosophiae antiquissimae et recentissimae
src.q: that we should examine whether spirit and body are of one nature and substance, and thus mutually convertible  into one another.
src.qo: annon spiritus & corpus unius sint naturæ & substantiæ, adeoque in se invicem convertibiles ?

src.l: Anne Conway, 1690, Principia philosophiae antiquissimae et recentissimae
src.q: annon spiritus & corpus unius sint naturæ & substantiæ, adeoque in se invicem convertibiles ?

s: Margaret Cavendish (Observations upon Experimental Philosophy, 1666) holds that Nature is 'a self-moving, and consequently a self-living and self-knowing infinite body', infinitely divisible, so that there are no atoms.

src.l: Margaret Cavendish, 1666, Observations upon Experimental Philosophy (with The Blazing World)
src.q: Nature is a self-moving, and consequently a self-living and self-knowing infinite body, divideable into infinite parts; yet I do not mean that these parts are Atomes

s: Cavendish (1666) says the inanimate part of matter is not self-moving and its motions are 'onely passive, not active', yet it has life and self-knowledge according to its own nature, since self-knowledge does not depend on motion: all parts of matter are living and knowing, but only the animate are self-moving.

src.l: Margaret Cavendish, 1666, Observations upon Experimental Philosophy (with The Blazing World)
src.q: In short, all parts or degrees of Matter are living and knowing, but not all are self-moving, but onely the animate.

src.l: Margaret Cavendish, 1666, Observations upon Experimental Philosophy (with The Blazing World)
src.q: its motions or actions are onely passive, not active

s: Cavendish (1666) argues that if nature has self-motion none of her parts can be called inanimate or soul-less, 'for Motion is the life and soul of Nature', and no part of nature's animate body can be dead or without motion.

src.l: Margaret Cavendish, 1666, Observations upon Experimental Philosophy (with The Blazing World)
src.q: none of her parts can be called inani- mate or soul-less: for Motion is the life and soul of Na- ture, and of all her parts

s: Spinoza (Ethics II, prop. 13 scholium, 1677) says what he has shown so far is quite general and pertains no more to humans than to other individuals, 'all of which, although in different degrees, are nevertheless animate' (quae omnia, quamvis diversis gradibus, animata tamen sunt).

src.l: Baruch Spinoza, 1915, Ethica (Latin original)
src.q: all of which, although in different degrees, are nevertheless animate
src.qo: quæ omnia, quamvis diversis gradibus, animata tamen sunt

src.l: Baruch Spinoza, 1915, Ethica (Latin original)
src.q: quæ omnia, quamvis diversis gradibus, animata tamen sunt

s: Thomas Willis (De anima brutorum, 1672) reports that Gassendi, following Epicurus, made the souls of animals corporeal, of the smoothest and roundest atoms that make fire and heat, and concluded that the soul is 'a certain little flame' (flammula): while it stays lit the animal lives, when extinguished it dies. Willis's own Chapter II holds the brute soul corporeal and fiery.

src.l: Thomas Willis, 1672, De anima brutorum
src.q: Finally, he concludes that the soul is therefore a certain little flame, or a type of most thin fire. As long as this flame thrives or remains lit, the animal lives. When it no longer thrives, or is extinguished, the animal dies.
src.qo: demum concludit animam proinde esse quandam flammulam, ignisve tenuissimi speciem, quæ quamdiu viget, seu manet accensa, tamdiu vivit animal

src.l: Thomas Willis, 1672, De anima brutorum
src.q: demum concludit animam proinde esse quandam flammulam, ignisve tenuissimi speciem, quæ quamdiu viget, seu manet accensa, tamdiu vivit animal

src.l: Thomas Willis, 1672, De anima brutorum
src.q: Animam Bruti eſse corpoream, & Igneam.

s: Gassendi (Syntagma, Physics, De anima, 1658) gathers the ancient senses of anima: it is used for air, Terence says it is 'breathed out' as a blast, wind or breath, Ovid calls an old woman's anima the breath that blows a fire into flame, and from this it is also called spirit.

src.l: Pierre Gassendi, 1658, Opera omnia, Tomus secundus (Syntagma philosophicum, Physica)
src.q: Hence Terence says the soul is "breathed out," as if it were a blast, a wind, or a breath.
src.qo: Heinc eadem Terentio dicitur efflari, quasi sit flatus, ventus, halitus; & expressius Ouidio Anima anilis dicitur flatus vetulæ ignem ad flammam excitantis.

src.l: Pierre Gassendi, 1658, Opera omnia, Tomus secundus (Syntagma philosophicum, Physica)
src.q: Heinc eadem Terentio dicitur efflari, quasi sit flatus, ventus, halitus; & expressius Ouidio Anima anilis dicitur flatus vetulæ ignem ad flammam excitantis.

s: Harvey (De generatione animalium, 1651; Robert Willis's English 1847) concludes that 'the life, therefore, resides in the blood', as scripture also says, because life and soul show themselves first in it and are last extinguished there; there 'the vital principle (anima) itself has its seat'.

src.l: William Harvey, Robert Willis (tr.), 1847, The Works of William Harvey (Sydenham Society)
src.q: The life, therefore, resides in the blood, (as we are also informed in our sacred writings,)² because in it life and the soul first show themselves, and last become extinct.

s: Harvey (De generatione, 1651; English 1847) says that whether the beginning of an animal is called egg or worm, the word 'primordium' should name that from which it is formed, as plants come from seeds, and that all these primordia have one common property, vitality.

src.l: William Harvey, Robert Willis (tr.), 1847, The Works of William Harvey (Sydenham Society)
src.loc: On the uterus and humours, p. 555, scan 655
src.q: all these “primordia” have one common property—that of vitality.

s: Harvey (De generatione, 1651; English 1847) still admits a class of animals with a generative fluid produced 'fortuitously, as it were', without distinction of sex, whose origin is spontaneous, comparing it with Aristotle's things made by accident.

src.l: William Harvey, Robert Willis (tr.), 1847, The Works of William Harvey (Sydenham Society)
src.q: Another class of animals has a generative fluid fortuitously, as it were, and without any distinction of sex ; the origin of such animals is spontaneous.

s: Redi (Esperienze intorno alla generazione degl'insetti, 1668) reports that dead scorpions watered with basil water produced flies, not scorpions, and in a well-sealed glass vessel neither worms, flies nor scorpions, confirming his view that from corpses, unless seed is brought upon them, no animal of any kind is ever born.

src.l: Francesco Redi, 1668, Esperienze intorno alla generazione degl'insetti
src.q: wherefore I continued more and more to confirm my opinion that from corpses, if the seed is not brought upon them, no animal of any kind is ever born.
src.qo: che da' cadaveri, se non vi è portato sopra il seme, non nasca mai animale di sorta alcuna

src.l: Francesco Redi, 1668, Esperienze intorno alla generazione degl'insetti
src.q: che da' cadaveri, se non vi è portato sopra il seme, non nasca mai animale di sorta alcuna

s: Hooke (Micrographia, 1665) admits as possible that since many contrivances go to make one complete animate body, some may be vitiated and the life of the whole destroyed while several of the constituting contrivances remain entire, and he finds no cogent argument that plant and animal are altogether heterogeneous.

src.l: Robert Hooke, 1665, Micrographia
src.q: For as there may be multitudes of contrivances that go to the making up of one compleat Animate body; so, That some of those coadjutors, in the perfect existence and life of it, may be vitiated, and the life of the whole destroyed, and yet several of the constituting contrivances remain intire

s: Sebastian Wirdig (Nova medicina spirituum, 1673) holds that natural motion presupposes life or a living principle and is perfected by the spirits; in the suffocated the spirits still move insensibly and radiate weakly, like fire in a glowing coal, the life that frogs, bears and marmots live in winter.

src.l: Sebastian Wirdig, 1673, Nova medicina spirituum
src.q: Natural motion presupposes life or a living principle; but motion is perfected by the benefit of the Spirits
src.qo: Motus naturalis præsupponit vitam seu principium vivens; motus autem beneficio Spirituum perficitur

src.l: Sebastian Wirdig, 1673, Nova medicina spirituum
src.q: Motus naturalis præsupponit vitam seu principium vivens; motus autem beneficio Spirituum perficitur

s: Nehemiah Grew (Cosmologia Sacra, 1701) argues that body is not vital as a substance: it cannot produce motion, much less life, which is greater, nor receive life as its proper adjunct, since life is distinct from and more excellent than motion and so needs an incorporeal subject.

src.l: Nehemiah Grew, 1701, Cosmologia Sacra
src.q: Body is not Vital, as it is Substantial: Or, it is not Productive of Life in it self, by virtue of its being a Substantial thing.

src.l: Nehemiah Grew, 1701, Cosmologia Sacra
src.q: For if Life be a Thing, distinct from, and more excellent than Motion; as I have a little before shewed, it is: It then requires a more Excellent, and so a distinct Subject

s: Against a story in which mechanism 'killed' matter: on SL's pages the mechanist and the animist of 1651-1666 give the SAME definition of life, motion (Hobbes: 'life is but a motion of Limbs'; Cavendish: 'Motion is the life and soul of Nature'), and disagree only about whether matter moves itself; the opponents of both (Wirdig 1673, Grew 1701) are those who say life is prior to and more than motion.

src.l: Thomas Hobbes, 1651, Leviathan (1651 first edition)
src.q: For seeing life is but a motion of Limbs

src.l: Margaret Cavendish, 1666, Observations upon Experimental Philosophy (with The Blazing World)
src.q: for Motion is the life and soul of Na- ture

src.l: Nehemiah Grew, 1701, Cosmologia Sacra
src.q: For if Body cannot produce Motion, which is the less

s: Against citing Harvey's 'omne vivum ex ovo' as the end of spontaneous generation: in De generatione (1651) Harvey still grants animals whose 'origin is spontaneous', and his primordium (egg or worm) is defined by vitality, not by parentage; the experimental denial on SL's pages is Redi's sealed vessels (1668).

src.l: William Harvey, Robert Willis (tr.), 1847, The Works of William Harvey (Sydenham Society)
src.q: the origin of such animals is spontaneous

src.l: Francesco Redi, 1668, Esperienze intorno alla generazione degl'insetti
src.q: from corpses, if the seed is not brought upon them, no animal of any kind is ever born
src.qo: che da' cadaveri, se non vi è portato sopra il seme, non nasca mai animale di sorta alcuna.

s: Tertullian (De anima 10, c. 210) defines living by breathing: to breathe is to drive breath (flatus) out of oneself, not to live is not to do so, so breathing is the mark of the living and belongs to the soul.

src.l: Tertullian, 1550, Tertulliani Scripta (1550)
src.q: Quid est, oro te, spirare: flatum, opinor, ex semetipso agere. Quid est non uiuere: flatum, opinor, ex semetipso non agere.

src.l: Tertullian, 1550, Tertulliani Scripta (1550)
src.q: What is it, I ask you, to breathe? It is, I believe, to drive breath from within oneself. What is it not to live? It is, I believe, not to drive breath from within oneself.
src.qo: Quid est, oro te, spirare: flatum, opinor, ex semetipso agere. Quid est non uiuere: flatum, opinor, ex semetipso non agere.

src.l: Tertullian, 1918, Ante-Nicene Fathers, Vol. 3 (Tertullian), ed. Roberts & Donaldson
src.q: It must, however, be characteristic of a dead man not to respire: to respire, therefore, is the characteristic of a living man.

s: Tertullian (De anima 11, c. 210) insists the soul made by God's breathing is properly flatus (breath), not spiritus in Scripture's sense, and accuses Hermogenes of turning flatus into spiritus so as to derive the soul from matter.

src.l: Tertullian, 1550, Tertulliani Scripta (1550)
src.q: Ita & animam quam flatum ex proprietate defendimus, spiritum nunc ex necessita- te pronunciamus. Cæterum aduersus Hermogenē, qui eam ex materia, non ex dei flatu conditit, flatum proprie tuemur.

src.l: Tertullian, 1918, Ante-Nicene Fathers, Vol. 3 (Tertullian), ed. Roberts & Donaldson
src.q: we on our side, even from that passage, maintain the soul to be breath and not the spirit, in the scriptural and distinctive sense of the spirit

s: Tertullian (De anima 7–8, c. 210) holds the soul is a body: the rich man tormented in hell (Luke 16) thirsts and begs a drop of water for his tongue, which he reads as the clearest evidence for the soul's corporeal nature.

src.l: Tertullian, 1918, Ante-Nicene Fathers, Vol. 3 (Tertullian), ed. Roberts & Donaldson
src.q: clearest evidence for the corporeal nature of the soul. In hell the soul of a certain man is in torment, punished in flames, suffering excruciating thirst

s: Tertullian (De anima 27, c. 210) holds that body and soul are conceived, formed and born together, with no moment's interval between them, so that the embryo is alive from conception.

src.l: Tertullian, 1918, Ante-Nicene Fathers, Vol. 3 (Tertullian), ed. Roberts & Donaldson
src.q: We indeed maintain that both are conceived, and formed, and perfectly simultaneously, as well as born together; and that not a moment's interval occurs in their conception

s: Gregory of Nyssa (De hominis opificio 8, 379) reads the order of Genesis 1 as teaching that the vital and psychic power (ζωτικὴ καὶ ψυχικὴ δύναμις) comes in three grades, the first only growing and nourishing, 'natural', found in plants, which have vital power without sensation.

src.l: Gregory of Nyssa, 1858, Patrologia Graeca vol. 44: Gregory of Nyssa (De hominis opificio)
src.q: Διδάσκει γὰρ ἡμᾶς διὰ τούτων ὁ λόγος, ἐν τρισὶ διαφοραῖς τὴν ζωτικὴν καὶ ψυχικὴν δύναμιν θεωρεῖσθαι. Ἡ μὲν γάρ τίς ἐστιν αὐξητική τε μόνον καὶ θρεπτική

src.l: Gregory of Nyssa, 1858, Patrologia Graeca vol. 44: Gregory of Nyssa (De hominis opificio)
src.q: For the discourse teaches us through these things that the vital and psychic power is to be considered in three differences. For one is only growth-producing and nourishing, bringing what is appropriate for the addition of those things which are nourished, which is called natural, and is considered in plants.
src.qo: Διδάσκει γὰρ ἡμᾶς διὰ τούτων ὁ λόγος, ἐν τρισὶ διαφοραῖς τὴν ζωτικὴν καὶ ψυχικὴν δύναμιν θεωρεῖσθαι. Ἡ μὲν γάρ τίς ἐστιν αὐξητική τε μόνον καὶ θρεπτική

s: Gregory of Nyssa (De hominis opificio 8, 379) maps the Apostle's 'body, soul and spirit' onto the three grades of life: body names the nourishing part, soul the sensing, spirit the intellectual; man is blended of all three.

src.l: Gregory of Nyssa, 1858, Patrologia Graeca vol. 44: Gregory of Nyssa (De hominis opificio)
src.q: ἀντὶ τοῦ θρεπτικοῦ μέρους τὸ σῶμα λέγων, τὸ δὲ αἰσθητικὸν τῇ ψυχῇ διασημαίνων, τὸ νοερὸν δὲ τῷ πνεύματι.

src.q: calling the nourishing part the "body," signifying the sensing part by the "soul," and the intellectual by the "spirit."
src.qo: ἀντὶ τοῦ θρεπτικοῦ μέρους τὸ σῶμα λέγων, τὸ δὲ αἰσθητικὸν τῇ ψυχῇ διασημαίνων, τὸ νοερὸν δὲ τῷ πνεύματι.

s: Cornelio Bellanda's Viaggio spirituale (1578) cites Augustine for the formula that as the soul is the whole life of the body, so God is the blessed life of the soul.

src.l: Bellanda, Cornelio, 1578, Viaggio spirituale, nel quale, facendosi passaggio da questa vita mortale ...
src.q: Augustine said: For just as the soul is the entire life of the body, so God is the blessed life of the soul.

s: Augustine (De civitate Dei XIII.23, 426) reads 1 Cor 15:45 as two states of the body: now the body is 'in animam viventem' (a living soul, an animal body), at the resurrection it will be 'in spiritum vivificantem' (a life-giving spirit), as Christ already is, who can no longer die.

src.l: Augustine, 1877, Saint Augustine: The City of God (De Civitate Dei)
src.q: Tunc ergo erit corpus in spiritum vivificantem, quod nunc est in animam viventem

src.l: Augustine, 1877, Saint Augustine: The City of God (De Civitate Dei)
src.q: The last Adam into a life-giving spirit, undoubtedly signifying Christ, who has already risen from the dead in such a way that he can now no longer die at all.
src.qo: Tunc ergo erit corpus in spiritum vivificantem, quod nunc est in animam viventem

s: Paul (1 Cor 15:45–46, c. 55) contrasts Adam, made εἰς ψυχὴν ζῶσαν (a living soul), with the last Adam, made εἰς πνεῦμα ζωοποιοῦν (a life-giving spirit), and says the ψυχικόν comes first, the πνευματικόν after; SL's English renders ψυχὴν ζῶσαν 'a living being' and ψυχικόν 'natural', so the word soul disappears.

src.l: Paul, 1633, Novum Testamentum Graece (Elzevir 1633, Textus Receptus)

src.l: Paul, 1633, Novum Testamentum Graece (Elzevir 1633, Textus Receptus)

s: Johann Franz Buddeus (Introductio ad historiam philosophiae Ebraeorum, 1702; ed. 1720), a Lutheran historian of philosophy, reports that the Kabbalists 'seem to admit five levels or, if you prefer, faculties' in the human soul, citing Luria via Kabbala denudata.

src.q: He calls this capacity of matter in an organized body (to distinguish it from the purely mechanical formative power that belongs to matter in general) a formative drive … which stands, as it were, under the higher guidance and direction of that original organization.
src.qo: zum Unterschiede von der ihr allgemein beiwohnenden, bloß mechanischen Bildungskraft

src.l: Immanuel Kant, 1922, Kritik der Urteilskraft (German)
src.q: zum Unterschiede von der ihr allgemein beiwohnenden, bloß mechanischen Bildungskraft

s: Oetinger (1762) equates Wolff's 'infinite power to form' with the ancients' vis plastica and argues that outside heat only awakens the seed while the formative force works from within.

src.l: Oetinger, Friedrich Christoph, 1762, Die Philosophie der Alten wiederkommend in der güldenen Zeit : worinnen von den unsichtbaren Anfängen des spiritus rectoris oder bildenden Geists in den Pflanzen ... gehandelt wird
src.q: That is exactly what the ancients say of the vis plastica … From the outside, there is nothing but heat, but this only awakens; it does not form.
src.qo: Was aber die Lebens- Kräfften seyen, ob es die formæ substantiales der Alten seyen, ob es der spiritus rector oder der Archaeus in allen Dingen seye

src.l: Oetinger, Friedrich Christoph, 1762, Die Philosophie der Alten wiederkommend in der güldenen Zeit : worinnen von den unsichtbaren Anfängen des spiritus rectoris oder bildenden Geists in den Pflanzen ... gehandelt wird
src.q: Was aber die Lebens- Kräfften seyen, ob es die formæ substantiales der Alten seyen, ob es der spiritus rector oder der Archaeus in allen Dingen seye

s: Schelling (Weltseele, 1st ed. 1798) rejects both a special Lebenskraft acting as a magical power and the derivation of organisation from 'dead' chemical forces, and demands both be united.

src.l: Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling, 1798, Von der Weltseele; eine Hypothese der höhern Physik (1st ed.)
src.q: which, acting as a magical power, cancels out all effects of the laws of nature within a living being … If, on the other hand, others explain the origin of all organization through "dead" chemical forces, they thereby destroy all of nature’s freedom in the acts of forming and organizing.
src.qo: Wenn dagegen andre den Ursprung aller Organisation aus todten chemischen Kräften erklären

src.l: Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling, 1798, Von der Weltseele; eine Hypothese der höhern Physik (1st ed.)
src.q: Wenn dagegen andre den Ursprung aller Organisation aus todten chemischen Kräften erklären

s: Schelling (1806 ed.) holds that the Bildungstrieb can never be an explanatory ground in natural science, only a reminder to seek the first cause of organisation outside organised matter and its 'dead, formative forces'.

src.l: Schelling, Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph von, 1806, Von der Weltseele
src.q: Thus, the formative drive can never serve as an explanatory ground in natural science, but only as a reminder to natural researchers to seek a first cause of organization not within organized matter itself (perhaps in its dead, formative forces), but outside of it.
src.qo: etwa in ihren todten, bilden- den Kräften

src.l: Schelling, Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph von, 1806, Von der Weltseele
src.q: etwa in ihren todten, bilden- den Kräften

s: Eckartshausen (1798), under the heading Lebenskraft, defines life as the effect of a force: the action of a vital stimulus on vital excitability, lasting while the two act together.

src.l: Karl von Eckartshausen, 1798, Ideen ueber das affirmative Princip des Lebens
src.q: Life is the effect of a force, the result of the action of a stimulus on an excitability — the action of the vital stimulus on vital excitability.
src.qo: Leben ist die Wirkung einer Kraft, die Folge der Einwirkung eines Reizes auf eine Erregbarkeit

src.l: Karl von Eckartshausen, 1798, Ideen ueber das affirmative Princip des Lebens
src.q: Leben ist die Wirkung einer Kraft, die Folge der Einwirkung eines Reizes auf eine Erregbarkeit

s: Mesmer's system as edited by Wolfart (1814) explains muscular irritability by a 'Lebensflut' or 'Lebensfeuer' brought by the nerve and distributed through the fibre.

src.l: Franz Anton Mesmer, Karl Christian Wolfart (ed.), 1814, Mesmerismus, oder System der Wechselwirkungen
src.q: It depends on an organization by means of which the life-fluid or the life-fire, brought along by the nerve and conducted through its infinitely divided branches distributed into all parts of the fiber, makes the vesicle swell
src.qo: mittelst welcher die Lebensflut oder das Lebensfeuer, durch den Nerven herbeigeführt

src.l: Franz Anton Mesmer, Karl Christian Wolfart (ed.), 1814, Mesmerismus, oder System der Wechselwirkungen
src.q: mittelst welcher die Lebensflut oder das Lebensfeuer, durch den Nerven herbeigeführt

s: Fechner (Nanna, 1848) traces the denial of plant souls to a spirit that rose out of nature and left it behind 'entseelt', soulless, overshooting an earlier view of nature as divinely ensouled.

src.l: Gustav Theodor Fechner, 1848, Nanna, oder über das Seelenleben der Pflanzen
src.q: Where all of nature is still regarded as divinely ensouled, it is much easier to recognize individual souls as particular manifestations of the general ensoulment than where, as with us, the divinely ensouled spirit has risen out of nature, soared above it, and left it behind soulless.
src.qo: der göttlich beseelte Geist aus der Natur heraus, über sie emporgestiegen ist, und sie entseelt zurückgelassen hat

src.l: Gustav Theodor Fechner, 1848, Nanna, oder über das Seelenleben der Pflanzen
src.q: der göttlich beseelte Geist aus der Natur heraus, über sie emporgestiegen ist, und sie entseelt zurückgelassen hat

s: Fechner (1848) rejects the fetus analogy against plant sensation: the fetus forms under a foreign Lebenskraft, while the plant grows by its own force and prepares its own living matter.

src.l: Gustav Theodor Fechner, 1848, Nanna, oder über das Seelenleben der Pflanzen
src.q: Der Fötus bildet sich unter dem Einflusse fremder Lebenskraft, schöpft seine Stoffe aus fremdem Lebensborne … die Pflanze wächst aus eigner Kraft, be- reitet sich selbst ihren lebendigen Stoff

s: Fechner (1848) lists naturalists who granted plants sensation (Percival, Smith, Bonnet, Hedwig, Ludwig) and Martius, who granted them a soul and its immortality.

src.l: Gustav Theodor Fechner, 1848, Nanna, oder über das Seelenleben der Pflanzen
src.q: Bonnet, Brolif, F. Hedwig, and Ludwig likewise lean toward attributing sensation to plants. … Martius attributes to plants not only a soul, but also an immortality of the same.
src.qo: Martius legt den Pflanzen nicht nur Seele, sondern auch eine Unsterblichkeit derselben bei.

src.l: Gustav Theodor Fechner, 1848, Nanna, oder über das Seelenleben der Pflanzen
src.q: Martius legt den Pflanzen nicht nur Seele, sondern auch eine Unsterblichkeit derselben bei.

s: Fechner (Zend-Avesta, 1851) treats the Earth as 'the being above us' and asks whether she should not have an eye turned to the heavens, better than creatures' short-sighted eyes.

src.l: Gustav Theodor Fechner, 1851, Zend-Avesta, oder über die Dinge des Himmels und des Jenseits
src.q: Should the Earth, the being above us, not also have an eye naturally directed upward toward the heavens, with which she can freely look around the sky?
src.qo: Sollte die Erde, das Wesen über uns, nicht auch ein von Natur aufwärts gegen den Himmel gerichtetes Auge haben

src.l: Gustav Theodor Fechner, 1851, Zend-Avesta, oder über die Dinge des Himmels und des Jenseits
src.q: Sollte die Erde, das Wesen über uns, nicht auch ein von Natur aufwärts gegen den Himmel gerichtetes Auge haben

s: Fechner's Little Book of Life After Death (1836; English c1904) opens: man lives three times, in continuous sleep, in alternation of sleep and waking, and in eternal waking.

src.l: Gustav Theodor Fechner, 1904, The Little Book of Life After Death (English, c1904)
src.q: MAN lives upon the earth not once, but three times. His first stage of life is a continuous sleep ; the second is an alternation between sleeping and waking ; the third is an eternal waking.

s: The introduction to the c1904 English Little Book reads Fechner's God as the totalised consciousness of the universe, of which the Earth's consciousness, and ours within it, are elements.

src.l: Gustav Theodor Fechner, 1904, The Little Book of Life After Death (English, c1904)
src.q: God, for Fechner, is the totalized … consciousness of the whole universe, of which the Earth's consciousness forms an element

s: Reichenbach (Der sensitive Mensch, 1854) argues that Od is not magnetism, since crystals, hands and plants show stronger odic force than many magnets.

src.l: Karl von Reichenbach, 1854, The Sensitive Man and His Relation to the Odic Force
src.q: if magnetism were identical with od, then the strength of the magnetic forces of a body at any given time would have to stand in a definite ratio to its odic force … Crystals, hands, and plants show odic forces of high and higher strength than many magnets
src.qo: Krystalle, Hände, Pflanzen zeigen odische Kräfte von hoher und höherer Stärke, als die vieler Magnete

src.l: Karl von Reichenbach, 1854, The Sensitive Man and His Relation to the Odic Force
src.q: Krystalle, Hände, Pflanzen zeigen odische Kräfte von hoher und höherer Stärke, als die vieler Magnete

s: Bichat (Recherches physiologiques sur la vie et la mort, 1800) defines life as the sum of the functions that resist death.

src.l: Xavier Bichat, 1800, Recherches physiologiques sur la vie et la mort
src.q: la vie est l’ensemble des fonctions qui résistent à la mort.

s: Bergson (L'Évolution créatrice, 1907) says the élan vital, traversing matter, would obtain everything at once if its power were unlimited, but it is finite and given once for all.

src.l: Henri Bergson, 1908, Creative Evolution
src.q: But the impetus is finite, and it was given once and for all. It cannot overcome all obstacles.
src.qo: Voilà ce que l'élan vital, traversant la matière, voudrait obtenir tout d'un coup. … Mais l'élan est fini, et il a été donné une fois pour toutes.

src.l: Henri Bergson, 1908, Creative Evolution
src.q: Voilà ce que l'élan vital, traversant la matière, voudrait obtenir tout d'un coup.

src.l: Henri Bergson, 1908, Creative Evolution
src.q: Mais l'élan est fini, et il a été donné une fois pour toutes.

s: Bergson (1907) splits contemporary neo-vitalism into the claim that pure mechanism is insufficient, authoritative when made by scientists such as Driesch or Reinke, and the hypotheses it superimposes on mechanism.

src.l: Henri Bergson, 1908, Creative Evolution
src.q: l'affirmation que le mécanisme pur est insuffisant, affirmation qui prend une grande autorité quand elle émane d'un savant tel que Driesch ou Reinke

s: Vaihinger (Philosophie des Als Ob, 1911) cites the vis dormitiva and the nisus formativus as the best-known 'auxiliary words' without factual value, yet too handy to discard.

src.l: Hans Vaihinger, 1924, Die Philosophie des Als Ob
src.q: Die bekanntesten Beispiele sind ja die vis dormitiva und der nisus formativus.

src.l: Hans Vaihinger, 1924, Die Philosophie des Als Ob
src.q: these auxiliary words are also merely logical repetitions without factual value
src.qo: Die bekanntesten Beispiele sind ja die vis dormitiva und der nisus formativus.

src.l: Hans Vaihinger, 1924, Die Philosophie des Als Ob
src.q: But to reject such expressions would be to fail to recognize their practical usefulness and handiness
src.qo: Die bekanntesten Beispiele sind ja die vis dormitiva und der nisus formativus.

s: Dahlke (Buddhism & Science, 1913) recalls a medicine in which working with 'vital energy' counted as unscientific and says the teleological view has since returned to medical thought.

src.l: Paul Dahlke, 1913, Buddhism & Science
src.q: At every opportunity, seasonable and unseasonable, it was declared that “to-day” we had no longer any need of a “vital energy,” that the mechanical view explained all that very much better

s: Huxley (Lay Sermons, 1870) says the spirit of Descartes's physiological passages is exactly that of the most advanced physiology of his day, and that the circulation is simply a matter of mechanism.

src.l: Thomas Henry Huxley, 1870, Lay Sermons, Addresses, and Reviews
src.q: The spirit of these passages is exactly that of the most advanced physiology of the present day … Beyond all question, the circulation of the blood is simply a matter of mechanism

s: La Mettrie (L'Homme machine, 1748; 1912 ed.) dismisses those who mock philosophers that regarded animals as machines and makes 'authentic reparation' to Descartes.

src.l: Julien Offray de La Mettrie, 1912, L'Homme machine (Man a Machine)
src.q: Let us leave the so-called Mr. Charp to mock those philosophers who looked upon animals as machines. How differently I think!
src.qo: Laissons donc le prétendu Mr. Charp se moquer des philosophes qui ont regardé les animaux, comme des machines. Que je pense différemment!

src.l: Julien Offray de La Mettrie, 1912, L'Homme machine (Man a Machine)
src.q: Laissons donc le prétendu Mr. Charp se moquer des philosophes qui ont regardé les animaux, comme des machines. Que je pense différemment!

s: Catharine Cook Smith (In Defense of Magic, 1930) writes that energy conservation and above all evolution brought the mechanical conception of the world into favour, explaining species by mechanical agencies.

src.l: Catharine Cook Smith, 1930, In defense of magic; the meaning and use of symbol and rite
src.q: It was believed that all phenomena could be explained mechanically by the laws of motion. The origin and transformation of living species were supposedly due to mechanical agencies

s: Against a two-sided 'mechanism versus vitalism' story: on Source Library's pages the protagonists refuse both horns. Schelling rejects a magical Lebenskraft and dead chemical forces alike, Kant's Blumenbach leaves mechanism a share, Schelling's Haller stands between mechanism and Stahl, and Bergson accepts vitalism's negative claim only.

src.l: Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling, 1798, Von der Weltseele; eine Hypothese der höhern Physik (1st ed.)
src.q: If, on the other hand, others explain the origin of all organization through "dead" chemical forces, they thereby destroy all of nature’s freedom in the acts of forming and organizing.

src.l: Immanuel Kant, 1922, Kritik der Urteilskraft (German)
Henri Bergson, 1908, Creative Evolution

s: 'Dead matter' is not, on the pages we hold, the mechanists' own word: Descartes says machine and 'Nature acting by the disposition of organs'; 'stupid' (More 1662), 'dead and senseless' (Cudworth 1678), 'dead Materiality' (Law 1740), 'rohe Materie' (Kant 1790) and 'todte Kräfte' (Schelling 1798) come from their critics or successors.

src.l: Rene Descartes, 1637, Discourse on the Method
src.q: it is Nature that acts in them according to the disposition of their organs

s: Pseudo-Albert's De secretis mulierum says life resides in the radical moisture: heat consumes it, and once it is consumed no medicine helps.

src.l: Albertus Magnus, 1662, De Secretis Mulierum et Virtutibus Herbarum, Lapidum et Animalium
src.q: Heat causes the radical moisture to evaporate; therefore, there must be a restoration of heat lest it consume the radical moisture entirely. If it did, death would follow, because once the radical moisture in which life resides is consumed, no medicines are of any use.
src.qo: consumpto humido radicali in quo consistit vita, nullae prosunt medicinae

src.l: Albertus Magnus, 1662, De Secretis Mulierum et Virtutibus Herbarum, Lapidum et Animalium
src.q: consumpto humido radicali in quo consistit vita, nullae prosunt medicinae

s: Roger Bacon explains ageing from hardship as a chain: illness and anxiety dry the natural moisture, which is the fuel of natural heat, so the heat cools and digestion fails.

src.l: Bacon, Roger, 1928, Hitherto Unpublished Works, Fascicle 8
src.q: For long-lasting illnesses and bad accidents dissolve and dry out the natural moisture, which is the fuel of natural heat; once the moisture is dried and dissolved, the natural heat is weakened and cooled; when it is weakened and cooled, the digestive power fails

s: Roger Bacon, following Isaac's book on fevers, places the moisture that feeds natural heat in the cavity of the heart and in its veins and arteries.

src.l: Bacon, Roger, 1928, Hitherto Unpublished Works, Fascicle 8
src.q: Sed queritur que sit ista humiditas et in quo loco est, a qua calor naturalis nutritur, et quod est eius fomentum. Hec humiditas est in concauitate cordis et in venis eius et in arteriis

s: Zwinger's Physiologia medica (1610) keeps the Galenic three spirits: the liver sends natural spirit through the veins, the heart vital spirit through the arteries, the brain animal spirit through the nerves.

src.l: Zwinger, Theodor, 1610, Physiologia Medica
src.q: Hepar spiritum Naturale per Venas, Cor spiritum Vitalem per Arterias, Cerebrum spiritum Animale per Neruos

s: The German verse Crede mihi (1625, after Norton's Ordinal) says the soul stays in the body while the three spirits (vital in the heart, natural in the liver, animal in the brain) keep it healthy, and departs when they no longer remain.

src.l: Thomas Norton, 1625, Crede mihi (German verse Ordinal)
src.q: So too does the soul remain, > Without strife or any resistance, In the body, at every hour, > And life is entirely healthy; But when these spirits now > No longer remain within the man, Then the soul departs from there as well, > According to the natural custom.

s: Varchi (lecture 'Sopra i calori') reports that many called natural heat 'life', because life lasts as long as natural heat, and heat lasts as long as the radical moisture that feeds it, like a flame on oil.

src.l: Benedetto Varchi, 1590, Lezzioni lette nell'Accademia Fiorentina (Sopra i calori)
src.q: It was also called "life" by many, perhaps because the life of each lasts as long as—and no longer than—its natural heat lasts, and the natural heat lasts as long as the radical moisture lasts, from which it feeds and nourishes itself continuously, not otherwise than the flame of oil
src.qo: Fu ancora chiamato da molti vita, forſe, perche tanto dura la vita di ciaſcuno, e non piu, quanto dura il ſuo caldo naturale, e tanto dura il caldo naturale quanto dura l'humido radicale, di che egli ſi paſce, e nutre continuamente, non altramente che la fiamma dell'olio, ò il fuoco delle legne

src.l: Benedetto Varchi, 1590, Lezzioni lette nell'Accademia Fiorentina (Sopra i calori)
src.q: Fu ancora chiamato da molti vita, forſe, perche tanto dura la vita di ciaſcuno, e non piu, quanto dura il ſuo caldo naturale, e tanto dura il caldo naturale quanto dura l'humido radicale, di che egli ſi paſce, e nutre continuamente, non altramente che la fiamma dell'olio, ò il fuoco delle legne

s: Cremonini (De calido innato, 1634) says the animate is preserved by nutrition, and the concoction of food is chiefly a boiling (elixatio) done by heat and moisture.

src.l: Cesare Cremonini, 1634, De calido innato et semine
src.q: for the preservation of the animate being must be brought about through nutrition. Nutrition occurs through the digestion of food. And the digestion of food, which contributes to nutrition, is primarily a boiling [elixatio], which boiling occurs through heat and moisture.
src.qo: debet enim fieri conſervatio animati per nutritionem. Nutritio fit per concoctionem alimenti. Et concoctio alimenti, quæ facit ad nutritionem, eſt præcipue elixatio, quæ elixatio fit per calidum, & humidum

src.l: Cesare Cremonini, 1634, De calido innato et semine
src.q: debet enim fieri conſervatio animati per nutritionem. Nutritio fit per concoctionem alimenti. Et concoctio alimenti, quæ facit ad nutritionem, eſt præcipue elixatio, quæ elixatio fit per calidum, & humidum

s: A Theatrum chemicum chapter 'De radicali humiditate' argues that the three humours (primigenial or radical, nutritive, elemental) are found not only in animate things but in metals too.

src.l: various, 1602, Theatrum chemicum
src.q: tres humores, primigenium videlicet seu radicalem, nutritium, & elementarem non solum in animatis, sed etiam in metallis reperiri

s: The Clangor buccinae (De alchimia opuscula, 1550) says the 'miracle' of making plants flower, thought contrary to the course of nature, is nothing other than pure natural heat infused into its own radical moisture; SL's note glosses calor naturalis as 'the body's own heat, which with the radical moisture was held to sustain growth and life'.

src.l: Anonymous, 1550, De alchimia opuscula complura (Clangor buccinae)
src.q: it is nothing other than pure natural heat calor naturalis infused into its own radical moisture
src.qo: non est aliud quam purus calor naturalis infusus in suo humido radicali

src.l: Anonymous, 1550, De alchimia opuscula complura (Clangor buccinae)
src.q: non est aliud quam purus calor naturalis infusus in suo humido radicali

s: Paracelsus (Volumen Paramirum, ch. VII) says every creature's food comes mixed with poison and the body has within it one who separates the poison from what it takes in: the Alchemist.

src.l: Paracelsus, 1904, Volumen Paramirum und Opus Paramirum (ed. 1904)
src.q: God has given every creature its own being and that which belongs to it. This is not for the sake of its own self-governance or the like, but for the sake of use—that which is necessary for it and which it must have—which is accompanied by poison.
src.qo: daß Gott einem jedlichen geschöpff hatt geben sein wesen, und was ihm zugehördt: Nit von wegen seins Selbstregiren oder dergleichen, sondern von wegen des gebrauchens, das ihm nottürfftig ist und haben muß, welchs mit gifft ist: dasselbig hatt im leib den, der diß gifft besondert, von dem, das der leib an sich nimmt

src.l: Paracelsus, 1904, Volumen Paramirum und Opus Paramirum (ed. 1904)
src.q: daß Gott einem jedlichen geschöpff hatt geben sein wesen, und was ihm zugehördt: Nit von wegen seins Selbstregiren oder dergleichen, sondern von wegen des gebrauchens, das ihm nottürfftig ist und haben muß, welchs mit gifft ist: dasselbig hatt im leib den, der diß gifft besondert, von dem, das der leib an sich nimmt

s: In the Buch Meteororum the Archeus in the stomach is a smith and a kitchen that makes male flesh in a man and female flesh in a woman from the same food; SL's term gloss calls it a 'vital force'.

src.l: Paracelsus, 1566, Das Buoch Meteororum
src.q: Ein ſchmidt vnd bereiten iſt im Magen/ der macht Menſchen fleiſch/ darauß/ nun hat er aber zwo arth an jm/ vnd iſt ein küchen

src.l: Paracelsus, 1566, Das Buoch Meteororum
src.q: but the Archeus Archeus; the "inner alchemist" or vital force that Paracelsus believed resided in the organs to separate the useful from the waste and direct growth is the one who prepares it for the person within their own Monarchy.
src.qo: Ein ſchmidt vnd bereiten iſt im Magen/ der macht Menſchen fleiſch/ darauß/ nun hat er aber zwo arth an jm/ vnd iſt ein küchen

s: Alexander von Suchten (1570) says man has a gift (donum) from God that Paracelsus calls the Archeus, whose office is to make human flesh from bread and blood from wine.

src.l: Alexander von Suchten, 1570, De secretis antimonii liber unus
src.q: Paracelsus heißt das Archeum. dises Archei ampt ist / das er auß brot menschen fleisch / auß wein blut mache

src.l: Alexander von Suchten, 1570, De secretis antimonii liber unus
src.q: man has a donum (gift), which is from God; Paracelsus calls this the Archeum. It is the office of this Archeus to make human flesh from bread, blood from wine
src.qo: Paracelsus heißt das Archeum. dises Archei ampt ist / das er auß brot menschen fleisch / auß wein blut mache

s: Under 'Vita longa' in De arcanis, Paracelsus says an annual herb can be renewed through its own prima materia before its decay, so that it stays green and fresh.

src.l: Paracelsus, 1589, Erster [- zehender] Theil der Bücher und Schrifften des edlen, hochgelehrten und bewehrten philosophi und medici Philippi Theophrasti Bombast von Hohenheim ...
src.q: So mag durch die Primam Materiam desselbigen Krautts / das Krautt vor seinem rechten Abdozren erneuert werden / das es Grün vnd Frisch bleibt

s: Maier (Atalanta fugiens, Discourse XXXII) says philosophers call their stone 'vegetable' because it vegetates, grows, increases and multiplies like a plant, and that the ignorant who deny stones grow measure the universe by their own grasp.

src.l: Michael Maier, 1617, Atalanta fugiens
src.q: Philosophi vocant lapidem suum vegetabilem, quia instar plantæ vegetet, crescat, augmentetur & multiplicetur

src.l: Michael Maier, 1617, Atalanta fugiens
src.q: Philosophers call their stone "vegetable," because it vegetates, grows, increases, and multiplies like a plant.
src.qo: Philosophi vocant lapidem suum vegetabilem, quia instar plantæ vegetet, crescat, augmentetur & multiplicetur

s: In De vita I.2 Ficino gives the physicians' definition of spiritus: a vapour of the blood, pure, subtle, warm and bright, made by the heart's heat from the finest blood, which flies to the brain where the mind uses it for the senses.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1529, De vita libri tres (Three Books on Life), Basel 1529
src.q: uapor quidã ſanguinis, purus, subtilis, calidus, & lucidus definitur

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1529, De vita libri tres (Three Books on Life), Basel 1529
src.q: which physicians define as a certain vapor of the blood, pure, subtle, warm, and bright. And from the heat of the heart itself, created from the most subtle blood, it flies to the brain, and there the mind uses it assiduously to exercise both internal and external senses.
src.qo: uapor quidã ſanguinis, purus, subtilis, calidus, & lucidus definitur

s: In De vita II.11 Ficino asks why old men, deprived of every other aid, should not suck the blood of a willing, healthy, cheerful, temperate youth, one or two ounces from a barely opened vein of the left arm, followed by as much sugar and wine.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1529, De vita libri tres (Three Books on Life), Basel 1529
src.q: Cur non & nostri senes omni uidelicet auxilio destituti, sanguinem adolescentis sugant? uolētis inquam adolescentis, sani, læti, temperati, cui sanguis quidem fit optimus, sed fortè nimius. Sugant igitur more hirudinum ex brachij sinistri uena uix aperta, unciam unam aut duas

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1529, De vita libri tres (Three Books on Life), Basel 1529
src.q: Why should our elderly, who are clearly deprived of every other aid, not suck the blood of a youth? A youth, I say, who is willing, healthy, joyful, and temperate, whose blood is excellent but perhaps excessive.
src.qo: Cur non & nostri senes omni uidelicet auxilio destituti, sanguinem adolescentis sugant? uolētis inquam adolescentis, sani, læti, temperati, cui sanguis quidem fit optimus, sed fortè nimius. Sugant igitur more hirudinum ex brachij sinistri uena uix aperta, unciam unam aut duas

s: Ficino (De vita II) says the moisture of the whole 'tree' of the body is preserved by preserving it in the roots, and prescribes a cake of the heart, liver, stomach, testicles and brain of chickens and capons, gilded with gold.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1561, Opera (Complete Works), Basel 1561

s: Ficino (De vita III) argues: nothing in the world is more tempered than heaven, nothing below more than the human body, nothing in the body more than spiritus; so tempered things refresh the life that remains in the spirit and conform it to the heavens.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1529, De vita libri tres (Three Books on Life), Basel 1529

src.q: Nothing in the world is more tempered than the heavens; nothing beneath the heavens is almost more tempered than the human body; nothing in this body is more tempered than the spiritus vital spirit. Therefore, through tempered things, life remaining in the spirit is refreshed.

s: Ficino (De vita II) says odour and spirit are both a kind of vapour, and since like feeds on like, the spirit and the spiritual man take the most nourishment from odours, which the old and thin especially need.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1529, De vita libri tres (Three Books on Life), Basel 1529

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1529, De vita libri tres (Three Books on Life), Basel 1529
src.q: Since, therefore, both odor and spirit are a certain kind of vapor, and like is nourished by like, it is not surprising that both the spirit and the spiritual person receive the greatest amount of nourishment from odors.
src.qo: Cum igitur uterq; videlicet odor et spiritus sit vapor quidam, et simile simili nutriatur, mi, rum et spiritus et spiritalis homo plurimum ab odoribus accipit alimentum

s: Ficino (De vita III.11) says the spiritual body is fed by four subtle elements: wine as earth, the scent of wine as water, song and sound as air, and light as fire.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1529, De vita libri tres (Three Books on Life), Basel 1529
src.q: For this, wine acts as earth; the very scent of wine performs the role of water; song and sound move the air; and light represents the fiery element.

s: Opening De vita III.11, Ficino tells scholars that the Moon gave them little matter but much Phoebean spirit, so that each of them is almost entirely spirit, a spiritual man masked in a small earthly body, whose spirit (on the same page) must be recalled to its subtlety in old age.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1529, De vita libri tres (Three Books on Life), Basel 1529

s: Ficino (De vita III) says the world-spirit is animated like any animal, and more effectively, which he says both Platonic arguments and Arab astrologers prove, and that by applying our spirit to the world-spirit through physical art and affection, celestial goods pass into our soul and body.

s: In the Latin Cornaro printed with Ramazzini's works, Cornaro says the ordered life is so useful, virtuous and holy that all should embrace it, being easy and most consonant with human nature; no follower need eat as little as he does, and he eats little because a tiny amount suffices.

src.l: Isidore of Seville, 1483, Etymologiae; De Summo Bono (1483 incunabulum)

s: Isidore (Etymologiae XI) distinguishes flesh from body by life: flesh is what lives, a body may be dead or never alive, and herbs and wood are bodies with life but not flesh; of the four elements in flesh, fire is in the vital heat (calor vitalis).

src.q: Flesh is composed of four elements: earth is in the flesh, air in the breath, moisture in the blood, and fire in the vital heat.

s: The twelfth-century De anima et spiritu (printed 1472 under Augustine's name) says the soul is named from animating, that is giving life to, the body, and that soul and spirit are one essence in man: 'spirit' names its nature, 'soul' its vivification.

src.l: Pseudo-Augustine, 1472, De anima et spiritu. Add: De ebrietate. De vanitate saeculi. De vita christiana
src.q: the soul is named from the fact that it animates the body, that is, it gives it life. … Soul and spirit are the same in man, although one calls it soul and the other spirit. For spirit refers to nature, and soul refers to the vivification.

s: Albertus Magnus (De vegetabilibus I.1.4, c. 1256) reports the view that a plant lives 'not by a soul, but by the vigour of growing and flowering from heat and natural moisture' (per vigorem virendi et florendi ex calore et humore naturali), so that 'life' said of plants would be equivocal.

src.l: Albertus Magnus, 1867, Alberti Magni De Vegetabilibus Libri VII
src.q: For they say that a plant lives not by a soul, but by the vigor of growing and flowering from heat and natural moisture.
src.qo: quod vivit⁴ planta non per animam, sed per vigorem virendi et florendi ex calore et humore naturali.

src.l: Albertus Magnus, 1867, Alberti Magni De Vegetabilibus Libri VII
src.q: quod vivit⁴ planta non per animam, sed per vigorem virendi et florendi ex calore et humore naturali.

s: Albertus (De vegetabilibus I) answers that the formal principle of plants uses a body diversified into organs (roots like a mouth, trunk, branches) and is therefore a soul, 'not a natural form only'; he rejects Democritus and Anaxagoras's intellectual soul in plants as absurd.

src.l: Albertus Magnus, 1867, Alberti Magni De Vegetabilibus Libri VII
src.q: Furthermore, every formal principle using a body diversified into organs is a soul. The formal principle of plants uses such a body; because of which there are roots in it—similar to a mouth—and trunks and branches and other organs having different functions: therefore, that principle is a soul, and not a natural form only.

s: In De mineralibus (c. 1250, printed 1542) Albertus argues stones are not ensouled because 'the primary function of a soul is life' and no trace of it is found in a stone: a stone does not take nourishment, having no pores, channels, roots or mouth.

src.l: Albertus Magnus, Ramon Lull, 1542, De secretis naturae sive quinta essentia. De mineralibus & rebus metallicis
src.q: Furthermore, the primary function of a soul is life, yet not even a trace of this is found in a stone.
src.qo: Adhuc autem primum opus animæ est vita, hoc autem secundum nullam sui differentiam inuenitur in lapide.

src.l: Albertus Magnus, Ramon Lull, 1542, De secretis naturae sive quinta essentia. De mineralibus & rebus metallicis
src.q: Adhuc autem primum opus animæ est vita, hoc autem secundum nullam sui differentiam inuenitur in lapide.

s: Albertus (De animalibus, c. 1258) says the formative virtue forms the heart first, 'which is the seat of life and soul' (cor quod est vitae et animae sedes), and the other members from it.

s: Albertus (De animalibus) argues the heart is the first member to live and the last to die, because 'the vital spirit remains longer in the heart' (spiritus vitalis diutius remanet in corde): nature closes the circle of life in the member where it began.

src.l: Albertus Magnus, 1916, De Animalibus Libri XXVI, Vol. 1 (Books I-XII)
src.q: For the vital spirit remains longer in the heart; for which reason it happens that all other members die before the heart, as if nature places in the act of life the final circle of life and concludes the beginning of life in the same member, which is the heart.
src.qo: Spiritus enim vitalis diutius remanet in corde: propter quod omnibus aliis membris prius accidit mori quam cordi, ac si natura in vitae actu ponat circulum ultimum vitae et principium vitae concludens in eodem membro quod est cor.

s: Avicenna (al-Shifāʾ, De anima, c. 1027) says the bodily psychic powers have as their 'first mount' (maṭiyya) a subtle body that penetrates the passages, and 'that body is the spirit (al-rūḥ)': a blocked passage stops motion, sense and imagination because the powers travel carried in a body.

src.l: Ibn Sina (Avicenna), 1027, al-Shifa (The Cure): Philosophy and Medicine
src.q: the bodily psychic powers have as their primary vehicle a subtle body, penetrating through the passages, spiritual [pneumatic] in nature, and that this body is the spirit (al-ruh).

s: Al-Ghazālī's Kīmiyā-yi saʿādat (c. 1105; Homes's English, 1873) says one cannot know death until one knows life, nor life until one knows the spirit; man has an animal spirit, whose fountain is the heart in the left breast, 'a delicate exhalation from the humors', and a human spirit of the nature of angels.

src.l: Al-Ghazali, Henry A. Homes (trans.), 1873, The Alchemy of Happiness
src.q: we cannot know what death is, until we know what life is: nor can we understand what life is, until we know what the spirit is.

src.l: Al-Ghazali, Henry A. Homes (trans.), 1873, The Alchemy of Happiness
src.q: The fountain of the animal spirit is in that heart which is in the left side of the breast, and is a piece of flesh. It is a delicate exhalation from the humors within the animal.

s: Roger Bacon (De retardatione accidentium senectutis, c. 1236–1260s) gives the cause hardest to remedy: natural heat lives in the natural moisture and is fed by it, but consumes it 'as the flame of a lamp consumes oil', and so is the cause of extinguishing itself.

src.l: Roger Bacon, 1928, De retardatione accidentium senectutis
src.q: For natural heat exists in natural moisture and is nourished by it; and when that moisture is dissolved, the heat is diminished and weakened. But natural heat gradually, successively, and accidentally dissolves and consumes it, and thus it is the cause of extinguishing itself
src.qo: Nam calor naturalis in humiditate existit naturali, et ab ea nutritur; et cum humiditas illa dissoluitur, calor minuitur et debilitatur. Sed calor naturalis illam paulatim et successiue accidentaliter dissoluit et consumit, et sic est causa extinguendi seipsum

src.l: Roger Bacon, 1928, De retardatione accidentium senectutis
src.q: Nam calor naturalis in humiditate existit naturali, et ab ea nutritur; et cum humiditas illa dissoluitur, calor minuitur et debilitatur. Sed calor naturalis illam paulatim et successiue accidentaliter dissoluit et consumit, et sic est causa extinguendi seipsum

s: Bacon (De retardatione) names two ways natural heat weakens: the wasting of natural moisture and the increase of foreign moisture from weak digestion; 'the innate heat exists within the natural moisture' and is extinguished by the foreign.

src.l: Roger Bacon, 1928, De retardatione accidentium senectutis
src.q: The innate heat exists within the natural moisture. It is extinguished by an increase of foreign moisture, which arises from a weakness in digestion.

s: Bacon (De retardatione) collects reports of men who lived 300, 500 and 900 years by medicines, Artephius's claim of 1,025 years, and a man with papal letters who looked thirty, and concludes 'we firmly hold that this great prolongation of life is possible and can be done by certain means'.

src.l: Roger Bacon, 1928, De retardatione accidentium senectutis
src.q: I have seen several trustworthy men who saw a man who had taken a magnificent medicine and lived for nine hundred and many other years. This man had papal letters to testify to this fact. I asked how old he appeared to be. I was told he looked like a man of thirty years.
src.qo: firmiter tenemus quod hec magna prolongatio vite possibilis est et potest fieri certis modis.

s: Bacon (De retardatione) adds a secret 'the ancient sages concealed': bread from wheat stored longer makes a purer moisture, further from corruption, and so with wine; men age faster in one land than another, so choose a place where foods keep.

src.l: Roger Bacon, 1928, De retardatione accidentium senectutis
src.q: euchemic bread made from wheat which is preserved longer generates a purer moisture and one Sl. f. 29v. further removed from corruption
src.qo: Eligendus est ergo locus in quo nutrientia diutius conseruantur

src.l: Roger Bacon, 1928, De retardatione accidentium senectutis
src.q: Eligendus est ergo locus in quo nutrientia diutius conseruantur

s: The Regimen senum et seniorum printed under Arnald of Villanova (Venice 1502, with Magninus's Regimen sanitatis) says the accidents of old age can be removed during the age of stability and their acceleration retarded afterwards, since 'calor innatus in humiditate existit naturali'.

src.l: Magninus Mediolanensis, 1192, Regimen sanitatis. Add: Arnoldus de Villa Nova: Phlebotomia. Hippocrates: Astronomia de infirmitatibus. Johannes de Zantvliet: De dietis. Nicolaus Salernitanus: Quid pro quo. Averroes: De venenis; De tyriaca. Hippocrates: Secreta. Arnoldus de Villa Nova: De vinis; Regimen senum et seniorum
src.q: From this weakness arise the accidents of old age which, if they occur during the time of stability, can be removed, and after that period, their acceleration can be delayed.
src.qo: accidentia proueniunt senectutis que in tempore consistendi si accidant possunt auferri et post illud eorum acceleratio potest retardari … calor innatus in humiditate existit naturali

src.l: Magninus Mediolanensis, 1192, Regimen sanitatis. Add: Arnoldus de Villa Nova: Phlebotomia. Hippocrates: Astronomia de infirmitatibus. Johannes de Zantvliet: De dietis. src.q: accidentia proueniunt senectutis que in tempore consistendi si accidant possunt auferri et post illud eorum acceleratio potest retardari … calor innatus in humiditate existit naturali

s: The same Regimen senum says the wise handed down two doctrines against the causes of old age: 'the science of regimen' and 'the science of the properties of certain things which the ancients concealed' — Bacon's phrase in De retardatione (quam antiqui sapientes occultaverunt).

src.l: Magninus Mediolanensis, 1192, Regimen sanitatis. Add: Arnoldus de Villa Nova: Phlebotomia. Hippocrates: Astronomia de infirmitatibus. Johannes de Zantvliet: De dietis. Nicolaus Salernitanus: Quid pro quo. Averroes: De venenis; De tyriaca. Hippocrates: Secreta. Arnoldus de Villa Nova: De vinis; Regimen senum et seniorum
src.q: the wise have handed down two doctrines regarding those things that obviate these causes. One is the science of regimen. The other is the science of the properties of certain things which the ancients concealed.
src.qo: Alia scientia est proprietatum quarumdam rerum quas antiqui occultauerunt

src.l: Magninus Mediolanensis, 1192, Regimen sanitatis. Add: Arnoldus de Villa Nova: Phlebotomia. Hippocrates: Astronomia de infirmitatibus. Johannes de Zantvliet: De dietis. s: As quoted in the Regimen senum (1502), Avicenna's definition of hygiene: 'the art of guarding health' secures a person from two things, from putrefaction and by defending the moisture 'lest it be dissolved quickly' (defensione humiditatis ne cito dissolvatur).

src.l: Magninus Mediolanensis, 1192, Regimen sanitatis. Add: Arnoldus de Villa Nova: Phlebotomia. Hippocrates: Astronomia de infirmitatibus. Johannes de Zantvliet: De dietis. Nicolaus Salernitanus: Quid pro quo. Averroes: De venenis; De tyriaca. Hippocrates: Secreta. Arnoldus de Villa Nova: De vinis; Regimen senum et seniorum
src.q: the art of guarding health provides security to a person from two things
src.qo: ars custodiendi sanitatem a duabus rebus securitatem prebet homini scilicet a phibitione penitus putrefactionis et defensione humiditatis ne cito dissoluat

src.l: Magninus Mediolanensis, 1192, Regimen sanitatis. Add: Arnoldus de Villa Nova: Phlebotomia. Hippocrates: Astronomia de infirmitatibus. Johannes de Zantvliet: De dietis. s: The Secretum secretorum (Latin, printed 1528) says all agree that whoever guards against superfluity and indigence by keeping equality and temperance receives health and 'length of days' (longitudinem dierum); whoever desires to live should acquire what is fitted to durability and preserves life.

src.l: Pseudo-Aristotle, 1528, Secreta Secretorum Aristotelis
src.q: All agree, therefore, that he who guards himself against superfluity and indigence by preserving equality and temperance will receive healthy salvation and length of days.
src.qo: qui igitur appetit vivere aut durare studeat acquirere quae durabilitati conveniunt & vitam conservent

src.l: Pseudo-Aristotle, 1528, Secreta Secretorum Aristotelis
src.q: qui igitur appetit vivere aut durare studeat acquirere quae durabilitati conveniunt & vitam conservent

s: Johannitius's Isagoge (Ḥunayn ibn Isḥāq, 9th c.; Latin MS, 14th c.) divides the virtue (virtus) three ways, 'natural, vital, and animal', the scheme the Latin physicians attached to the three spirits.

src.l: Hunain ibn Ishaq (Johannitius), 1350, Ioannitii Introductio ad artem parvam Galeni (Latin MS)
src.q: The virtue is therefore divided in three ways: for it is natural, vital, and animal.

s: A Latin medical miscellany (Wellcome MS.531, part of uncertain date, 14th–17th c.) derives the natural spirit in the liver 'from the vapor of perfected blood' and the spiritual spirit in the heart, and says that while moisture remains the soul cannot be separated from the body, 'for life stands by moisture and death by dryness' (vita stat per humiditatem et mors per siccitatem).

src.l: Unknown, 14th–17th century, Composite manuscript of medical works in Italian and Latin (Medical Miscellany), Wellcome MS.531
src.q: The natural spirit is born in the liver from the vapor of perfected blood
src.qo: nā vita stat p humiditatem et mors per siccitāte

src.l: Unknown, 14th–17th century, Composite manuscript of medical works in Italian and Latin (Medical Miscellany), Wellcome MS.531
src.q: it is impossible for the soul to be separated from the body; for life stands by moisture and death by dryness.
src.qo: nā vita stat p humiditatem et mors per siccitāte

src.l: Unknown, 14th–17th century, Composite manuscript of medical works in Italian and Latin (Medical Miscellany), Wellcome MS.531
src.q: nā vita stat p humiditatem et mors per siccitāte

s: Robert Grosseteste (De luce, c. 1225) holds that 'the first corporeal form, which some call corporeity' is light, which diffuses itself in every direction so that a sphere of light is generated at once from a point; light is 'not a form that follows corporeity, but it is corporeity itself'.

src.l: Robert Grosseteste, Ludwig Baur (ed.), 1912, Die Philosophischen Werke des Robert Grosseteste, Bischofs von Lincoln
src.q: I consider the first corporeal form, which some call corporeity, to be light.
src.qo: Formam primam corporalem, quam quidam corporeitatem vocant, lucem esse arbitror.

src.l: Robert Grosseteste, Ludwig Baur (ed.), 1912, Die Philosophischen Werke des Robert Grosseteste, Bischofs von Lincoln
src.q: Formam primam corporalem, quam quidam corporeitatem vocant, lucem esse arbitror.

src.l: Robert Grosseteste, Ludwig Baur (ed.), 1912, Die Philosophischen Werke des Robert Grosseteste, Bischofs von Lincoln
src.q: Therefore, light is not a form that follows corporeity, but it is corporeity itself.

s: Hildegard of Bingen (Physica IV.1, c. 1150–60) says that at sunrise 'the greenness of the earth and the grasses' (viriditas terre et graminum) is strongest, and herbs suck in this greenness 'as strongly as a lamb drinks milk', so the day's heat can ripen it for fruit.

src.l: Hildegard of Bingen, 1533, Physica - Hildegard von Bingen
src.q: At that time, the greenness of the earth and the grasses is at its strongest, because the air is still cold and the sun is already warm. The herbs drink in this greenness as strongly as a lamb drinks milk
src.qo: Et tunc viriditas terre et graminum maxime vigent, quia aer tunc adhuc frigidus est et sol iam calidus, et tunc herbe viriditatem tam fortiter sugunt, ut agnus qui lac sugit

src.l: Hildegard of Bingen, 1533, Physica - Hildegard von Bingen
src.q: Et tunc viriditas terre et graminum maxime vigent, quia aer tunc adhuc frigidus est et sol iam calidus, et tunc herbe viriditatem tam fortiter sugunt, ut agnus qui lac sugit

s: In the modern German introduction to Hildegard's Physica, SL's English adds a translator's note glossing viriditas as 'the "greening power" or life-force inherent in all living things'; the German says only 'Grünkraft (viriditas)', and Hildegard's own usage on scan 245 is the greenness of earth and grasses.

src.l: Hildegard of Bingen, 1533, Physica - Hildegard von Bingen
src.q: the endowment of plants and trees through their greening power
src.qo: Ausstattung der Pflanzen und Bäume durch deren Grünkraft (viriditas)

src.l: Hildegard of Bingen, 1533, Physica - Hildegard von Bingen
src.q: Ausstattung der Pflanzen und Bäume durch deren Grünkraft (viriditas)

s: In SL's c. 1280 manuscript of the Latin Canon (book 59e68f94…, scan 73), on the vital virtue reaching the members, SL's English says the soul 'is not destroyed by reason of the life-force'; the Latin abbreviation on the scan reads 'rōne uīt̄as' (ratione vitae / vitalitatis?), not a 'force'.

src.l: Avicenna (Ibn Sina), Gerard of Cremona (trans.), 1280, Canon Medicinae (c. 1280 MS)
src.q: Once the vital virtue arrives, it prevents the animal powers in the members from being destroyed. Thus, a soul still exists even if it is not in a state of use; it is not destroyed by reason of the life-force
src.qo: rōne uīt̄as

src.l: Avicenna (Ibn Sina), Gerard of Cremona (trans.), 1280, Canon Medicinae (c. 1280 MS)
src.q: rōne uīt̄as

s: Pietro d'Abano (Conciliator, c. 1303, printed 1472) says the formative power builds the heart first and turns the purest blood into 'the spermatic nature called radical moisture', in which the innate heat, compounded of fiery and celestial heat, subsists, encompassing it 'like a form encompassing matter'.

src.l: Pietro d'Abano, 1472, Conciliator differentiarum philosophorum et praecipue medicorum
src.q: In this moisture, the innate heat calidum innatum —composed of both fiery and "celestial" heat—subsists. It encompasses that moisture everywhere, like a form encompassing matter.

s: A treatise in Constantine the African's Opera (11th c., Basel 1536) says 'the spirit which is in the ventricles of the heart is the cause of life, breath, and pulse', the vital spirit born from the heart, while the spirit proceeding from the brain to the members is called animal and is nourished by the heart's spirit.

src.l: Constantinus Africanus, 1536, Constantini Africani Opera, Vol. I
src.q: it is clear that the spirit which is in the ventricles of the heart is the cause of life, breath, and pulse; this is of the vital spirit, whose birth is from the heart.

src.l: Constantinus Africanus, 1536, Constantini Africani Opera, Vol. I
src.q: The spirit, however, which proceeds from the brain and passes to the other members of the body is called animal

s: Against reading medieval light metaphysics as a theory of life: Grosseteste's De luce makes light the first form of BODY (corporeity, three-dimensional extension), not of living things; life in the same century is defined by self-motion (Aquinas) or by heat in moisture (physicians), so 'life as light' is a modern conflation.

src.l: Robert Grosseteste, Ludwig Baur (ed.), 1912, Die Philosophischen Werke des Robert Grosseteste, Bischofs von Lincoln
src.q: Corporeity, indeed, is that which is necessarily followed by the extension of matter according to three dimensions

src.l: Thomas Aquinas, 1484, Summa theologiae: Pars prima
src.q: From which it is clear that those are properly living things which move themselves according to some species of motion

s: Against saying 'for medieval physicians life WAS a heat-and-moisture balance': in the same texts heat and moisture are the soul's instrument or subject, and the heart's gift alongside life (Avicenna lists life, innate heat and spirit as three); and Albertus reports the bare heat-and-moisture account of plant life as an opinion to be rejected in favour of a soul.

src.l: Ibn Sina (Avicenna), 1027, al-Shifa (The Cure): Philosophy and Medicine
src.q: each one of them receives life, innate heat, and the spirit from the heart.

src.l: Albertus Magnus, 1867, Alberti Magni De Vegetabilibus Libri VII
src.q: therefore, that principle is a soul, and not a natural form only.

s: Helen Wilmans (A Search for Freedom, 1898) uses 'aliveness' as a noun for a felt condition of her own childhood, which she says showed not in bodily activity but in love of living things and a pang at killing anything: the earliest use of the English noun for a felt quality that a search of SL pages turns up.

src.l: Helen Wilmans, 1898, A Search for Freedom
src.loc: ch. V, "Brother Findlay comes to town"; scan 94
src.q: The aptest word I can apply to myself as a child is "aliveness." I was — in my own way — tremendously alive. That this aliveness was not expressed in great bodily activity is no reason for doubting that the condition existed.

s: Thomas Troward (Edinburgh Lectures on Mental Science, 1904) coins 'livingness' as a quality that in one sense admits no degrees and in another is entirely a question of degree, a plant's livingness being very different from an animal's.

src.l: Thomas Troward, 1909, The Edinburgh Lectures on Mental Science
src.q: There is, of course, one sense in which the quality of livingness does not admit of degrees; but there is another sense in which it is entirely a question of degree.

s: Troward (The Creative Process in the Individual, 1910) makes 'feeling of aliveness' the first state of Spirit before creation: since in the beginning there is nothing but Spirit, its primary feeling of aliveness must be that of being alive all over.

src.l: Thomas Troward, 1910, The Creative Process in the Individual
src.q: since in the beginning there is nothing except Spirit, its primary feeling of aliveness must be that of being alive all over

s: Yogi Ramacharaka (W. W. Atkinson, The Science of Psychic Healing, 1906) prescribes rubbing and swinging the hands until they have 'that undefinable feeling of "aliveness" and being full of Energy' before a pranic treatment: aliveness as a sensation produced on purpose.

src.l: Yogi Ramacharaka (William Walker Atkinson), 1893, The Science of Psychic Healing
src.q: Rub the hands to-gether briskly for a few minutes, and then swing them to-and-fro a little while, until they have that undefinable feeling of "aliveness" and be-ing full of Energy.

s: William Walker Atkinson (Thought Vibration, 1906), in a chapter titled 'Asserting the Life-Force', treats lack of life as a felt deadness of ambition, energy and interest that the reader can end by will: 'Wake up and display a few signs of life!'

src.l: William Walker Atkinson, 1908, Thought Vibration, or The Law of Attraction in the Thought World
src.loc: ch. IX, "Asserting the Life-Force", p. 62; scan 97
src.q: Now I wish to put LIFE into you. Many of you have been going along as if you were dead—no ambition—no energy—no vitality—no interest—no life. This will never do. You are stagnating. Wake up and display a few signs of life!

s: Charles Brodie Patterson (Living Waters, 1912) defines being 'truly alive' as consciousness of oneness with the Divine Life: the life one lives is not one's own but the life of the Infinite manifesting through one.

src.l: Charles Brodie Patterson, 1912, Living Waters; or, Rivers to the Ocean
src.q: The man who is truly alive is the man who is conscious of his oneness with the Divine Life.

s: Warren Felt Evans (The Divine Law of Cure, 1881) defines life as a spiritual force, 'not, as formerly supposed, a fluid', yet different from the ordinary forces of nature: the mind-cure definition of life, which also makes all force a manifestation of a primal Life.

src.l: Warren Felt Evans, 1884, The Divine Law of Cure
src.loc: ch. VIII, "Origin and conservation of life-force", p. 58; scan 60
src.q: It is now a well-established principle in philosophy that all life is a force, and it is equally certain to the intuitive reason that all force in the universe is a manifestation of some primal Life

s: Evans (The Mental Cure, 1869) reverses the materialist order: why should life result from organization rather than organization from the vital force? Theories that derive life from organization or fibre contractility take effects for causes.

src.l: Warren Felt Evans, 1869, The Mental Cure: Illustrating the Influence of the Mind on the Body
src.q: But why is life supposed to result from organization, rather than organization from the vital force, whatever it may be? Others have referred it to the contractility of the fibres. In these theories there is the error of taking effects for causes.
