s: William James (Varieties of Religious Experience, 1902, Conclusions) endorses as the purely subjective vindication of religion the view that 'not God, but life, more life' is the end of religion and the love of life the religious impulse.

src.l: William James, 1902, The Varieties of Religious Experience
src.q: Not God, but life, more life, a larger, richer, more satisfying life, is, in the last analysis, the end of religion. The love of life, at any and every level of development, is the religious impulse.

s: James (Varieties, 1902, 'The Religion of Healthy-Mindedness') reports that the mind-cure movement relies on the conquering efficacy of courage, hope and trust and a contempt for doubt, fear and worry, and that its disciples' practical experience 'forms to-day a mass imposing in amount'.

src.l: William James, 1902, The Varieties of Religious Experience
src.q: of healthy-minded attitudes as such, in the conquering efficacy of courage, hope, and trust, and a correlative contempt for doubt, fear, worry, and all nervously pre- cautionary states of mind.

s: Jung (Psychologische Typen, 1921) defines libido as nothing other than the energy of the life-process (Energie des Lebensablaufes), whose laws are the laws of life-energy: a quantitative formula for life phenomena that, like physical energy, passes through every transformation.

src.l: C. G. Jung, 1921, Psychologische Typen
src.loc: ch. V (the type problem in poetry); scan 293
src.q: which is intended to mean nothing other than the energy of the life-process. Its laws are the laws of life-energy. Libido as a concept of energy is a quantitative formula for life phenomena
src.qo: So auch der Libidobegriff, der nichts anderes bedeuten will, als die Energie des Lebensablaufes. Seine Gesetze sind die Gesetze der Lebensenergie.

src.l: C. G. Jung, 1921, Psychologische Typen
src.q: So auch der Libidobegriff, der nichts anderes bedeuten will, als die Energie des Lebensablaufes. Seine Gesetze sind die Gesetze der Lebensenergie.

s: Jung (Versuch einer Darstellung der psychoanalytischen Theorie, 1913) widens libido to 'the energy of life activity in general' (Energie der Lebenstätigkeit überhaupt), first at work in the child's nutritive zone, in sucking, before it opens new paths of need and satisfaction.

src.l: C. G. Jung, 1913, Versuch einer Darstellung der psychoanalytischen Theorie
src.loc: Lecture on infantile sexuality, p. 38; scan 48
src.q: We find the libido as the energy of life activity in general working in the child initially in the zone of the nutritional function.
src.qo: Die Libido als Energie der Lebenstätigkeit überhaupt finden wir beim Kinde zunächst in der Zone der Ernährungsfunktion an der Arbeit.

src.l: C. G. Jung, 1913, Versuch einer Darstellung der psychoanalytischen Theorie
src.q: Die Libido als Energie der Lebenstätigkeit überhaupt finden wir beim Kinde zunächst in der Zone der Ernährungsfunktion an der Arbeit.

s: Jung (Wandlungen und Symbole der Libido, part II, 1912) describes a compulsion that leads a quantity of libido (Libidobetrag) away from sexual activity and creates symbolic, approximately valid substitutes for what is lost: libido as a quantity that can be moved.

src.l: C. G. Jung, Sigmund Freud (eds.), 1912, Jahrbuch für psychoanalytische und psychopathologische Forschungen, Bd. IV (Jung, Wandlungen und Symbole der Libido, part II)
src.loc: Wandlungen und Symbole der Libido, p. 199; scan 204
src.q: leads a certain amount of libido away from the actual sexual activity and creates symbolic and approximately valid substitutes for what has been lost.
src.qo: einen gewissen Libidobetrag von der eigentlichen Sexualbetätigung weg und schafft für das Verlorene symbolischen und annähernd gültigen Ersatz

src.l: C. G. Jung, Sigmund Freud (eds.), 1912, Jahrbuch für psychoanalytische und psychopathologische Forschungen, Bd. IV (Jung, Wandlungen und Symbole der Libido, part II)
src.q: einen gewissen Libidobetrag von der eigentlichen Sexualbetätigung weg und schafft für das Verlorene symbolischen und annähernd gültigen Ersatz

s: Rudolf Steiner (Theosophie, 1904; English 1910) names the species-forming force that moulds changing materials into a lasting form 'life-force', adding that 'in theosophical literature it is called Prana': life as a form-giving force, and prāṇa recast as the Lebenskraft of German biology.

src.l: Rudolf Steiner, 1910, Theosophy: An Introduction to the Supersensible Knowledge of the World and the Destination of Man
src.loc: ch. I, "The essential nature of man"; scan 45
src.q: This species-forming force will here be called LIFE-FORCE (in theosophical literature it is called “Prana”’). Just as the mineral forces express themselves in crystals, so the life-force expresses itself in the species or form of plant and animal life.

s: Steiner (Theosophy, note to p. 23) records that to speak of 'life-force' (Lebenskraft) was lately the mark of an unscientific mind, that some science now inclines back to it, and that it is not the same as the forces of nature (Naturkräfte).

src.l: Rudolf Steiner, 1910, Theosophy: An Introduction to the Supersensible Knowledge of the World and the Destination of Man
src.q: To speak of "life-force" (Lebenskraft) was regarded a short time back as the mark of an unscientific mind. But one begins to find here and there in science to-day a tendency which is not averse from the idea of a "life-force" such as was accepted in former times.

s: Besant and Leadbeater (Occult Chemistry, 1908) say the physical atom is formed by the flow of the life-force and vanishes with its ebb; were the flow checked for an instant, the physical world would vanish.

src.l: Annie Besant, C. W. Leadbeater, 1908, Occult Chemistry: Clairvoyant Observations on the Chemical Elements
src.q: formed by the flow of the life-force * and vanishes with its ebb. When this force arises in 'space' †—the apparent void which must be filled with subtance of some kind, of inconceivable tenuity—atoms appear ; if this be artificially stopped for a single atom, the atom disappears

s: Leadbeater (The Chakras, 1927, 'The absorption of vitality') describes the 'vitality globule', inconceivably minute but so brilliant that anyone looking at the sky over the sea can see these points of light darting in all directions: vitality as a visible particle absorbed by the body.

src.l: C. W. Leadbeater, 1927, The Chakras: A Monograph
src.loc: ch. III, "The absorption of vitality: the globule"; scan 80
src.q: THE vitality globule, though inconceivably minute, is so brilliant that it can be seen even by those who are not in the ordinary sense clairvoyant.

s: Bergson (L'Évolution créatrice, 1907) answers why vision recurs on independent lines of evolution: it is carried out by the original élan of life, and 'life is, above all, a tendency to act upon brute matter', in a direction not predetermined.

src.l: Henri Bergson, 1908, Creative Evolution
src.q: we would answer that life is, above all, a tendency to act upon brute matter. The direction of this action is undoubtedly not predetermined
src.qo: nous répondrions que la vie est, avant tout, une tendance à agir sur la matière brute.

src.l: Henri Bergson, 1908, Creative Evolution
src.q: nous répondrions que la vie est, avant tout, une tendance à agir sur la matière brute.

s: Blavatsky (Secret Doctrine I, 1888), quoting an 'Occult Embryology', gives Jiva (life) a five-fold function: joined to the lowest principle in the mineral atom, to Prana in the plant, to further principles in the animal, and complete only in man.

src.l: Helena Petrovna Blavatsky, 1888, The Secret Doctrine Vol. I
src.q: in the vegetable particle, with their second the Prana (life), in the animal, with all these plus the third and the fourth, in man, the germ must receive the fruition of all the five

s: Scheler (Der Formalismus in der Ethik, 1913–16) objects to Spencer that an intellect sprung from life for one species can never make life itself intelligible, as the part cannot explain the whole; life must be transcendent to it, and Spencer's picture shows only how a tool would make organisms like a machine.

src.l: Max Scheler, 1916, Der Formalismus in der Ethik und die materiale Wertethik
src.loc: Part II, section on vital values and Spencer; scan 305
src.q: an understanding that has sprung from life for a specific species, namely the human species, can never make life itself understandable—no more than the part can explain the whole—and that life must necessarily be transcendent to it
src.qo: daß ein Verstand, der für eine bestimmte Art, eben für die Menschenart, aus dem Leben entsprungen ist, niemals das Leben selbst verständlich machen kann

src.l: Max Scheler, 1916, Der Formalismus in der Ethik und die materiale Wertethik
src.q: daß ein Verstand, der für eine bestimmte Art, eben für die Menschenart, aus dem Leben entsprungen ist, niemals das Leben selbst verständlich machen kann

s: Scheler (Über Ressentiment, 1912) turns the Darwinian picture over: the Umwelt to which we adapt our tools is only the corner of the universe our vital organization has chosen for itself, not a whole to which all living beings have 'adapted'.

src.l: Max Scheler, 1912, Ressentiment
src.loc: ch. on the ressentiment in the modern world view; scan 100
src.q: The "environment" to which we adapt our tools is factually only the corner that our vital organization has chosen for itself in the whole of the universe
src.qo: Die »Umwelt«, an die wir unsere Werkzeuge anpassen, ist faktisch nur die Ecke, die sich unsere vitale Organisation im Ganzen des Alls erwählt hat

src.l: Max Scheler, 1912, Ressentiment
src.q: Die »Umwelt«, an die wir unsere Werkzeuge anpassen, ist faktisch nur die Ecke, die sich unsere vitale Organisation im Ganzen des Alls erwählt hat

s: Hereward Carrington (Yoga Philosophy, 1923) cites William James's essay 'The Energies of Men' as showing that we use only a small fraction of the energies within ourselves, and offers hypnotism as a way to bring the inner 'inexhaustible stores' to the surface.

src.l: Hereward Carrington, 1923, Yoga Philosophy: An Outline of the Secret Hindu Teachings
src.q: William James has an essay entitled "The Energies of Men," and he shows in this very illuminating essay that we use only a small fraction of the energies within ourselves.

s: Bergson (Essai sur les données immédiates de la conscience, 1889) separates the time of the exact sciences, which reduces to a number, from real duration (durée réelle), whose apparent quantity is truly a quality and cannot be shortened by an instant without changing what fills it.

src.l: Henri Bergson, 1908, Essai sur les données immédiates de la conscience
src.loc: ch. III, 'La durée réelle et la prévision', p. 131; scan 165
src.q: on identifie inconsciemment le temps dont il est question dans les sciences exactes, et qui se réduit à un nombre, avec la durée réelle, dont l'apparente quantité est véritablement une qualité

s: Jung (Psychologie der Dementia praecox, 1907) borrows Pierre Janet's 'abaissement de la tension psychologique' for the effect of sleep's 'désintérêt pour la situation présente' (Bergson, Claparède) on association: lowered mental tension, not lost force, explains the dream's associations.

src.l: C. G. Jung, 1907, Über die Psychologie der Dementia praecox: ein Versuch
src.q: Die Wirkung des „desinteret" auf die Assoziationstätigkeit ist das „abaissement de la tension psyehologiojie" (Jauet)

s: John Woodroffe (Shakti and Shakta, 1918; 3rd ed. 1927) reads Western science as converging on the Shākta view: life exists throughout, the division between 'dead' and 'living' matter has no existence in fact, and every particle vibrates with unending Energy.

src.l: John Woodroffe (Arthur Avalon), 1927, Shakti and Shakta, 3rd ed.
src.q: Life exists throughout, but manifests in various ways. The arbitrary division which has been drawn between "dead" and "living" matter has no existence in fact

s: William Q. Judge (The Ocean of Theosophy, 1893) distinguishes Jiva, 'life' in general derived from the Supreme Life and applied also to the living soul, from Prana, which is more particular, and denies that a body holds a definite amount of this 'Life Energy'.

src.l: William Q. Judge, 1893, The Ocean of Theosophy
src.loc: ch. on the seven principles, p. 38; scan 52
src.q: Jiva means "life", and also is applied to the living soul, for the life in general is derived from the Supreme Life itself. Jiva is therefore capable of general application, whereas Prana is more particular.

s: Critique: on Source Library pages the English noun 'aliveness' for a felt quality arrives through New Thought (Wilmans 1898, Ramacharaka 1906, Troward 1910), where it means a sensation one can raise by will or rubbing the hands and a quality that comes in degrees. A history organised by 'aliveness' risks reading every tradition through mind-cure's assumption that life is a felt, gradable, cultivable quality.

src.l: Helen Wilmans, 1898, A Search for Freedom
src.q: The aptest word I can apply to myself as a child is "aliveness."

src.l: Thomas Troward, 1909, The Edinburgh Lectures on Mental Science
src.q: it is entirely a question of degree

s: Critique: Jung calls libido a 'quantitative formula' for life phenomena of differing intensity, but names no unit, measurement or conservation law; 'life-energy' borrows physics' authority for what remains a metaphor of intensity, the same move the older Lebenskraft made.

src.l: C. G. Jung, 1921, Psychologische Typen
src.q: Die Libido als Energiebegriff ist eine quantitative Formel für die Lebenserscheinungen, die bekanntlich von verschiedener Intensität sind.

s: Gilbert (De magnete V.12, 1600) argues that because living bodies spring from earth and sun, and herbage sprouts unsown from soil exposed on a tower, sun and earth cannot give what they lack: they awaken souls and so are themselves ensouled.

src.l: William Gilbert, 1893, On the Loadstone and Magnetic Bodies (tr. P. F. Mottelay, 1893)
src.q: since living bodies spring from earth and sun and by them are animate ... it is not likely that they (sun and earth) can do that which is not in themselves; but they awaken souls, and consequently are themselves possessed of souls.

s: Gilbert (1600) calls it pitiable if soul is denied the stars and earth while granted to the worm, the ant, plants and morels, since nothing is excellent that has no soul; without globe-souls there would be no life, motion, coherence, sympathy or generation.

src.l: William Gilbert, 1893, On the Loadstone and Magnetic Bodies (tr. P. F. Mottelay, 1893)
src.q: Pitiable is the state of the stars, abject the lot of earth, if this high dignity of soul is denied them, while it is granted to the worm, the ant, the roach, to plants and morels

src.l: William Gilbert, 1893, On the Loadstone and Magnetic Bodies (tr. P. F. Mottelay, 1893)
src.q: else there were neither life, nor prime act, nor move- ment, nor unition, nor order, nor coherence, nor conactus, nor sympathia, nor any generation

s: Gilbert (1600) identifies the earth's magnetic force with 'the formate soul or animate form of the globes': without senses yet without error or disease, it exerts an unending, constant, directive action through the whole mass and propagates generation and decay on the surface; hence Thales rightly called the loadstone animate.

src.l: William Gilbert, 1893, On the Loadstone and Magnetic Bodies (tr. P. F. Mottelay, 1893)
src.q: the earth's magnetic force and the formate soul or animate form of the globes, that are without senses, but without error and without the injuries of ills and diseases, exert an unending action, quick, definite, constant, directive, motive, imperant, harmonious, through the whole mass of matter

s: Patrizi (Pampsychia V, Nova de universis philosophia, 1591) rejects the rational/irrational division of souls: every soul comes from intellect, or is a part of the world soul, which is 'reason through and through', so no soul, not even a brute's or a plant's, is irrational by nature.

src.l: Francesco Patrizi, 1593, Nova de universis philosophia (Venice 1593)
src.q: this distinction of rational and irrational soul is in no way approved by us. For we believe that no soul is by its nature irrational.
src.qo: Nobis uero distinctio hæc animi rationa- lis, & irrationalis minime probatur. Nullum enim animũ sui natura irrationalem esse exi- stimamus.

src.l: Francesco Patrizi, 1593, Nova de universis philosophia (Venice 1593)
src.q: Nobis uero distinctio hæc animi rationa- lis, & irrationalis minime probatur. Nullum enim animũ sui natura irrationalem esse exi- stimamus.

s: Campanella (De sensu rerum II.12, written c. 1604, printed 1620) holds that light and heat are the most sensitive of all beings and that the whole world feels, more in some places and less in others, as an animal feels differently in its parts.

src.l: Tommaso Campanella, 1620, De sensu rerum et magia (Frankfurt 1620)
src.q: It is fitting to consider light and heat as the most sensitive of all beings that are in the world, above all others. It is fitting also to believe that the whole world feels, in some places more, in others less
src.qo: Mundum quoque sentire totum, alibi magis, alibi minus, sicuti animal in variis partibus vario sentire modo declaratum est.

src.l: Tommaso Campanella, 1620, De sensu rerum et magia (Frankfurt 1620)
src.q: Mundum quoque sentire totum, alibi magis, alibi minus, sicuti animal in variis partibus vario sentire modo declaratum est.

s: Campanella's chapter list for De sensu rerum (1620) states his definition: all beings derive their motion from fire, the motive soul is a warm spirit, and concoction, nutrition, growth and decay show that the spirit is the soul; the soul is the body's mistress and guest, not its form (human mind excepted).

src.l: Tommaso Campanella, 1620, De sensu rerum et magia (Frankfurt 1620)
src.loc: Table of chapters, book II chs. 8, 10, 18 (scans 10-11)
src.q: That all beings derive their motion from fire, and that the motive soul is a warm spirit.

src.l: Tommaso Campanella, 1620, De sensu rerum et magia (Frankfurt 1620)
src.loc: Table of chapters, book II ch. 10 (scan 10)
src.q: through concoction, nutrition, growth, and decay, the spirit is shown to be the soul
src.qo: 10. Ex concoctione,nutritione, augmento & decremento spiritum esse animam :

s: Campanella (De sensu rerum II, 1620) argues that the act of Venus, which makes all senses languish while the spirit flows together to enjoy pleasure, proves that the sensing spirit is one and continuous through all the sense organs, as air is through sounding pipes.

src.l: Tommaso Campanella, 1620, De sensu rerum et magia (Frankfurt 1620)
src.q: the act of Venus, which makes all the senses languish, well proves that the sensing spirit is unique, which flows together to enjoy pleasure
src.qo: At Veneris actus, qui sensus omnes languere facit, bene probat, sentientem spiritum esse vnicum qui confluit ad fruendum voluptate

src.l: Tommaso Campanella, 1620, De sensu rerum et magia (Frankfurt 1620)
src.q: At Veneris actus, qui sensus omnes languere facit, bene probat, sentientem spiritum esse vnicum qui confluit ad fruendum voluptate

s: Fernel (De abditis rerum causis I, 1548) calls the innate spirit or heat 'the maker and the bond of life' (vitae opifex et vinculum) and argues it cannot come from the body's temperament: a freshly killed animal's parts keep their temperament but have lost that heat and spirit, so it must flow from a more divine nature.

src.l: Jean Fernel, 1548, De abditis rerum causis libri duo (Paris 1548)
src.q: this innate spirit or heat, which is both the maker and the bond of life, cannot be considered as something received from the temperament of the body's parts.

src.l: Jean Fernel, 1548, De abditis rerum causis libri duo (Paris 1548)
src.q: insitus is siue spiritus siue calor, qui vitæ est & opifex & vinculum, non poterit partium corporis temperamento acceptus refer- ri.

src.l: Jean Fernel, 1548, De abditis rerum causis libri duo (Paris 1548)
src.q: Instead, these things must have flowed from a more divine nature.

s: Ficino (De vita II, 1489) tells the old to seek the sun in winter like sheep and streams in summer like birds, to live among green, sweet-smelling plants which, being alive and breathing, breathe out to increase man's spirit, and to dwell among pines, olives and vines, since evergreen long-lived trees lend long life by shade, vapour, fruit and wood.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1489, De triplici vita (Florence 1489)
src.q: Let them frequently spend time among green and sweet-smelling plants. For these, being living and breathing, breathe forth their essence to increase the spirit  of man.
src.qo: Frequẽter iter uirẽtes uerſẽ- tur plantas: & ſuauiter redolentes. Hę nanq; ui- uentes, ſpiranteſq; ꝑſpirant ad ſpiritũ hoĩs augẽ- dum.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1489, De triplici vita (Florence 1489)
src.q: Frequẽter iter uirẽtes uerſẽ- tur plantas: & ſuauiter redolentes. Hę nanq; ui- uentes, ſpiranteſq; ꝑſpirant ad ſpiritũ hoĩs augẽ- dum.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1489, De triplici vita (Florence 1489)
src.q: it is probable that trees naturally endowed with long life—especially if they remain green even in winter—will benefit you toward a long life through their shade, their vapor, their fresh fruit, their wood, and any other timely use.
src.qo: Frequẽter iter uirẽtes uerſẽ- tur plantas: & ſuauiter redolentes. Hę nanq; ui- uentes, ſpiranteſq; ꝑſpirant ad ſpiritũ hoĩs augẽ- dum.

s: Bacon (Historia vitae et mortis, 1623) rejects the old view that life runs down by a fixed decline: in youth everything in an animal is repaired whole, so that the matter of repair might be almost eternal if the manner of repair did not fail; with age repair becomes unequal, some parts mending well and others badly.

src.l: Bacon, Francis, 1623, Historia vitae et mortis
src.q: everything in an Animal, during  Adolescence and Youth,  is repaired entirely; nay,  even for a time, they are increased in  Quantity, and improved in Quality;  so that the Matter of Repair   might be almost eternal,  if the Manner of Repair  did not  fail.
src.qo: vt Materia Repa- rationis, quasi æterna esse posset, si Modus Reparatio- nis non intercideret.

src.l: Bacon, Francis, 1623, Historia vitae et mortis
src.q: vt Materia Repa- rationis, quasi æterna esse posset, si Modus Reparatio- nis non intercideret.

s: Among his operations for long life Bacon (1623) condenses the spirits two ways: opium by putting them to flight, nitre by cold and 'freshness'; nitre's subordinates are things with an earthy scent, like good earth newly dug and turned.

src.l: Bacon, Francis, 1623, Historia vitae et mortis
src.loc: Operation on the spirits, printed p. 233 (scan 243)
src.q: Nitre, which condenses the spirits by Cold and a certain freshness  (as the Moderns call it); it also has its own subordinates. | | 54 | The subordinates to Nitre are all things that exhibit a somewhat Earthy Scent; such as is the scent of pure and good earth, recently dug up and turned over.
src.qo: Nitrum, quod condenſat     ſpiritus per Frigus, & quandam     (vt Moderni loquuntur) Freſcu-     ram

src.l: Bacon, Francis, 1623, Historia vitae et mortis
src.q: Nitrum, quod condenſat     ſpiritus per Frigus, & quandam     (vt Moderni loquuntur) Freſcu-     ram

s: In De la causa (1584, dialogue 3) Teofilo makes the universal intellect the 'first and principal faculty' of the world soul and the universal physical efficient cause: one and the same, it fills the whole, lights the universe and directs nature to produce its species, as our intellect produces rational ideas; the Platonists call it the world's smith.

src.l: Giordano Bruno, 1888, Le opere italiane (De la causa, principio et uno)
src.loc: De la causa, dial. 3, printed p. 231 (scan 236)
src.q: the universal physical efficient cause is the universal intellect. This is the first and principal faculty of the soul of the world, which is the universal form of that soul.

src.l: Giordano Bruno, 1888, Le opere italiane (De la causa, principio et uno)
src.q: Dico l'efficiente phisico uniuersale essere l' in- telletto uniuersale, che é la prima et principal facultá del anima del mondo, la quale é forma uniuersale di quello.

s: Bruno (De vinculis in genere, c. 1591) denies that the bond (vinculum) of love is shape, proportion of limbs or pure colour, since beauty and love fade while shape remains: the bond lies in a harmony and a 'co-disposition' between the one who binds and the one bound.

src.l: Giordano Bruno, 1891, Latin Works Vol. III (On Magic, On Bonds)
src.q: The bond, therefore, exists in a certain harmony, not only of the limbs with one another, but  also in a certain "co-disposition" , so to speak, between the captor and the captured.
src.qo: Vinculum ergo est in quadam convenientia non tantum membrorum ad invicem, sed et in quadam rapientis et rapti condispositione, ut ita dicam.

src.l: Giordano Bruno, 1891, Latin Works Vol. III (On Magic, On Bonds)
src.q: Vinculum ergo est in quadam convenientia non tantum membrorum ad invicem, sed et in quadam rapientis et rapti condispositione, ut ita dicam.

s: Agrippa (De occulta philosophia I.34, 1533) says that when many scattered things conforming to one star and Idea are rightly applied together, a singular gift is poured from the Idea into the matter so prepared 'by way of the world soul', provided the matter is under a harmony like the one that first infused its virtue.

src.l: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, 1533, De occulta philosophia libri tres (1533)
src.q: when you properly apply many things to a specific species or individual, things which are scattered but conform to the same lowest Idea and star, a singular gift is soon poured in from that Idea. This occurs through the mediation of the anima mundi world soul into the matter
src.qo: mox per materiam hanc ita opportune paratam singulare munus ab idea infunditur per rationem animæ mundi.

src.l: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, 1533, De occulta philosophia libri tres (1533)
src.q: mox per materiam hanc ita opportune paratam singulare munus ab idea infunditur per rationem animæ mundi.

s: Mercuriale (De arte gymnastica IV, 1569) reports Aristotle's rule that bodies should be exercised more in summer, because then the natural heat is sluggish and digests poorly, so the native heat must be excited by exercise and sweat drawn out lest residues putrefy; clear skies strengthen the spirits, 'friends to light'.

src.l: Girolamo Mercuriale, 1587, De arte gymnastica libri sex (Venice 1587)
src.q: the native heat must be more greatly excited by exercise so that it may digest more properly
src.qo: exercitatione calor natiuus magis excitandus, ut concoquat honestius, magisq. sudor motu proliciendus

src.l: Girolamo Mercuriale, 1587, De arte gymnastica libri sex (Venice 1587)
src.q: exercitatione calor natiuus magis excitandus, ut concoquat honestius, magisq. sudor motu proliciendus

src.l: Girolamo Mercuriale, 1587, De arte gymnastica libri sex (Venice 1587)
src.q: the spirits—being by their own nature friends to light—are strengthened, and the mind is refreshed.
src.qo: exercitatione calor natiuus magis excitandus, ut concoquat honestius, magisq. sudor motu proliciendus

s: Ficino (Platonic Theology IV, 1482) argues that just as people seeing iron move but not the magnet would think it moved itself, those ignorant of the spheres' souls think bodies move by themselves; since no craftsman moves limbs as rightly as bodies move in the world, they must be moved 'not by an inert quality alone but by an artful nature'.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1561, Opera (Complete Works), Basel 1561
src.q: it is necessary that those bodies are moved and guided not by a lifeless quality alone, but by an artistic nature.
src.qo: necessarium est illa corpuscula non ab inerti qualitate solummodo, uerùm etiam ab artificiosa natura moueri & duci.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1561, Opera (Complete Works), Basel 1561
src.q: necessarium est illa corpuscula non ab inerti qualitate solummodo, uerùm etiam ab artificiosa natura moueri & duci.

s: Mylius (Basilica medica, 1618) states that all things live by innate heat (omnia vivunt beneficio caloris insiti), seen in animals and in plants where the sun excites it, and that this heat is not elemental: the coldest plants, poppy and hemlock, still live, so their life is 'from a diviner principle'.

src.l: Johann Daniel Mylius, 1618, Opus medico-chymicum: Basilica medica (Frankfurt 1618)
src.q: all things live by the benefit of innate heat, which is proven because, when that is extinguished, life perishes at the same time.
src.qo: omnia viuere beneficio caloris insiti, quod probatur, quia illo extincto, perit simul vita. … Ergo à Diuiniore principio hæc vita est.

src.l: Johann Daniel Mylius, 1618, Opus medico-chymicum: Basilica medica (Frankfurt 1618)
src.q: omnia viuere beneficio caloris insiti, quod probatur, quia illo extincto, perit simul vita.

src.l: Johann Daniel Mylius, 1618, Opus medico-chymicum: Basilica medica (Frankfurt 1618)
src.q: Ergo à Diuiniore principio hæc vita est.

s: Bacon's account of Telesio (De principiis atque originibus, c. 1612) gives Telesio's two conjugations of co-essential natures: the Hot, Luminous, Rare and Mobile, seated in heaven and the Sun, against the Cold, Opaque, Dense and Immobile, seated in the earth; heat and cold are the sources, the rest emanations.

src.l: Francis Bacon, 1653, Scripta in naturali et universali philosophia (Amsterdam 1653), incl. De principiis atque originibus
src.loc: De principiis, on Parmenides and Telesius, printed p. 240 (scan 263)
src.q: heat and cold are the source, the others are emanations), but nevertheless they are perpetually accompanying and inseparable. These are: the Hot, the Luminous, the Rare, and the Mobile. And again, four opposed to these: the Cold, the Opaque, the Dense, and the Immobile.
src.qo: ſed tamen perpetuo concomitantes & inſeparabiles. Eas eſſe, Calidum, Lucidum, Rarum, Mobile. Et quatuor rurſus his oppoſitas, Frigidum, Opacum, Denſum, Immobile.

s: Agrippa (De occulta philosophia II.55, 1533) argues it would be absurd for flies and little worms to be worthy of life and have souls while the whole, perfect world neither lives nor has a soul; and who but the lifeless would deny that earth and water live, since they generate, vivify and nourish trees, plants and animals, plainly so in things born without seed?

src.l: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, 1550, De occulta philosophia libri III (1550)
src.q: It would be absurd if every imperfect little body, every tiny particle of the world, and even the lowliest animals—such as flies and little worms—were worthy of life and possessed souls, yet the world itself (a complete, perfect, total, and most noble body) neither lived nor possessed a soul.
src.qo: absurdum foret, quòd imperfecta quæq; corp la, & mundi particulæ, & uilissima quæq; anima muscæ & uermiculi, uita digna sint, uitam possidea nimam habeat, mundum ipsum integrum, perfectu totale, ac nobilissimum corpus, neq; uiuere, neq; an habere.

src.l: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, 1550, De occulta philosophia libri III (1550)
src.q: For who, unless they lack life themselves, would deny that the earth and water live? From themselves they generate, give life to, nourish, and increase innumerable trees, plants, and living creatures.
src.qo: Quis enim, nisi uita terram & aquam neget uiuere, quæ ex se innume arbores, plantas, animantesq; generant, uiuificant, nu unt, augent?

s: Fernel (Physiologia IV.12, De spiritu et innato calido, 1554) holds that every similar part of the body, while the animal lives, is furnished with innate heat and a prior spirit and can never subsist without them, and that the innate heat and spirit implanted in each part are governed by those flowing in from elsewhere.

src.l: Jean Fernel, 1566, Opera medicinalia (incl. Physiologia, 1566 printing)
src.q: every similar part  is equipped with innate heat and a prior spirit, and that it can never exist while it is alive without the aid of these.
src.qo: PARTEM unamquamque similarem innato calido & priori spiritu instructam esse quoad in uita sit animans, neque citra opem illorum posse unquā consistere

src.l: Jean Fernel, 1566, Opera medicinalia (incl. Physiologia, 1566 printing)
src.q: PARTEM unamquamque similarem innato calido & priori spiritu instructam esse quoad in uita sit animans, neque citra opem illorum posse unquā consistere

s: Cornaro (Discorsi della vita sobria, 1558; Latin in Ramazzini's Opera) reports that at 78, persuaded to raise his daily food from twelve to fourteen ounces and his drink from fourteen to sixteen, he turned melancholic and choleric within ten days, fell into a 35-day fever, and recovered only by returning to his exact rule of life.

src.l: Bernardino Ramazzini, 1739, Complete Medical and Physiological Works
src.q: the measure of all daily food—namely bread, egg yolk, meat, and a side dish—was exactly weighed at twelve ounces, I increased it by two ounces to fourteen; I increased the measure of drink, which was fourteen ounces, to sixteen
src.qo: me curavi sola regula illa vivendi, etsi jam essem annorum 78.

src.l: Bernardino Ramazzini, 1739, Complete Medical and Physiological Works
src.q: me curavi sola regula illa vivendi, etsi jam essem annorum 78.

s: Ficino (De vita II, 1489), citing Isaac and Galen, says well-tempered wine restores the natural humour and fosters heat; it should be mixed with water for the young, less for the old, and not at all for cold old men, since cold, hard old age is heated and softened by unmixed wine 'as iron by fire'.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1489, De triplici vita (Florence 1489)
src.q: it restores the natural humor, fosters internal heat, and balances both. Mixing such wine with water is more necessary for the young, less for the old, and for cold old men, not at all.
src.qo: Frigida nā qꝫ duraqꝫ ſenectus (ut inquit plato) ita mero fer uet atqꝫ mollitur: ſicut uel igne ferruz: uel aqua lupini.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1489, De triplici vita (Florence 1489)
src.q: Frigida nā qꝫ duraqꝫ ſenectus (ut inquit plato) ita mero fer uet atqꝫ mollitur: ſicut uel igne ferruz: uel aqua lupini.

s: Ficino (De vita II, 1489) explains why green refreshes: the ray of sight is kindled in the eyes' water, and in green things the sun's implanted light still keeps a spring-like moisture and a subtle water full of hidden light; so frequent use of green recreates the spirit of sight and, through it, the animal spirit.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1489, De triplici vita (Florence 1489)
src.q: In these green things, indeed, the indwelling light of the sun still retains a youthful  moisture and a subtle water full of a certain hidden light.
src.qo: In quibus ſane uiridibus ſo- lis lumen inſitum adhuc uernum ſecum habet humorem, aquamque ſubtilem occulto quodã lumine plenam.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1489, De triplici vita (Florence 1489)
src.q: In quibus ſane uiridibus ſo- lis lumen inſitum adhuc uernum ſecum habet humorem, aquamque ſubtilem occulto quodã lumine plenam.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1489, De triplici vita (Florence 1489)
src.q: the frequent use of green things—since it recreates the spirit of sight, which is the chief part of the animal spirit —also refreshes the animal spirit itself.
src.qo: In quibus ſane uiridibus ſo- lis lumen inſitum adhuc uernum ſecum habet humorem, aquamque ſubtilem occulto quodã lumine plenam.

s: Bacon's table of youth and age (Historia vitae et mortis, 1623) sets the young spirit 'plentiful and swelling, dense and green' (densus et viridis) against the old spirit 'scant and meagre, sharp and thin', beside dewy juices against raw and watery ones; ageing is a change in the spirit's quantity and texture.

src.l: Bacon, Francis, 1623, Historia vitae et mortis
src.loc: Differences of youth and age, printed p. 398 (scan 408)
src.q: In the young, the  spirit is plentiful and swelling; in the old, it is scant and meager. In the young, the spirit is dense and fresh; in the old, it is sharp and thin.
src.qo: Iu- ueni Spiritus Multus, & Turgescens ; Seni Paucus, & Ieiu- nus : Iuueni Spiritus Densus, & Viridis ; Seni Acris, & Rarus

src.l: Bacon, Francis, 1623, Historia vitae et mortis
src.q: Iu- ueni Spiritus Multus, & Turgescens ; Seni Paucus, & Ieiu- nus : Iuueni Spiritus Densus, & Viridis ; Seni Acris, & Rarus

s: Patrizi (Pampsychia V, 1591), defending reason in brute souls, says all animals speak except fish and some reptiles, each species with the instruments nature gave it, expressing the soul's inner passions by voice as we do; not understanding their language no more proves they lack speech than our ignorance of foreign tongues proves foreigners mute.

src.l: Francesco Patrizi, 1593, Nova de universis philosophia (Venice 1593)
src.q: For all animals speak, with the exception of fish and the reptiles we have already mentioned. They do not speak, perhaps, in the human tongue, nor with such articulated sounds, but each species speaks according to the instruments of speech granted to it by nature.
src.qo: Loquuntur enim præter piſces, & quæ diximus reptilia, animalia omnia. Non quidem humana lingua, nec tum forte dearticulata, loquuntur tamen ſua ſpecie quæque, prout ei ſermonis inſtrumenta ſunt tributa a natura cuique.

s: Campanella (De sensu rerum I.1, 1620) argues from 'whatever is in the effects is in the causes': plant and animal have spirit, heat, motion and subtlety from the sun and matter from the earth, and have nothing not in their causes; sense is not a mode of existence but an essential thing and an active power, so sun and earth must sense.

src.l: Tommaso Campanella, 1620, De sensu rerum et magia (Frankfurt 1620)
src.q: the plant and the animal have spirit, heat, motion, and subtlety from the Sun, and matter from the Earth, fashioned by the art of the solar sense. Yet they have nothing that is not in the causes
src.qo: At sensus non videtur esse modus quidam Existentiæ, veluti sunt aliæ figuræ, sed res essentialis, visque actiua, vt mox palam fiet. Idcirco solem sentire necesse est & terram.

src.l: Tommaso Campanella, 1620, De sensu rerum et magia (Frankfurt 1620)
src.q: At sensus non videtur esse modus quidam Existentiæ, veluti sunt aliæ figuræ, sed res essentialis, visque actiua, vt mox palam fiet. Idcirco solem sentire necesse est & terram.

s: Campanella's chapter list (De sensu rerum I.5-6, 1620) holds that without sense the world would be chaos with no generation or corruption, and that the operations in which things show sense come not from God, angels, the world soul or the active intellect but from the natural forms themselves, though not without God.

src.l: Tommaso Campanella, 1620, De sensu rerum et magia (Frankfurt 1620)
src.q: The operations of things, in which their sense is manifested, do not proceed from God, nor from Angels, nor from the World Soul, nor from the active intellect, as others believe; but from the natural forms themselves—yet they do not happen without God.

s: Against the seed that modern panpsychism descends from Renaissance world-soul doctrine: the 1590-1620 'everything is alive' positions rest on different grounds that sometimes exclude each other. Patrizi derives all souls from intellect and the world soul; Gilbert gives the globes their own formate souls; Campanella puts sense in each thing's natural form and explicitly denies that the world soul is its operator.

src.l: Tommaso Campanella, 1620, De sensu rerum et magia (Frankfurt 1620)
src.q: do not proceed from God, nor from Angels, nor from the World Soul, nor from the active intellect, as others believe; but from the natural forms themselves

src.l: Francesco Patrizi, 1593, Nova de universis philosophia (Venice 1593)
src.q: every soul comes from intellect.
src.qo: esse est iam demonstratum.

s: Goethe (Versuch die Metamorphose der Pflanzen, 1790, §119) sums up his method: the diverse-seeming organs of the sprouting and flowering plant are all explained from a single organ, the leaf, and even the seed-enclosing fruits are derived from the leaf-form.

src.l: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, 1790, Versuch die Metamorphose der Pflanzen zu erklären
src.q: Just as we have now sought to explain the diverse-appearing organs of the sprouting and flowering plant all from a single one—namely the leaf, which usually develops at every node—so too have we ventured to derive those fruits, which typically enclose their seeds firmly within themselves, from the form of the leaf
src.qo: So wie wir nun die verſchiedenſcheinenden Organe der ſproſſenden und blühenden Pflanze alle aus einem einzigen nehmlich dem Blatte, welches ſich gewöhnlich an jedem Knoten ent- / wickelt, zu erklären geſucht haben

src.l: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, 1790, Versuch die Metamorphose der Pflanzen zu erklären
src.q: So wie wir nun die verſchiedenſcheinenden Organe der ſproſſenden und blühenden Pflanze alle aus einem einzigen nehmlich dem Blatte, welches ſich gewöhnlich an jedem Knoten ent- / wickelt, zu erklären geſucht haben

s: Goethe (Metamorphose der Pflanzen, 1790, §73) describes the plant's growth from seed to fruit as an alternation of expansion and contraction: stem leaves expand, the calyx contracts, the petals expand again.

src.l: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, 1790, Versuch die Metamorphose der Pflanzen zu erklären
src.q: we thereby explain once more that principle of alternating expansion and contraction. From the seed to the highest development of the stem leaf, we first noticed an expansion; thereafter, we saw the calyx arise through a contraction, and the petals through a subsequent expansion.
src.qo: Vom Samen bis zu der höchsten Entwickelung des Stengelblattes, bemerkten wir zuerst eine Ausdehnung, darauf sahen wir durch eine Zusammenziehung den Kelch entstehen, die Blumenblätter

s: Goethe (Italienische Reise, Palermo, April 1787; Insel ed. 1913) recalls his 'old whim' of finding the Urpflanze among the plants of the public garden, reasoning that one must exist, or he could not know a form to be a plant at all unless all were formed after one pattern.

src.l: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, 1913, Goethes italienische Reise
src.q: could I not discover the Urpflanze primordial plant among this host? One must surely exist! How else would I recognize that this or that formation is a plant, if they were not all formed according to one pattern?
src.qo: Eine solche muß es denn doch geben! Woran würde ich sonst erkennen, daß dieses oder jenes Gebilde eine Pflanze sei, wenn sie nicht alle nach einem Muster gebildet wären?

src.l: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, 1913, Goethes italienische Reise
src.q: Eine solche muß es denn doch geben! Woran würde ich sonst erkennen, daß dieses oder jenes Gebilde eine Pflanze sei, wenn sie nicht alle nach einem Muster gebildet wären?

s: Ritter's first book (Weimar, 1798) states its thesis in its title: proof that a constant galvanism accompanies the life process (Lebensproceß) in the animal kingdom.

src.l: Johann Wilhelm Ritter, 1798, Beweis, daß ein beständiger Galvanismus den Lebensproceß in dem Thierreich begleite
src.q: Proof, that a constant Galvanism the life process in the animal kingdom accompanies.
src.qo: Beweis, daſs ein beständiger Galvanismus den Lebensproceſs in dem Thierreich begleite.

src.l: Johann Wilhelm Ritter, 1798, Beweis, daß ein beständiger Galvanismus den Lebensproceß in dem Thierreich begleite
src.q: Beweis, daſs ein beständiger Galvanismus den Lebensproceſs in dem Thierreich begleite.

s: Ritter (Fragmente aus dem Nachlasse eines jungen Physikers, 1810, nos. 322–324) proposes that the galvanic circuit animal part–moisture–animal part is probably respiration itself, and that animal life is a constant state of galvanism between the solid and fluid parts of the body.

src.l: Johann Wilhelm Ritter, 1810, Fragmente aus dem Nachlasse eines jungen Physikers, Vol. I
src.q: 323. The Galvanic process in the circuit [Kette]: animal part—moisture—animal part (the circuit of the first kind), is likely the respiration process itself. 324. Animal life is a constant state of Galvanism between the solid and fluid parts of the body.

s: Ritter (Fragmente, 1810, no. 78) sets all nature on one great scale, atmosphere, plant kingdom, animal kingdom, 'todte Natur', ranked by how many individuals each realm has and whether they are fluid and make one, or solid and many.

src.l: Johann Wilhelm Ritter, 1810, Fragmente aus dem Nachlasse eines jungen Physikers, Vol. I
src.q: Everything forms one great scale: at- mosphere — plant kingdom — animal kingdom — inanimate nature . The animal kingdom has fewer individuals, the plant kingdom more.
src.qo: 78. Alles bildet eine große Scale: At- mosphäre — Pflanzenreich — Thierreich — todte Natur.

src.l: Johann Wilhelm Ritter, 1810, Fragmente aus dem Nachlasse eines jungen Physikers, Vol. I
src.q: 78. Alles bildet eine große Scale: At- mosphäre — Pflanzenreich — Thierreich — todte Natur.

s: Schelling (Erster Entwurf, 1799) holds that life comes about 'as it were against the will of external nature' (invita natura externa), by tearing itself loose from it, so that most influences thought life-promoting, such as air, are really a consuming process that seeks to subject living matter to chemical forces.

src.l: Schelling, Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph von, 1799, Erster Entwurf eines Systems der Naturphilosophie
src.q: Life, wherever it is established, occurs as it were against the will of external nature , through a breaking away from it. External nature will therefore fight against life; most external influences that are considered life-promoting are actually destructive to life
src.qo: Das Leben, wo es zu Stande kommt, kommt gleichsam wider den Willen der äufsern Natur (invita natura externa), durch ein Losreifsen von ihr, zu Stande. Die äufsre Natur also wird gegen das Leben ankämpfen

src.l: Schelling, Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph von, 1799, Erster Entwurf eines Systems der Naturphilosophie
src.q: Das Leben, wo es zu Stande kommt, kommt gleichsam wider den Willen der äufsern Natur (invita natura externa), durch ein Losreifsen von ihr, zu Stande. Die äufsre Natur also wird gegen das Leben ankämpfen

s: Schelling (Erster Entwurf, 1799) writes that if nature is only visible spirit (der sichtbare Geist), spirit must become visible in it once the identity of matter is abolished and duplicity restores a world; he then asks how 'this dream' helps physics.

src.l: Schelling, Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph von, 1799, Erster Entwurf eines Systems der Naturphilosophie
src.q: And if nature is only visible spirit, then spirit in general must become visible in it (just as beauty emerges in it as soon as the mechanism of natural laws allows), as soon as the identity of matter is abolished
src.qo: Und wenn die Natur nur der sicht- bare Geist ist

src.l: Schelling, Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph von, 1799, Erster Entwurf eines Systems der Naturphilosophie
src.q: Und wenn die Natur nur der sicht- bare Geist ist

s: Schelling (Von der Weltseele, 1798) concludes that the principle which keeps the inorganic and organic worlds continuous and links the whole of nature into one universal organism is the being that the most ancient philosophy hailed as the common soul of nature (the world soul).

src.l: Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling, 1798, Von der Weltseele; eine Hypothese der höhern Physik (1st ed.)
src.q: Since this principle maintains the continuity of the inorganic and the organic worlds and links the whole of nature into a universal organism, we recognize in it once again that being which the most ancient philosophy presciently hailed as the common soul of nature
src.qo: Da nun dieses Princip die Continuität der anorgischen und der organischen Welt unterhält, und die ganze Natur zu einem allgemeinen Organismus verknüpft, so erkennen wir aufs Neue in ihm jenes Wesen, das die älteste Philosophie als die gemeinschaftliche Seele der Natur ahnend begrüßte

src.l: Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling, 1798, Von der Weltseele; eine Hypothese der höhern Physik (1st ed.)
src.q: Da nun dieses Princip die Continuität der anorgischen und der organischen Welt unterhält, und die ganze Natur zu einem allgemeinen Organismus verknüpft, so erkennen wir aufs Neue in ihm jenes Wesen, das die älteste Philosophie als die gemeinschaftliche Seele der Natur ahnend begrüßte

s: In the preface kept in the 1806 edition of Von der Weltseele, Schelling divides the treatise in two: the first part seeks the force of nature shown in general changes, the second the positive principle of organization and life, with the shared result that one and the same principle connects inorganic and organic nature.

src.l: Schelling, Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph von, 1806, Von der Weltseele
src.q: The second section undertakes to find the positive principle of organization and life. The shared result of these sections is that one and the same principle connects inorganic and organic nature.

s: Schelling (Erster Entwurf, 1799) states that the essence of every organism is not an absolute activity, such as is thought under the concept of Lebenskraft, but an activity mediated by receptivity, because the organism's existence is not a being but a constant being-reproduced, which only contrary external influences keep from exhausting itself in its product.

src.l: Schelling, Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph von, 1799, Erster Entwurf eines Systems der Naturphilosophie
src.q: The existence of the organism is not a state of being, but a constant state of being reproduced. Organic activity would exhaust itself in its product, just as in a dead object the activity exhausts itself in its product
src.qo: Nun besteht aber das Wesen alles Organismus darinn, dafs er keine absolute Thätigkeit sey, (dergleichen z. B. mit dem Begriff der Lebenskraft gedacht wird, sondern eine durch Receptivität vermittelte Thätigkeit, denn das Bestehen des Organismus ist nicht ein Seyn, sondern ein beständiges Reproducirtwerden.

src.l: Schelling, Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph von, 1799, Erster Entwurf eines Systems der Naturphilosophie
src.q: Nun besteht aber das Wesen alles Organismus darinn, dafs er keine absolute Thätigkeit sey, (dergleichen z. B. mit dem Begriff der Lebenskraft gedacht wird, sondern eine durch Receptivität vermittelte Thätigkeit, denn das Bestehen des Organismus ist nicht ein Seyn, sondern ein beständiges Reproducirtwerden.

s: Fechner (Nanna, 1848) argues that if plants have souls and sensations they no longer stand in nature like blind eyes or deaf ears, and nature, through whom God's living breath (lebendiger Odem) blows, beholds and feels herself as many times over as there are souls in her.

src.l: Gustav Theodor Fechner, 1848, Nanna, oder über das Seelenleben der Pflanzen
src.q: she, through whom God’s living breath blows. How different this is, if plants have souls and sen- sations; no longer standing in nature like blind eyes or deaf ears, within her—nature—who beholds and feels herself as many times over as there are souls within her to perceive her
src.qo: ſie, durch die Gottes lebendiger Odem weht. Wie anders dieß, wenn die Pflanzen Seelen haben und empfin- den; nicht mehr wie blinde Augen, taube Ohren in der Natur daſtehen

src.l: Gustav Theodor Fechner, 1848, Nanna, oder über das Seelenleben der Pflanzen
src.q: ſie, durch die Gottes lebendiger Odem weht. Wie anders dieß, wenn die Pflanzen Seelen haben und empfin- den; nicht mehr wie blinde Augen, taube Ohren in der Natur daſtehen

s: Fechner (Nanna, 1848) allows that every plant cell leads its own individual life, but as a life subordinate to a higher individuality, and quotes Goethe's Metamorphose: every living thing is not a single thing but a plurality, an assembly of living independent beings.

src.l: Gustav Theodor Fechner, 1848, Nanna, oder über das Seelenleben der Pflanzen
src.q: every cell of the plant from leading its own individual life in a certain way. It is simply a life subordinate to a higher individuality. Goethe expresses this aptly enough in his Metamorphosis of Plants: "Every living thing is not a single unit, but a multiplicity
src.qo: Jedes Lebendige ist kein Einzelnes, sondern eine Mehrheit; selbst in so- sofern es uns als Individuum erscheint, bleibt es doch eine Versammlung von lebendigen selbstständigen Wesen

src.l: Gustav Theodor Fechner, 1848, Nanna, oder über das Seelenleben der Pflanzen
src.q: Jedes Lebendige ist kein Einzelnes, sondern eine Mehrheit; selbst in so- sofern es uns als Individuum erscheint, bleibt es doch eine Versammlung von lebendigen selbstständigen Wesen

s: Fechner (Zend-Avesta, 1851) sums up that the Earth agrees with us in every mark of an ensouled individual being, while the differences make her appear a living, more independent, more individual being in a higher sense than we are, our own life falling short in fullness and depth.

src.l: Gustav Theodor Fechner, 1851, Zend-Avesta, oder über die Dinge des Himmels und des Jenseits
src.q: the equally conspicuous differences between us and the Earth all combine to make the Earth appear as a living, more independent, more individually distinct being in a higher sense than we are ourselves, whereas our own life falls far short in fullness and depth
src.qo: die Erde als ein in höherem Sinne lebendiges, selbstständigeres, individueller geartetes Wesen erscheinen zu lassen, als wir selbst sind, wogegen unser eigenes Leben an Fülle und Tiefe sehr in Nachtheil steht

src.l: Gustav Theodor Fechner, 1851, Zend-Avesta, oder über die Dinge des Himmels und des Jenseits
src.q: die Erde als ein in höherem Sinne lebendiges, selbstständigeres, individueller geartetes Wesen erscheinen zu lassen, als wir selbst sind, wogegen unser eigenes Leben an Fülle und Tiefe sehr in Nachtheil steht

s: Hegel (Encyklopädie, 1st ed. 1817, before §261) divides organic nature into three: the universal image of life, the geological organism (the Earth); particular subjectivity, vegetable nature; and individual concrete subjectivity, animal nature.

src.l: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel, 1817, Encyklopaedie der philosophischen Wissenschaften im Grundrisse (1st ed.)
src.q: the universal image of life; the geological organism; b) as particular or formal subjectivity, the vegetable nature; c) as individual concrete subjectivity, animal nature.
src.qo: das allgemeine Bild des Lebens; der geologische Organismus; b) als besondere oder formelle Subjecti- vität, die vegetabilische, c) als einzelne concrete Subjectivität, animalische Natur.

src.l: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel, 1817, Encyklopaedie der philosophischen Wissenschaften im Grundrisse (1st ed.)
src.q: das allgemeine Bild des Lebens; der geologische Organismus; b) als besondere oder formelle Subjecti- vität, die vegetabilische, c) als einzelne concrete Subjectivität, animalische Natur.

s: Hegel (Encyklopädie, 1817, §284) argues that because the living animal is a subject, the simple negativity of the point-like One, its assimilation of food can be neither mechanical nor chemical, since in those processes substances, conditions and activity stay external to one another and lack living absolute unity.

src.l: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel, 1817, Encyklopaedie der philosophischen Wissenschaften im Grundrisse (1st ed.)
src.q: Since the animal is a subject and thus the simple negativity of the point-like One, assimilation can be neither mechanical nor chemical in nature.
src.qo: Da dieses ein Subject hiemit, die einfache Negativität des punctuellen Eins ist, so kann die Assimilation weder mechanischer, eben so wenig als chemischer Natur seyn

src.l: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel, 1817, Encyklopaedie der philosophischen Wissenschaften im Grundrisse (1st ed.)
src.q: Da dieses ein Subject hiemit, die einfache Negativität des punctuellen Eins ist, so kann die Assimilation weder mechanischer, eben so wenig als chemischer Natur seyn

s: Schelling (Von der Weltseele, 1798), right after quoting Goethe's Metamorphose (1790) on the alternation of expansion and contraction, lays down as a law that the last goal of nature in every organization is gradual individualization (das allmählige Individualisiren).

src.l: Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling, 1798, Von der Weltseele; eine Hypothese der höhern Physik (1st ed.)
src.q: It can therefore be established as a law that the ultimate goal of nature in every organization is gradual individualization
src.qo: Es kann also als Gesetz aufgestellt werden, daß das letzte Ziel der Natur in jeder Organisation das allmählige Individualisiren ist

src.l: Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling, 1798, Von der Weltseele; eine Hypothese der höhern Physik (1st ed.)
src.q: Es kann also als Gesetz aufgestellt werden, daß das letzte Ziel der Natur in jeder Organisation das allmählige Individualisiren ist

s: Schelling (Von der Weltseele, 1798) asks the reader to renounce from the start any purely physical explanation of the general conflict of negative and positive principles, out of which alone a system of nature develops harmoniously.

src.l: Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling, 1798, Von der Weltseele; eine Hypothese der höhern Physik (1st ed.)
src.q: Let us therefore, from the very beginning, solemnly renounce any purely physical explanation of that general conflict between negative and positive principles, from which alone a system of nature harmoniously develops.
src.qo: Lasset uns also gleich anfangs feyerlich Verzicht thun auf eine physikalische Erklärung jenes allgemeinen Conflictes negativer Principien mit positiven, aus welchem allein ein System der Natur harmonisch sich entwickelt.

src.l: Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling, 1798, Von der Weltseele; eine Hypothese der höhern Physik (1st ed.)
src.q: Lasset uns also gleich anfangs feyerlich Verzicht thun auf eine physikalische Erklärung jenes allgemeinen Conflictes negativer Principien mit positiven, aus welchem allein ein System der Natur harmonisch sich entwickelt.

s: Schelling (Von der Weltseele, 1806 ed.) treats the Earth's magnetic polarity as the most original appearance of a universal dualism that physics must simply presuppose, appearing lower in electrical polarity and lastly in living organizations, where it forms a new world.

src.l: Schelling, Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph von, 1806, Von der Weltseele
src.q: This dualism already appears on a much deeper level in electrical polarity, until it finally disappears — at least to the common eye — in the heterogeneity diverse nature of two types of air near the Earth, and lastly in living organisms, where it forms a new world.
src.qo: und zuletzt in den belebten Organisationen, (wo er eine neue Welt bildet)

src.l: Schelling, Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph von, 1806, Von der Weltseele
src.q: und zuletzt in den belebten Organisationen, (wo er eine neue Welt bildet)

s: Tylor (Primitive Culture, 1871; 1920 printing) reports that Oken hit on a definition almost identical in form to the savage's and Porphyry's: 'What sounds, announces its spirit' (Was tönt, gibt seinen Geist kund), but meant it as a modern philosopher, not of a spirit apart from matter.

src.l: Edward Burnett Tylor, 1871, Primitive Culture, Vol. II
src.q: Oken hit upon a definition almost identical in form, that ‘ What sounds, announces its spirit ’ (‘ Was tönt, gibt seinen Geist kund ’).

s: Fechner (Büchlein vom Leben nach dem Tode, 1836; 2nd ed. 1852) holds that all our acting and willing in this world is calculated only to create for us an organism which we shall behold and use as our self in the following world, as the embryo builds the body it will use after birth.

src.l: Gustav Theodor Fechner, 1852, Das Büchlein vom Leben nach dem Tode (2nd ed.)
src.q: Our entire acting and willing in this world is likewise only calculated to create for us an organism which we shall behold and use as our self in the following world.
src.qo: Unser ganzes Handeln und Wollen in dieser Welt ist eben so nur berechnet, uns einen Organismus zu schaffen, den wir in der folgenden Welt als unser Selbst erblicken und brauchen sollen.

src.l: Gustav Theodor Fechner, 1852, Das Büchlein vom Leben nach dem Tode (2nd ed.)
src.q: Unser ganzes Handeln und Wollen in dieser Welt ist eben so nur berechnet, uns einen Organismus zu schaffen, den wir in der folgenden Welt als unser Selbst erblicken und brauchen sollen.

s: Fechner's Little Book (English c1904, footnote for physiologists) puts the child's creative principle before birth not in what will live on after birth but in what is cast off at birth, the placenta and membranes, like the body of man in death; the young human grows out of its activity as its continuation.

src.l: Gustav Theodor Fechner, 1904, The Little Book of Life After Death (English, c1904)
src.q: The creative principle of the child lies, before birth, not in that which after birth will continue to live on with him, which indeed now is only dependence, the product, but in that which at birth will remain behind and be cast off, like the body of man in death

src.l: Gustav Theodor Fechner, 1852, Das Büchlein vom Leben nach dem Tode (2nd ed.)
src.q: was vom Kinde bei der Geburt in Rückstand bleiben und verderben wird, wie der Leib des Menschen im Tode (placenta cum funiculo umbilicali, velamentis ovi eorumque liquoribus)

s: Fechner (Nanna, 1848) sets out, in order to reject it, the philosophers' neat schema of nature's stages: man has spirit or reason over Lebenskraft and soul, the animal Lebenskraft and soul, the plant mere Lebenskraft, while the crystal lacks even that and is wholly dead, given over to mechanical process.

src.l: Gustav Theodor Fechner, 1848, Nanna, oder über das Seelenleben der Pflanzen
src.q: The animal, one stage lower, must be content with vital force and soul; the plant, yet another stage lower, with mere vital force ; the crystal then also lacks vital force; it is entirely dead, fallen prey merely to mechanical processes.
src.qo: Das Thier, eine Stufe niedriger, hat ſich mit Lebens= kraft und Seele zu begnügen; die Pflanze, noch eine Stufe niedriger, mit der bloßen Lebenskraft; dem Krystall fehlt dann auch noch die Lebenskraft; er iſt ganz todt

src.l: Gustav Theodor Fechner, 1848, Nanna, oder über das Seelenleben der Pflanzen
src.q: Das Thier, eine Stufe niedriger, hat ſich mit Lebens= kraft und Seele zu begnügen; die Pflanze, noch eine Stufe niedriger, mit der bloßen Lebenskraft; dem Krystall fehlt dann auch noch die Lebenskraft; er iſt ganz todt

s: Fechner (Zend-Avesta, 1851) narrates the modern separation in stages: soul and spirit become two parts, the body scorns the soul and says 'my Lebenskraft will do', then the Lebenskraft is stripped from it too and mechanical force does everything, so the whole grows ever clearer in detail and ever deader as a whole.

src.l: Gustav Theodor Fechner, 1851, Zend-Avesta, oder über die Dinge des Himmels und des Jenseits
src.q: Yet the body now also scorns the soul, which one wishes to leave to it only as a remnant, and says: "My vital force will do just as well"; then, finally, the vital force is also stripped away from it, and at last, everything is done by mechanical force .
src.qo: Doch der Leib verschmäht nun auch die Seele, die man ihm nur als Rest lassen will, und spricht: meine Lebenskraft thut’s wohl auch; da zieht man ihm endlich auch die Lebenskraft ab, und Alles thut zuletzt seine mechanische Kraft.

src.l: Gustav Theodor Fechner, 1851, Zend-Avesta, oder über die Dinge des Himmels und des Jenseits
src.q: Doch der Leib verschmäht nun auch die Seele, die man ihm nur als Rest lassen will, und spricht: meine Lebenskraft thut’s wohl auch; da zieht man ihm endlich auch die Lebenskraft ab, und Alles thut zuletzt seine mechanische Kraft.

s: Fechner (Zend-Avesta, 1851) ties the antagonism that runs from body to soul in our organism to the law of the conservation of 'lebendige Kraft' (vis viva), which SL's English renders 'kinetic energy'; he expects the antagonism to hold in the wider organism of the world into which ours is built.

src.l: Gustav Theodor Fechner, 1851, Zend-Avesta, oder über die Dinge des Himmels und des Jenseits
src.q: That antagonism—indisputably dependent on the law of the conservation of kinetic energy —which shows itself in our narrow organism and extends from the body to the soul, will indisputably express itself in the world at large, or the broader organism
src.qo: Jener, unstreitig von dem Gesetze der Erhaltung der lebendigen Kraft abhängige, Antagonismus, der sich in unserm engen Organismus zeigt und vom Körper auf die Seele erstreckt

src.l: Gustav Theodor Fechner, 1851, Zend-Avesta, oder über die Dinge des Himmels und des Jenseits
src.q: Jener, unstreitig von dem Gesetze der Erhaltung der lebendigen Kraft abhängige, Antagonismus, der sich in unserm engen Organismus zeigt und vom Körper auf die Seele erstreckt

s: Against filing Romantic Naturphilosophie under 'vital force' vitalism: on SL's pages Schelling (1799) defines the organism against Lebenskraft as an absolute activity, Hegel (1817) refuses mechanical and chemical assimilation without positing any force, and Fechner (1848, 1851) treats Lebenskraft as the philosophers' remnant of a soul on the way to mechanism.

src.l: Schelling, Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph von, 1799, Erster Entwurf eines Systems der Naturphilosophie
src.q: it is not an absolute activity, such as is thought of with the concept of life force

src.l: Gustav Theodor Fechner, 1851, Zend-Avesta, oder über die Dinge des Himmels und des Jenseits
src.q: then, finally, the vital force is also stripped away from it, and at last, everything is done by mechanical force

s: Against a single Romantic doctrine of a living Earth or world soul: Schelling (1798) recognises the 'common soul of nature' only as a principle of continuity, Hegel (1817) calls the Earth the universal IMAGE of life (Bild des Lebens), not a living subject, and only Fechner (1851) makes the Earth a living being more individual than we are.

src.l: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel, 1817, Encyklopaedie der philosophischen Wissenschaften im Grundrisse (1st ed.)
src.q: das allgemeine Bild des Lebens; der geologische Organismus

src.l: Gustav Theodor Fechner, 1851, Zend-Avesta, oder über die Dinge des Himmels und des Jenseits
src.q: make the Earth appear as a living, more independent, more individually distinct being in a higher sense than we are ourselves
src.qo: die Erde als ein in höherem Sinne lebendiges, selbstständigeres, individueller geartetes Wesen erscheinen zu lassen, als wir selbst sind,

s: Walter Scott, The Hermetic Writings, Volume 1 (1926), on pneuma: states the Stoic extension of pneuma to the vehicle of life in the whole cosmos.

src.l: Walter Scott, 1926, The Hermetic Writings, Volume 1
src.q: ASCLEPIUS In some passages of Aristotle, the term πνεῦμα is used in this way. The Stoics extended its meaning to signify also the vehicle of life in the Cosmos as a whole, which they regarded as a single living organism.
src.qo: ASCLEPIUS passages of Aristotle. The Stoics extended its meaning, and used it to signify also the vehicle of life in the Kosmos as a whole, which they regarded as a single living organism.

s: John Actuarius, Actuarius, On Urines (Byzantine diagnostic medicine) (1450), on pneuma: a Byzantine physician's own words on psychic pneuma as the carrier of sensation.

src.l: John Actuarius, 1450, Actuarius, On Urines (Byzantine diagnostic medicine)
src.q: Therefore, since the sensory power of the soul and the psychic pneuma [spirit] remain within it, this pneuma [spirit], whenever things fall upon the senses from the outside, makes them be what they are.
src.qo: τῆς τοίνυν αἰσθητικῆς δυνάμεως τῆς ψυχῆς καὶ ψυχικοῦ πνεύματος ἐν αὐτῇ μενούσης πνεύματι. τοῦτο δὴ πνεῦμα. ὅταν ἐκ τῶν ἔξω προσπίπτοντα ταῖς αἰσθήσεσι ποιοῦντος εἶναι αὐτῶν.

s: Walter Scott, The Hermetic Writings, Volume 1 (1926), on pneuma: pneuma as vehicle of soul, its vital element fire, in the Stoic system.

src.l: Walter Scott, 1926, The Hermetic Writings, Volume 1
src.q: " πνεῦμα (spirit/breath) is the vehicle of ψυχή (soul), and the vital element of πνεῦμα is fire. The heavenly bodies are no doubt considered to be composed of fire, as in the Stoic system, and the writer’s view seems to be that they send forth vitalizing fire, which coalesces with the upper air to form πνεῦμα.

s: Henri II Estienne, Thesaurus of the Greek Language (Vol. 3) (1572), on pneuma: Renaissance lexicon definition: in living beings, the breath of life.

src.l: Henri II Estienne, 1572, Thesaurus of the Greek Language (Vol. 3)
src.q: See Empneō [to inspire]. Πνεῦμα, ατος, τό, Breath, blast, spirit: but particularly in living beings, the breath of life. Mostly the blast of winds, or wind.
src.qo: Πνεῦμα, ατος, τό, Flamen, Flatus, Spiritus: peculiariter autē in animantibus Anhelitus. Plerunque Ventorū flatus, vel Ventus.

s: Lenz, Christian Friedrich, First Physical Dissertation on the Bond Connecting Soul and Body (1717), on psychē: Plato via 1717 dissertation: the self-moving is the substance and definition of soul, soul as principle of life.

src.l: Lenz, Christian Friedrich, 1717, First Physical Dissertation on the Bond Connecting Soul and Body
src.q: 344 D: ἀθανάτὲ δὲ πεφασμένε, τῆς ὑφ' ἑαυτῦ κινμένε, ψυχῆς ἐσίαν τε καὶ λόγον τῦτο αὐτό τις λέγων οὐκ αἰχυνεται [When therefore it appears that what moves itself is immortal, the person who says that this itself is the substance and definition of the soul does not blush].

s: Justus Lipsius, Six Books of Politics (1604), on psychē: Hermetic ladder matter-air-soul-mind-God, translated context.

src.l: Justus Lipsius, 1604, Six Books of Politics
src.q: That Hermes, truly thrice-greatest in these divine matters: Ὕλης μὲν τὸ λεπτομερέστερον, ἀὴρ. ἀέρος δὲ, ψυχή. ψυχῆς δὲ, νοῦς. νοῦ δὲ, ὁ Θεός.
src.qo: Hermes ille verè Ter maximus in his diuinis: Ὕλης μὲν τὸ λεπτομερέστερον, ἀὴρ. ἀέρος δὲ, ψυχή. ψυχῆς δὲ, νοῦς. νοῦ δὲ, ὁ Θεός.

s: Plato, Phaedo (1890), on psychē: states where the word psyche as a person's true self came from.

src.l: Plato, 1890, Phaedo
src.q: It is sufficiently established that the use of the word ψυχή [soul/spirit] to express a living man’s true personality is Orphic in its origin, and came into philosophy from mysticism.

s: Scott, Walter, Hermetica, Volume II: Notes on the Corpus Hermeticum (1925), on psychē: Hermetic doctrine of soul separating from mind after death.

src.l: Scott, Walter, 1925, Hermetica, Volume II: Notes on the Corpus Hermeticum
src.q: CORPVS HERMETICVM The νοῦς [mind] is separated from the ψυχή [soul]. The νοῦς then ascends to the sun, from where it originally came; the ψυχή is left on the moon, and retains for a time a dreamlike life of its own, but sooner or later fades away and is resolved into the substance of the moon.
src.qo: νοῦς is separated from the ψυχή. The νοῦς then ascends to the sun, whence it originally came; the ψυχή is left on the moon, and retains for a time a dreamlike life of its own, but sooner or later fades away, and is resolved into the substance of the moon.

s: Aristoteles, On the Soul (1500), on vegetative soul: Aristotle's own statement: the vegetative soul is the first and most common power, by which living is present in all.

src.l: Aristoteles, 1500, On the Soul
src.q: On the Vegetative Soul Clearly, one must speak first of nourishment and generation. The vegetative soul is the first for other animate things, and it is the most common power of the soul, according to which living is present in all.
src.qo: De Anima vegetativa Clare primo de alimēto et gnātione dicendū est. Uegetatlua em anima et alijs animatis pria est. et maxime cōmunis potētia aie fm quā inest viuere omnib'.

s: Judah Leon Abravanel, Dialoghi di amore, composti per Leone medico, di natione hebreo, et dipoi fatto christiano. (1545), on vegetative soul: Leone Ebreo: the anima vegetativa causes germination, nourishment, growth and generation in plants.

src.l: Judah Leon Abravanel, 1545, Dialoghi di amore, composti per Leone medico, di natione hebreo, et dipoi fatto christiano.
src.q: with greater equality, and with less excess of any of them, they not only have the forms of the mixture, but also receive more excellent forms, such as the animate ones, and first those of the anima vegetativa [vegetative soul], which cause in plants germination, nourishment, and growth on every side, and the generation of similar ones with the seed and branch of the generator.
src.qo: & con manco eccesso d'ogn'uno di loro, non solamente hanno le forme della mistion, ma ancor riceuono forme piu eccellenti, come sono l'animate, & prima quelle dell'anima uegetatiua, che causano nelle piante la germinatione, il nutrimento, & il crescimento per ogni lato, & la generatione delle simili con la semenza & ramo del generante,

s: Hartmann, Johann, Disputationes chymico-medicae (1614), on vegetative soul: 1614 chymical medicine: one anima vegetabilis hidden in the seed regrows shoots every year.

src.l: Hartmann, Johann, 1614, Disputationes chymico-medicae
src.q: In the same way, one and the same anima vegetabilis [vegetative soul] in number, which originally lay hidden in the seed and produced the individual body of the plant from moisture impregnated with attracted spirits, pushes out and restores new shoots, leaves, branches, flowers, and fruits from the root every year.
src.qo: quae primitus in semine delitescens ex humore spiritibus impregnato allecto individuum plantae corpus extulit, quotannis ex radice novos surculos, folia, ramos, flores, & fructus protrudit, ac restituit.

s: William Harvey, Exercises on the Motion of the Heart (1651), on vegetative soul: Harvey: even an unfertile egg has a vegetative soul.

src.l: William Harvey, 1651, Exercises on the Motion of the Heart
src.q: On the Generation of Animals concedes that a vegetative soul is present in the egg, even an unfertile one: while he says, Females and all things that live possess a vegetative power of the soul, as has been said more often: wherefore this egg (he speaks of the unfertile one), like the conception of a plant, is perfect;
src.qo: concedit animam vegetativam in ovo, etiam subventaneo, inesse: dum ait, Vegetalem animæ virtutem obtinent & fœminæ, & omnia quæ vivunt, ut sæpius dictum est:

s: Suidas, The Lexicon of Suidas (1854), on entelechy: Suidas' lexicon definition: the perfection and form of the underlying subject.

src.l: Suidas, 1854, The Lexicon of Suidas
src.q: ἐντελέχεια [entelechy/actuality]: The perfection and the form of the underlying subject, that is, the form that arises in the matter from such a composition of elements.
src.qo: ἐντελέχεια ἡ τελειότης καὶ τὸ εἶδος τοῦ ὑποκειμένου, τουτέστι τὸ εἶδος τὸ ἐπιγινόμενον ἐκ τῆς τοιᾶσδε συνθέσεως τῶν στοιχείων τῇ ὕλῃ.

s: Diogène Laërce, Diogenous Laertiou Peri biōn, dogmatōn kai apophthegmatōn tōn en philosophia eudokimēsantōn biblia 10 (1593), on entelechy: Diogenes Laertius: Aristotle's soul as first entelechia of a natural organic body.

src.l: Diogène Laërce, 1593, Diogenous Laertiou Peri biōn, dogmatōn kai apophthegmatōn tōn en philosophia eudokimēsantōn biblia 10
src.q: He said the soul is incorporeal: and the first entelechia [actuality/perfection], that is, the perfection of a natural and organic body having life in potentiality: which according to him is twofold.
src.qo: Animam esse incorpoream dixit: et primam, ἐντελέχειαν, hoc est perfectionem, corporis naturalis et organici, potentia vitam obtinentis: quae secundum eum duplex est.

s: Leibnitz, Gottfried Wilhelm von, Essais de theodicée sur la bonté de Dieu (1714), on entelechy: Leibniz on the word's origin and Barbarus' rendering perfectihabia.

src.l: Leibnitz, Gottfried Wilhelm von, 1714, Essais de theodicée sur la bonté de Dieu
src.q: The same Philosopher gave the soul the generic name of Entelechie [Entelechy] or act. This word Entelechy apparently draws its origin from the Greek word which means perfect, and it is for this reason that the famous Hermolaus Barbarus expressed it in Latin word for word by perfectihabia [the possession of perfection], for the Act is an accomplishment of power: and he had no need to consult the Devil, as they say he did, to learn only that.

s: Leibnitz, Gottfried Wilhelm von, Essais de theodicée sur la bonté de Dieu (1714), on entelechy: Leibniz revives entelechy as a permanent force or conatus.

src.l: Leibnitz, Gottfried Wilhelm von, 1714, Essais de theodicée sur la bonté de Dieu
src.q: I have shown elsewhere that the notion of Entelechy [a vital principle of activity] is not entirely to be despised, and that, being permanent, it carries with it not only a simple active faculty, but also what one may call force or conatus [striving or inclination], from which the action itself must follow, if nothing prevents it.

s: Morienus; Bernard Trevisanus; Arnaldus de Villanova, Alchemical Collection: Morienus, Bernard of Treviso, Arnaldus (1574), on spiritus: Morienus/Bernard: spiritus as the bond and fire of nature holding soul and body together.

src.l: Morienus; Bernard Trevisanus; Arnaldus de Villanova, 1574, Alchemical Collection: Morienus, Bernard of Treviso, Arnaldus
src.q: and the sulphur is the spiritus [spirit] and the sal [salt] the corpus, the mercurius the anima [soul], and the spiritus is the vinculum [bond] that holds the anima and the corpus together, and the spiritus is the ignis [fire] of nature that drives the mercurium into the corpus, and the sal is the fixum [fixed part] of nature that retains the spiritum and the animam.
src.qo: u. d. Sulphur ist d. Spiritus und d. Sal d. Corpus, d. Mercurius d. Anima, u. d. Spiritus ist d. Vinculum so d. Anima u. d. Corpus zusammen hält, u. d. Spiritus ist d. Ignis d. Naturae so d. Mercurium in d. Corpus treibt, u. d. Sal ist d. Fixum d. Naturae so d. Spiritum u. d. Animam behelt.

s: Paracelsus, Erster [- zehender] Theil der Bücher und Schrifften des edlen, hochgelehrten und bewehrten philosophi und medici Philippi Theophrasti Bombast von Hohenheim ... (1589), on spiritus: body from earth, spiritus from heaven and God; many kinds of spirits.

src.l: Paracelsus, 1589, Erster [- zehender] Theil der Bücher und Schrifften des edlen, hochgelehrten und bewehrten philosophi und medici Philippi Theophrasti Bombast von Hohenheim ...
src.q: The body is of the earth, the Spiritus [spirit] is from heaven and from God, etc. It is further to be known that there are many kinds of spirits, and each one is different from the other.

s: Basilius, Fratris Basilii Valentini ... chymische Schriften alle so viel derer verhanden (1700), on spiritus: Basil Valentine: the alchemists' volatile distillate rising into the flask.

src.l: Basilius, 1700, Fratris Basilii Valentini ... chymische Schriften alle so viel derer verhanden
src.q: But when the phlegma is over, give it a stronger fire, and a great white spiritus [spirit] comes up into the flask, almost looking like the white spiritus vitrioli [spirit of vitriol], but it does not fall into the phlegma.
src.qo: wann aber die phlegma herüber/ so gieb ihm ein stär- cker Feuer/ so kommt ein grosser weisser spiritus oben in den Kolben/ fast anzusehen wie der weisse spiri- tus vitrioli, fället aber nicht in die phlegma,

s: Laurent Ventura; Petrus Bonus Ferrariensis, Book of Perfect Chemical Knowledge — Czech Alchemy (1579), on spiritus: Czech alchemy: mercury as fixed, volatile, world and body spirit.

src.l: Laurent Ventura; Petrus Bonus Ferrariensis, 1579, Book of Perfect Chemical Knowledge — Czech Alchemy
src.q: Mercury is the spiritus fixus [fixed spirit], and mercury is the spiritus volatilis [volatile spirit], and mercury is the spiritus mundi [spirit of the world], and mercury is the spiritus corporis [spirit of the body], and mercury is the spiritus animae [spirit of the soul], and mercury
src.qo: a rtuť gest spiritus fixus, a rtuť gest spiritus volatilis, a rtuť gest spiritus mundi, a rtuť gest spiritus corporis,
