s: Paracelsus, Paracelsus: De Peste Tractatus (1613), on vital spirits: Job Kornthauer's gloss on Paracelsus (1613): nature and the vital spirits fight a plague poison.

src.l: Paracelsus, 1613, Paracelsus: De Peste Tractatus
src.q: The other pestis [plague] breaks out through the virtus expultrix [expulsive power], because either the poison is not so strong that nature and the spiritus vitales [vital spirits] can overcome the poison and drive it out from itself, or it is often driven out per medicamenta [through medicines] which come to the aid of the vital spirits.
src.qo: Die ander pestis dringet herauß/ per virtutem expultricem, dies weil/ entweder das Gifft nicht so starck ist/ daß also die Natur und spiritus vitales das Gifft uberwindet/ und von jhr hinauß treibet: Oder aber wirt offt per medicamenta so den spiritibus vitalibus zu

s: Anonymous, German Chemical Theater (1728), on vital spirits: keeping the vital spirits at the natural digestive heat.

src.l: Anonymous, 1728, German Chemical Theater
src.q: And so it is likewise situated when the spiritus vitales [vital spirits] have no movement. Therefore, it behooves a conscientious physician to strive particularly for the one thing, how he may maintain the modum [mode] of the spiritum vitalium [vital spirits] at the natural digestive heat in a good state;
src.qo: Und so ist es eben- falls beschaffen/ wenn die Spiritus Vitales keine Bewegung haben. Derowegen kommet es eis nem gewissenhafften Medico zu/ nach dem eini- gen sonderlich zu streben/ wie er den Modum, derer Spiritum vitalium,

s: Unknown, Defensions-Articul oder Eygentl. Bericht, was zu Beschützung des Gottesdienstes sub utraque von den Herrn Rittern ... deß Königreichs Böhmen, welche den Leib und das Blut unsers Herrn Jesu Christi unter beyderley gestalt empfangen bey großer Versamblung auff dem Prager Schloß anno 1618 beschlossen (1618), on vital spirits: where the vital spirits were believed to hide: the red globules.

src.l: Unknown, 1618, Defensions-Articul oder Eygentl. Bericht, was zu Beschützung des Gottesdienstes sub utraque von den Herrn Rittern ... deß Königreichs Böhmen, welche den Leib und das Blut unsers Herrn Jesu Christi unter beyderley gestalt empfangen bey großer Versamblung auff dem Prager Schloß anno 1618 beschlossen
src.q: The red globules are those particles that give the blood its red color, and in which, as many believe, the spiritus vitales [vital spirits] lie hidden.
src.qo: Rubri autem globuli sunt illæ particulæ, quæ sanguini colorem rubrum conciliant, et in quibus, ut multi volunt, spiritus vitales latent.

s: [s.n.], Von den Träumen und Nachtwandlern (1784), on vital spirits: Lebensgeister and temperament, 1784.

src.l: [s.n.], 1784, Von den Träumen und Nachtwandlern
src.q: b) On the other hand, the Lebensgeister [vital spirits] in a sanguinisch [sanguine] temperament also bring about fleeting thoughts, just as c) the Nervensaft [nervous fluid] of a melancholisch [melancholic] temperament causes a slowness in the progression of representations.
src.qo: b) Hingegen bewirken die Lebensgeister bey einem sanguinischen Temperamente, auch flüchtige Gedanken, so wie c) der Nervensaft eines melancholischen Temperaments in dem Gange der Vor- stellungen eine Langsamkeit bewirket.

s: Lemnius, Levinus, Hidden miracles of nature: and various documents of things, explained in two books with probable reason and skillful conjecture, which are not so much for the use as for the delight of the studious and eager reader (1559), on animal spirits: 1559 Latin physician: the animal spirit carries the strength of nerves and muscles from the brain.

src.l: Lemnius, Levinus, 1559, Hidden miracles of nature: and various documents of things, explained in two books with probable reason and skillful conjecture, which are not so much for the use as for the delight of the studious and eager reader
src.q: Thus it happens that the body is carried aloft by the impulse of the animal spirit spiritus animalis; according to ancient and medieval medicine, a refined substance that resides in the brain and flows through the nerves to control movement and sensation, which contains and protects the strength of the nerves and muscles (that is, the duty of sensing and moving) within the brain.
src.qo: Quò fit vt corpus ſpiritus animalis impulſu, qui neruorum ac muſculorum robur, hoc eſt, ſentiendi mouendique munus in cerebro continet ac tuetur, in ſublime feratur,

s: Rene Descartes, Discourse on the Method (1637), on animal spirits: Descartes himself: the esprits animaux distributed into the muscles move the limbs.

src.l: Rene Descartes, 1637, Discourse on the Method
src.q: and for the fantaisie [imagination], which can variously change them, and compose new ones, and by the same means, distributing the esprits animaux [animal spirits] into the muscles, cause the limbs of this body to move, in as many different ways, and as appropriately to the objects that present themselves to its senses, and to the internal passions that are within it, as our own can move without the will directing them.
src.qo: & pour la fantaifie, qui les peut diuerfement changer, & en compofer de nouuelles, & par mefme moyen, diftribuant les efpris animaux dans les mufcles, faire mouuoir les membres de ce cors, en autant de diuerfes façons, & autant a propos des obiets qui fe prefentent à fes fens, & des paffions interieures qui font en luy, que les noftres fe puiffent mouuoir fans que la volonté les conduife.

s: Mornay, Philippe de, De la vérité de la religion chrestienne (1585), on animal spirits: 1585 French: animals lose life with their blood because the animal spirits depart with it.

src.l: Mornay, Philippe de, 1585, De la vérité de la religion chrestienne
src.q: Of the Truth Animals certainly lose life and action with their blood, for with it the esprits animaux [animal spirits, the vital essence believed to animate the body] depart.
src.qo: De la verité loger luy est osté. Les animaux certes perdent la vie & l'action auec le sang, car auec iceluy les esprits animaux s'en vont:

s: René Descartes, Opera Philosophica (1672), on animal spirits: Descartes' Latin: the nerves and brain contain a very subtle wind called spiritus animales.

src.l: René Descartes, 1672, Opera Philosophica
src.q: and they contain, as does the brain itself, a certain very subtle air or wind, which is expressed by the name of spiritus animales [animal spirits].
src.qo: & continent, ut & ipſum cerebrum, certum quendam aërem aut ventum ſubtiliſſimum, qui ſpirituum animalium nomine exprimitur.

s: Nemesius of Emesa; Nicasius Ellebodius (trans.), On the Nature of Man, one book, now first published and translated into Latin (1565), on innate heat: Nemesius: breathing exists to preserve the innate heat, a doctrine stated plainly.

src.l: Nemesius of Emesa; Nicasius Ellebodius (trans.), 1565, On the Nature of Man, one book, now first published and translated into Latin
src.q: The need is twofold: the preservation of the innate heat, and the nourishment of the psychic spirit. The preservation of the natural heat consists of both inhalation and exhalation;
src.qo: χρεία μὲν διττή· φυλακή τε τῆς ἐμφύτου θερμασίας, καὶ θρέψις τοῦ ψυχικοῦ πνεύματος. ἀλλ' ἡ μὲν φυλακὴ τῆς κατὰ φύσιν θερμότητος διά τε τῆς εἰσπνοῆς καὶ τῆς ἐκπνοῆς συνίσταται·

s: Bacon, Roger, Hitherto Unpublished Works, Fascicle 8 (1928), on innate heat: Roger Bacon on old age: grey hair comes from the weakening of natural heat, the waning the gloss describes.

src.l: Bacon, Roger, 1928, Hitherto Unpublished Works, Fascicle 8
src.q: Weakening of natural heat due to the course of nature (partly curable), Graying hair happens because of the weakening of the heat that leaves the body.
src.qo: Weakening of natural heat due to course of nature (partly curable), Canicies autem est propter debilitatem caloris qui exit a corpore;

s: Petrus de Abano, De venenis. Ed: Guilielmus Haldenhoff (1498), on innate heat: Petrus de Abano: natural heat is the soul's instrument and resists poisons.

src.l: Petrus de Abano, 1498, De venenis. Ed: Guilielmus Haldenhoff
src.q: of the calor innatus [innate heat] is such that it also resists hot poisons, not in a complexional way, but in a formal way. This is because natural heat informs and is regulated by our soul, which moves toward life by means of natural heat as its own instrument.
src.qo: calor innatus: adeo q etiam venenis calidis repugnat non cōplerionaliter: sed formaliter: quia calor naturalis informat: est regulat ab anima nostra que mouet ad vitaz mediante calore naturali tanq3 suo instrumento:

s: Fludd, Robert, Dr. Fludds Answer to M. Foster or, the squesing of parson Fosters sponge (1631), on innate heat: Fludd: calidum innatum by whose power every creature exists, carried in radical moisture.

src.l: Fludd, Robert, 1631, Dr. Fludds Answer to M. Foster or, the squesing of parson Fosters sponge
src.q: vertue is that Calidum innatum, or Naturall heate, by whose vertue euery creature doth exist, and the volatile vehicle, in which it is carried, is that Humidum Radicale, or Radicall Moisture, or Humidity,

s: Zwinger, Theodor, Physiologia Medica (1610), on innate heat: Zwinger: innate heat and radical moisture as the foundations of all vital functions.

src.l: Zwinger, Theodor, 1610, Physiologia Medica
src.q: These two are the calidum innatum [innate heat] and the humidum radicale [radical moisture], which serve as the foundations of all vital functions.

s: Kircher, Athanasius, The Minor Art of Consonance and Dissonance (1662), on radical moisture: remedies strengthen and preserve the radical moisture and heat: the medical doctrine in practice.

src.l: Kircher, Athanasius, 1662, The Minor Art of Consonance and Dissonance
src.q: , invented both with proof and with characterization, which strengthen and preserve the humidum radicale [radical moisture], heat, etc. The greater community these remedies have with the limbs with which they harmonize, the more powerfully will they strengthen them, just as in music, consonances are more perfect the closer they come to the unison.

s: Anonymous, The Golden Art, Called Chemistry (1572), on radical moisture: early alchemical claim: other things lose their radical humidity in fire, the stone does not.

src.l: Anonymous, 1572, The Golden Art, Called Chemistry
src.q: because all other things are consumed in fire and lose their humiditas radicalis [radical humidity]. The said stone, however, alone and entirely in the fire, is always improved and its goodness grows;
src.qo: quia omnes aliæ res in igne comburuntur, & amittunt humiditatem radicalem. Dictus verò lapis totus solus in igne semper melio- ratur & crescit eius bonitas:

s: anonymous, Hermetisches Journal (1802), on radical moisture: what the ancients called it: universal balsam, panacea, mercury of life.

src.l: anonymous, 1802, Hermetisches Journal
src.q: The ancients call the Humidum radicale [radical moisture] the Universal Balsam [original: "Balsamum catholicum"], the most precious nature-elixir, the Panacea, and the Mercurium Vitae [Mercury of Life].
src.qo: Die Alten nennen das Humidum radicale den Universalbalsam (Balsamum catholicum) das überkostbare Natur-Elixir, die Panacee, den Mercurium Vitae.

s: Paracelsus (1493-1541), Erster [- zehender] Theil der Bücher und Schrifften des edlen, hochgelehrten und bewehrten philosophi und medici Philippi Theophrasti Bombast von Hohenheim ... / [Erster bis sechster Theil.] (1589), on archeus: Paracelsus: the human archei transform ingested tartar, the inner craftsman at work.

src.l: Paracelsus (1493-1541), 1589, Erster [- zehender] Theil der Bücher und Schrifften des edlen, hochgelehrten und bewehrten philosophi und medici Philippi Theophrasti Bombast von Hohenheim ... / [Erster bis sechster Theil.]
src.q: the external Tartars our Tartars become, that is, that the external Tartars come into us through food and drink, afterwards becoming Tartara humana [human Tartars] in us: and because of the Archei humani [human internal alchemist], in whom there is transformation, it changes in another way in the transplantation.

s: Jan Baptist van Helmont, Daybreak, or the New Rise of the Art of Medicine (1659), on archeus: Van Helmont: archei as masters of transformation.

src.l: Jan Baptist van Helmont, 1659, Daybreak, or the New Rise of the Art of Medicine
src.q: The Archei [internal organizers] (certain masters of transformation) are partly like one another, and partly unlike; nevertheless, they do not receive nor replace one another except for their own benefit and love.
src.qo: De Archei (eenige werckmeesters ter verwefentheydt) zijn malkanderen eensdeels gelijck, en eensdeels ongelijck: nochtans en ontfangen, noch en vervangen sy malkanderen niet, dan uyt eygener baet en liefde.

s: Paracelsus (1493-1541), Erster [- zehender] Theil der Bücher und Schrifften des edlen, hochgelehrten und bewehrten philosophi und medici Philippi Theophrasti Bombast von Hohenheim ... / [Erster bis sechster Theil.] (1589), on archeus: Paracelsus: the archeus is like man and lies in the four elements.

src.l: Paracelsus (1493-1541), 1589, Erster [- zehender] Theil der Bücher und Schrifften des edlen, hochgelehrten und bewehrten philosophi und medici Philippi Theophrasti Bombast von Hohenheim ... / [Erster bis sechster Theil.]
src.q: But what we should know concerning Confortativis [strengthening medicines] is taught by the Explanation Archei [explanation of the internal alchemist/nature spirit], who is just like man and lies in the four elements.
src.qo: Was wir aber de Confortativis sollen wissen/ lehret die Explanation Archei, der also ist gleich dem Menschen/ und ligt in den vier Elementen/

s: Marci z Kronlandu, Jan Marek, Restored Ancient Philosophy (1676), on archeus: archei moved unequally by impressions, fear and anger.

src.l: Marci z Kronlandu, Jan Marek, 1676, Restored Ancient Philosophy
src.q: occasional cause may have fear in this archeus, anger or madness in that one, and in another no movement at all. This is because the archei are moved unequally by impressions.

s: [Dolhopff, Georg Andreas], Animal Microcosmic Stone. Or, the Highest Medicine, from the Little World of the Human Body: Together with a Little Treatise on the Urine of Man (1681), on mumia: Paracelsian distinction: a mumia prepared from a living body.

src.l: [Dolhopff, Georg Andreas], 1681, Animal Microcosmic Stone. Or, the Highest Medicine, from the Little World of the Human Body: Together with a Little Treatise on the Urine of Man
src.q: Now, however, to speak further of the Mumia, you should know that yet another Mumia exists: namely, the Mumia that is separated and prepared from a living body.
src.qo: Nun aber weiter von dem Mumia zu reden / solt ihr wissen / daß noch ein ander Mumia vorhanden ist / nemlich die Mumia, die von einem lebendigen Leib separirt und præparirt wird.

s: Paracelsus, Theophrastus, Opera. Bücher und Schrifften (1616), on mumia: living mumia makes a body act like a magnet: the basis of sympathetic cures.

src.l: Paracelsus, Theophrastus, 1616, Opera. Bücher und Schrifften
src.q: For every Corpus [body] to which a living Mumia [vital corpse-essence] is brought from a human, that same Corpus immediately becomes like a magnet.
src.qo: Dann ein jedes Corpus, dem ein lebendige Mumia wird bey gebracht von ei- nem Menschen/dasselbige Corpus, wird als bald zu einem Magneten.

s: Unknown, Hundert acht und dreyßig neu-entdeckte und vollkommen bewährte Geheimnüsse, Oder allerhand magische, spagyrische, sympathetische und antipathetische Kunst-Stücke ... (1726), on mumia: a practical sympathetic cure through the mumia.

src.l: Unknown, 1726, Hundert acht und dreyßig neu-entdeckte und vollkommen bewährte Geheimnüsse, Oder allerhand magische, spagyrische, sympathetische und antipathetische Kunst-Stücke ...
src.q: Sympathetic cure through the Mumia [mummy (a medicinal preparation)]. When a person has such cruel tearing in a limb that the flesh even wastes away, there is nothing better than to tie a white birch bark around the limb and leave it for 24 hours, thereafter remove it, and in the following evening and morning smear it with the following spirit of mummy, so the tearing will pass and the flesh will grow again.
src.qo: Sympathetische Cur durch die Mumia. Wann ein Mensch das grausame Reissen in einem Gliede hat, daß so gar das Fleisch ihme verschwindet, so ist nichts bessers, als daß man eine weisse Bircken-Rinde um das Glied binde, und 24. Stunden also lasse, hernach davon nehme, folgendes Abends und Morgens mit folgendem Mumien-Geiste überschmiere, so wird das Reissen vergehen, und das Fleisch wieder wachsen.

s: Paracelsus, Erster [- zehender] Theil der Bücher und Schrifften des edlen, hochgelehrten und bewehrten philosophi und medici Philippi Theophrasti Bombast von Hohenheim ... (1589), on mumia: Paracelsus on mumia dying out of a sick body as it rots while alive.

src.l: Paracelsus, 1589, Erster [- zehender] Theil der Bücher und Schrifften des edlen, hochgelehrten und bewehrten philosophi und medici Philippi Theophrasti Bombast von Hohenheim ...
src.q: So it is also to be understood with Mumia, which also dies a natural death out of illness itself. For all strength departs from such a person, the blood drains away, the body begins to rot even while still alive: the blood also, and all other strengths, decrease;

s: Dorn, Gerhard, Chymisticum artificium naturae (1568), on natural balsam: Dorn: the natural balsam is implanted in all bodies.

src.l: Dorn, Gerhard, 1568, Chymisticum artificium naturae
src.q: Indeed, "uncorrupted nature" here refers to the natural balsam [the inherent life-force or preservative fluid in living things] naturally implanted in all bodies.

s: Anonymous, Theatrum chemicum, praecipuos selectorum auctorum tractatus de chemiae et lapidis philosophici antiquitate, veritate, iure, praestantia, & operationibus, continens: in gratiam verae chemiae, et medicinae chemicae studiosorum ... congestum, et in sex partes seu volumina digestum; singulis voluminibus, suo auctorum et librorum catalogo primis pagellis: rerum vero & verborum indice postremis annexo. Volumen primum [- sextum] / Volumen primum. (1659), on natural balsam: balsam of life defined as natural heat tempered with radical moisture; its failing causes disease.

src.l: Anonymous, 1659, Theatrum chemicum, praecipuos selectorum auctorum tractatus de chemiae et lapidis philosophici antiquitate, veritate, iure, praestantia, & operationibus, continens: in gratiam verae chemiae, et medicinae chemicae studiosorum ... congestum, et in sex partes seu volumina digestum; singulis voluminibus, suo auctorum et librorum catalogo primis pagellis: rerum vero & verborum indice postremis annexo. Volumen primum [- sextum] / Volumen primum.
src.q: It is truly nothing other than the failing of the balsami vitae naturalis [natural balsam of life], due to a lack or excess of its fuel. We say that the balsam of life is the balanced mixture of the calidi naturalis [natural heat] with its radicali humido [radical moisture].

s: Dorn, Gerhard, Chymisticum artificium naturae (1568), on natural balsam: Dorn: the body's natural balsam must be nourished by balsam, like by like.

src.l: Dorn, Gerhard, 1568, Chymisticum artificium naturae
src.q: But if they are to serve as nourishment, they must be presented with the body, for all parts of the body, both the thicker and the more subtle, must be nourished by things similar to themselves: namely, salt by salt, sulfur by sulfur, and natural balsam by balsam.
src.qo: Verùm si alimento de- beant esse, cum corpore sunt exhibenda, nam partes corporis omnes tam crassiores quàm subtiles sibi similibus nutriri debent, utpote sal sale, sulphure sulphur, & balsamum natu- rale balsamo.

s: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, Three Books on Occult Philosophy (1551), on world soul: Agrippa: the world has a soul on which all lower things depend.

src.l: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, 1551, Three Books on Occult Philosophy
src.q: For what else do these verses seem to mean, than that the world not only has a spirit and a soul, but also participates in the divine mind? Philosophers on the soul of the world. And that the origin, power, and vigor of all lower things depend upon that very soul of the world?
src.qo: Quid enim hi uersus aliud uelle uidentur, quā mundū non modo habere spiritum & animam,sed etiam mentis diuinæ esse participē, atq; Philosophi de anima mundi. omnium inferiorum originem, uirtutem, vigoremq;,ab ipsa mundi anima dependere?

s: Giordano Bruno, Latin Works Vol. III (On Magic, On Bonds) (1891), on world soul: Bruno: poets and philosophers grant that heaven and world are animate.

src.l: Giordano Bruno, 1891, Latin Works Vol. III (On Magic, On Bonds)
src.q: Concerning the soul of the world and of worldly things according to the magic of the ancients. 73r It has been granted by the most noble poets and the wisest philosophers that the heaven and the world are animate—that is, possessed of a soul—as are the celestial bodies that we see.
src.qo: Caelum et mundum esse animatum, insuper et caelestia quae videntur corpora, nobilissimis poëtis et sapientissimis philosophis est concessum,

s: Vladimir Solovyov, Collected Works, Vol. 9 (1907), on world soul: concise definition: the world as a living being with perceptions and feelings.

src.l: Vladimir Solovyov, 1907, Collected Works, Vol. 9
src.q: World Soul (ψυχὴ τοῦ κόσμου [soul of the world], anima mundi [soul of the world], Weltseele [world soul]) is the unified inner nature of the world, thought of as a living being possessing aspirations, perceptions, and feelings.
src.qo: Міровая душа (ψυχὴ τοῦ κόσμου, anima mundi, Weltseele)—единая внутренняя природа міра, мыслимая какъ живое существо, обладающее стремленіями, представленіями и чувствами.

s: Orpheus (ed. Abel), Orphic Hymns and Argonautica (1885), on world soul: Orphic reading of Bacchus as the anima mundi.

src.l: Orpheus (ed. Abel), 1885, Orphic Hymns and Argonautica
src.q: The disciples of Orpheus are read to have interpreted this fiction by asserting that Bacchus is to be understood as nothing other than the anima mundi [Soul of the World].

s: Ficino, Marsilio, Les trois livres de la vie (1582), on spirit of the world: Ficino (French 1582): images join our spirit to the stars through the Spirit of the World.

src.l: Ficino, Marsilio, 1582, Les trois livres de la vie
src.q: The Arabs say that when we manufacture images well and properly, if our spirit is very attentive to the work through imagination and effect, it joins itself to the stars with the Spirit of the World [Spiritus Mundi], and with the rays of the stars, through which the spirit of the world acts.
src.qo: Les Arabes disent que quand nous fabriquons bien & proprement les Images, si par l'imagination & l'effect nostre esprit est fort attentif à l'œuure, il se conioint aux Estoilles auecques l'Esprit du Monde, & auecques les rayons des Estoilles, par lesquels agit l'esprit du monde

s: anonymous, Mercurii zweyfacher Schlangen-Stab, das ist: I. Glücks-Ruthe. II. Menstruum seu solvens universale philosophicum (1679), on spirit of the world: spiritus mundi as food of life taken in through air and food.

src.l: anonymous, 1679, Mercurii zweyfacher Schlangen-Stab, das ist: I. Glücks-Ruthe. II. Menstruum seu solvens universale philosophicum
src.q: In the Animal Kingdom: This moistening and bringing of this Spiritus Mundi [spirit of the world] to their nourishment occurs both through the Aura [breath of air] (in which such food of life is abundantly contained) as well as in the enjoyment of food and drink according to their nature, because in all things such Spiritus Mundi [spirit of the world] is contained.
src.qo: Beschihet diese Befeuchtigung und Zubringung dieses Spiritus Mundi, zu ihrem Nutriment so wol per Auram (darinnen solche Lebens-Speiß häuffig enthalten ist /) als auch in Genießung ihrer Natur gemäßen Speiß und Trancks/ weiln in allen Dingen solcher Spiritus Mundi begriffen.

s: Khunrath, Heinrich, Catholic Magnesia of the Philosophers (1599), on spirit of the world: catching the spirit of the world from the air for the Stone.

src.l: Khunrath, Heinrich, 1599, Catholic Magnesia of the Philosophers
src.q: Here one must also keep in mind that some say one should and must catch the Spiritus Mundi secretissimum [most secret spirit of the world] for the Philosophical STONE from the air, or from the firmament of heaven, into certain materials which are specifically placed there for this purpose by the artificial arrangement of the artist.
src.qo: Allhier fellet ein auch mit zugedencke / das etliche sprechen / man solle vnd müsse Spiritum Mundi secretissimum, den Geheimbsten Geist der Weld / zum Philosophischen LSEIN / aus dem Lufft / oder aber vom Firmament des Himmels / in gewisse Materias, so auff kunstliche anordnung des Artisten darzu insonderheit hingestellet werden / erst fohen.

s: Ficino, Marsilio, Les trois livres de la vie (1582), on spirit of the world: Ficino: life drawn from world soul and world spirit by art and medicine.

src.l: Ficino, Marsilio, 1582, Les trois livres de la vie
src.q: And in this third book, the life that we draw from the soul of the world [anima mundi] and the spirit of the world [spiritus mundi], by means of art and medicine.
src.qo: Et en ce tiers, de la vie que nous tirons de l'ame du monde, & de l'esprit du monde, par le moyen de l'art, & de la medecine.

s: Antonius Andreae; Thomas Aquinas, Questions on the Three Principles / On Being and Essence (1475), on seminal reasons: Augustine via scholastic: Levi was in his fathers' loins through seminal reasons.

src.l: Antonius Andreae; Thomas Aquinas, 1475, Questions on the Three Principles / On Being and Essence
src.q: The first conclusion: although a seminal reason exists in matter, it is not the matter itself. I prove this thus: because Augustine, in the eighteenth book of De Genesi [On Genesis], says that Levi was in the loins of his fathers through seminal reasons;

s: Vladimir Solovyov, The Justification of the Good (1918), on seminal reasons: names the Stoic origin: the seed of Reason, logoi spermatikoi.

src.l: Vladimir Solovyov, 1918, The Justification of the Good
src.q: That which to the senses and sensibility is a deceptive appearance contains for reason ‘a reflection of the Idea,’ according to Plato, or ‘the seed of Reason,’ according to the Stoics (λόγοι σπερματικοί).

s: Bonaventura, Centiloquium Newly Printed (1503), on seminal reasons: scholastic definition: seminal and natural reasons the same in reality, differing in definition.

src.l: Bonaventura, 1503, Centiloquium Newly Printed
src.q: Similarly, natural reasons and seminal reasons are the same in reality, but they differ in definition: for "seed" refers to that from which something comes, while "nature" refers to that by which it comes.
src.qo: Similiter naturales rationes et seminales idem sunt re : sed differunt ra- tione : quia semē dicitur ex quo : natura vt a quo .

s: Hermes Trismegistus | Jamblichus | Proclus, The Divine Pymander, Asclepius, and On the Mysteries (1532), on seminal reasons: Ficino's Neoplatonic use: the soul gives rationes seminales to the body.

src.l: Hermes Trismegistus | Jamblichus | Proclus, 1532, The Divine Pymander, Asclepius, and On the Mysteries
src.q: Even while the soul is present in the body, neither the soul itself nor the rationes seminales [seed-reasons or formative principles] which it gives to the body suffer anything.
src.qo: Anima neque etiam dum adest corpori, patitur uel ipsa quicquid, uel rationes seminales, quas ipsa corpori tradit.

s: Paracelsus, The Works of Paracelsus, Volume 6: On Spagyric Preparations and Alchemical Transmutation (1590), on quintessence: Paracelsus: the quintessence separated from brandy by water bath, the wine-distillation method.

src.l: Paracelsus, 1590, The Works of Paracelsus, Volume 6: On Spagyric Preparations and Alchemical Transmutation
src.q: this brandy per Balneum [by water bath], and the quinta Essentia remains at the bottom in the form of an oil, separated from all the like.

s: Reusner, Hieronymus, Pandora: The Noblest Gift of God (1598), on quintessence: Reusner: the fifth essence heals sores, fistula and cancer.

src.l: Reusner, Hieronymus, 1598, Pandora: The Noblest Gift of God
src.q: Then the quinta essentia [fifth essence] will remain for you at the bottom, prettier and more beautiful than all gold. The same is good for healing sores and the corrosive or gnawing pests, just as the quinta essentia [fifth essence] of the mercurii [mercury] can heal fistula and cancer, and many others more.
src.qo: so wird dir die quinta essentia im boden bleiben / Hübscher vnd schöner dann alles Gold / dieselb ist gut die schäden zu heilen / vnd die corrosiuischen oder fressenden pre- sten / wie auch die quinta essentia des Mercurij die Fistel vnd den Krebs hei- len / vnd andere viel mehr.

s: Faust, Johannes Michael, New Alchemical Compendium, or Pandora Explained (1706), on quintessence: Faust: the quintessence draws life and health into the body from the Sun and stars.

src.l: Faust, Johannes Michael, 1706, New Alchemical Compendium, or Pandora Explained
src.q: **The Second Canon of this First Book reveals the sanctity of this mastery of the fifth essence / how and in what manner our quintessence is adorned by the Sun and the stars / so that their wonderful influence and the flowing-in of life and health into our body may be increased / and first regarding the mastery of the action.

s: Reusner, Hieronymus, Pandora: The Noblest Gift of God (1598), on quintessence: Reusner: the art of extracting the fifth essence from quicksilver and vitriol.

src.l: Reusner, Hieronymus, 1598, Pandora: The Noblest Gift of God
src.q: 209 The Art and Knowledge of extracting the quintam essentiam [fifth essence] from Quicksilver and Roman Vitriol. THe Almighty and Supreme God has ordained it so that the fifth essence of vitriol and of cuperose [copper vitriol/blue vitriol] be extracted, invisibly, with the quicksilver.

s: Magus Incognito (William Walker Atkinson), The Secret Doctrine of the Rosicrucians (1918), on plastic nature: quotes Cudworth's argument for a Plastic Nature against chance, mechanism and constant miracles.

src.l: Magus Incognito (William Walker Atkinson), 1918, The Secret Doctrine of the Rosicrucians
src.q: > "Therefore, since neither all things are produced fortuitously, or by the unguided mechanism of matter, nor God himself may be reasonably thought to do all things immediately and miraculously, it may well be concluded that there is a Plastic Nature under him, which, as an inferior and subordinate instrument, doth grudgingly execute that part of his providence which consists in the regular and orderly motion of matter;

s: William Harvey, Exercises on the Motion of the Heart (1651), on plastic nature: Harvey on the vis plastica of fertile eggs, the formative power at work.

src.l: William Harvey, 1651, Exercises on the Motion of the Heart
src.q: For just as fertile eggs are changed by their inherent vis plastica [formative force] into colliquamentum [embryonic liquid] (which later passes into blood), so subventanea [wind-eggs] are corrupted at the same time and putrefy.

s: Colonne, François-Marie-Pompée, Les principes de la nature, ou de la generation des choses (1731), on plastic nature: names natura plastica as the formative spirit or industrious nature.

src.l: Colonne, François-Marie-Pompée, 1731, Les principes de la nature, ou de la generation des choses
src.q: This is what the Academicians called Form, that is to say, the formative spirit, and many Ancients and others more modern have named Natura Plastica [Plastic Nature], or the industrious nature.

s: Libavius, Andreas, The Singular Works of Andreas Libavius, Part 1: On the Nature of Metals and Amber (1599), on plastic nature: Libavius says what the formative power is not.

src.l: Libavius, Andreas, 1599, The Singular Works of Andreas Libavius, Part 1: On the Nature of Metals and Amber
src.q: 306 The formative power [vis plastica] is not the soul of one assisting and fashioning its own organ for itself, nor is it a part of the sun, or the soil, or the heavens, etc.

s: Schelling, Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph von, Von der Weltseele (1806), on formative drive: Schelling defines what the concept of the formative drive implies.

src.l: Schelling, Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph von, 1806, Von der Weltseele
src.q: — The question arises: how does the general formative power of matter transition into a formative drive? The concept of the formative drive Bildungstrieb [the innate impulse in living organisms to develop and maintain their form] implies that formation does not occur blindly — that is, solely through forces inherent to matter as such — but that to the necessity inherent in these forces, the contingency of a foreign influence is added.

s: Schelling, Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph von, Erster Entwurf eines Systems der Naturphilosophie (1799), on formative drive: Schelling: sensibility, irritability and formative drive as branches of one force.

src.l: Schelling, Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph von, 1799, Erster Entwurf eines Systems der Naturphilosophie
src.q: And so it would surely be time to point out that sequence of levels in inorganic nature as well, and to justify the thought that the organic forces—sensibility, irritability, and formative drive Bildungstrieb [the innate impulse in living things to take on a specific form]—are all only branches of One Force, just as, without doubt, in light, in electricity, and so on, only One Force emerges in its various appearances.

s: Anonymous, Gotha Scholarly Journals for the Year 1781 (1781), on formative drive: 1781 report of Blumenbach researching the drive in the year he named it.

src.l: Anonymous, 1781, Gotha Scholarly Journals for the Year 1781
src.q: Blumenbach has been researching the formative drive, and only in this past February discovered an uncommonly simple method of reproduction in Haller’s Conferva cespitosa [tufted conferva (a type of algae)], a furry moss, on which Bonnet found his already-drawn earthworms 36 years ago.

s: Arthur Schopenhauer, Die Welt als Wille und Vorstellung (1818), on formative drive: Schopenhauer: the will acting blindly in the snail as formative impulse.

src.l: Arthur Schopenhauer, 1818, Die Welt als Wille und Vorstellung
src.q: In us, the Will acts according to motives, but in the snail it still acts blindly, as a formative impulse[original: "Bildungstrieb"; an innate biological drive toward growth and organization] directed outward.

s: Anonymous, Gotha Scholarly Journals for the Year 1781 (1781), on vital principle: 1781 report of Barthez's principium vitale as one driving force for all motions of the living body.

src.l: Anonymous, 1781, Gotha Scholarly Journals for the Year 1781
src.q: to light, when we tell them that he assumes, once and for all, a common driving force for all possible movements in the living body of man and for all functions of its parts, which he calls the principium vitale [vital principle], and with which he hopes to solve or burst all other physiological knots of doubt.

s: Marquis de Puysegur, On Animal Magnetism (1807), on vital principle: animal magnetism acts directly on the principe vital, which keeps equilibrium or health.

src.l: Marquis de Puysegur, 1807, On Animal Magnetism
src.q: One should never compare the effect of medicines to the effect of magnetic action, since the former act first on organs, while the latter always acts immediately on the principe vital [vital principle], to which it communicates the impression of a movement that is analogous to it, and which only serves to add to the efforts it is constantly making of its own accord to maintain equilibrium or health.

s: Samuel Hahnemann, Organon of the Healing Art (1921), on vital principle: Hahnemann's Lebensprincip tuned by the remedy.

src.l: Samuel Hahnemann, 1921, Organon of the Healing Art
src.q: for the greatest possible acceleration of the cure, but with the caution that the degree of potency of each dose varies slightly from that of the previous and subsequent doses, so that the vital principle Lebensprincip [the animating force of the organism], which is to be tuned to the similar medicinal disease, can never feel itself excited and outraged toward adverse counter-effects, as always happens with unmodified repeated doses, especially when repeated

s: Henri Bergson, Creative Evolution (1908), on vital principle: Bergson's critique: the vital principle as a foreman repairing the body's faults.

src.l: Henri Bergson, 1908, Creative Evolution
src.q: that it would take only the absence or deviation of one of them for nothing to function anymore, the mind's first movement is to have this army of little workers overseen by a wise foreman, the "principe vital [vital principle]," who would repair the faults committed at every instant, correct the effect of distractions, and put things back in place:

s: Schelling, Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph von, Erster Entwurf eines Systems der Naturphilosophie (1799), on vital force: Schelling argues the organism's non-chemical cause is an immaterial principle, the Lebenskraft.

src.l: Schelling, Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph von, 1799, Erster Entwurf eines Systems der Naturphilosophie
src.q: Now, the cause which partly cancels and partly changes the chemical forces and laws of matter in the organism cannot itself be a material one, since every matter itself is subject to the chemical process—therefore, it is an immaterial principle, which is rightly called Lebenskraft [vital force].

s: Schelling, Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph von, Von der Weltseele (1806), on vital force: Schelling sides with the defenders of the life force against chemical physiologists.

src.l: Schelling, Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph von, 1806, Von der Weltseele
src.q: I believe that after such discoveries, it is no longer to be regarded as a fiction when one—like the defenders of the life force [Lebenskraft], who in this regard are far superior to the chemical physiologists—ascribes to the universally distributed principles of nature a completely different activity in living organization than they show in inorganic nature.

s: Ernst Haeckel, The Riddle of the Universe (1901), on vital force: Haeckel's retrospective on Haller and the 'erroneous' vis vitalis.

src.l: Ernst Haeckel, 1901, The Riddle of the Universe
src.q: In postulating, however, a special "sensitive force or sensibility" for neural action, and a special "irritability" for muscular movement, Haller gave strong support to the erroneous idea of a specific "vital force" (vis vitalis).

s: Karl von Reichenbach, The Sensitive Man and his Relation to the Odic Force, Volume II (1855), on vital force: Reichenbach places his Od nearest to the Lebenskraft.

src.l: Karl von Reichenbach, 1855, The Sensitive Man and his Relation to the Odic Force, Volume II
src.q: Of all dynamids [forces or powers], Od is the one that comes closest to the Lebenskraft [life force], to this complex of as-yet-unexplored forces.

s: Николай Лосский, Bergson's Intuitive Philosophy (1922), on élan vital: Bergson's élan vital as the unity behind the divergent organic world.

src.l: Николай Лосский, 1922, Bergson's Intuitive Philosophy
src.q: Bergson calls it by the words élan vital [vital impetus/life force]. Thanks to the unity of the "vital impetus," the entire organic world is a harmonious whole, though, admittedly, not at all perfect: unity is the starting point of organic life, it lies in its past, and in the process of development, due to resistances encountered on the path, especially from dead matter, the stream $^1$) Creative Evolution, 24—26;

s: Semyon Lyudvigovich Frank, Introduction to Philosophy (1923), on élan vital: being as change and creative impulse (élan vital).

src.l: Semyon Lyudvigovich Frank, 1923, Introduction to Philosophy
src.q: According to the doctrine of the well-known modern philosopher Bergson, the foundation of being is not something unchanging, but is the very essence of change, time, effectiveness, or creativity—the very effort of doing, the creative impulse (élan vital) [vital impetus].

s: Николай Лосский, Bergson's Intuitive Philosophy (1922), on élan vital: individuals developing different sides of the original vital impetus.

src.l: Николай Лосский, 1922, Bergson's Intuitive Philosophy
src.q: In the organic world, there is a tendency toward individualization, where some individuals develop one side of the original vital impetus predominantly, others another.

s: Lewis Spence, An Encyclopaedia of Occultism (1920), on animal magnetism: a new era in the doctrine of a magnetic fluid.

src.l: Lewis Spence, 1920, An Encyclopaedia of Occultism
src.q: The whole soul and the whole body are contained in the hands as a medium of influence." Mesmerism or Animal Magnetism.—In the latter half of the eighteenth century a new era was inaugurated in connection with the doctrine of a magnetic fluid.

s: Joseph Philippe François Deleuze, Histoire critique du magnétisme animal (1813), on animal magnetism: 1813 critic: the magnetic state is a nervous crisis.

src.l: Joseph Philippe François Deleuze, 1813, Histoire critique du magnétisme animal
src.q: DU MAGNÉTISME ANIMAL. the marvelous that this state presents can lead those who observe it to the most absurd consequences, if they do not look upon it as a simple nervous crisis, which is in the natural order, and which cannot lead to the discovery of knowledge foreign to that which we receive through the senses.

s: Eckartshausen, Karl von, Aufschlüsse zur Magie (1791), on animal magnetism: 1791: animal magnetism and electricity as the means of the animal economy.

src.l: Eckartshausen, Karl von, 1791, Aufschlüsse zur Magie
src.q: and this means is electricity and thierischer Magnetismus [animal magnetism]. That plus- and minus-electricity is the natural consequence of the disruption of the animal economy is most convincingly proven by the experiments made with electricity on those suffering from fever.

s: Schelling, Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph von, Von der Weltseele (1806), on animal electricity: Schelling: the most irritable organ reveals galvanism, which is more general than imagined.

src.l: Schelling, Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph von, 1806, Von der Weltseele
src.q: What changes bodies produce in one another through mere contact, we do not see in most cases because we have neither instruments nor organs to indicate this to us: in this case, the most irritable of all organs indicates it to us. Galvanism [Galvanismus] is therefore something far more general than is usually imagined. — The analogies force themselves upon us.

s: Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling, First Outline of a System of the Philosophy of Nature (1799), on animal electricity: Schelling contrasts animal galvanism with its negative in plants.

src.l: Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling, 1799, First Outline of a System of the Philosophy of Nature
src.q: The plant will be only negatively galvanizable. (Galvanism, it is said, does not extend over the plant kingdom. Why not? It becomes only the negative of animal galvanism in the plant.

s: Frank Podmore, Modern Spiritualism: A History and a Criticism, Vol. I (1902), on odic force: Podmore defines odyle/odic force and the sensations of light and temperature it was said to produce.

src.l: Frank Podmore, 1902, Modern Spiritualism: A History and a Criticism, Vol. I
src.q: For the effluence assumed to produce these sensations he proposed the name odyle, or odic force. The sensations were broadly of two kinds—vague feelings of temperature, which were either pleasant or unpleasant, and quite definite perceptions of light and colour.

s: Karl von Reichenbach, The Sensitive Man and His Relation to the Odic Force (1854), on odic force: Reichenbach himself on the polarity of odic light in sunbeams.

src.l: Karl von Reichenbach, 1854, The Sensitive Man and His Relation to the Odic Force
src.q: It follows from all this that the odic [related to the Odic force] component of sunbeams can be polarized; that the transmitted light possesses predominantly od-negative [negative Odic force] properties, while the reflected light possesses predominantly od-positive [positive Odic force] properties;

s: Atwood, Mary Anne, A  Suggestive Inquiry into the Hermetic Mystery : with a Dissertation on the more Celebrated of the Alchemical Philosophers ... (1920), on odic force: Atwood on Od as a 'new imponderable' that few believed in.

src.l: Atwood, Mary Anne, 1920, A  Suggestive Inquiry into the Hermetic Mystery : with a Dissertation on the more Celebrated of the Alchemical Philosophers ...
src.q: for though experiments of recent date seem to supply concurrent evidence, and the phenomena of Mesmerism have helped to force again on the minds of the more observing portion of mankind the supposition of a "New Imponderable," or "Odic Force," yet few believe;

s: Eliphas Lévi, Transcendental Magic: Doctrine and Ritual, Vol. 1 (1861), on astral light: Lévi: the great magical agent preserves all imprints and images.

src.l: Eliphas Lévi, 1861, Transcendental Magic: Doctrine and Ritual, Vol. 1
src.q: We have said that in the great magical agent, which is the lumière astrale [astral light], all imprints of things are preserved, all images formed either by rays or by reflections.

s: Guaita, Stanislas de, Le serpent de la Genèse. Première septaine (livre I). Le temple de Satan (1891), on astral light: Guaita: the fluid governing instincts, dispenser of elementary life, agent of birth and death.

src.l: Guaita, Stanislas de, 1891, Le serpent de la Genèse. Première septaine (livre I). Le temple de Satan
src.q: ¹ In the first esoteric sense, it is the Lumière astrale [Astral Light], that implacable fluid which governs the instincts; that universal dispenser of elementary life, the fatal agent of birth and death;

s: H.P. Blavatsky, Theosophical Glossary (1906), on astral light: Theosophy's take: the invisible region surrounding the globe.

src.l: H.P. Blavatsky, 1906, Theosophical Glossary
src.q: The reader must not confuse it with the ASTRAL SOUL, another name for the lower Manas, or Kama-Manas so-called, the reflection of the HIGHER Ego. Astral Light (Occult.). The invisible region that surrounds our globe, as it does every other,

s: Eliphas Lévi, Transcendental Magic: Doctrine and Ritual, Vol. 1 (1861), on astral light: Lévi: what we truly will remains written in the astral light.

src.l: Eliphas Lévi, 1861, Transcendental Magic: Doctrine and Ritual, Vol. 1
src.q: everything that we truly will, that is to say, everything that we confirm by our acts, remains written in the astral light [the universal fluidic medium], where our reflections are preserved;

s: Balthasar Bekker, The Enchanted World (1694), on ruach: states the Hebrew ruah means both spirits and winds.

src.l: Balthasar Bekker, 1694, The Enchanted World
src.q: ,, ble Spirits, the Hebrew term רוח ruah ,, having these two meanings, that of Spirits & that of winds.) ,, The Angels, ,, being therefore immaterial, are essentially ,, distinguished among themselves in dignity, ,, as if by degrees, some being above ,, others, to which the Author makes application of these words: For a higher than the highest regardeth, and there be higher than they.

s: Overbeck, Johann Daniel; Gläsener, Justus Martin, Dissertatio Philologico-Theologica De Trinitate In Scriptis Cabbalistarum Et Rabbinorum Non Christiana, Sed Mere Platonica (1741), on ruach: Ruach ha-Qodesh as a divine breathing that moved the prophets.

src.l: Overbeck, Johann Daniel; Gläsener, Justus Martin, 1741, Dissertatio Philologico-Theologica De Trinitate In Scriptis Cabbalistarum Et Rabbinorum Non Christiana, Sed Mere Platonica
src.q: Ruach Ha-Qodesh or Holy Spirit among the Jews is a certain gift of prophecy, or, to express it in the words of Vitringa g): "It is a divine thing or a certain breathing, which affected the Prophets, and the last degree of prophetic revelation.

s: Columna, Petrus (Galatinus), Work on the Secrets of Catholic Truth Against Jewish Obstinacy (1518), on ruach: oldest: Galatinus glosses Ruah ha-Qodesh as spirit of holiness.

src.l: Columna, Petrus (Galatinus), 1518, Work on the Secrets of Catholic Truth Against Jewish Obstinacy
src.q: ורוח הקדש ve-Ruach ha-Qodesh, that is, and the Holy Spirit. Or even if we call it "the Holy Spirit," as they more frequently do: רוח הקדש Ruah ha-Qodesh, that is, the Spirit of Holiness, or of the Sanctuary.

s: Richtenfels, Johannes, Promotoris Edlen Ritters von Orthopetra ...Theosophischer Wunder-Saal, Des in die unvergleichliche Schönheit Der Underirdischen Königin Juno inniglich verliebten Uberirdischen Königs Magniphosauri. Das ist: Theosophischer Schau-Paltz [!], Des entdeckten geistlichen Lebens und Wesens aller Creaturen, Insonderheit des Brodt- und Weines (1709), on ruach: the ruach that hovered over the waters of creation.

src.l: Richtenfels, Johannes, 1709, Promotoris Edlen Ritters von Orthopetra ...Theosophischer Wunder-Saal, Des in die unvergleichliche Schönheit Der Underirdischen Königin Juno inniglich verliebten Uberirdischen Königs Magniphosauri. Das ist: Theosophischer Schau-Paltz [!], Des entdeckten geistlichen Lebens und Wesens aller Creaturen, Insonderheit des Brodt- und Weines
src.q: The answer is in the joyous and living echo of the Holy Spirit, the Spirit (רוח) [Hebrew: Ruach/Spirit] which hovered over the waters of the first creation, Gen.

s: Yiśrā'ēl Ben-Moše, Kabbalistic Disputation on the Soul and the Rhythmic Work of Abraham Ibn Ezra (1635), on breath of life: Kabbalistic reading: the nishmat chayim breathed in makes man a nephesh.

src.l: Yiśrā'ēl Ben-Moše, 1635, Kabbalistic Disputation on the Soul and the Rhythmic Work of Abraham Ibn Ezra
src.q: Whence that vivifying spirit is called in scripture נשמת חיים [Neschamah], the breath of life: from which that corporeal spirit becomes living, and thence it is denominated Nephesh, as if נפשה [diffused], namely from that vivifying spirit: According to that in Genesis 2, verse 7: "And he breathed into his face the נשמת חיים [breath of life]: then immediately it is subjoined: "And man became a Nephesh.

s: Francesco Giorgi (Giorgio Veneto), Three songs on the harmony of the whole world. With a recently added index of them (1545), on breath of life: 1545: 'breath of lives' plural means every kind of life was contained in it.

src.l: Francesco Giorgi (Giorgio Veneto), 1545, Three songs on the harmony of the whole world. With a recently added index of them
src.q: Hence, not without mystery, Scripture says that God, when he gave life to man, breathed into his face the breath, or soul of lives, which the Hebrews call נשמת חיים nif-mat haiim: it says "of lives," so that it may be intimated that in that breath, or soul, which was infused, every kind of life was contained, which pertains to the whole man himself.

s: Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan (1651 first edition) (1651), on breath of life: Hobbes: the breath of life signifies only that God gave him life.

src.l: Thomas Hobbes, 1651, Leviathan (1651 first edition)
src.q: breathed into his nostrils (spiraculum vitæ) the breath of life, and man was made a living soul. There the breath of life inspired by God, signifies no more, but that God gave him life;

s: Paracelsus, Erster [- zehender] Theil der Bücher und Schrifften des edlen, hochgelehrten und bewehrten philosophi und medici Philippi Theophrasti Bombast von Hohenheim ... (1589), on breath of life: Paracelsus: God gives life through the spiraculum vitae and takes it back through the spiraculum mortis.

src.l: Paracelsus, 1589, Erster [- zehender] Theil der Bücher und Schrifften des edlen, hochgelehrten und bewehrten philosophi und medici Philippi Theophrasti Bombast von Hohenheim ...
src.q: Thus, just as God breathed life into the flesh through the Spiraculum Vitae [breath of life]; thus He takes it back through the Spiraculum Mortis [breath of death], and the spirit remains what it was before, with the addition that it is embodied in the flesh: because of which addition it separates itself from the angels, and from the heavenly spirits, into a special stall.

s: Avicenna (Ibn Sina), القانون في الطب (al-Qānūn fī al-Ṭibb / Canon of Medicine) (1076), on rūḥ: Avicenna: the rūḥ moving inward under grief causes fainting fever.

src.l: Avicenna (Ibn Sina), 1076, القانون في الطب (al-Qānūn fī al-Ṭibb / Canon of Medicine)
src.q: Faint-related day fever may occur from the movement of the rūḥ [spirit] inward and its congestion therein due to excessive grief, until it causes fainting.

s: Jurjānī, ʻAlī ibn Muḥammad, al-Sayyid al-Sharīf, 1340-1413, Sharḥ al-Mawāqif (1455), on rūḥ: Jurjānī: the animal spirit generated from the vapours of the humours.

src.l: Jurjānī, ʻAlī ibn Muḥammad, al-Sayyid al-Sharīf, 1340-1413, 1455, Sharḥ al-Mawāqif
src.q: This requires an equilibrium of the animal spirit rūḥ ḥaywānī [a subtle vapor that carries life], which is generated from the vapors of the humors.

s: Duncan Black Macdonald, The Religious Attitude and Life in Islam (1909), on rūḥ: the Qur'anic verse 'the spirit is of the affair of my Lord'.

src.l: Duncan Black Macdonald, 1909, The Religious Attitude and Life in Islam
src.q: This belongs apparently to the rūḥ of man, for, in explanation, Qurʾān, xvii, 87, is again quoted: “Say, ‘The spirit (rūḥ) is of the affair of my Lord.

s: Ali Çelebi, Kınalızade, 1510-1571, Ahlâk-ı alâ'î (1564), on rūḥ: Kınalızade: animal and natural spirits linking heart and liver.

src.l: Ali Çelebi, Kınalızade, 1510-1571, 1564, Ahlâk-ı alâ'î
src.q: For example, the liver is necessary to find life through the "animal spirit" ruh-i hayvani, yet it is dependent on the heart. The heart, in being nourished by the "natural spirit" ruh-i tabii, is dependent on the liver.

s: Various Taoist Masters, Essence of the Taoist Canon (1922), on qi: Daoist canon: humans receive the qi of Heaven and Earth; original qi.

src.l: Various Taoist Masters, 1922, Essence of the Taoist Canon
src.q: 2. Nourishing Qi Humans receive the Qi of Heaven and Earth to be born. There must be a portion of Original Vitality Yuanqi (元氣). The fundamental life force inherited from one's parents.

s: attributed to Huangdi, Commentary on the Yellow Emperor's Classic: Spiritual Pivot (Huangdi Neijing Lingshu), Vol 1 (1587), on qi: guarding the spirit as guarding blood and qi in medicine.

src.l: attributed to Huangdi, 1587, Commentary on the Yellow Emperor's Classic: Spiritual Pivot (Huangdi Neijing Lingshu), Vol 1
src.q: The superior practitioner guards the spirit, which means guarding the excess or deficiency of the patient’s blood and Qi 氣 (qì): the vital life force or energy that flows through the body to determine whether to supplement or drain.

s: Han, Wŏn-jin, 1682-1751, Kyŏngŭi kimunnok (1722), on qi: Korean Neo-Confucian dispute over qi versus principle.

src.l: Han, Wŏn-jin, 1682-1751, 1722, Kyŏngŭi kimunnok
src.q: Shen both mistake Qi [vital energy/matter] for Principle. To explain "the marvel of Principle through Principle" or "Principle containing Principle"—these theories are all incorrect.

s: 張介賓, 景岳全書·卷二十~卷二十一 (vol 12) (1609), on qi: calm non-action lets qi flow properly.

src.l: 張介賓, 1609, 景岳全書·卷二十~卷二十一 (vol 12)
src.q: Only by remaining calm, indifferent, and free from purposeful action can the Qi [vital energy] flow properly. Afterward, use salty and bitter flavors to transform the grain, and then the stool will pass.

s: 尹真人 Yin Zhenren (attrib.), 性命雙修萬神圭旨 :4卷. [China] : 吳之鶴, 明萬曆43 [1615]. (1615), on jing (essence): 1615: sages refine jing, qi and shen to preserve their bodies.

src.l: 尹真人 Yin Zhenren (attrib.), 1615, 性命雙修萬神圭旨 :4卷. [China] : 吳之鶴, 明萬曆43 [1615].
src.q: Therefore, the Sages and Worthies maintain the Jie Ding Hui [Precepts, Concentration, and Wisdom] to empty their hearts, and they refine the Jing Qi Shen [Essence, Vitality, and Spirit] to preserve their bodies.

s: 高濂, 遵生八牋·卷一 (vol 1) (1596), on jing (essence): jing, qi and shen as the three internal treasures.

src.l: 高濂, 1596, 遵生八牋·卷一 (vol 1)
src.q: The scripture says: essence, qi [vital energy], and spirit form the three inner treasures; the ears, eyes, and mouth form the three outer treasures.

s: 柳華陽 Liu Huayang (b. 1736), 柳華陽. 華陽金仙證論 ; 慧命經. [China : s.n.], 清嘉慶4 [1799] 補刊本. (1799), on jing (essence): 1794: essence, qi and spirit contained in heart and kidneys.

src.l: 柳華陽 Liu Huayang (b. 1736), 1799, 柳華陽. 華陽金仙證論 ; 慧命經. [China : s.n.], 清嘉慶4 [1799] 補刊本.
src.q: However, terms like Kan and Li [Water and Fire], Lead and Mercury, or Essence, Qi, and Spirit [Jing, Qi, Shen] are all fully contained within the Heart and the Kidneys.

s: Annambhatta (trans. James R. Ballantyne), Compendium of Logic (Tarka Sangraha) (1851), on prāṇa: classical definition: the air circulating within the body is called prana, named variously by its accidents.

src.l: Annambhatta (trans. James R. Ballantyne), 1851, Compendium of Logic (Tarka Sangraha)
src.q: || Original Text || śarīrānta:saṃcārī vāyu:prāṇa: sacaiko'pyupādhibhedātprāṇāpānādisaṃjñāṃ labhate। || Translation || The air that circulates within the body is called breath (prāṇa).

s: Vasugupta; Kṣemarāja, comm., Shiva Sutra Vimarshini (1911), on prāṇa: Kashmir Shaiva practice: resting in the middle breath between prana and apana.

src.l: Vasugupta; Kṣemarāja, comm., 1911, Shiva Sutra Vimarshini
src.q: "By relying on the middle breath madhyama-prāṇa which is between the path of inhalation prāṇa and exhalation apāna, and by supporting oneself on the power of knowledge jñāna-śakti, one attains the posture āsana situated there.

s: Anonymous, བསྟན་འགྱུར། སྡེ་དགེ། རྒྱུད་འགྲེལ། ཀི (Derge Tengyur, vol. 32) (1982), on prāṇa: Tibetan tantric commentary: the life-force breath rising from the navel produces speech.

src.l: Anonymous, 1982, བསྟན་འགྱུར། སྡེ་དགེ། རྒྱུད་འགྲེལ། ཀི (Derge Tengyur, vol. 32)
src.q: In that way, the vital breath [prāṇa] known as the "life-force" arising from the region of the navel is stirred by the intellect. Because of the desire to grasp external objects, the eight locations of articulation are touched, and the letters are produced.

s: Vraj Vallabha Dwivedi (ed.), The Heart of the Yogini (1965), on prāṇa: lists the ten vital airs headed by prana.

src.l: Vraj Vallabha Dwivedi (ed.), 1965, The Heart of the Yogini

s: Sushruta, सुश्रुतसंहिता (Suśruta Saṃhitā) (1833), on ojas: Sushruta on the nature of ojas: cool, white, oily, the best seat of life.

src.l: Sushruta, 1833, सुश्रुतसंहिता (Suśruta Saṃhitā)
src.q: Here are the verses: The nature of ojas. Ojas is soma-like [lunar/cooling], oily, white, cool, stable, and spreading; it is distinct, soft, and is considered the best seat of life.

s: Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna (trans.), An English Translation of the Sushruta Samhita, Based on Original Sanskrit Text (1907), on ojas: Sushruta: ojas permeates the body and its loss brings emaciation and dissolution.

src.l: Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna (trans.), 1907, An English Translation of the Sushruta Samhita, Based on Original Sanskrit Text
src.q: The whole body with its limbs and members is permeated with Ojas, and a loss or diminution in its natural quantity leads to the gradual emaciation (and ultimate dissolution) of organism.

s: Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna (trans.), An English Translation of the Sushruta Samhita, Based on Original Sanskrit Text (1907), on ojas: Ojas as the quintessence of all bodily tissues, identified with vital power.

src.l: Kaviraj Kunja Lal Bhishagratna (trans.), 1907, An English Translation of the Sushruta Samhita, Based on Original Sanskrit Text
src.q: The quintessence of all the fundamental principles of the body, starting with lymph chyle and ending with semen, is called the Ojas, which is identical with what is termed "vital power.

s: Charaka; Avinash Chandra Kaviratna (trans.), Charaka-Samhita (1890), on ojas: Charaka: in the eighth month ojas passes between mother and foetus.

src.l: Charaka; Avinash Chandra Kaviratna (trans.), 1890, Charaka-Samhita
src.q: In the eighth month the fœtus draws from the mother, and the mother draws from the fœtus, through the juice-bearing ducts, again and again, that ingredient (dhatu) which is called ojas.

s: Vāgbhaṭa, The Compendium of Alchemical Jewels (1927), on ojas: Vagbhata's rasashastra: a remedy that increases ojas.

src.l: Vāgbhaṭa, 1927, The Compendium of Alchemical Jewels
src.q: It increases the Ojas [vital essence] and tissues, provides strength, and destroys anemia. It is wholesome, removes all poisons, eliminates artificial toxins, and cures chronic diarrhea and similar ailments.

s: Gheranda, Gheranda Samhita (Sanskrit-English) (1915), on kuṇḍalinī: the goddess sleeping in the Muladhara as a serpent of three and a half coils.

src.l: Gheranda, 1915, Gheranda Samhita (Sanskrit-English)
src.q: The great goddess Kuṇḍalinī, the energy of Self, Ātma-śakti [spiritual force], sleeps in the Mūlādhāra [base center/rectum]; she has the form of a serpent having three coils and a half.

s: Sarngadeva, Ocean of Music, Volume 1 (1898), on kuṇḍalinī: 13th-c.: within the root lotus; straightened to the Brahmarandhra she bestows immortality.

src.l: Sarngadeva, 1898, Ocean of Music, Volume 1
src.q: [120] Within that Root Lotus resides the Kundalini, the Creative Power of the Absolute (Brahma-shakti). When she is brought to straightness all the way to the Opening of the Absolute (Brahma-randhra), she bestows immortality.

s: Abhinavagupta, The Light of the Tantras (1918), on kuṇḍalinī: Abhinavagupta: the subtle kundalini power rises in union with Shiva.

src.l: Abhinavagupta, 1918, The Light of the Tantras
src.q: To explain: the supreme, subtle Kundalini power kuṇḍalinī śakti, having attained a state of friction and union saṃghaṭṭa with Shiva—a state characterized by mutual harmony and the condition of the "churning rod"—rises up.

s: Gheranda, Gheranda Samhita (Sanskrit-English) (1915), on kuṇḍalinī: practice: breath retention wakes the serpent and it rises.

src.l: Gheranda, 1915, Gheranda Samhita (Sanskrit-English)
src.q: By restraining the breath by Kumbhaka [breath retention] in this way, the Serpent Kuṇḍalinī, feeling suffocated awakes and rises upwards to the Brahmarandhra [the aperture at the crown of the head].

s: Anonymous, བསྟན་འགྱུར། སྡེ་དགེ། གསོ་རིག ཧེ (Derge Tengyur, vol. 198) (1982), on rlung (wind): names the five kinds of wind, the core doctrine.

src.q: When each of the humors, such as rlung [wind/Vata] and the others, undergoes increase, balance, or decrease, they form six combinations as follows: 1.

s: Robert Henry Codrington, The Melanesians (1891), on mana: Codrington's definition of mana as a power beyond ordinary men, attaching to people and objects.

src.l: Robert Henry Codrington, 1891, The Melanesians
src.q: ‘Mana.’ beyond the ordinary power of men, outside the common processes of nature; it is present in the atmosphere of life, attaches itself to persons and to things, and is manifested by results which can only be ascribed to its operation.

s: Edward Shortland, Maori Religion and Mythology (1854), on mana: Maori usage: the mana of the land obtained by the chief who took possession.

src.l: W.D. Westervelt, 1916, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes

src.l: W.D. Westervelt, 1915, Legends of Gods and Ghosts (Hawaiian Mythology)

src.l: Vogel, Paul Joachim Siegmund, 1793, Versuch über die Religion der alten Ägypter und Griechen

s: Henri L. Joly, Legend in Japanese Art (1908), on kami: Kami as protective deities of the soil and spirit of food.

src.l: Henri L. Joly, 1908, Legend in Japanese Art
src.q: Several of the Kami are protective deities of the soil: Uga no Mitama no Mikoto is the spirit of food. Sukuna hikona no Kami, the scarecrow god.

src.l: Ō no Yasumaro, 712, Kojiki (古事記), Vol. 1

s: Manuzio, Paolo, Catullus, with the Commentary of Marc-Antoine Muret, Tibullus, and Propertius (1558), on genius loci: Virgil: praying to the genius of the place.

src.l: Manuzio, Paolo, 1558, Catullus, with the Commentary of Marc-Antoine Muret, Tibullus, and Propertius

The same author: > Thus having spoken, he binds his temples with a leafy branch, > And prays to the genius of the place, and to Earth, the first of gods, > And the nymphs, and the rivers still unknown.

s: Wagner, Bernhard; Silberrad, Johann Paul, Dissertation on the Natural Knowledge of Angelic Existence (1688), on genius loci: 1688: a tutelary genius assigned to every region and city.

src.l: Wagner, Bernhard; Silberrad, Johann Paul, 1688, Dissertation on the Natural Knowledge of Angelic Existence
src.q: They assigned a certain Tutelary Genius not only to individual men, but also to every kingdom, province, region, city, and people, whom they called the Genius of the place, who presided over it as a patron and protector, promoting good things for it and averting evils.

s: Gisbert Cuper, Three Books of Observations (1670), on genius loci: daemones presiding over places were called genii loci.

src.l: Gisbert Cuper, 1670, Three Books of Observations

s: Iamblichus; tr. Theodor Hopfner, On the Secret Teachings (1922), on daimōn: Iamblichus: one daemon rules over all the part-daemons within us.

src.l: Iamblichus; tr. Theodor Hopfner, 1922, On the Secret Teachings
src.q: For whatever you choose to bring forward as proof for your (opposing) claim—that there are many daemons set over different parts of the body, a daemon of health, of beauty, and of the other states of our limbs, and that finally a single daemon is placed as a common overseer over all these (part- and limb-)daemons—this you must only understand as an argument for the rule of a single (and unified) daemon over all that is in us.

s: Proclus, Diadochus, 412-485, Commentary on the First Alcibiades of Plato (1820), on daimōn: Proclus: Plato found Love called a great daimon in Orpheus.

src.l: Proclus, Diadochus, 412-485, 1820, Commentary on the First Alcibiades of Plato
src.q: And it seems to me that Plato, having found this same god in Orpheus—who is called both Love and a great daimon—also loved such a hymn regarding Love himself.

s: Plato, Phaedo (1890), on daimōn: the guardian daemon that stands by every man from birth (Menander).

src.l: Plato, 1890, Phaedo
src.q: 67 c 5 n. ὁ ἑκάστου δαίμων [each person's daemon]: cp. for the mystic doctrine of the guardian δαίμων [guardian spirit] Menander (fr. 550 Kock) A daemon stands by every man immediately upon his birth as a guide of life.

src.l: Cicero, Marcus Tullius, 1488, On Duties
src.q: As the stoici [Stoics] teach, the universe functions as a single city governed by divine reason. If we are parts of this greater whole, then the interests of the individual must be subordinate to the interests of the entire human family.

src.l: Cicero, Marcus Tullius, 1488, On Duties

We should follow nature in this, that we seek and demonstrate the common utility with our duties, such as sharing one's property with others, one work for another, and one labor for another, so that the society and union of humans may be kept steady, firm, and undivided.
