(1728), on Galenic medicine: states the doctrine: Galenists hold bodies consist of four temperaments and fluids.

src.l: Roth-Scholtz, Friedrich (1687-1736), 1728, Deutsches theatrum chemicum, auf welchem der berühmtesten Philosophen und Alchymisten Schrifften, die von dem Stein der Weisen, von Verwandlung der schlechten Metalle in bessere ... handeln ... vorgestellet werden / Zweyter Theil.
src.q: And this is also the consideration why the Galenists claim the bodies consist of four temperaments and fluids. For after a great deal of earth or water comes into the mixture, as if from the accidental origins, the body becomes either melancholic, cold, and dry;

s: Daniel Sennert, On the Consensus and Dissensus of Chemists with Aristotelian and Galenic Scholars, Book I (1619), on Galenic medicine: Sennert defines pseudo-Galenists who rely on Galen's authority over reason and experience.

src.l: Daniel Sennert, 1619, On the Consensus and Dissensus of Chemists with Aristotelian and Galenic Scholars, Book I
src.q: Pseudo-Galenists, who they are. Pseudo-Galenici [false Galenists] are that stubborn race of men who think that nothing is to be accepted unless it is found in Galen, and in judging truth and falsehood, they rely not so much on reason and experience as on the authority of Galen.

s: Retzel, Georg Friedrich, Der Geheimen Natur eröffnete Pforten und deroselben würckende Eigenschafften in Gut und Böse (1718), on Galenic medicine: Paracelsian complaint about the Galenists' long compound prescriptions.

src.l: Retzel, Georg Friedrich, 1718, Der Geheimen Natur eröffnete Pforten und deroselben würckende Eigenschafften in Gut und Böse
src.q: I do not know upon what foundation the old Galenici [Galenists; followers of traditional herbal medicine] devised such extensive composita [compounds] and long recepta [prescriptions].

s: Conring, Hermann, On the Ancient Hermetic Medicine of the Egyptians and the New Medicine of the Paracelsians (1648), on Paracelsian medicine: Conring: the Paracelsians call the four humours empty names, the core doctrinal break.

src.l: Conring, Hermann, 1648, On the Ancient Hermetic Medicine of the Egyptians and the New Medicine of the Paracelsians
src.q: Both of which are Paracelsian. Now, indeed, mention is made more than once in ancient Hermetic writings of the humors of our body—blood, phlegm, black and yellow bile—which the Paracelsians nevertheless dare to pronounce as nothing but empty names;

s: Andreas Libavius, Necessary Appendix to the Synthesis of Chemical Secrets (1615), on Paracelsian medicine: Libavius berates the Paracelsians for damning Galen and the ancient antidotes.

src.l: Andreas Libavius, 1615, Necessary Appendix to the Synthesis of Chemical Secrets
src.q: But truly, you Paracelsians, who damn Galen, ascribe fables to him, explode ancient antidotes—even if not of Galenic invention—wish for the lengthy canons of the ancients to be sent to the vinegar jar, and call the disciples of Hippocrates who do not agree with you Momuses [mockers] and incarnate devils—to all of which you have diabolically smeared your pages—must I cajole you with some pleasant and soft touch?

s: Colberg, Ehregott Daniel, Das platonisch-hermetische Christenthum (1709), on Paracelsian medicine: Colberg: Paracelsists set against Aristotelians and Galenists.

src.l: Colberg, Ehregott Daniel, 1709, Das platonisch-hermetische Christenthum
src.q: others, however, supposed that the Rosicrucian brothers were nothing but Paracelsists [followers of Paracelsus] who wanted to gain status for Paracelsus and his followers against the Aristotelians and Galenists [traditional university scholars and physicians] and draw them to their side.

s: Kunckel von Löwenstern, Johann, Collegium physico-chymicum experimentale, oder Laboratorium chymicum (1738), on Helmontian medicine: Kunckel names the Helmontian as a school beside the Cartesian, with Helmont's gas and blas.

src.l: Kunckel von Löwenstern, Johann, 1738, Collegium physico-chymicum experimentale, oder Laboratorium chymicum
src.q: This one is a Helmontian, that one a Cartesian, and so on. One has gas and blas [the formative force of the stars, according to van Helmont].

s: Herman Boerhaave, Elements of Chemistry (1732), on Helmontian medicine: Boerhaave disputes a specific Helmontian chemical claim.

src.l: Herman Boerhaave, 1732, Elements of Chemistry
src.q: Not as the Helmontians claim, that here the Sulfur of Wine has associated itself with the alkaline salt: for in my experiments, the water seeks the salt as long as water is in the alcohol, and the alcohol is rejected.

s: Anonymous, Chemical Theater, Volume Six (1661), on Helmontian medicine: the reception: Helmont's writings as a new light in medicine.

src.l: Anonymous, 1661, Chemical Theater, Volume Six
src.q: Although it has come to pass by the immense mercy of our God that, in this century, a singular and clear light in Medicine has shone forth for us unworthy men for the comfort of the sick, through Johannes Baptista Helmontius, and that it has been recognized and held dear by very many physicians greedy for the truth, and for the sake of this Light have read and considered the Helmontian writings not unwillingly;

s: Becher, Johann Joachim, Chymisches Laboratorium oder unter-erdische Naturkündigung (1680), on Helmontian medicine: Becher's verdict that Helmont measured nature by imagination, not experience.

src.l: Becher, Johann Joachim, 1680, Chymisches Laboratorium oder unter-erdische Naturkündigung
src.q: I, however, concede to him that he was not ignorant in theory, even if Doctor Helmontius behaved in practice in a Helmontian manner and measured the nature of things not according to experience but according to his imagination.

s: Knorr von Rosenroth, Christian, Kabbala denudata, seu, doctrina Hebraeorum transcendentalis et metaphysica atque theologica : opus antiquissimae philosophiae barbaricae variis speciminibus refertissimum ... (1677), on Cambridge Platonism: More: the Hylarchic Principle or Spirit of Nature orders the material world.

src.l: Knorr von Rosenroth, Christian, 1677, Kabbala denudata, seu, doctrina Hebraeorum transcendentalis et metaphysica atque theologica : opus antiquissimae philosophiae barbaricae variis speciminibus refertissimum ...
src.q: From this place, I surmise that Metatron may correspond to what I call the Hylarchic Principle [the ruling principle of matter], or the Spirit of Nature, which is the immediate decorator and orderer of the material World.

s: Knorr von Rosenroth, Christian (1636-1689), Kabbala denudata, seu, doctrina Hebraeorum transcendentalis et metaphysica atque theologica : opus antiquissimae philosophiae barbaricae variis speciminibus refertissimum ... / Tomus secundus. (1677), on Cambridge Platonism: More hopes the hylarchic principle will not slacken search for mechanical causes.

src.l: Knorr von Rosenroth, Christian (1636-1689), 1677, Kabbala denudata, seu, doctrina Hebraeorum transcendentalis et metaphysica atque theologica : opus antiquissimae philosophiae barbaricae variis speciminibus refertissimum ... / Tomus secundus.
src.q: I hope that my demonstrations of the principle called Hylarchic [the ruling principle of matter], which I have elaborated with such care and effort, will not slacken human industry in searching out the mechanical reasons of nature that are truly present.

s: Wilhelm Windelband, A History of Modern Philosophy (1919), on Cambridge Platonism: what the Cambridge Platonists held about innate moral ideas.

src.l: Wilhelm Windelband, 1919, A History of Modern Philosophy
src.q: The Cambridge Platonists, who from a psychological point of view considered moral ideas to be "innate," saw the norm of morality in the reasonable nature of man given by God and his ever-higher perfection.

s: Julien Offray de La Mettrie, L'Homme machine (Man a Machine) (1912), on Stahl's animism: La Mettrie challenges the Stahlians on how the soul could execute so many bodily movements: the doctrine stated by its opponent.

src.l: Julien Offray de La Mettrie, 1912, L'Homme machine (Man a Machine)
src.q: Now, I beg, or rather I defy, the Stahlians to tell me—they who know so well everything our soul can do—how it would be possible for it to execute so quickly so many movements, movements that take place so far from it, and in so many

s: Maine de Biran, Philosophical Works of Maine de Biran (1841), on Montpellier vitalism: Maine de Biran on Barthez's principle of life and sensibility in each organ.

src.l: Maine de Biran, 1841, Philosophical Works of Maine de Biran
src.q: I grasp first a principal idea in the theory of Barthez on this subject. The state of sleep is characterized, according to this author, by a concentration of the principle of life and sensibility in each of the partial organs that this principle animates, and between which it also establishes a true solidarity, a reciprocal sympathy, more or less intimate in the state of waking.

s: Wilhelm Wundt, Logic: An Investigation of the Principles of Knowledge (1907), on vitalism: vitalism as middle link between animism and mechanism.

src.l: Wilhelm Wundt, 1907, Logic: An Investigation of the Principles of Knowledge
src.q: 562 According to this origin, vitalism forms a kind of middle link between animism and mechanism. With the former, it assumes purpose-acting forces in living beings;

s: Galen, On the Natural Faculties (1916), on vitalism: Galen's Vitalists: nature precedes the formed body.

src.l: Galen, 1916, On the Natural Faculties
src.q: However, according to the first school mentioned (the Vitalists), nature is not something that appears after the body is formed; rather, it is much earlier and older than the body itself.

s: Henri Bergson, Creative Evolution (1908), on vitalism: Bergson on why vitalism's position is difficult.

src.l: Henri Bergson, 1908, Creative Evolution
src.q: THE EVOLUTION OF LIFE But the truth is that the position of vitalism is made very difficult by the fact that there is neither purely internal finality nor absolutely clear-cut individuality in nature.

s: Wilhelm Wundt, Logic: An Investigation of the Principles of Knowledge (1907), on vitalism: physiology's fight against vitalism ending in mechanical teleology.

src.l: Wilhelm Wundt, 1907, Logic: An Investigation of the Principles of Knowledge
src.q: And, in fact, recent physiology has accomplished this by initially rejecting all teleology in its fight against the preceding vitalism, only to end up itself, forced by the nature of its objects of investigation, in mechanical teleology.

s: Schelling, Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph von, Erster Entwurf eines Systems der Naturphilosophie (1799), on Naturphilosophie: Schelling 1799: Naturphilosophie as speculative physics.

src.l: Schelling, Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph von, 1799, Erster Entwurf eines Systems der Naturphilosophie
src.q: Least of all should someone judge who does not even know what Naturphilosophie [Natural Philosophy] or speculative Physik [Speculative Physics] means to the author.

s: Schelling, Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph von, Von der Weltseele (1806), on Naturphilosophie: Von der Weltseele: the doctrine spread under the name Naturphilosophie.

src.l: Schelling, Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph von, 1806, Von der Weltseele
src.q: We can present it as a pure impression of the most general principles of that doctrine which, under the name of Naturphilosophie [Philosophy of Nature], has indeed received a very rapid expansion, but has truly been recognized very little in its essence.

s: Wilhelm Dilthey, Poetry and Experience (1907), on Naturphilosophie: 1907: formation of Naturphilosophie in the Jena ferment.

src.l: Wilhelm Dilthey, 1907, Poetry and Experience
src.q: place them in relation to the simultaneous expressions of Friedrich Schlegel, Schleiermacher, and Schelling. The years from Fichte’s activity in Jena to the formation of the Naturphilosophie [philosophy of nature] and then, a few years later, the philosophy of the moral world, represent a period of immense fermentation and the boldest designs to subject the positive sciences of nature and spirit to the principles of the Wissenschaftslehre [theory of science].

s: Gustav Theodor Fechner, On the Physical and Philosophical Atomic Theory (1855), on Naturphilosophie: 1855 critic: their gaze conjures the things themselves.

src.l: Gustav Theodor Fechner, 1855, On the Physical and Philosophical Atomic Theory
src.q: Certainly, great insights have emerged from Schelling and Hegel. But everything dissolves into futility or first requires a firm shape and foundation, because their gaze, instead of being directed sharply at things, wants to conjure up the things themselves.

s: Henri Bergson, Creative Evolution (1908), on Bergson's creative evolution: Bergson's own opening of Creative Evolution: mechanism and finality, the self known inwardly.

src.l: Henri Bergson, 1908, Creative Evolution
src.q: CREATIVE EVOLUTION 1 CHAPITRE PREMIER On the evolution of life. — Mechanism and finality. The existence of which we are most certain and which we know best is incontestably our own, for of all other objects we have notions that might be judged external and superficial, while we perceive ourselves internally, deeply.

s: Ernst Cassirer, The Philosophy of Symbolic Forms, Part 3: The Phenomenology of Knowledge (1929), on Bergson's creative evolution: Cassirer: Bergson's doctrine opposes vitalism to mechanism, after Schelling.

src.l: Ernst Cassirer, 1929, The Philosophy of Symbolic Forms, Part 3: The Phenomenology of Knowledge
src.q: Bergson’s doctrine is in agreement with Schelling’s philosophy of nature, from which it has indirectly received strong and decisive stimuli¹, above all in one point: it opposes vitalism to mechanism;

s: Max Scheler, Ressentiment (1912), on Bergson's creative evolution: Scheler: Bergson uncovered the error of the mechanical theory of life.

src.l: Max Scheler, 1912, Ressentiment
src.q: It is the fundamental error of the mechanical theory of life—principally uncovered by Bergson—that the phenomena of life are to be grasped and explained with concepts and forms of perception that are peculiar to a "reason" that has itself only been formed in the service of the life activity peculiar to man and is completely dependent on its directions of activity¹.

s: Raphson, Joseph, Universal Analysis of Equations (1702), on hylozoism: Raphson 1702: the hylozoists and their supposed origin in Strato, as Cudworth framed it.

src.l: Raphson, Joseph, 1702, Universal Analysis of Equations
src.q: The Hylozoists introduced another kind of Panhylism [the doctrine that all matter is alive]; to whom, as it seemed to most, Strato of Lampsacus, commonly called the Physicist, gave origin.

s: Helena Petrovna Blavatsky, The Secret Doctrine Vol. I (1888), on hylozoism: Blavatsky defines hylozoism as all matter being in some sense alive.

src.l: Helena Petrovna Blavatsky, 1888, The Secret Doctrine Vol. I
src.q: Hylozoism the philosophical doctrine that all matter is in some sense alive, when philosophically understood, is the highest aspect of Pantheism.

s: Ernst Haeckel, The Riddle of the Universe (1901), on hylozoism: Haeckel traces hylozoism to the Ionian philosophers.

src.l: Ernst Haeckel, 1901, The Riddle of the Universe
src.q: still, we do not meet a definite philosophical expression of it until the hylozoism of the Ionic philosophers, in the first half of the sixth century before Christ.

s: Wilhelm Wundt, Logic: An Investigation of the Principles of Knowledge (1907), on hylozoism: Wundt: philosophical hylozoism taught the eternity of life.

src.l: Wilhelm Wundt, 1907, Logic: An Investigation of the Principles of Knowledge
src.q: In a form essentially different from this, philosophical hylozoism has taught the eternity of life at all times. Even if its primary concern was more to rescue life for all of nature than to explain it, the latter—or rather the possibility of being able to do without such an explanation—was usually considered a welcome byproduct.

s: Н.А. Бердяев, Sub Specie Aeternitatis: Philosophical, Social, and Literary Essays (1907), on panpsychism: Berdyaev: panpsychism as an ontology of a hierarchy of spiritual monads.

src.l: Н.А. Бердяев, 1907, Sub Specie Aeternitatis: Philosophical, Social, and Literary Essays
src.q: " This is fully compatible with spiritualism or panpsychism [the view that mind or spirit is the primary reality of all things] in ontology, which teaches that being consists of a complex, interacting hierarchy of concrete spiritual entities, spiritualized monads [indivisible, fundamental units of reality], united into a

s: Damaskios, The Life of the Philosopher Isidoros by Damaskios of Damascus (1911), on panpsychism: Neoplatonist pantheism was basically a panpsychism.

src.l: Damaskios, 1911, The Life of the Philosopher Isidoros by Damaskios of Damascus
src.q: 66, 27 Soul] The main topic of the Neoplatonists, whose pantheism was basically a panpsychism [the view that all things possess a soul]. Consequently, judging by the surviving remnants, our biography seems to have been more of a "psychography"—that is, a depiction of the souls of the people appearing in it—than an exact recording of their external life circumstances.

s: Ernst Cassirer, The Philosophy of Symbolic Forms, Part 3: The Phenomenology of Knowledge (1929), on panpsychism: Cassirer distinguishes universal animation from universal ensoulment.

src.l: Ernst Cassirer, 1929, The Philosophy of Symbolic Forms, Part 3: The Phenomenology of Knowledge
src.q: consciousness imprints the form of life upon everything it grasps, this mode of universal animation Allbelebung [enlivening of all] is by no means synonymous with universal ensoulment Allbeseelung [ensouling of all] from the beginning.

s: Edward Burnett Tylor, Primitive Culture: Researches into the Development of Mythology, Philosophy, Religion, Art, and Custom, Vol. I (1871), on animism: Tylor's own definition in Primitive Culture.

src.l: Edward Burnett Tylor, 1871, Primitive Culture: Researches into the Development of Mythology, Philosophy, Religion, Art, and Custom, Vol. I
src.q: Thus Animism, in its full development, includes the belief in controlling deities and subordinate spirits, in souls, and in a future state, these doctrines practically resulting in some kind of active worship.

s: Henry Whitehead, The Village Gods of South India (1921), on animism: the animist's question of placing his soul among other souls.

src.l: Henry Whitehead, 1921, The Village Gods of South India
src.q: "The vital question for the Animist," he says, "is how to place his own soul in relation to the souls surrounding him, and to their powers, which are partly injurious and and partly useful, with as little danger and as much advantage to himself as possible.

s: Hermann Jacobi (trans.), Jaina Sutras, Part 2 (SBE Vol. 45) (1895), on animism: Jaina belief that earth, water, fire and wind have souls, labelled animistic.

src.l: Hermann Jacobi (trans.), 1895, Jaina Sutras, Part 2 (SBE Vol. 45)
src.q: Such a mark is the animistic belief that nearly everything is possessed of a soul; not only have plants their own souls, but particles of earth, cold water, fire, and wind also.

s: Samuel Marinus Zwemer, The Influence of Animism on Islam (1920), on animism: soul-stuff in nails, teeth and spittle.

src.l: Samuel Marinus Zwemer, 1920, The Influence of Animism on Islam
src.q: ISLAM AND ANIMISM finger nails are connected with the soul and have spiritual value (p. 38). Also the teeth (p. 39). Spittle, perspira- tion, tears and the other excretions of the body all contain soul-stuff (pp. 40-47) and one may see in all the supersti- tions of the animist the same practices that are related of Mohammed the Prophet and his companions in Moslem Tradition.

s: Ptolemy, Vat.gr.1594 (900), on microcosm and macrocosm: Byzantine: man as a small world, his proportions referred to the world's.

src.l: Ptolemy, 900, Vat.gr.1594
src.q: Viewing man as a kind of small world mikrokosmos [microcosm] within the great world, we likewise refer the proportions within him to the proportions within the world.

s: Abrabanel, Jehuda, Philosophy of Love (1595), on microcosm and macrocosm: Leone Ebreo: man is an image of the whole universe, hence Microcosmos.

src.l: Abrabanel, Jehuda, 1595, Philosophy of Love
src.q: The truth is such that Man is an image of the entire universe: and therefore the Greeks name him Microcosmos|original: "Microcosmos," from the Greek words for "small" and "world": which signifies a little world: but also Man, and even every other

s: Franz Kieser; Paracelsus; Albertus Magnus, Chemical Kabbalah — Kieser, Paracelsus & Albertus Magnus, post-1606 (1610), on microcosm and macrocosm: man is the microcosm not in form but in all powers and virtues.

src.l: Franz Kieser; Paracelsus; Albertus Magnus, 1610, Chemical Kabbalah — Kieser, Paracelsus & Albertus Magnus, post-1606
src.q: To understand this correctly: man is the Microcosmus [little world], not in form and physical substance, but in all powers and virtues, just as the great world is.

s: Paracelsus, Erster [- zehender] Theil der Bücher und Schrifften des edlen, hochgelehrten und bewehrten philosophi und medici Philippi Theophrasti Bombast von Hohenheim ... (1589), on microcosm and macrocosm: Paracelsus: the star of the microcosm governs the heavenly star.

src.l: Paracelsus, 1589, Erster [- zehender] Theil der Bücher und Schrifften des edlen, hochgelehrten und bewehrten philosophi und medici Philippi Theophrasti Bombast von Hohenheim ...
src.q: so also the star of the Microcosmus [the little world/man] governs and overcomes the stella coelestis [heavenly star]. For you should know here that God did not create the planets and all other stars of the heaven with the intention that they should govern man and be his heart, but for the service of man, so that they serve him like other creatures.

s: Weigel, Valentin, [Greek: Gnothi seauton]. Nosce teipsum. Erkenne dich selbst (1615), on microcosm and macrocosm: man carries within him everything in heaven and earth.

src.l: Weigel, Valentin, 1615, [Greek: Gnothi seauton]. Nosce teipsum. Erkenne dich selbst
src.q: Shows and points out that man is a Microcosmus [microcosm], the greatest work of God under heaven. He is the little world and carries everything within him that is found in heaven and earth, and even beyond.

s: Albertus Magnus, De Secretis Mulierum et Virtutibus Herbarum, Lapidum et Animalium (1662), on spontaneous generation: Albertus: equivocal generation, earth producing a mouse.

src.l: Albertus Magnus, 1662, De Secretis Mulierum et Virtutibus Herbarum, Lapidum et Animalium
src.q: Note that in the sixth book of the Metaphysics, generation is divided thus: some is univocal|The "standard" way of reproduction where like produces like, such as a human giving birth to a human, and some is equivocal|Spontaneous generation, where the cause and the result are different species, such as earth producing a mouse.

s: Erastus, Thomas, Disputationum de nova medicina Philippi Paracelsi (1572), on spontaneous generation: Erastus: univocal vs equivocal generation from decaying matter.

src.l: Erastus, Thomas, 1572, Disputationum de nova medicina Philippi Paracelsi
src.q: 227 FF 2 ERASTUS: Generation is known by philosophers to be of two kinds: univocal [like producing like, as a human begetting a human] and equivocal [spontaneous generation from decaying matter].

s: Henry Baker, The Microscope Made Easy (1743), on spontaneous generation: Baker: the doctrine and how microscopes overturned it.

src.l: Henry Baker, 1743, The Microscope Made Easy
src.q: Equivocal or spontaneous Generation, that is, a Production of Plants without Seeds, and of living Creatures without any other Parents but Accident and Putrefaction, however absurd it may seem to us, was an Opinion that prevailed, almost universally, till Microscopes overturn'd it; by demonstrating that all Plants have their Seeds, and all Animals their Eggs: whence other Plants and other Animals, exactly of the same Species, are perpetually and unalterably produced.

s: Anton de Bary (1831-1888), Untersuchungen über die Brandpilze und die durch sie verursachten Krankheiten der Pflanzen (1853), on spontaneous generation: de Bary: fungi once thought to arise by Urzeugung, now refuted.

src.l: Anton de Bary (1831-1888), 1853, Untersuchungen über die Brandpilze und die durch sie verursachten Krankheiten der Pflanzen
src.q: and while in earlier times all fungi were thought to arise through spontaneous generation (Urzeugung), this theory has lost its footing ever since Ehrenberg's ³) discoveries, the more research has progressed and the more the tools and methods of investigation have been improved.

s: Potier, Michael, The Hermetic-Philosophical Messenger Bringing Joyful and Unheard-of News (1622), on growth of metals: metals grow, so they have seed and can be multiplied.

src.l: Potier, Michael, 1622, The Hermetic-Philosophical Messenger Bringing Joyful and Unheard-of News
src.q: because nothing grows without a seed. Metals grow, as experience testifies. Therefore, metals have a seed. Now for the second: Whatever has a seed can be multiplied through it.

s: Böhme, Jakob, Böhme, Jakob: Trost-Schrift, von vier Complexionen (1621), on growth of metals: Böhme: metals grow because their tincture drives them.

src.l: Böhme, Jakob, 1621, Böhme, Jakob: Trost-Schrift, von vier Complexionen
src.q: There the tincture of the metals always wants to flee from the earthly part, especially when the evil constellation touches it, and wants to go out from the center [the core of its being]. From this it comes that the metals grow, for their tincture drives their

s: anonymous, Tractatus chymicus antiquissimus & vere aureus (1721), on growth of metals: metals generated in the bowels of the earth by mercurial vapour.

src.l: anonymous, 1721, Tractatus chymicus antiquissimus & vere aureus
src.q: The generatio Metallorum [birth of metals] in the bowels of the earth happens by the action of a Mercuriali halitu [mercurial vapor or breath].

s: Becher, Johann Joachim, Subterranean Physics (1738), on growth of metals: alchemists can achieve the true generation of metals.

src.l: Becher, Johann Joachim, 1738, Subterranean Physics
src.q: Whence even the Alchemists themselves, through the true art of Alchemy, using the aforementioned principles—or rather, using things derived from those principles—sometimes achieve the* TRUE GENERATION OF METALS.

s: Sushruta, सुश्रुतसंहिता (Suśruta Saṃhitā) (1833), on Āyurveda: Susruta: Ayurveda is so named because life exists in it; its purpose is curing the sick and protecting the healthy.

src.l: Sushruta, 1833, सुश्रुतसंहिता (Suśruta Saṃhitā)
src.q: The purpose of Ayurveda is the eradication of disease in those afflicted and the protection of the healthy." (27) Ayurveda Āyurveda [the science of life] is so named because life āyus [life/longevity] exists within it, or because it imparts knowledge of life.

s: Sushruta, सुश्रुतसंहिता (Suśruta Saṃhitā) (1833), on Āyurveda: an Ayurvedic doctrine stated: the count of bones in the body.

src.l: Sushruta, 1833, सुश्रुतसंहिता (Suśruta Saṃhitā)
src.q: With 32 teeth and 3 small bones in each ear, they total 238, and 8 sesamoid bones, making them 246. And according to the Ayurvedic view. There are 120 bones in the four limbs (hands and feet), 117 in the torso, and 63 above the neck.

s: Bhūdeb Mukharjī (Mookerji), Rasa-Jala-Nidhi, or Ocean of Indian Chemistry & Alchemy, vol. 1 (1891), on Āyurveda: 1891 plea that Ayurveda can only recover its glory through Indian medical chemistry.

src.l: Bhūdeb Mukharjī (Mookerji), 1891, Rasa-Jala-Nidhi, or Ocean of Indian Chemistry & Alchemy, vol. 1
src.q: PREFACE While anxious for the revival of Ayurvedic culture in India, let me sound a note of warning to the authorities of the different Ayurvedic institutions, which have been started during the present decade, that unless and until the greatest stress is laid upon the revival of Indian Chemistry of medicine, as outlined in the present work, there is not the slightest chance of recovering the glory which Ayurveda lost about a thousand years ago.

s: Svatmarama, Hathayogapradipika (Sanskrit, 1867) (1867), on haṭha yoga: Hathapradipika: uniting prana and apana is pranayama, which is hatha yoga.

src.l: Svatmarama, 1867, Hathayogapradipika (Sanskrit, 1867)
src.q: The union of these two, the Out-breath Prāṇa and the In-breath Apāna, is called Breath Control Prāṇāyāma, which is Hatha Yoga. The science that explains this is Hatha Yoga.

s: Svatmarama, Light on the Yoga of Force with Commentaries (1450), on haṭha yoga: Svatmarama: dissolving breath and mind brings liberation.

src.l: Svatmarama, 1450, Light on the Yoga of Force with Commentaries
src.q: ( 134 ) IN THE LIGHT ON HAṬHA YOGA Root Text: The man who brings these two—the breath and the mind—to dissolution, he attains liberation; no other does, by any means whatsoever.

s: E.T. Sturdy, Aphorisms of Narada: An Inquiry Into Love (1896), on haṭha yoga: Hatha yoga as a physiological process preparing the body for higher yoga.

src.l: E.T. Sturdy, 1896, Aphorisms of Narada: An Inquiry Into Love
src.q: Gîtâ, VI, 19. 4. Hatha Yoga—an almost entirely physiological process, by which the body may be prepared for the higher forms of yoga,

src.q: Hatha Yoga was promoted and practised by Matsendra Nath and Goraksh Nath and their followers, and by many sects of ascetics in this country (India).

s: Anonymous, བསྟན་འགྱུར། སྡེ་དགེ། དཀར་ཆག (Derge Tengyur, vol. 213) (1982), on Tibetan medicine: Tengyur catalogue: the Science of Healing accomplishes longevity and freedom from disease.

src.q: Regarding the second field of knowledge, the Science of Healing Sowa Rigpa [the traditional Tibetan science of medicine], which accomplishes the well-being of longevity and freedom from disease: This section explains the necessity of entering into the Science of Healing and the nature of the treatises that teach it.

s: Gangtey Monastery Collection, Jo bo rje'i rnam thar (1700), on Tibetan medicine: Atisha skilled in Sowa Rigpa, with treatment of humans, elephants and horses.

src.l: Gangtey Monastery Collection, 1700, Jo bo rje'i rnam thar

s: More, Henry, Ethical Handbook, Comprising the Principal Rudiments of Moral Philosophy (1695), on mechanical philosophy: Descartes's view that all phenomena arise from matter and local motion.

src.l: More, Henry, 1695, Ethical Handbook, Comprising the Principal Rudiments of Moral Philosophy
src.q: That other opinion of Descartes, which seems to savor less of piety, is this: namely, that all the Phenomena of the world—not even excepting Plants or the organic bodies of Animals—can arise from merely Mechanical principles (that is, solely from local Motion and Matter);

s: Benedictus de Spinoza, Posthumous Works (1677), on mechanical philosophy: forms and qualities best explained from mechanical principles.

src.l: Benedictus de Spinoza, 1677, Posthumous Works
src.q: We are also occupied with composing a History of the Mechanical Arts, holding it as certain that the forms and qualities of things can best be explained from Mechanical Principles.

s: Colonne, François-Marie-Pompée, Les principes de la nature, ou de la generation des choses (1731), on mechanical philosophy: mechanical philosophers' preformation answer to generation.

src.l: Colonne, François-Marie-Pompée, 1731, Les principes de la nature, ou de la generation des choses
src.q: Our Mechanical Philosophers, seeing this impossibility in their Mechanics, have cleverly extricated themselves by saying that the animal was entirely formed within the sperm of the bird.

s: Babbage, Charles, The Ninth Bridgewater Treatise: A Fragment (1838), on mechanical philosophy: denial of the mechanical philosophers' authority over the universe.

src.l: Babbage, Charles, 1838, The Ninth Bridgewater Treatise: A Fragment
src.q: > "We may thus, with the greatest propriety, deny to the mechanical philosophers and mathematicians of recent times any authority with regard to their views of the administration of the universe;

s: Bacon, Roger, The Greater Work (1733), on regimen of health: Roger Bacon: medicine can provide a regimen of health for all ages, including the elderly.

src.l: Bacon, Roger, 1733, The Greater Work
src.q: For the art of medicine can do no more than provide a sufficient regimen of health suitable for all ages. Although famous authors have spoken insufficiently regarding the proper regimen for the elderly, such a regimen was nonetheless within the reach of the medicinal art.

s: Various (Galen, Hippocrates, et al.), Articella (1519), on regimen of health: Articella: the threefold mode of governing the healthy.

src.l: Various (Galen, Hippocrates, et al.), 1519, Articella
src.q: ¶ On the regimen of health. There is a triple mode for governing the healthy: those prepared to fall ill, those beginning to be ill, and the failing.

On certain surgical cases. To these are Added (1628), on regimen of health: 1628: a suitable regimen of the six non-naturals.

src.q: This can be achieved first through a refined lifestyle and a suitable regimen of the six non-naturals: a historical medical concept referring to factors within a person's control: air, food/drink, sleep/wakefulness, motion/rest, excretion/retention, and passions of the mind.

s: Sanctorius Sanctorius, On Static Medicine (1701), on regimen of health: Sanctorius on Celsus's advice about using the non-naturals sparingly or in excess.

src.l: Sanctorius Sanctorius, 1701, On Static Medicine
src.q: The opinion of Celsus [Aulus Cornelius Celsus] is not safe for everyone, namely that the use of the six res non naturales [non-naturals: factors such as air, food/drink, sleep/waking, exercise/rest, evacuation/repletion, and mental state] should be sometimes sparse and sometimes excessive.

s: Christian Wolff, Moral Philosophy or Ethics (1752), on the sober life: Wolff: Cornaro cured himself at 87 by returning to his diet.

src.l: Christian Wolff, 1752, Moral Philosophy or Ethics
src.q: Finally, that diseases can be cured by diet, Cornaro proved by his own example, who, when departing from his usual diet in the eighty-seventh year of his age, had fallen into a very serious disease, recovered by returning to his usual diet, having used no other medicine.

s: Bernardino Ramazzini, Complete Medical and Physiological Works (1739), on the sober life: Ramazzini on the commendation of the sober life and Speroni's objections.

src.l: Bernardino Ramazzini, 1739, Complete Medical and Physiological Works
src.q: Therefore, by reasons and examples, it is sufficiently clear what great commendation a sober life is worthy of; wherefore it is to be wondered how Spero Speronius wrote a letter to our author, in which he contends, with various arguments—ingenious ones, however—to disprove this sober life.

s: Böhmer, Georg Rudolph, Systematic Library of Writers on Natural History, Economics, and Related Arts and Sciences (1786), on the sober life: Berger's sober-life diet of no more than 14 ounces a day.

src.l: Böhmer, Georg Rudolph, 1786, Systematic Library of Writers on Natural History, Economics, and Related Arts and Sciences
src.q: Berger also included in his Dissertation de commodis vitae sobriae [Dissertation on the benefits of the sober life] (1705) a description of the strictest diet, which does not exceed 14 ounces within 24 hours.

s: Roger Bacon, Unpublished Works of Roger Bacon (Opus Tertium, Opus Minus, Compendium Studii) (1859), on prolongation of life: Roger Bacon: the science teaches prolonging life; we die early for want of regimen.

src.q: Therefore, the precepts most necessary for prolonging life avoid equally—on this side, resolution; on that side, suffocation and putrefaction.

src.l: 高濂, 1596, 遵生八牋·卷十 (vol 8)
src.q: Master Gao stated: "Knowing what harms the body and mind brings the efficacy of extending one's years: Harmonizing and regulating oneself through the twenty-four hours, and protecting oneself morning and evening, can extend one's years.

src.l: Bacon, Roger, 1928, Hitherto Unpublished Works, Fascicle 8
src.q: at the table or elsewhere, the virtues of the stars may be led, which make stellar the foods and drinks and species and medicines and stones and herbs, which men worthy of perpetual health and the prolongation of life might use, so that the defect of the regimen which we contracted from infancy may be repaired suddenly, and the passions of old age be long delayed, and when they can no longer be delayed, they may be mitigated when they come, so that they do not inflict

src.l: Maier Arcana, 1798, Imperial Privileged Empire Gazette
src.q: Whoever knows even to a small degree the excellence and the value of the book: The Art of Prolonging Human Life by Hufeland, must surely also be overcome by the wish that the principles contained therein might be spread everywhere for the general human welfare, which, however, at the somewhat high price of that book, will likely be difficult to happen.

src.l: Antonio Beccadelli (Panormita), 1908, Hermaphroditus (Latin-German edition)

s: Galen, Epitome of the Complete Works of Galen (1548), on care of old age: Galen epitome: gerocomice resists the drying of the heart that ends life.

src.l: Galen, 1548, Epitome of the Complete Works of Galen
src.q: which task pertains to gerocomice [the art of caring for the elderly]. This indeed proposes to itself, so far as it is possible, to resist and prohibit the body of the heart from drying out to such a degree that it is devoid of all work.

s: Dubois, Jacques, Ordo et ordinis ratio in legendis Hippocratis & Galeni libris (1561), on care of old age: places gerocomy, the care of the elderly, under both hygiene and therapeutics, citing Galen.

src.l: Dubois, Jacques, 1561, Ordo et ordinis ratio in legendis Hippocratis & Galeni libris
src.q: Therefore, Galen mentions these in his books on preserving health and on therapeutics. Gerocomy, or the care of the elderly, may also rightly be assigned to both, that is, to Hygiene and Therapeutics.

s: Girolamo Mercuriale, De arte gymnastica libri sex (Amsterdam ed.) (1672), on medical gymnastics: Mercuriale defines true gymnastics as a part of medicine.

src.l: Girolamo Mercuriale, 1672, De arte gymnastica libri sex (Amsterdam ed.)
src.q: DE ARTE GYMNASTICA Lib. I. N we have proposed to treat true gymnastics, which was already defined by us as a part of medicine, and since there are other types of gymnastics concerning almost the same things, I think it is necessary to hold a discussion about these very things, so that once this is done, the diversity of all may be distinguished most easily.

s: Anonymous, Weekly News of Learned Matters, 1749 (1749), on medical gymnastics: Felici: the art of gymnastics is necessary to keep the body healthy and strong.

s: Girolamo Mercuriale, De arte gymnastica libri sex (1573), on medical gymnastics: Mercuriale on medical gymnastics as distinct from athletic and military.

src.l: Girolamo Mercuriale, 1573, De arte gymnastica libri sex

s: Ulstad, Philip|Campesius, Joannes Antonius, Coelum philosophorum, seu liber de secretis naturae. Directorium summae summarum medicinae (1572), on elixir of life: it takes away the illnesses of old age, hence called elixir vitae.

s: Ruland jr., Martin, Prolegomena of Alchemy, or Chemical Problems Clarified by Ninety-One Questions with the True Method of Preparing the Philosopher's Stone (1607), on universal medicine: Libavius: the proof of a universal medicine has been longed for through all memory.
