s: Patrizi (Pampsychia I, Nova de universis philosophia) says the Greeks named with one word, psychē, what the Latins named with two, animus and anima, and that both etymologies err from respiration: the Greeks derived psychē from psychein, to cool, the Latins animus and anima from aura, wind.

src.l: Francesco Patrizi, 1593, Nova de universis philosophia (Venice 1593)
src.q: Error hic vterque a respiratione venit.

src.l: Francesco Patrizi, 1593, Nova de universis philosophia (Venice 1593)
src.q: That which the ancient Greeks signified with the single name psychē soul, the Latins expressed with two: animus mind/spirit and anima soul. ... Both these errors stem from respiration. ... From wind, animus was formed, and from cooling, psychē.
src.qo: Error hic vterque a respiratione venit.

s: Natta (De immortalitate animae, 1564) reports the grammarians' rule that anima is that by which we live and animus that by which we are wise, so that life can exist without animus, as in the insane, but not without anima; he adds that great writers use the two words promiscuously.

src.l: Marcus Antonius Natta, 1564, M. Antonii Nattae Astensis Opera: De immortalitate animae libri V (Venice: Paolo Manuzio)
src.loc: De immortalitate animae I, dialogue Mar./Atha.; scan 25 (printed p. 4)
src.q: Si Grammaticis credimus , anima est , qua uiuimus , animus quo sapimus : uel anima est uitæ , animus consilij . hinc dicunt posse uitam sine animo existere , ut in furiosis uidemus , sed non sine anima .

src.l: Marcus Antonius Natta, 1564, M. Antonii Nattae Astensis Opera: De immortalitate animae libri V (Venice: Paolo Manuzio)
src.q: If we believe the grammarians, anima is that by which we live, animus is that by which we are wise; or, anima is of life, animus of counsel. Hence they say that life can exist without animus, as we see in the insane, but not without anima.
src.qo: Si Grammaticis credimus , anima est , qua uiuimus , animus quo sapimus : uel anima est uitæ , animus consilij . hinc dicunt posse uitam sine animo existere , ut in furiosis uidemus , sed non sine anima .

s: In the Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad (III.2) Indra says 'I am prāṇa, meditate on me as the conscious self (prajñātman)', identifies prāṇa with life and immortality, and says there is life only as long as prāṇa dwells in the body: here breath and self are one.

src.l: F. Max Müller (tr.), 1879, The Upanishads, Part 1 (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 1)
src.q: I am prâna, meditate on me as the conscious self (pragñâtman), as life, as immortality. Life is prâna, prâna is life. ... As long as prâna dwells in this body, so long surely there is life.

s: Chāndogya Upaniṣad VI.11.3: the body withers and dies when the living self (jīva) has left it, but the jīva does not die; Śaṅkara's school reads the verse to mean that birth and death belong to the body only.

src.l: F. Max Müller (tr.), 1879, The Upanishads, Part 1 (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 1)
src.q: This (body) indeed withers and dies when the living Self has left it; the living Self dies not.

src.l: Śaṅkarācārya, Sureśvarācārya, Sāyaṇa, A. Mahadeva Sastri (trans.), 1903, The Taittiriya Upanishad with the Commentaries of Shankaracharya, Suresvaracharya and Sayana (Mysore)
src.q: when devoid of jíva, forsooth, this body dies, jíva never dies,

s: The Taittirīya commentary tradition (Śaṅkara and successors, English 1903) treats prāṇa, the air that makes a man breathe in and out, as part of the non-self that has a birth (Vedānta-sūtra II.iv.8), while the jīva is not born: breath and self are split.

src.l: Śaṅkarācārya, Sureśvarācārya, Sāyaṇa, A. Mahadeva Sastri (trans.), 1903, The Taittiriya Upanishad with the Commentaries of Shankaracharya, Suresvaracharya and Sayana (Mysore)
src.loc: Prāṇamaya-kośa, 'Prana has a birth'; scan 443 (printed p. 411)
src.q: That the vital principle (Prana) dwelling within the physical body—which has been proved to be the non-self—has a birth has been determined as follows in the Vedanta-sutra II. iv. 8

src.l: Śaṅkarācārya, Sureśvarācārya, Sāyaṇa, A. Mahadeva Sastri (trans.), 1903, The Taittiriya Upanishad with the Commentaries of Shankaracharya, Suresvaracharya and Sayana (Mysore)
src.loc: 'Jiva is not of the Creation'; scan 584 (printed p. 552)
src.q: Therefore birth and death pertain to the body.

s: A gloss on the Zuozhuan's 'at birth the first transformation is called po; once po is born, its yang is called hun', quoted in Zhang Jiushao's Lixue leibian, makes po the sentience in the first gathering of essence and blood and hun the spirit in the warm qi that follows; joined they make a living thing, dispersed the hun becomes shen and the po gui.

src.l: 張九韶 Zhang Jiushao, Ming (Siku quanshu copy), 理學類編 Lixue leibian, juan 4–6 (vol 2)
src.loc: juan 5, 魂魄 (gloss on Zuozhuan Zhao 7); scan 50
src.q: 既生魄陽曰魂者既生此魄便有 暖氣其間有神者名之曰魂也二者既合然後有物

src.l: 張九韶 Zhang Jiushao, Ming (Siku quanshu copy), 理學類編 Lixue leibian, juan 4–6 (vol 2)
src.q: once this po is born, there is warm vital energy. That which possesses spirit within it is named the hun ethereal soul. When the two combine, only then is there a living thing.
src.qo: 既生魄陽曰魂者既生此魄便有 暖氣其間有神者名之曰魂也二者既合然後有物

s: The Xingming guizhi (1615) defines hun as the spirit of qi, that by which mouth and nose breathe, and po as the spirit of essence (jing), that by which eyes and ears see and hear; hun is the yang spirit (sun), po the yin spirit (moon).

src.l: 尹真人 Yin Zhenren (attrib.), 1615, 性命雙修萬神圭旨 :4卷. [China] : 吳之鶴, 明萬曆43 [1615].
src.loc: Diagram of the Hun and Po (魂魄圖); scan 65
src.q: 魂者氣之神有清有濁口鼻之所 以呼吸者呼為陽伸吸為陰屈也 魄者精之神有虛有實耳目之所 以視聽者

src.l: 尹真人 Yin Zhenren (attrib.), 1615, 性命雙修萬神圭旨 :4卷. [China] : 吳之鶴, 明萬曆43 [1615].
src.q: is the spirit of the breath. It has both clear and turbid aspects. It is that which the mouth and nose use to breathe.
src.qo: 魂者氣之神有清有濁口鼻之所 以呼吸者呼為陽伸吸為陰屈也 魄者精之神有虛有實耳目之所 以視聽者

s: Descartes (Discours V, 1637) supposes a body with no vegetative or sensitive soul, only a fire without light kindled in the heart like the heat of damp hay or new wine, and finds in it all the functions that exist in us independently of thought, owing nothing to the soul.

src.l: René Descartes, 1912, Discourse on Method, Meditations, Principles of Philosophy (Everyman, Dent/Dutton)
src.q: vegetative or sensitive soul, beyond kindling in the heart one of those fires without light, such as I had already described, and which I thought was not different from the heat in hay that has been heaped together before it is dry

src.l: René Descartes, 1912, Discourse on Method, Meditations, Principles of Philosophy (Everyman, Dent/Dutton)
src.q: I found precisely all those which may exist in us independently of all power of thinking, and consequently without being in any measure owing to the soul

s: Leibniz (Monadology §70, 1714) concludes that each living body has a dominant entelechy, which in an animal is the soul, while its members are full of other living beings each with its own dominant entelechy or soul: soul is put back into the machine at every scale.

src.l: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, Robert Latta, 1898, The Monadology and Other Philosophical Writings (Latta)
src.q: Hence it appears that each living body has a dominant entelechy, which in an animal is the soul; but the members of this living body are full of other living beings, plants, animals, each of which has also its dominant entelechy or soul

src.l: Michael Gottlieb Hansch, 1728, G. G. Leibnitii Principia philosophiae more geometrico demonstrata
src.loc: def. CCII–CCIII and scholion II; scan 73
src.q: A true substance, such as an animal, is composed of an immaterial soul and an organic body; and it is the composite of these two that is called a unity in itself

s: A 1709 Halle disputation under Stahl calls the living body synergon and energon with the physician's art and names an energy immanent in the living body, 'indeed, making it such' (living), which only intensifies and redirects its customary vital operations against disease.

src.l: Georg Ernst Stahl (praeses), Gottfried Bateldt (respondent), 1709, Disputatio medica inauguralis de abstinentia medici (Halle)
src.q: *imma- nens* certè VIVO corpori, imò hoc tale reddens, ENER- GIA

src.l: Georg Ernst Stahl (praeses), Gottfried Bateldt (respondent), 1709, Disputatio medica inauguralis de abstinentia medici (Halle)
src.q: This power, however it may be judged, is certainly inherent in the LIVING body—indeed, it is what makes the body living.
src.qo: *imma- nens* certè VIVO corpori, imò hoc tale reddens, ENER- GIA

s: Plato's Timaeus (34b) has the god set soul in the middle of the world's body, stretch it through the whole, and wrap the body round with it from outside, making one self-sufficient, revolving heaven.

src.l: Plato, 1902, Platonis Opera (Republic, Timaeus, Critias)
src.q: ψυχὴν δὲ εἰς τὸ μέσον αὐτοῦ θεὶς διὰ παντός τε ἔτεινεν καὶ ἔτι ἔξωθεν τὸ σῶμα αὐτῇ περιεκάλυψεν

src.l: Plato, 1902, Platonis Opera (Republic, Timaeus, Critias)
src.q: He placed the soul in the center of it and extended it through the whole, and also covered the body with it from the outside.
src.qo: ψυχὴν δὲ εἰς τὸ μέσον αὐτοῦ θεὶς διὰ παντός τε ἔτεινεν καὶ ἔτι ἔξωθεν τὸ σῶμα αὐτῇ περιεκάλυψεν

src.l: Plato, Thomas Taylor (trans.), 1793, The Cratylus, Phaedo, Parmenides, and Timaeus of Plato
src.q: But placing soul in the middle of the world, he extended it through the whole: and besides this, he externally invested the body of the universe with soul

s: Opening Ennead IV.3, Plotinus sets out a view he will examine: as each part of us shares our soul, so we, being parts of the whole, share as parts in the soul of the universe, which cares for everything inanimate.

src.l: Plotinus, Thomas Taylor (trans.), 1817, Select Works of Plotinus (with Synesius on Providence)
src.q: since we have the relation of parts to the whole, participate as parts of the soul of the universe

s: Plotinus (Ennead IV.3.9) says the cosmos lies in a soul that sustains it, no part of it without soul, 'moistened with life, like a net in water', and that there never was a time when the universe held together without Soul.

src.l: Plotinus, Thomas Taylor (trans.), 1817, Select Works of Plotinus (with Synesius on Providence)
src.q: in soul which sustains it, and no part of it is destitute of soul; being moistened with life, like a net in water.

src.l: Plotinus, Stephen MacKenna (tr.), 1917, The Enneads of Plotinus, Vol. I
src.q: there never was a time when this All was without Soul, never a time when the frame of the universe held together in the absence of Soul

s: Ficino's Platonic Theology (book IV; 1491 ed.) says that Platonists and Peripatetics alike grant souls to the celestial spheres, and that it is clearly established among Platonists that the elemental spheres are alive too.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1491, Theologia Platonica de immortalitate animarum
src.q: Cæleftes ſphæras habere animas, non modò Platonici, ſed omnes etiã Peripatetici confiteantur

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1491, Theologia Platonica de immortalitate animarum
src.q: Although it is clearly established among the Platonists that the spheres of the elements are alive
src.qo: Cæleftes ſphæras habere animas, non modò Platonici, ſed omnes etiã Peripatetici confiteantur

s: Ficino (De vita III.3; 1498 ed.) argues that the world's body is alive everywhere, as its motion and generation show, so it lives through a soul present to it everywhere, with a spirit between that soul and its body as in us.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1498, De vita libri tres (De triplici vita); Apologia; Quod necessaria sit ad vitam securitas
src.q: Profecto mundanum corpus quantum ex motu generationeque apparet est ubique uiuum

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1498, De vita libri tres (De triplici vita); Apologia; Quod necessaria sit ad vitam securitas
src.q: Indeed, the worldly body, as far as appears from its motion and generation, is alive everywhere
src.qo: Profecto mundanum corpus quantum ex motu generationeque apparet est ubique uiuum

s: Henry More (Immortality of the Soul III.12, in the 1662 Collection) defines the Spirit of Nature as an incorporeal substance without sense or animadversion that pervades all the matter of the universe and exercises a plastic power in it.

src.l: Henry More, 1662, A Collection of Several Philosophical Writings of Dr. Henry More
src.loc: Immortality of the Soul III.12.1 (printed p. 193); scan 579
src.q: The Spirit of Nature therefore, according to that notion I have of it, is, A substance incorporeal, but without Sense and Animadversion, pervading the whole Matter of the Universe, and exercising a Plastical power therein

s: More (Immortality of the Soul III.12.2) argues from the unison-string experiment and the soul's unity in its own body that there is a principle 'we call The Spirit of Nature, or the inferiour Soul of the World', to which such phenomena are to be resolved.

src.l: Henry More, 1662, A Collection of Several Philosophical Writings of Dr. Henry More
src.loc: Immortality of the Soul III.12.2 (printed p. 194); scan 580
src.q: there is some such Principle as we call The Spirit of Nature, or the inferiour Soul of the World

s: Fechner opens Über die Seelenfrage (1861) by listing the sub-questions of how far the soul-realm extends through nature: are humans, animals, plants, stones, heavenly bodies, the world ensouled?

src.l: Gustav Theodor Fechner, 1861, Über die Seelenfrage: ein Gang durch die sichtbare Welt, um die unsichtbare zu finden
src.q:
Sind die Pflanzen beseelt?
Sind die Steine. beseelt?
Sind die Weltkörper beseelt?
Ist die Welt beseelt?

src.l: Gustav Theodor Fechner, 1861, Über die Seelenfrage: ein Gang durch die sichtbare Welt, um die unsichtbare zu finden
src.q: Are plants ensouled? Are stones ensouled? Are celestial bodies ensouled? Is the world ensouled?
src.qo:
Sind die Pflanzen beseelt?
Sind die Steine. beseelt?
Sind die Weltkörper beseelt?
Ist die Welt beseelt?

s: Fechner (Seelenfrage, 1861) names what resists an ensouled Earth: common opinion balks at a being so dry and without free will, and natural science sees the Earth as a purely astronomical, geological, meteorological and physical being.

src.l: Gustav Theodor Fechner, 1861, Über die Seelenfrage: ein Gang durch die sichtbare Welt, um die unsichtbare zu finden
src.q: Der gemeinen Ansicht namentlich widerstrebt es, ein so trocknes, keine Spur von freier Willkühr verrathen- des, Wesen wie die Erde beseelt zu denken.

s: Fechner (Seelenfrage, 1861) diagnoses the loss of the world soul: once the finite loses its bond in the infinite, souls fall apart monadically, and instead of one world soul there is a world of soul-dust (Seelenstaub).

src.l: Gustav Theodor Fechner, 1861, Über die Seelenfrage: ein Gang durch die sichtbare Welt, um die unsichtbare zu finden
src.q: Die Seelen fallen monadisch aus einander, statt einer Weltseele giebt’s eine Welt aus Seelenstaub

s: Whytt (Observations on Nervous Disorders, 1765) derives the nervous symptoms from a 'sentient and sympathetic power of the nerves', a general sympathy through the whole system, and declines speculation on its nature.

src.l: Robert Whytt, 1765, Observations on the Nature, Causes and Cure of those Disorders which have been commonly called Nervous, Hypochondriac, or Hysteric
src.q: is a general sympathy which prevails through the whole system; so there is a particular and very remarkable consent between various parts of the body. From this sentient and sympathetic power of the nerves, I have endeavour- ed to deduce the various symptoms

s: Whytt (1765) accepts that muscles and blood vessels possess 'irritability, or a power of alternate contraction', and sorts the motions of living animals into only two kinds: voluntary, and involuntary from stimuli.

src.l: Robert Whytt, 1765, Observations on the Nature, Causes and Cure of those Disorders which have been commonly called Nervous, Hypochondriac, or Hysteric
src.q: appear evidently to be possessed of irritability, or a power of alternate con- traction. 7. THERE are only two kinds of mo- tion observed in the bodies of living a- nimals, viz. voluntary, and involunta- ry from stimuli.

s: Bichat (Recherches physiologiques sur la vie et la mort, 1800) finds the definition of life not in abstractions but in a general view: 'la vie est l'ensemble des fonctions qui résistent à la mort'; living bodies survive only by a permanent principle of reaction, 'unknown in its nature', known by its phenomena.

src.l: Xavier Bichat, 1800, Recherches physiologiques sur la vie et la mort
src.q: On cherche dans des considérations abstraites la définition de la vie; on la trouvera, je crois, dans cet aperçu général : la vie est l’ensemble des fonctions qui résistent à la mort.

src.l: Xavier Bichat, 1800, Recherches physiologiques sur la vie et la mort
src.q: bientôt ils succomberoient s’ils n’avoient en eux un principe permanent de réaction. Ce principe est celui de la vie; inconnu dans sa nature, il ne peut être apprécié que par ses phénomènes

s: Krüger's Träume (1st ed. 1754; this ed. 1758) gives a physician the line that the doctor need not deal with the soul, since the body's motions come from its Reizbarkeit or Irritabilität, 'a property of the matter of the animal body, for which no sensation is required'.

src.l: Johann Gottlob Krüger, 1758, D. Joh. Gottlob Krügers Träume
src.q: the movements of the body come from its irritability or irritabilitas irritability, which is a property of the matter of the animal body, for which no sensation is required.
src.qo: und die Bewegungen des Körpers kommen von sei- ner Reizbarkeit oder Irritabilität, welches eine Eigenschaft der Materie des thierischen Kör- pers ist, wozu keine Empfindung erfordert wird.

src.l: Johann Gottlob Krüger, 1758, D. Joh. Gottlob Krügers Träume
src.q: und die Bewegungen des Körpers kommen von sei- ner Reizbarkeit oder Irritabilität, welches eine Eigenschaft der Materie des thierischen Kör- pers ist, wozu keine Empfindung erfordert wird.

s: Gleichen-Rußwurm (Metaphysische Kezereien, 1796) fears that Haller's discovery of an unfelt Reizbarkeit of the muscles will breed physiological errors, since from it men at once concluded that muscles have no feeling.

src.l: Carl Heinrich von Gleichen-Rußwurm, 1796, Metaphysische Kezereien
src.q: Ich fürchte, daß die Hallerische Entdeckung der von uns nicht gefühlten Reizbarkeit unserer Muskeln, zu manchem physiologischen Irrthume Anlaß geben wird.

s: Condorcet (Outlines of the Progress of the Human Mind, 1794–95) lists Haller's irritability, a property 'common to almost every organic substance', among the few indubitable physiological truths of the age, set against the succession of mechanical, chemical and 'organical' explanations.

src.l: Marquis de Condorcet, 1795, Outlines of an Historical View of the Progress of the Human Mind (English tr.)
src.q: thofe in which irritability only refides, a property difcovered by Haller Haller, and common to almoft every organic fubftance : thefe facts are the whole of what phyfiology has been enabled to difcover, by indubitable obfervations

s: Augustin's tabular history of medicine (1801) logs under 1749 'Hallers Entdeckungen den Bau, den Nutzen und die Lebenskraft des Zellgewebes betreffend': by 1801 the word Lebenskraft is applied backward to Haller's work on cellular tissue.

src.l: Friedrich Ludwig Augustin, 1801, Vollständige Uebersicht der Geschichte der Medicin in tabellarischer Form
src.q: Hallers Entdeckungen den Bau, den Nutzen und die Lebenskraft des Zellgewebes betreffend.

src.l: Friedrich Ludwig Augustin, 1801, Vollständige Uebersicht der Geschichte der Medicin in tabellarischer Form
src.q: Haller's discoveries concerning the structure, utility, and vital force of cellular tissue.
src.qo: Hallers Entdeckungen den Bau, den Nutzen und die Lebenskraft des Zellgewebes betreffend.

s: Wenzel (Unterhaltungen, 1800) has a dialogue speaker argue that if life is Lebenskraft put into activity, then life is at the same time a gradual dying, since that activity consumes the force.

src.l: Gottfried Immanuel Wenzel, 1800, Unterhaltungen über die auffallendsten neuern Geistererscheinungen, Träume und Ahndungen
src.loc: ch. VII 'Ist dem Menschen ein Ziel seines Lebens bestimmt'; scan 107
src.q: Wenn das Leben die in Thätigkeit, in Wirksamkeit versetzte Lebenskraft ist, so scheint es, man müsse hieraus die Folge ziehen, daß es auch zugleich ein allmähliges Sterben sey

s: Eckartshausen (Mysterien der Religion, 1823 ed.) names 'Weltgeist, Lebensluft, Sauerstoffgas' the stimulating principle that alone gives life, acting only where Erregbarkeit is present; life lasts as long as the life-excitable substance is consumed by the life-stimulus.

src.l: Karl von Eckartshausen, 1823, Über die wichtigsten Mysterien der Religion
src.q: Weltgeist, Lebensluft, Sauerstoffgas ist das reizende allein das Leben gebende Principium. Es reizt aber nur unter dem bedingten Gesetze, daß Erregbarkeit vorhanden ist.

src.l: Karl von Eckartshausen, 1823, Über die wichtigsten Mysterien der Religion
src.q: The duration of life is therefore equal to the duration of the consumption of the life-excitable substance by the life-stimulus.
src.qo: Weltgeist, Lebensluft, Sauerstoffgas ist das reizende allein das Leben gebende Principium. Es reizt aber nur unter dem bedingten Gesetze, daß Erregbarkeit vorhanden ist.

s: Hahnemann (Organon §15, 5th ed. 1833, as revised on this scan) calls the life of the body a 'geistartige, unsern Körper belebende Dynamis (Lebenskraft)' and holds that the organism is the material tool of life but that organism and Lebenskraft form one unity, split only in thought.

src.l: Samuel Hahnemann, 1833, Organon der Heilkunst (5th ed., with revisions toward the 6th)
src.q: Das Leiden der krankhaft verstimmten, geistartigen, unsern Körper belebenden Dynamis (Lebenskraft) im unsichtbaren Innern

src.l: Samuel Hahnemann, 1833, Organon der Heilkunst (5th ed., with revisions toward the 6th)
src.q: The organism is indeed a material tool for life, but without being enlivened by the instinctually feeling and ordering vital force, just as the vital force is unthinkable without the organism; consequently, both form a unity
src.qo: Das Leiden der krankhaft verstimmten, geistartigen, unsern Körper belebenden Dynamis (Lebenskraft) im unsichtbaren Innern

s: The 1879 appendix to Deleuze's Practical Instruction quotes the judgement that 'the theories of Brown and Darwin are founded upon the doctrine of accumulated and exhausted excitability or sensorial power', a re-description of Cullen's agent.

src.l: J. P. F. Deleuze, Thomas C. Hartshorn (tr.), 1879, Practical Instruction in Animal Magnetism (tr. Hartshorn), with a new appendix
src.q: The theories of Brown and Darwin are founded upon the doctrine of accumulated and exhausted excitability or sensorial power; only another mode of describing the same agent referred to by Cullen.

s: Huxley ('On the Physical Basis of Life', lecture 1868, in Lay Sermons 1870) declares protoplasm 'the formal basis of all life', the potter's clay that remains clay, so that all living powers are cognate.

src.l: Thomas Henry Huxley, 1870, Lay Sermons, Addresses, and Reviews
src.loc: 'On the Physical Basis of Life'; scan 145
src.q: Protoplasm, simple or nucleated, is the formal basis of all life. It is the clay of the potter: which, bake it and paint it as he will, remains clay

s: Huxley (1868/1870) asks what better philosophical status 'vitality' has than 'aquosity', and mocks it with Scriblerus's 'meat roasting quality' of the meat-jack: a word for a property of living matter is no cause.

src.l: Thomas Henry Huxley, 1870, Lay Sermons, Addresses, and Reviews
src.loc: 'On the Physical Basis of Life'; scan 153
src.q: What better philosophical status has “vitality” than “aquosity”? And why should “vitality” hope for a better fate than the other “itys” which have disappeared

s: Haeckel (Welträthsel 1899; English Riddle of the Universe 1901) sketches the vitalism that ruled from the mid-18th century: some vital processes physico-chemical, others the work of a special vital force, 'a self-contained force (archaeus), unknown in inorganic nature, which compelled ordinary forces into its service'.

src.l: Ernst Haeckel, 1901, The Riddle of the Universe
src.q: it was a self-contained force (archaeus), unknown in inorganic nature, which compelled ordinary forces into its service.

s: Haeckel (1899/1901) reports that 'distinguished biologists' were reintroducing vital force under another name; Reinke calls the directive or dominant forces 'vital forces' against physical forces, and other neovitalists posit a 'supreme' engineer.

src.l: Ernst Haeckel, 1901, The Riddle of the Universe
src.q: he calls “vital forces,” in opposition to physical forces, the directive or dominant forces.

s: Du Prel (Philosophie der Mystik, 1884) holds that with his 'transcendental subject' two problems frowned upon by modern science revive, teleology and Lebenskraft, though not in the old form, and calls the long dispute an idle quarrel over words.

src.l: Carl du Prel, 1884, Die Philosophie der Mystik
src.q: Mit dem transcendentalen Subjekt leben also zwei Probleme wieder auf, Teleologie und Lebenskraft, die zwar in der modernen Naturwissenschaft verpönt sind; aber sie leben keineswegs in der alten Gestalt auf.

src.l: Carl du Prel, 1884, Die Philosophie der Mystik
src.q: I can only see an idle dispute over words in the long conflict of opinions on this point
src.qo: Mit dem transcendentalen Subjekt leben also zwei Probleme wieder auf, Teleologie und Lebenskraft, die zwar in der modernen Naturwissenschaft verpönt sind; aber sie leben keineswegs in der alten Gestalt auf.

s: Kardec's Livre des Esprits (1857) answers whether the vital principle is a cause or a property of organised matter: 'both'; life is an effect produced by an agent acting on matter, and the agent without matter is not life, as matter cannot live without it.

src.l: Allan Kardec, 1857, Le Livre des Esprits
src.q: La vie est un effet produit par l'action d'un agent sur la matière; cet agent, sans la matière, n'est pas la vie, de même que la matière ne peut vivre sans cet agent.

s: Bibra (Die narkotischen Genussmittel, 1855) writes that the word Stoffwechsel had gained a real meaning only in the last two decades, and that Liebig gave the impetus with his Thierchemie (1842) and Chemische Briefe.

src.l: Ernst von Bibra, 1855, Die narkotischen Genussmittel und der Mensch
src.q: so sind es wieder kaum zwei Decennien, seit welchen der Ausdruck „Stoffwechsel“ eine wirkliche Bedeutung erhalten hat.

src.l: Ernst von Bibra, 1855, Die narkotischen Genussmittel und der Mensch
src.q: Everyone knows that Liebig provided the impetus for this through his works
src.qo: so sind es wieder kaum zwei Decennien, seit welchen der Ausdruck „Stoffwechsel“ eine wirkliche Bedeutung erhalten hat.

s: Bichat (1800) makes life a ratio: 'the measure of life is ... the difference that exists between the effort of external powers and that of internal resistance'; the child has a surplus of reaction, the old man's internal principle weakens until all proportion ceases.

src.l: Xavier Bichat, 1800, Recherches physiologiques sur la vie et la mort
src.q: The measure of life is therefore, in general, the difference that exists between the effort of external powers and that of internal resistance.
src.qo: La mesure de la vie est donc en général, la différence qui existe entre l'effort des puissances extérieures, et celui de la résistance intérieure.

s: Bichat (1800) divides life into two modifications, one common to vegetable and animal, the other proper to the animal: the organic and the animal life.

src.l: Xavier Bichat, 1800, Recherches physiologiques sur la vie et la mort
src.q: Division of Life into Animal and Organic. Such is life considered in its entirety; examined in greater detail, it offers us two remarkable modifications. One is common to the vegetable and the animal, the other is the special share of the latter.
src.qo: Telle est la vie considérée dans sa totalité ; examinée plus en détail, elle nous offre deux modifications remarquables. L'une est commune au végétal et à l'animal, l'autre est le partage spécial de ce dernier.

s: Reil (Archiv für die Physiologie I.3, p. 173, as quoted by Schelling, Weltseele 1798) argues that if a bodily substance were the principle of contractility it should show it when isolated, yet no substance does: 'Der Sauerstoff hat für sich weder Irritabilität noch Contractilität'; Schelling calls this the most ingenious objection to the oxygen theory of irritability.

src.l: Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling, 1798, Von der Weltseele; eine Hypothese der höhern Physik (1st ed.)
src.q: Allein wir finden in der Natur keinen „Stoff, der für sich und abgesondert die Phä- „nomene, die wir thierische Contractilität nennen, „hervorbrächte.

src.l: Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling, 1798, Von der Weltseele; eine Hypothese der höhern Physik (1st ed.)
src.q: Yet we find in nature no substance which, by itself and isolated, produces the phenomena we call animal contractility. Oxygen, by itself, has neither irritability nor contractility
src.qo: Allein wir finden in der Natur keinen „Stoff, der für sich und abgesondert die Phä- „nomene, die wir thierische Contractilität nennen, „hervorbrächte.

s: Krüger's Träume (1758 ed.) reports the Stahlian explanation of a violent febrile pulse: the Stahlians say the soul drives the blood about so violently.

src.l: Johann Gottlob Krüger, 1758, D. Joh. Gottlob Krügers Träume
src.q: Die Stahlianer sagen, daß die Seele das Blut darum so heftig herumtriebe,

src.l: Johann Gottlob Krüger, 1758, D. Joh. Gottlob Krügers Träume
src.q: The Stahlian physicians say that the soul drives the blood about so violently because
src.qo: Die Stahlianer sagen, daß die Seele das Blut darum so heftig herumtriebe,

s: Hermippus redivivus (English 1744), citing Boerhaave's Institutiones §1053–54, states that 'the Body is a Pneumatico-hydraulic Machine, composed of Fluids and Solids', health arising from the proper motion of the one and due circulation of the other.

src.l: Johann Heinrich Cohausen, 1744, Hermippus redivivus: or, the Sage's Triumph over Old Age and the Grave (English ed.)
src.q: Reaſon and Experience have convinced us, that the Body is a Pneumatico-hy- draulic Machine, compoſed of Fluids and Solids, and that a good Conſtitution, or healthy Diſpo- ſition ariſes from the proper Motion of the one, and a due Circulation of the other.

s: Hermippus redivivus (Latin 1742, English 1744) takes up a Roman inscription that the long-lived Hermippus 'owed his Vivacity to the Nourishment he received from the Breath of Girls', and proposes to examine the nature and force of human breath as a means of prolonging life.

src.l: Johann Heinrich Cohausen, 1744, Hermippus redivivus: or, the Sage's Triumph over Old Age and the Grave (English ed.)
src.q: the long-lived Hermippus owed his Vivacity to the Nourishment he received from the Breath of Girls, or if we take in the various Readings of the Inscription to the Breath of young People of both Sexes.

s: Teichmeyer (Elementa anthropologiae, Jena, early 18th c.) states 'Corpus humanum est machina hydraulico-pnevmatica': named, like mills, from its motive forces, since its solids are moved by blood, spirits and breathed air.

src.l: Hermann Friedrich Teichmeyer, n.d., Elementa Anthropologiae
src.q: Corpus humanum est machina hydraulico-pnevmatica.

src.l: Hermann Friedrich Teichmeyer, n.d., Elementa Anthropologiae
src.q: Because its solid parts are moved by fluids, namely by blood and spirits, as well as by the air which we receiv
src.qo: Corpus humanum est machina hydraulico-pnevmatica.

s: Huxley (1868/1870) writes that the matter of life breaks up into carbonic acid, water and ammonia 'in consequence of that continual death which is the condition of its manifesting vitality'.

src.l: Thomas Henry Huxley, 1870, Lay Sermons, Addresses, and Reviews
src.loc: 'On the Physical Basis of Life'; scan 151
src.q: Thus the matter of life, so far as we know it (and we have no right to speculate on any other), breaks up, in consequence of that continual death which is the condition of its manifesting vitality

s: Against the story that the critics 'killed' vital force: on SL's pages what dies is the explanatory WORD (Huxley's 'vitality' as 'aquosity', 1868; Lebenskraft 'verpönt' by 1884), while the definition of life through its relation to death runs unbroken from Bichat (1800) through Wenzel (1800) to Huxley's own 'continual death' (1868), and the force returns as Reinke's Dominanten (1899).

src.l: Thomas Henry Huxley, 1870, Lay Sermons, Addresses, and Reviews
src.q: in consequence of that continual death which is the condition of its manifesting vitality

src.l: Xavier Bichat, 1800, Recherches physiologiques sur la vie et la mort
src.q: la vie est l’ensemble des fonctions qui résistent à la mort.

s: Haller's irritability did not side with vitalism or mechanism: within a few decades it was used to dismiss the soul from medicine (Krüger, 1754/58), attacked as a source of error for splitting motion from feeling (Gleichen, 1796), logged as an observed fact amid shifting explanations (Condorcet, 1794), and praised by Schelling as inexplicable mechanically (1806).

src.l: Johann Gottlob Krüger, 1758, D. Joh. Gottlob Krügers Träume
src.q: welches eine Eigenschaft der Materie des thierischen Kör- pers ist, wozu keine Empfindung erfordert wird.

src.l: Carl Heinrich von Gleichen-Rußwurm, 1796, Metaphysische Kezereien
src.q: zu manchem physiologischen Irrthume Anlaß geben wird.

s: Aristotle (De juventute et senectute 24 [18 in Hammond], 479a29, c. 350 BCE) defines birth as the first participation of the nutritive soul in heat and life as the persistence (μονή) of that participation; death is the exhaustion or quenching of the heat. Life by what it HAS and keeps: a heat held by the nutritive soul.

src.l: Aristotle, William A. Hammond (trans.), 1902, Aristotle's Psychology: De Anima and Parva Naturalia
src.q: BIRTH, then, is the original suffusion of the nutritive soul with heat, and life is the maintenance of this heat.

src.l: Aristotle, 1495, Aristotelis Opera, Vol. 3 (Aldine: De anima, Parva naturalia, De motu animalium)
src.q: γένεσις μὲν οὖν ἐστιν ἡ πρώτη μέθεξις σὺν τῷ θερμῷ τῆς θρεπτικῆς ψυχῆς· ζωὴ δὲ μονὴ ταύτης·

s: Aristotle (De juventute 4, 469b, c. 350 BCE) says every member and the whole animal body has congenital heat, so that living animals are warm and dead ones cold, and places the source of that heat in the heart. Life by what it HAS: congenital heat in a ruling organ.

src.l: Aristotle, William A. Hammond (trans.), 1902, Aristotle's Psychology: De Anima and Parva Naturalia
src.q: Every member and the entire animal body possess to a certain degree congenital heat. Consequently we see that during life animals are warm, but when dead and deprived of life they are cold.

s: Aristotle (De juventute 3, 469a, c. 350 BCE) says that the principle by which a thing is called an animal is the same as that by which it is said to live, and that the mark of sensation is the mark of a living body; with the life-principle in the heart, the sensory principle must be there too. For animals, life is defined by what they DO: sense.

src.l: Aristotle, William A. Hammond (trans.), 1902, Aristotle's Psychology: De Anima and Parva Naturalia
src.q: For that by virtue of which we call a thing an animal is the same as that by virtue of which we say that it lives, and the differential mark of sensation is the same as the differential mark of a living body.

s: Pietro d'Abano (Conciliator, diff. 'on long life', c. 1310; printed 1472) opens his account of what life is with a Neoplatonic definition from the commentary on the Liber de causis: life is a procession from eternal, quiet Being and the first motion, reaching the generable things below through intermediaries; and 'to live is to be for living things', so life is the form and substance of the living. Life by what it IS PART OF: an emanation from the First Cause.

src.l: Pietro d'Abano, 1472, Conciliator differentiarum philosophorum et praecipue medicorum
src.q: Life is a procession proceeding from the eternal, quiet Being, and the first movement, such as that of the intelligences and the heavens, and consequently reaching into these lower things that are born and decay through certain intermediaries from the first cause.
src.qo: Vita est pcessio pcedens ab ente sem pitno quieto

src.l: Pietro d'Abano, 1472, Conciliator differentiarum philosophorum et praecipue medicorum
src.q: Vita est pcessio pcedens ab ente sem pitno quieto

s: Abano (Conciliator, c. 1310) gives two lower, 'more material' definitions beside the Neoplatonic one: from De anima, life is the consistency maintained through nourishment; and, for the more perfect animals, from Alfred of Sareshel's De motu cordis, life is a continuous motion flowing from the heart into the other members. Life by what it DOES: feeding, and the heart's motion.

src.l: Pietro d'Abano, 1472, Conciliator differentiarum philosophorum et praecipue medicorum
src.q: Life is the consistency maintained through nourishment.
src.qo: Vita est cōsistentia p alimē tum

src.l: Pietro d'Abano, 1472, Conciliator differentiarum philosophorum et praecipue medicorum
src.q: Life is a continuous motion flowing from the heart into the other members.
src.qo: Vita est cōsistentia p alimē tum

src.l: Pietro d'Abano, 1472, Conciliator differentiarum philosophorum et praecipue medicorum
src.q: Vita est cōsistentia p alimē tum

s: Abano (Conciliator, c. 1310) makes heat and moisture and their proportion the primary formal causes of life and its length, and rejects rival causes (a hot dry place, much blood, a large body) as causes only per accidens, because 'life is measured by heat and moisture'. Life by what it HAS: a proportioned heat and moisture.

src.l: Pietro d'Abano, 1472, Conciliator differentiarum philosophorum et praecipue medicorum
src.q: It is only a cause insofar as blood contains heat and moisture, which is the essential cause of life.

s: Hermann Conring (De calido innato sive igne animali, 1647) holds innate heat to be evident to touch: all animals are warm even before birth and lay that heat aside only with life. Life by what it HAS: an implanted, connate heat.

src.l: Conring, Hermann, 1634, De calido innato sive igne animali
src.loc: ch. on whether innate heat exists; scan 21
src.q: For all animals, even before they are brought forth into the light, are warm in a remarkable way: nor do they lay aside that heat except with life.
src.qo: neque illum deponunt calorem nisi cum vitâ.

src.l: Conring, Hermann, 1634, De calido innato sive igne animali
src.q: neque illum deponunt calorem nisi cum vitâ.

s: Conring (1647) grants that vital heat feeds on fuel like common fire, but denies that the heat forms the body's parts: formation is the work of a far more excellent faculty, as Galen taught, and the elementary qualities are, likely, only its instruments, the shaper being something else.

src.l: Conring, Hermann, 1634, De calido innato sive igne animali
src.q: But the formation of parts is not the work of heat, but of a far more excellent
src.qo: At formatio partium non opus est caloris, sed facultatis longe prestantioris

src.l: Conring, Hermann, 1634, De calido innato sive igne animali
src.q: At formatio partium non opus est caloris, sed facultatis longe prestantioris

s: Cesare Cremonini (De calido innato et semine, 1634) answers an objection with the conditional 'if life consists in heat and moisture, every living thing is of a hot and moist complexion', and affirms that it does: old age, a diminution of life, tends to cold and dry, and death is nothing but cold and dry. Life by what it HAS: heat and moisture.

src.l: Cesare Cremonini, 1634, De calido innato et semine
src.q: The response must be of this kind: if life consists in heat and moisture, there is no doubt that every living thing is of a hot and moist complexion.
src.qo: si vita consistit in calido, & humido non est dubium, omne vivens esse complexionis calidæ & humidæ.

src.l: Cesare Cremonini, 1634, De calido innato et semine
src.q: si vita consistit in calido, & humido non est dubium, omne vivens esse complexionis calidæ & humidæ.

s: Paracelsus (De vita longa I.1, lectures c. 1527; printed 1560/1566) says the ancients never defined life, then defines it: life is nothing else than a certain balsamic mummy (Mummia Balsamita) that preserves the mortal body from worms and corruption, with an impressed mixture of the liquor of salts. Life by what it HAS: a preserving substance, a balsam.

src.l: Paracelsus, Gerhard Dorn (ed.), 1566, Libri V de vita longa
src.q: But so that I may finally define what life is: In truth, life is nothing else but a certain Balsamic Mummy
src.qo: Nihil me- hercle uita eſt aliud, niſi Mummia quæ- dam Balſamita, conſeruans mortale cor- pus à mortalibus

src.l: Paracelsus, Gerhard Dorn (ed.), 1566, Libri V de vita longa
src.q: Nihil me- hercle uita eſt aliud, niſi Mummia quæ- dam Balſamita, conſeruans mortale cor- pus à mortalibus

s: Jan Baptist van Helmont (Ortus medicinae, 'Vita longa', 1648) defines life as a light and a formal beginning (lumen & initium formale) by which a thing acts as it was commanded to act, infused by the Creator in an instant; it is not a fiery light and does not consume the radical moisture, and is as vital in a fish as in a lion. Life by what it HAS (a created light) and what it DOES (act as commanded); against the heat-and-moisture definition.

src.l: Jan Baptist van Helmont, 1648, Ortus Medicinae
src.q: First, therefore, life is a light and a formal beginning by which a thing acts as it has been commanded to act.
src.qo: Inprimis ergo vita est lumen & initium formale, quo res agit, quod agere jussa est.

src.l: Jan Baptist van Helmont, 1648, Ortus Medicinae
src.q: However, it is not a fiery light, nor combustible, nor is it a consumer of the radical moisture .
src.qo: Inprimis ergo vita est lumen & initium formale, quo res agit, quod agere jussa est.

src.l: Jan Baptist van Helmont, 1648, Ortus Medicinae
src.q: Inprimis ergo vita est lumen & initium formale, quo res agit, quod agere jussa est.

s: Van Helmont (1648) refuses to distinguish the form of a living thing from its life (except in the human mind), and finds life at every level: a 'mute' life in minerals, which show by signs that they live and die, a more unfolded life in seeds, and a third in plants that grow and multiply. Life by what it IS PART OF: a created order where every form is a life.

src.l: Jan Baptist van Helmont, 1648, Ortus Medicinae
src.q: Therefore, I do not distinguish the "form" in living things from "life" itself, except in both cases for the human mind.

src.l: Jan Baptist van Helmont, 1648, Ortus Medicinae
src.q: To be sure, a certain kind of life is "mute" and scarcely appears, such as that which occurs in minerals

s: Francis Bacon (Historia vitae et mortis, 1623) separates the lifeless spirits diffused through flesh, bone and membrane, which remain in a corpse, from the vital spirit, which governs them but is far different: whole and standing by itself (integralis, et per se constans). Life by what it HAS: one continuous vital spirit over many dead ones.

src.l: Bacon, Francis, 1623, Historia vitae et mortis
src.q: But the Vital Spirit, although it governs these others and shares a certain harmony with them, is far different from them; it is whole and exists independently.
src.qo: At Spiritus Vitalis, ta- metsi eos regat, & quendam habeat cum illis Consensum, longè alius est ab ipsis ; Integralis, & per se Con- stans.

src.l: Bacon, Francis, 1623, Historia vitae et mortis
src.q: At Spiritus Vitalis, ta- metsi eos regat, & quendam habeat cum illis Consensum, longè alius est ab ipsis ; Integralis, & per se Con- stans.

s: Bacon (1623) defines the difference of the living by continuity: lifeless spirits are cut off and trapped in denser body, like air in snow or foam, while the vital spirit is continuous with itself through channels and never wholly blocked, either branched through fine ducts or also gathered in a cell. Life by how what it HAS is ORGANIZED: one connected spirit.

src.l: Bacon, Francis, 1623, Historia vitae et mortis
src.q: But the Vital Spirit is entirely continuous within itself, moving through certain channels through which it flows, and is never completely blocked off.
src.qo: At Spiritus Vitalis omnis ſibi continuatur, per quoſdam Canales, per quos perme- at, nec totalitèr intercipitur.

src.l: Bacon, Francis, 1623, Historia vitae et mortis
src.q: At Spiritus Vitalis omnis ſibi continuatur, per quoſdam Canales, per quos perme- at, nec totalitèr intercipitur.

s: William Harvey (De motu cordis, 1628, printed in the 1660 De generatione volume) calls the auricles, especially the right, the first movers of the blood and 'the first living and the last dying' (primum vivens & ultimum moriens). Life is located by what it DOES: the motion that starts first and stops last.

src.l: William Harvey, 1660, Exercitationes anatomicae de generatione animalium (with De motu cordis)
src.q: but the auricles are the primary movers of the blood, especially the right one, the first to live and the last to die (as stated before).
src.qo: sed motores primi sanguinis ſunt auriculæ, præsertim dextra, pri- mum vivens & ultimum moriens

src.l: William Harvey, 1660, Exercitationes anatomicae de generatione animalium (with De motu cordis)
src.q: sed motores primi sanguinis ſunt auriculæ, præsertim dextra, pri- mum vivens & ultimum moriens

s: Ralph Cudworth (True Intellectual System, 1678) ranks the plastic and vegetative life of nature as the lowest of all lives, below the sensitive, and argues that because plastic nature is a life it must be incorporeal. Life by what it IS PART OF: a hierarchy of incorporeal lives in which forming bodies is the lowest rung.

src.l: Ralph Cudworth, 1678, The true intellectual system of the universe: the first part; wherein, all the reason and philosophy of atheism is confuted; and its impossibility demonstrated. By R. Cudworth, D.D.
src.q: The Plastick and Vegetative Life of Nature the Lowest of all Lives, and Inferiour to the Sensitive.

src.l: Ralph Cudworth, 1678, The true intellectual system of the universe: the first part; wherein, all the reason and philosophy of atheism is confuted; and its impossibility demonstrated. By R. Cudworth, D.D.
src.q: forasmuch as the Plastick Nature is a Life, it must needs be Incorporeal.

s: Jan Marek Marci of Kronland, the author of the 'Ancient Philosophy Restored' (Philosophia vetus restituta, 1662; 1676 ed.), examining van Helmont's archeus, argues that if the splendor the archeus produces is a ray of light, the archeus will have light and so life and soul of itself, needing nothing alien. Life by what it HAS: light.

src.l: Marci z Kronlandu, Jan Marek, 1676, Restored Ancient Philosophy
src.q: And because splendor is a ray of light, the archeus will have light, and consequently life and soul, not needing anything alien to itself
src.qo: Et quia splendor est radius lucis, habe- bit archeus lucem ac proinde vitam & animam ex se alienæ haud indi- gus

src.l: Marci z Kronlandu, Jan Marek, 1676, Restored Ancient Philosophy
src.q: Et quia splendor est radius lucis, habe- bit archeus lucem ac proinde vitam & animam ex se alienæ haud indi- gus

s: Kant (Kritik der Urteilskraft §65, 1790) says an organized being is not merely a machine, which has only moving force, but has in itself a self-propagating formative power (bildende Kraft) that organizes materials; 'analogue of art' says too little, 'analogue of life' comes closer but runs into a dilemma. Life by what it DOES to matter: organize it; Kant declines to call this life outright.

src.l: Immanuel Kant, 1922, Kritik der Urteilskraft (German)
src.q: An organized being is therefore not merely a machine, for a machine has only moving power; rather, it possesses within itself formative power
src.qo: Ein organisiertes Wesen ist also nicht bloß Maschine, denn die hat lediglich bewegende Kraft, sondern es d) besitzt in sich bildende Kraft … Näher tritt man vielleicht dieser unerforschlichen Eigenschaft, wenn man sie ein Analogon des Lebens nennt

src.l: Immanuel Kant, 1922, Kritik der Urteilskraft (German)
src.q: Ein organisiertes Wesen ist also nicht bloß Maschine, denn die hat lediglich bewegende Kraft, sondern es d) besitzt in sich bildende Kraft

src.l: Immanuel Kant, 1922, Kritik der Urteilskraft (German)
src.q: Näher tritt man vielleicht dieser unerforschlichen Eigenschaft, wenn man sie ein Analogon des Lebens nennt

s: Kant (Kritik der Urteilskraft §66, 1790) states the principle that is also the definition of organized beings: an organized product of nature is one in which everything is an end and reciprocally also a means, and nothing in it is in vain or due to blind mechanism. The living is defined by what it IS: a whole whose parts are reciprocally ends and means.

src.l: Immanuel Kant, 1922, Kritik der Urteilskraft (German)
src.q: This principle, which is also the definition of such beings, states: An organized product of nature is one in which everything is an end and, reciprocally, also a means.
src.qo: Ein organisiertes Produkt der Natur ist das, in wel- chem alles Zweck und wechselseitig auch Mittel ist.

src.l: Immanuel Kant, 1922, Kritik der Urteilskraft (German)
src.q: Ein organisiertes Produkt der Natur ist das, in wel- chem alles Zweck und wechselseitig auch Mittel ist.

s: Schelling (Von der Weltseele, 1798) argues that what is the principle of life (Princip des Lebens) cannot itself be a product of life, so physiologists who seek the ground of life in the nerves must put it outside the body; yet a body absolutely passive toward life is a senseless concept, since passivity is only a lack of resistance. Life defined by a RELATION: an outer cause met by the organism's own resistance.

src.l: Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling, 1798, Von der Weltseele; eine Hypothese der höhern Physik (1st ed.)
src.q: that which is the principle of life Princip des Lebens cannot itself be a product of life
src.qo: das, was Princip des Lebens ist, nicht selbst Product des Lebens seyn kann

src.l: Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling, 1798, Von der Weltseele; eine Hypothese der höhern Physik (1st ed.)
src.q: das, was Princip des Lebens ist, nicht selbst Product des Lebens seyn kann

s: Schopenhauer (Die Welt als Wille und Vorstellung IV, 1818; 1844 ed.) recalls the truth set out at the start of Book IV: to the will to live (Wille zum Leben), life itself is always certain, as its mere image or mirror. Life by what it IS PART OF: the appearance of a blind will.

src.l: Arthur Schopenhauer, 1818, Die Welt als Wille und Vorstellung
src.q: to the will to live life itself is always certain as its mere image or mirror
src.qo: daß dem Willen zum Leben das Leben ſelbſt, als ſein bloßes Abbild oder Spiegel, immer gewiß iſt

src.l: Arthur Schopenhauer, 1818, Die Welt als Wille und Vorstellung
src.q: daß dem Willen zum Leben das Leben ſelbſt, als ſein bloßes Abbild oder Spiegel, immer gewiß iſt

s: Bergson (L'Évolution créatrice, 1907) says that in reality life is a movement and materiality the inverse movement, each simple: matter an undivided flux, and life an undivided current that traverses it, cutting living beings out of it. Life by what it DOES: a movement against the descent of matter.

src.l: Henri Bergson, 1908, Creative Evolution
src.q: In reality, life is a movement, materiality is the inverse movement, and each of these two movements is simple
src.qo: En réalité la vie est un mouvement, la matérialité est le mouvement inverse, et chacun de ces deux mouvements est simple

src.l: Henri Bergson, 1908, Creative Evolution
src.q: En réalité la vie est un mouvement, la matérialité est le mouvement inverse, et chacun de ces deux mouvements est simple

s: Nietzsche (a note of 1887 printed in Der Wille zur Macht, 1922 ed.) says nothing in life has value except the degree of power, 'provided that life itself is the will to power'. Life by what it IS: will to power, stated as a premise in a hypothetical.

src.l: Friedrich Nietzsche, 1922, Der Wille zur Macht
src.q: There is nothing in life that has value, except for the degree of power—provided, of course, that life itself is the will to power.
src.qo: Es giebt Nichts am Leben, was Werth hat, ausser dem Grade der Macht — gesetzt eben, dass Leben selbst der Wille zur Macht ist.

src.l: Friedrich Nietzsche, 1922, Der Wille zur Macht
src.q: Es giebt Nichts am Leben, was Werth hat, ausser dem Grade der Macht — gesetzt eben, dass Leben selbst der Wille zur Macht ist.

s: Nietzsche (Unzeitgemässe Betrachtungen, 1873–76; German only on SL) says those who see in their inner vision no new forms, only old ones behind them, 'serve history, but not life, and are dead before they have died'; true, fruitful life now means feeling music within. Life by what it DOES: bring forth new forms.

src.l: Friedrich Nietzsche, 1873, Unzeitgemässe Betrachtungen
src.q: so dienen sie der Historie, aber nicht dem Leben, und sind todt, bevor sie gestorben sind

s: Dilthey (Das Erlebnis und die Dichtung, 1906; 1907 ed.) narrows Erlebnis: any of the poet's countless states of life may be called an Erlebnis psychologically, but he means only those moments, or their connections, that unlock for the poet a trait of life; ideas serve the poet only as they make his experiences intelligible. Life by what it IS for a subject: lived experience disclosing itself.

src.l: Wilhelm Dilthey, 1907, Poetry and Experience
src.q: Each of the countless states of life through which the poet passes can be designated as an Erlebnis … this expression is intended to denote only those moments of his existence, or the connections among them, that unlock for him a trait of life.
src.qo: Jeder der unzähligen Lebenszustände, durch die der Dichter hindurchgeht, kann in psychologischem Sinne als Erlebnis bezeichnet werden

src.l: Wilhelm Dilthey, 1907, Poetry and Experience
src.q: Jeder der unzähligen Lebenszustände, durch die der Dichter hindurchgeht, kann in psychologischem Sinne als Erlebnis bezeichnet werden

s: Whitehead (Process and Reality, 1929) says 'Life is a bid for freedom': the problem life presents is how there can be originality, and the doctrine of an enduring soul is 'exactly the irrelevant answer', since it makes the soul no more original than a stone. Life by what it DOES: originality in response, not a soul it has.

src.l: Alfred North Whitehead, 1929, Process and Reality
src.q: Life is a bid for freedom: an enduring entity binds any one of its occasions to the line of its ancestry. The doctrine of the enduring soul with its permanent characteristics is exactly the irrelevant answer to the problem which life presents.

s: Whitehead (1929) argues that the nature of life is not to be sought by identifying it with some society of occasions defined by a common character: an 'entirely living' nexus is, in respect of its life, not social, and lacks the genetic power of societies, though it may be supported by them. Life is not a kind of THING; it is what happens in the interstices of organisms.

src.l: Alfred North Whitehead, 1929, Process and Reality
src.q: So far we have argued that the nature of life is not to be sought by its identification with some society of occasions, which are living in virtue of the defining characteristic of that society. An 'entirely living' nexus is, in respect to its life, not social.

s: Whitehead (1929) says organic bodies have their parts coordinated by a peculiar vividness of mutual inheritance, and that the difference between a living organism and its inorganic environment is only one of degree, but a degree that makes all the difference, in effect a difference of quality. Life by what it IS PART OF: one continuum of organism with the inorganic.

src.l: Alfred North Whitehead, 1929, Process and Reality
src.q: In a sense, the difference between a living organism and the inorganic environment is only a question of degree; but it is a difference of degree which makes all the difference—in effect, it is a difference of quality.

s: Against 'each era's definition of life': on SL's pages the 17th century alone holds at least four incompatible definitions side by side: heat and moisture (Cremonini 1634, Conring 1647), a self-continuous spirit (Bacon 1623), a created light and form that does not consume radical moisture (van Helmont 1648), and an incorporeal plastic life (Cudworth 1678); and Abano (c. 1310) already lists four on one page. A spine of one definition per era is a retrospective tidying.

src.l: Jan Baptist van Helmont, 1648, Ortus Medicinae
src.q: However, it is not a fiery light, nor combustible, nor is it a consumer of the radical moisture .

src.l: Pietro d'Abano, 1472, Conciliator differentiarum philosophorum et praecipue medicorum
src.q: Regarding the first, it should be known that "life" is spoken of in three ways

s: Against reading Schopenhauer, Nietzsche, Dilthey and Whitehead as the next entries after Aristotle, Bacon and Kant in one series of 'definitions of life': the earlier texts define the living body (zōē: nourishment, heat, spirit, organization), while Schopenhauer's will to live, Nietzsche's will to power and Dilthey's Erlebnis define life as lived and valued (bios, Leben as Erleben). Kant explicitly defines the organized product, not life, and Dilthey's 'trait of life' is a poet's experience. A single spine joins two different questions.

src.l: Wilhelm Dilthey, 1907, Poetry and Experience
src.q: that unlock for him a trait of life.

src.l: Immanuel Kant, 1922, Kritik der Urteilskraft (German)
src.q: An organized product of nature is one in which everything is an end and, reciprocally, also a means.

s: Plato's Phaedo (105c–d, c. 380 BCE) answers 'what, when present in a body, makes it alive?' with 'soul', and adds that whatever soul takes possession of, it always comes bringing life to it (φέρουσα ζωήν): soul is not life itself but its carrier, and so cannot admit death.

src.l: Plato, Harold North Fowler (trans.), 1913, Euthyphro, Apology, Crito, Phaedo, Phaedrus (Loeb)
src.q: "What causes the body in which it is to be alive?" "The soul," he replied. "Is this always the case?" "Yes," said he, "of course." "Then if the soul takes possession of anything it always brings life to it?"

src.l: Plato, Harold North Fowler (trans.), 1913, Euthyphro, Apology, Crito, Phaedo, Phaedrus (Loeb)
src.q: Ἡ ψυχὴ ἄρα ὅτι ἂν αὐτὴ κατάσχῃ, ἀεὶ ἥκει ἐπ’ ἐκεῖνο φέρουσα ζωήν;

s: In the Phaedrus (245c–e) Plato makes self-motion the essence and definition of soul: a body moved from without is soulless (ἄψυχον), one moved from within, of itself, is ensouled (ἔμψυχον); the self-mover is the beginning of motion and so ungenerated and immortal.

src.l: Plato, Harold North Fowler (trans.), 1913, Euthyphro, Apology, Crito, Phaedo, Phaedrus (Loeb)
src.q: For every body which derives motion from without is soulless, but that which has its motion within itself has a soul, since that is the nature of the soul

src.l: Plato, Harold North Fowler (trans.), 1913, Euthyphro, Apology, Crito, Phaedo, Phaedrus (Loeb)
src.q: πᾶν γὰρ σῶμα, ᾧ μὲν ἔξωθεν τὸ κινεῖσθαι, ἄψυχον, ᾧ δὲ ἔνδοθεν αὐτῷ ἐξ αὑτοῦ, ἔμψυχον, ὡς ταύτης οὔσης φύσεως ψυχῆς

s: Plato's Laws X (895c–896a, c. 350 BCE) makes the life test explicit: a thing of earth, water or fire that moves itself is to be called alive (ζῆν), whatever has soul in it is alive, and the definition (λόγος) of soul is 'the motion able to move itself'.

src.l: Plato, R. G. Bury (trans.), 1926, Laws, vol. 2 (Books 7–12) (Loeb)
src.q: What you ask me is, whether we are to speak of a thing as "alive" when it moves itself?

src.l: Plato, R. G. Bury (trans.), 1926, Laws, vol. 2 (Books 7–12) (Loeb)
src.q: Well then, when we see soul in things, must we not equally agree that they are alive?

src.l: Plato, R. G. Bury (trans.), 1926, Laws, vol. 2 (Books 7–12) (Loeb)
src.q: ὁπόταν ψυχὴν ἔν τισιν ὁρῶμεν, μῶν ἄλλο ἢ ταὐτὸν τούτῳ; ζῆν ὁμολογητέον;

src.l: Plato, R. G. Bury (trans.), 1926, Laws, vol. 2 (Books 7–12) (Loeb)
src.q: Can we give it any other definition than that stated just now—"the motion able to move itself"?

s: Heraclitus (B36, via Clement, Strom. VI.16) puts soul inside the cycle of the elements: 'to souls it is death to become water', and from water, in turn, soul comes to be; soul is a phase of transformation, not a separate principle.

src.l: Hermann Diels, 1912, Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker
src.q: To souls it is death to become water, and to water it is death to become earth, but from earth comes water, and from water, soul.
src.qo: ψυχῆισιν θάνατος ὕδωρ γενέσθαι, ὕδατι δὲ θάνατος γῆν γενέσθαι, ἐκ γῆς δὲ ὕδωρ γίνεται, ἐξ ὕδατος δὲ ψυχή.

src.l: Hermann Diels, 1912, Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker
src.q: ψυχῆισιν θάνατος ὕδωρ γενέσθαι, ὕδατι δὲ θάνατος γῆν γενέσθαι, ἐκ γῆς δὲ ὕδωρ γίνεται, ἐξ ὕδατος δὲ ψυχή.

s: Numenius (in Porphyry, Cave of the Nymphs 10) reports that Heraclitus said becoming moist is delight or death for souls, the delight being their fall into birth, and elsewhere that 'we live their death and they live our death' (B77/B62): living and dying are one exchange seen from two sides.

src.l: Hermann Diels, 1912, Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker
src.loc: Heraclitus B77 (Numenius fr. 35, Porph. antr. nymph. 10); scan 114
src.q: Whence Heraclitus also said that for souls it is a delight or death to become moist; their delight is the fall into birth. But elsewhere he says: we live their death and they live our death.
src.qo: ζῆν ἡμᾶς τὸν ἐκείνων θάνατον καὶ ζῆν ἐκείνας τὸν ἡμέτερον θάνατον

src.l: Hermann Diels, 1912, Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker
src.q: ζῆν ἡμᾶς τὸν ἐκείνων θάνατον καὶ ζῆν ἐκείνας τὸν ἡμέτερον θάνατον

s: Empedocles (B110.10, c. 450 BCE) tells his pupil 'know that all things have thought (φρόνησις) and a share of understanding': sentience is not the mark that divides the living from the rest but is spread through everything.

src.l: Empedocles, William Ellery Leonard (trans.), 1908, The Fragments of Empedocles
src.q: For know: All things have fixed intent and share of thought.

src.l: Empedocles, William Ellery Leonard (trans.), 1908, The Fragments of Empedocles
src.q: πάντα γὰρ ἴσθι φρόνησιν ἔχειν καὶ νώματος αἶσαν.

s: Empedocles (B111) promises his pupil knowledge of 'drugs that are a defence against ills and old age' (γήραος ἄλκαρ), power over winds and rain, and the power to bring back from Hades the strength of a dead man: the earliest Greek text on SL that treats prolonging and restoring life as a learnable art.

src.l: Empedocles, William Ellery Leonard (trans.), 1908, The Fragments of Empedocles
src.q: And thou shalt master every drug that e’er Was made defense ’gainst sickness and old age—

src.l: Empedocles, William Ellery Leonard (trans.), 1908, The Fragments of Empedocles
src.q: φάρμακα δ’ ὅσσα γεγᾶσι κακῶν καὶ γήραος ἄλκαρ

src.l: Empedocles, William Ellery Leonard (trans.), 1908, The Fragments of Empedocles
src.q: From Hades beckon the might of perished men.

s: A Stoic argument printed in SVF II.1013 grades unified bodies by what holds them together, hexis (stones, wood), physis (plants) or psychē (animals), and argues from cosmic sympathy (moon and tides, a cut finger affecting the whole body) that the world is a unified body which changes too much to be held by mere hexis; it must be ensouled.

src.l: Hans von Arnim (ed.), 1964, Stoicorum Veterum Fragmenta, vol. 2: Chrysippus
src.q: But in unified bodies, there is a certain sympathy, if, when a finger is cut, the whole body is affected together. The world, therefore, is a body of unified things.
src.qo: καὶ ἕξεως μὲν ὡς λίθοι καὶ ξύλα, φύσεως δὲ καθάπερ τὰ φυτά, ψυχῆς δὲ τὰ ζῶα

src.l: Hans von Arnim (ed.), 1964, Stoicorum Veterum Fragmenta, vol. 2: Chrysippus
src.q: καὶ ἕξεως μὲν ὡς λίθοι καὶ ξύλα, φύσεως δὲ καθάπερ τὰ φυτά, ψυχῆς δὲ τὰ ζῶα

src.l: Hans von Arnim (ed.), 1964, Stoicorum Veterum Fragmenta, vol. 2: Chrysippus
src.q: But the world admits noteworthy changes, sometimes the environment becoming freezing, sometimes hot, sometimes arid, sometimes moist, and sometimes otherwise changing according to the motions of the heavens. Therefore, the world is not held together by a simple hexis.
src.qo: καὶ ἕξεως μὲν ὡς λίθοι καὶ ξύλα, φύσεως δὲ καθάπερ τὰ φυτά, ψυχῆς δὲ τὰ ζῶα

s: Cicero's Stoic Balbus (De natura deorum II.30) argues that since sense and reason are found in parts of the world, they must be present more keenly in its ruling part: 'it is necessary that the world is wise' and therefore a god; the world's heat is purer than 'this heat of ours' by which living things are kept and thrive.

src.l: Marcus Tullius Cicero, 1494, De natura deorum and other philosophical works
src.q: For this reason, it is necessary that the world is wise, and that nature, encompassing and holding all things, excels in the perfection of reason, and therefore the world is a god
src.qo: Quo circa sapientem esse mundum necesse est

src.l: Marcus Tullius Cicero, 1494, De natura deorum and other philosophical works
src.loc: De natura deorum II.30, Latin; scan 36
src.q: Quo circa sapientem esse mundum necesse est

s: Lucretius (DRN III.177–180) answers what the mind and soul are with a body: 'extremely fine and formed of exceedingly minute bodies', shown by how fast thought moves; life needs no principle beyond small, mobile atoms held in a frame, and so it ends when the frame no longer holds them.

src.l: Lucretius, H. A. J. Munro (ed., trans.), 1864, De rerum natura (Munro text and notes)
src.q: First of all, I say that it is extremely fine and consists of exceedingly minute bodies.
src.qo: principio esse aio persuptilem atque minutis perquam corporibus factum constare.

src.l: Lucretius, H. A. J. Munro (ed., trans.), 1864, De rerum natura (Munro text and notes)
src.q: principio esse aio persuptilem atque minutis perquam corporibus factum constare.

s: Galen (On the Natural Faculties III.10, c. 180 CE) concludes that four faculties, attraction, retention, alteration and excretion, are necessary to every part of the body that is nourished, and calls them the 'handmaids of nutrition': what the living part does is draw in what is proper to it and reject what is foreign.

src.l: Galen, 1916, On the Natural Faculties
src.q: It has been demonstrated that these four faculties—attraction, retention, alteration, and excretion—are necessary for every part of the body that requires nourishment. For this reason, we have called these powers the handmaids of nutrition .
src.qo: For these four faculties have been shown to be necessary for every part which is to be nourished ; this is why we have called these faculties the handmaids of nutrition.

s: Philo (Quaestiones in Genesim I.4–5, c. 40 CE, extant in Armenian; Aucher's Latin in Richter's 1828 edition) reads Gen 2:7 as: the moulded, sensible man was formed from dust as by a potter and obtained a soul when God breathed life into his face, so that his nature is a mixture of corruptible and incorruptible; the breath goes to the face because the fountain of animal form is sensation, which is in the face.

src.l: Philo of Alexandria, J. B. Aucher (Latin of the Armenian), C. E. Richter (ed.), 1828, Philonis Judaei Opera Omnia, Vol. 6 (Quaestiones in Genesim, Latin)
src.q: he obtained a soul by God breathing life into his face … so that the temperament of nature was a mixture of the corruptible and the incorruptible
src.qo: animam autem sortitus est insufflante deo P. A. vitam in eius vultum, ita ut commixtum esset temperamentum naturae ex corruptibili et incorruptibili.

src.l: Philo of Alexandria, J. B. Aucher (Latin of the Armenian), C. E. Richter (ed.), 1828, Philonis Judaei Opera Omnia, Vol. 6 (Quaestiones in Genesim, Latin)
src.q: animam autem sortitus est insufflante deo P. A. vitam in eius vultum, ita ut commixtum esset temperamentum naturae ex corruptibili et incorruptibili.

src.l: Philo of Alexandria, J. B. Aucher (Latin of the Armenian), C. E. Richter (ed.), 1828, Philonis Judaei Opera Omnia, Vol. 6 (Quaestiones in Genesim, Latin)
src.q: the fountain of animal form is sensation, and sensation (as a whole) is in the face
src.qo: Adhaec animalis formae fons est sensus, sensus autem (totalis) in facie est.

s: Ibn Gabirol's Fons vitae (11th c., Latin of John of Spain and Gundissalinus; Baeumker 1895) ends: asked the fruit of this study, the Master answers 'escape from death and attachment to the origin of life', reached by withdrawing from sensibles into intelligibles and hanging one's whole being on the Giver of goodness; the title's 'source of life' is the divine origin.

src.l: Solomon ibn Gabirol (Avicebron), Clemens Baeumker (ed.), 1895, Avencebrolis Fons Vitae
src.q: Disciple. What is the fruit we will obtain from this study? Master. The escape from death and the attachment to the origin of life.
src.qo: D. Quis est fructus quem consequemur ex hoc studio? M. Euasio mortis et applicatio ad originem uitae.

src.l: Solomon ibn Gabirol (Avicebron), Clemens Baeumker (ed.), 1895, Avencebrolis Fons Vitae
src.q: D. Quis est fructus quem consequemur ex hoc studio? M. Euasio mortis et applicatio ad originem uitae.

s: Avicenna's Compendium de anima (Latin of Andrea Alpago, Venice 1546), ch. 5: a living body is a natural composite body distinguished from a non-living one by its soul, not by its body; the soul is therefore a form, forms are perfections, and the soul is the first perfection (the principle of operations, not the operations) of a natural body.

src.l: Avicenna (Ibn Sina), Andrea Alpago (trans.), 1546, Compendium de anima
src.q: a living body is a natural composite body which is distinguished from a non-living body by its soul, and not by its body … The principle or source is the first perfection, while the operation or resulting impression is the second.
src.qo: corpus uiuens est corpus cõ positum naturale, quod distinguitur a non uiuente per animã suam, non per corpus suum

src.l: Avicenna (Ibn Sina), Andrea Alpago (trans.), 1546, Compendium de anima
src.q: corpus uiuens est corpus cõ positum naturale, quod distinguitur a non uiuente per animã suam, non per corpus suum

s: Ibn Tufayl's Hayy ibn Yaqzan (12th c.; Pococke's Arabic-Latin edition, 1671): when the doe that nursed him dies, Hayy cuts open her chest with stones and reeds to find the seat of the affliction, passes the lungs, opens the heart and finds two cavities: the right full of clotted blood, the left empty; what he seeks is 'the thing specific to this place', without which he cannot manage for the twinkling of an eye.

src.l: Ibn Tufayl, Edward Pococke (ed. and Latin trans.), 1671, حي بن يقظان / Philosophus Autodidactus
src.q: When he split it open, he found two cavities: one on the right side and one on the left. … The one on the right was full of clotted blood, while the one on the left was empty, containing nothing. … My object is the thing specific to this place, without which I cannot manage for the twinkling of an eye
src.qo: والذي من الجهة اليسري خال لاشي فيه … انما مطلوبي الشي الذي يختص به هذا الموضع الذي لا استغني عنه طرفة عين

src.l: Ibn Tufayl, Edward Pococke (ed. and Latin trans.), 1671, حي بن يقظان / Philosophus Autodidactus
src.q: والذي من الجهة اليسري خال لاشي فيه

src.l: Ibn Tufayl, Edward Pococke (ed. and Latin trans.), 1671, حي بن يقظان / Philosophus Autodidactus
src.q: انما مطلوبي الشي الذي يختص به هذا الموضع الذي لا استغني عنه طرفة عين

s: Hayy concludes that what he sought had been in the empty chamber and departed, and that its departure was the doe's cessation of perception and movement; he comes to see that his mother was that departed thing, the source of all her actions, and that the body was only its tool, like the stick he fought beasts with, so his attachment passes from the body to its possessor and mover.

src.l: Ibn Tufayl, Edward Pococke (ed. and Latin trans.), 1671, حي بن يقظان / Philosophus Autodidactus
src.q: I see only that my object was in it, then it departed and left it vacant. … At that moment, that which occurred to this body happened, such as the cessation of function and the loss of perception and movement.
src.qo: ما اري الا ان مطلوبي كان فيه فارتحل عنه واخلاه … وان هذا الجسد بجانبه انما هو كالآلة لذلك

src.l: Ibn Tufayl, Edward Pococke (ed. and Latin trans.), 1671, حي بن يقظان / Philosophus Autodidactus
src.q: This body beside him was merely like a tool for it, in the place of the stick he had taken to fight the wild beasts. His attachment shifted from the body to the possessor of the body and its mover.

s: Taught by fire, and by the warmth of animals in life and their coldness after death, Hayy guesses the departed thing is of fire's substance; he binds a live animal, opens its heart's left cavity and finds it full of a vaporous air like white mist, hot enough to burn his finger; the animal dies at once, and he concludes this moist vapour was what moved it, present in every animal, and that its separation is death.

src.l: Ibn Tufayl, Edward Pococke (ed. and Latin trans.), 1671, حي بن يقظان / Philosophus Autodidactus
src.q: it occurred to him that the thing which had departed from the heart of his mother the gazelle, who had raised him, was of the substance of this existing thing, or of something of its genus. This was confirmed in his mind by what he saw of the heat of the animal during its lifetime, and its coldness after its death
src.qo: فراي ذلك الفراغ مملوا بهوا بخاري شبه الضباب الابيض فادخل اصبعه فيه فوجده من الحرارة في حد كان يحرقه ومات ذلك الحيوان علي الفور فصح عنده ان ذلك البخار الرطب هو الذي كان يحرك هذا الحيوان

src.l: Ibn Tufayl, Edward Pococke (ed. and Latin trans.), 1671, حي بن يقظان / Philosophus Autodidactus
src.q: He saw that void space full of a vaporous air, like a white mist. He inserted his finger into it and found it to be so hot that it burned him, and that animal died on the spot. So it became clear to him that this moist vapor was what had moved this animal
src.qo: فراي ذلك الفراغ مملوا بهوا بخاري شبه الضباب الابيض فادخل اصبعه فيه فوجده من الحرارة في حد كان يحرقه ومات ذلك الحيوان علي الفور فصح عنده ان ذلك البخار الرطب هو الذي كان يحرك هذا الحيوان

s: Dissecting living and dead animals, Hayy finds that each animal, though many in organs, senses and motions, is one through that spirit (al-rūḥ) which spreads from one source to all the organs, which serve it as tools serve a hunter; 'that animal spirit is one', seeing through the eye, hearing through the ear.

src.l: Ibn Tufayl, Edward Pococke (ed. and Latin trans.), 1671, حي بن يقظان / Philosophus Autodidactus
src.q: every individual of the animal species, even if it is complex in its organs and varied in its senses and movements, is one through that spirit whose source is from one location, and its division into the other organs emanates from it. All the organs are merely serving it or acting on its behalf.
src.qo: فانه واحد بذلك الروح الذي مبدؤه من قرار واحد … كذلك ذلك الروح الحيواني واحد

src.l: Ibn Tufayl, Edward Pococke (ed. and Latin trans.), 1671, حي بن يقظان / Philosophus Autodidactus
src.q: Likewise, that animal spirit is one, and if it acts through the tool of the eye, its action is seeing
src.qo: فانه واحد بذلك الروح الذي مبدؤه من قرار واحد … كذلك ذلك الروح الحيواني واحد

s: Kaviratna's 1890 English of Caraka (Sūtrasthāna 1) renders the āyus verse plainly as 'The union of body, senses, mind, and soul is called Life', and his note glosses its synonyms: dhāri as holding together the elements, nityaga as continually going away, anubandha as a link in the chain of rebirths.

src.l: Charaka; Avinash Chandra Kaviratna (trans.), 1890, Charaka-Samhita
src.q: The union of body, senses, mind, and soul is called Life. The latter is known again by the names of Dhāri, Jivita, Nityaga, and Anubandha.

src.l: Charaka; Avinash Chandra Kaviratna (trans.), 1890, Charaka-Samhita
src.q: Nityaga (always going), because it is continually running or going away; Anubandha (tie or link), because this life is a link in the endless chain of individual existence.

s: Caraka (Sū. 1, Kaviratna 1890): mind, soul and body, this trinity called the person, rests on union like three sticks standing by one another's support; everything rests on it, and it is the subject of the Science of Life.

src.l: Charaka; Avinash Chandra Kaviratna (trans.), 1890, Charaka-Samhita
src.q: Mind, soul, and body, this trinity, called person, resteth on union like three sticks (standing with one another’s support.) Upon that (trinity) everything rests.

s: Anquetil-Duperron's Latin Oupnek'hat (1802, from Dara Shikoh's Persian of the Upanishads) retells the senses' submission to prāṇa: all the senses said to the pran, 'you sustain everything; you are our lord; we are all from you'; the senses set into the pran in sleep and it makes them appear again on waking.

src.l: Abraham-Hyacinthe Anquetil-Duperron (trans.), Dara Shikoh (Persian), 1802, Oupnek'hat (id est, Secretum tegendum), Vol. 2
src.q: All the senses said to the pran: You are the one sustaining everything; you are our master; we are all from you. … And because all the senses, at the time of sleep, make their setting into the pran and go down
src.qo: Omnes sensus cum pran dixerunt, quòd; tu super habens (sustentans) omne ; tu dominus noster es ; nos omnes ex te sumus.

src.l: Abraham-Hyacinthe Anquetil-Duperron (trans.), Dara Shikoh (Persian), 1802, Oupnek'hat (id est, Secretum tegendum), Vol. 2
src.q: Omnes sensus cum pran dixerunt, quòd; tu super habens (sustentans) omne ; tu dominus noster es ; nos omnes ex te sumus.

s: Zhuangzi ch. 18 'Perfect Happiness' (Giles 1889): drumming on a bowl after his wife's death, Zhuangzi says she existed before birth without form or substance, then substance was added to spirit, the substance took form, then came birth, and now by a further change she is dead, like the sequence of the four seasons.

src.l: Zhuang Zhou, Herbert A. Giles (trans.), 1889, Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer
src.q: she had already existed in a previous state before birth, without form, or even substance; that while in that unconditioned condition, substance was added to spirit; that this substance then assumed form; and that the next stage was birth.

src.l: Zhuang Zhou, Herbert A. Giles (trans.), 1889, Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer
src.q: Life is a loan with which the borrower does but add more dust and dirt to the sum total of existence. Life and death are as day and night

s: Huainanzi (139 BCE; 1595 Huainan honglie jie with Gao You's commentary): when a tree dies its green leaves it, but what made the tree live is not the tree; 'what gives life to life has never died; only what it produced dies'; the interlinear commentary says what made it live is Heaven, and what fills the form is qi, not the form.

src.l: 劉安 Liu An, 高誘 Gao You (comm.), 1595, 淮南鴻烈解 Huainan hong lie jie
src.q: When a tree dies, its green color leaves it. But that which caused the tree to grow, is it the tree itself? … That which gives life to life has never died; it is only that which is produced that dies

s: Spinoza (Ethics III, prop. 6, 1677) holds that each thing, as far as it is in itself, strives to persevere in its being: the striving belongs to every individual thing, not to living things alone.

src.l: Baruch Spinoza, 1915, Ethica (Latin original)
src.loc: Ethica III, prop. VI; scan 85 (printed p. 70)
src.q: Each thing, as far as it lies within itself, strives to persevere in its being.
src.qo: Unaquæque res, quantum in se est, in suo esse perseverare conatur.
