s: Spinoza (Ethics III, prop. 7, 1677) identifies the conatus by which each thing strives to persevere in its being with nothing but the thing's own actual essence: a thing is its striving.

s: Spinoza (Ethics III, prop. 8, 1677) says the striving to persevere involves no finite time but an indefinite duration: a thing destroyed by no external cause would go on existing by the same power by which it now exists, so death always comes from outside.

src.loc: Ethica III, prop. VIII and demonstration; scan 86
src.q: The striving by which each thing strives to persevere in its being involves no finite time, but an indefinite duration. ... if it is destroyed by no external cause, it will continue to exist by the same power by which it already exists

s: Spinoza (Ethics III, prop. 9 scholium, 1677) names the conatus Will when it is referred to the mind alone and Appetite when referred to mind and body together, and says this appetite is the very essence of man.

src.l: Baruch Spinoza, 1915, Ethica (Latin original)
src.loc: Ethica III, prop. IX scholium; scan 86
src.q: This striving, when it is related to the Mind alone, is called Will; but when it is related to both the Mind and the Body together, it is called Appetite. This appetite is therefore nothing other than the very essence of man
src.qo: Hic conatus, cum ad Mentem solam refertur, Voluntas appellatur, sed cum ad Mentem et Corpus simul refertur, vocatur Appetitus; qui proinde nihil aliud est quam ipsa hominis essentia

s: Leibniz (Monadology §72, 1714) holds that the soul changes its body only gradually, never being stripped of all its organs at once; animals undergo metamorphosis but never metempsychosis, there are no disembodied souls, and God alone is without body.

src.l: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, 1930, The Monadology of Leibniz (English translation with commentary)
src.q: Thus the soul changes its body only gradually and by degrees, so that it is never suddenly despoiled of all its organs. And while in animals there is often metamorphosis, there is never metempsychosis, nor transmigration of souls. There are no disembodied souls, no bodiless genii. God alone is without body.

s: Leibniz (Monadology §73, 1714) concludes that there is neither absolute birth nor complete death, in the sense of a separation of soul and body: what we call births are developments and unfoldings, what we call deaths are foldings and shrinkages.

src.l: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, 1930, The Monadology of Leibniz (English translation with commentary)
src.q: there is neither absolute birth nor complete death in the precise meaning of the separation of the soul and body. What we call births are developments and unfoldings, and what we call deaths are foldings and shrinkages.

s: Leibniz (Monadology §74, 1714) cites recent research on plants, insects and animals to deny spontaneous generation from chaos or putrefaction, holds that organic bodies come always from seeds with some preformation, and calls conception a great transformation of an animal that already existed.

src.l: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, 1930, The Monadology of Leibniz (English translation with commentary)
src.q: natural organic bodies are not spontaneously produced from a chaos or from putrefaction but always from seeds or germs. In these seeds there can be no doubt there is already some preformation before their germination. ... Conception is a means of a great transformation of disposition which makes it become an animal of another kind.

s: The 1930 commentator on the Monadology reads its rejection of disembodied souls as resting on the impossibility of defining existence except as activity: 'anything is what it does', so separating living from thinking or body from mind is a reductio ad absurdum.

src.l: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, 1930, The Monadology of Leibniz (English translation with commentary)
src.q: The logical basis of the monadic conception is the impossibility of defining existence except in terms of activity. Anything is what it does.

s: La Mettrie (L'Homme machine, 1748) asks whether organisation would suffice for everything and answers 'yes, once again', because thought visibly develops with the organs and matter can acquire the faculty of feeling.

src.q: Would organization, therefore, be sufficient for everything? Yes, once again; since thought develops visibly with the organs

s: La Mettrie (L'Homme machine, 1748) lists observations that the flesh of animals palpitates after death, that muscles cut from the body retract when pricked, and that a frog's heart torn from the body beats for an hour or more and beats again when pricked.

src.l: Julien Offray de La Mettrie, 1748, L'Homme Machine
src.q: All the flesh of Animals palpitates after death ... Muscles separated from the body withdraw when pricked. ... One only needs to prick the heart, and this hollow muscle beats again.
src.qo: Toutes les chairs des Animaux palpitent après la mort ... il n'y a qu'à piquer le cœur, & ce muscle creux bat encore.

src.q: Toutes les chairs des Animaux palpitent après la mort ... il n'y a qu'à piquer le cœur, & ce muscle creux bat encore.

s: La Mettrie (L'Homme machine, 1748) concludes from these facts that every little fibre or part of an organised body moves by a principle proper to it, whose action does not depend on the nerves.

src.l: Julien Offray de La Mettrie, 1748, L'Homme Machine
src.q: every little fiber or part of organized bodies moves by a principle that is proper to it, and whose action does not depend on the nerves

s: La Mettrie (L'Homme machine, 1748) notes that polyps, cut up, regenerate within eight days into as many animals as there are pieces, and says he is glad this discovery upsets the naturalists' system of generation.

src.l: Julien Offray de La Mettrie, 1748, L'Homme Machine
src.q: Polypes do more than move after sectioning; they reproduce within eight days into as many Animals as there are severed parts.
src.qo: Les Polypes font plus que de se mouvoir, après la Section; ils se reproduisent dans huit jours en autant d'Animaux, qu'il y a de parties coupées.

s: Dutens (Origine des découvertes, 1796 ed.) expounds Buffon's system, by his own account in Buffon's own terms: a nutritive and productive matter spread everywhere, made of organic particles always active and tending to organisation, which take forms through an internal mould, with no pre-existing germs; generation and corruption are only the association and disunion of similar parts.

src.l: Louis Dutens, 1796, Origine des découvertes attribuées aux modernes
src.loc: §67 Exposition du systême de M. de Buffon; scan 62
src.q: This nutritive and productive matter is universally spread everywhere, and is composed of ... that are always active, constantly tending toward organization, and taking different forms of their own accord according to the circumstances.
src.qo: Cette matière nutritive & productive est universellement répandue par-tout, & composée de particules organiques toujours actives, tendantes sans cesse à l'organisation, & prenant d'elles-mêmes des formes différentes, suivant les circonstances

s: Goethe (Metamorphose der Pflanzen, 1790, §§3-4) argues that a plant's ability to step backwards (as when stamens turn into petals in a double flower) reveals the laws of transformation by which nature produces one part through another and presents the most varied forms by modifying a single organ; this effect he calls the metamorphosis of plants.

src.l: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, 1790, Versuch die Metamorphose der Pflanzen zu erklären
src.q: we learn the laws of transformation by which nature produces one part through another and presents the most varied forms through the modification of a single organ.

s: William James ('The Energies of Men', 1906–7; SL edition On Vital Reserves, 1911) takes 'second wind' as evidence that past the first layer of fatigue we tap 'a level of new energy', and infers that the organism holds stored-up reserves of energy ordinarily not called upon: most of us live 'unnecessarily near our surface'.

src.l: William James, 1911, On Vital Reserves: The Energies of Men; The Gospel of Relaxation
src.q: We have evidently tapped a level of new energy masked until then by the fatigue-obstacle usually obeyed.

src.l: William James, 1911, On Vital Reserves: The Energies of Men; The Gospel of Relaxation
src.q: our organism has stored-up reserves of energy that are ordinarily not called upon, but that may be called upon ... Most of us continue living unnecessarily near our surface.

s: James (1906–7; 1911 ed.) makes felt aliveness a variable everyone knows: we feel more or less alive on different days, energies slumber that the day does not call forth, and compared with what we ought to be we are 'only half awake'; men habitually use only a small part of the powers they possess.

src.l: William James, 1911, On Vital Reserves: The Energies of Men; The Gospel of Relaxation
src.q: Everyone is familiar with the phenomenon of feeling more or less alive on different days.

src.l: William James, 1911, On Vital Reserves: The Energies of Men; The Gospel of Relaxation
src.q: Compared with what we ought to be, we are only half awake. Our fires are damped, our drafts are checked.

s: James (1906–7; 1911 ed.) says a man who energizes below his normal maximum fails by so much to profit by 'his chance at life', and that energy is measured by quality as well as quantity: everyone feels his total power rise when he passes to a higher qualitative level of life (writing above walking, thinking above writing, deciding above thinking).

src.l: William James, 1911, On Vital Reserves: The Energies of Men; The Gospel of Relaxation
src.q: a man who energizes below his normal maximum fails by just so much to profit by his chance at life ... Everyone feels that his total power rises when he passes to a higher qualitative level of life.

s: James (1906–7; 1911 ed.) names what releases the reserves: when men rise above their usual level, either some unusual stimulus fills them with emotional excitement or some idea of necessity induces an extra effort of will; 'excitements, ideas, and efforts' carry us over the dam, and the usual level is an inveterate habit of inferiority to our full self.

src.l: William James, 1911, On Vital Reserves: The Energies of Men; The Gospel of Relaxation
src.q: the habit of inferiority to our full self ... Excitements, ideas, and efforts, in a word, are what carry us over the dam.

s: In 'The Book of the Machines' (Butler, Erewhon, 1872) an Erewhonian writer argues that machines' having little consciousness now is no security against the 'ultimate development of mechanical consciousness' (a mollusc has not much either), and asks who can say a vapour engine has not a kind of consciousness, or where consciousness begins and ends.

src.l: Samuel Butler, 1872, Erewhon, or, Over the Range
src.q: against the ultimate development of mechanical consciousness, in the fact of machines possessing little consciousness now. A mollusc has not much consciousness.

src.l: Samuel Butler, 1872, Erewhon, or, Over the Range
src.q: But who can say that the vapour engine has not a kind of consciousness ? Where does consciousness begin, and where end? Who can draw the line? Who can draw any line?

s: The Erewhonian treatise (Butler, Erewhon, 1872, 'The Machines' chapters) applies the old marks of a living body to the steam engine: it must be fed and consumes its food by fire as man does, supports its combustion by air, and has a pulse and circulation; man's body is only the older and more versatile of the two.

src.l: Samuel Butler, 1872, Erewhon, or, Over the Range
src.q: The vapour-engine must be fed with food and consume it by fire even as man consumes it ; it supports its combustion by air as man supports it ; it has a pulse and circulation as man has.

s: The Erewhonian treatise (Butler, Erewhon, 1872) answers the objection that machines cannot reproduce: as the humble bee is part of the clover's reproductive system, so man may be part of that of the machines; few creatures reproduce after their own kind, and machines have 'the germ of a true reproductive system'.

src.l: Samuel Butler, 1872, Erewhon, or, Over the Range
src.q: The humble bee is a part of the reproductive system of the clover. ... then why not we part of that of the machines ?

s: Schopenhauer (Die Welt als Wille und Vorstellung IV, 1818; 1844 ed.) says that as walking is a constantly checked falling, so the life of our body is only a continually checked dying, a death always postponed; every breath wards off death, which wins in the end.

src.l: Arthur Schopenhauer, 1818, Die Welt als Wille und Vorstellung
src.loc: Book IV (Bejahung und Verneinung des Willens), printed p. 351; scan 388
src.q: das Leben unsers Leibes nur ein fortdauernd gehemmtes Sterben, ein immer aufgeschobener Tod ist

s: A Nietzsche note (Der Wille zur Macht §13–14, 1922 ed.) says that the most extreme nihilism places the value of things in their having no reality behind them, being only a symptom of strength in those who posit values, 'a simplification for the purpose of life'; the next note says values change in relation to the growth of power of the one who posits them.

src.l: Friedrich Nietzsche, 1922, Der Wille zur Macht
src.q: sondern dass sie nur ein Symptom von Kraft auf Seiten der Werth-Ansetzer sind, eine Simplifikation zum Zweck des Lebens. 14. Die Werthe und deren Veränderung stehen im Verhältniss zu dem Macht-Wachsthum des Werthsetzenden.

s: Bergson (L'Évolution créatrice, 1907, 'De la signification de la vie') says that from amoeba to the top of the series animal life consists in procuring a store of energy and spending it, through matter as supple as possible, in variable and unforeseen directions; the plant alone gathers solar energy, so that all life appears as an effort to accumulate energy and then release it.

src.l: Henri Bergson, 1908, Creative Evolution
src.loc: De la signification de la vie, printed p. 275; scan 293
src.q: la vie animale consiste 1° à se procurer une provision d'énergie, 2° à la dépenser, par l'entremise d'une matière aussi souple que possible, dans des directions variables et imprévues.

src.l: Henri Bergson, 1908, Creative Evolution
src.loc: De la signification de la vie, printed p. 275; scan 293
src.q: De sorte que la vie tout entière, animale et végétale, dans ce qu'elle a d'essentiel, apparaît comme un effort pour accumuler de l'énergie et pour la lâcher ensuite

s: Whitehead (Process and Reality, 1929) defines the primary meaning of 'life' as the origination of conceptual novelty, novelty of appetition; a society is 'living' only derivatively, by including living occasions, and may be more or less living, with no absolute gap between living and non-living societies.

src.l: Alfred North Whitehead, 1929, Process and Reality
src.q: In accordance with this doctrine of 'life,' the primary meaning of 'life' is the origination of conceptual novelty—novelty of appetition. ... A 'living society' is one which includes some 'living occasions.'

s: Scheler (Der Formalismus in der Ethik, 1913–16) sets out vital values as a second value modality above the pleasant: their object-values are spanned by the opposition of the noble (edel) and the common (gemein), and their states are the modes of Lebensgefühl, the feeling of ascending and descending life, of health and sickness, of age and death, of weariness and vigour.

src.l: Max Scheler, 1916, Der Formalismus in der Ethik und die materiale Wertethik
src.q: Als eine zweite Wertmodalität hebt sich der Inbegriff von Werten des vitalen Fühlens heraus. ... als Zustände gehören dazu alle Modi des Lebensgefühls (z. B. das Gefühl des »aufsteigenden« und des »niedergehenden« Lebens, das Gesundheits- und Krankheitsgefühl, das Alters- und Todesgefühl

src.l: Max Scheler, 1916, Der Formalismus in der Ethik und die materiale Wertethik
src.q: as states, this includes all modes of life-feeling (e.g., the feeling of "ascending" and "descending" life, the feeling of health and sickness, the feeling of age and death, feelings like "weary," "vigorous," etc.)

s: Dilthey (Einleitung in die Geisteswissenschaften, 1883) finds the elements of society and history in 'Lebenseinheiten', psycho-physical individuals, each a world; unlike the hypothetical particles of natural science, these units are given as facts in inner experience, and their study is the most fundamental group of the human sciences.

src.l: Wilhelm Dilthey, 1883, Einleitung in die Geisteswissenschaften, Bd. 1
src.q: Die Analysis findet in den Lebenseinheiten, den psychophysischen Individuis die Elemente, aus welchen Gesellschaft und Geschichte sich aufbauen

src.l: Wilhelm Dilthey, 1883, Einleitung in die Geisteswissenschaften, Bd. 1
src.q: Individua, psycho-physische Ganze, deren jedes von jedem anderen unterschieden, deren jedes eine Welt ist.

src.l: Wilhelm Dilthey, 1883, Einleitung in die Geisteswissenschaften, Bd. 1
src.q: Analysis finds in the units of life, the psycho-physical individuals, the elements from which society and history are built
src.qo: Die Analysis findet in den Lebenseinheiten, den psychophysischen Individuis die Elemente, aus welchen Gesellschaft und Geschichte sich aufbauen

s: Crowther's Yoruba Vocabulary (1852) glosses ẹ̀mí (printed Emmí) as 'life, breath, spirit, influence', with the blessing 'May God give you a long life!' (li ẹmmi gigun, lit. 'with long ẹ̀mí') and the proverb that the ẹ̀mí of a spring makes the brook flow: one word for breath, the length of a life, and the moving power of water.

src.l: Samuel Ajayi Crowther, 1852, A Vocabulary of the Yoruba Language
src.q: Emmí, s. life, breath, spirit, influence.—Ki Ọlọrun ki ofu ’ọ li ẹmmi gigun, “May God give you a long life!”—Emmí abata ni imu odò iṣan, “The influence of a fountain makes the brook flow.”

s: Farrow (1926) lists Elemi, 'The Owner of Breath', among the Yoruba names of the Supreme Being, and glosses emi as 'breath' or 'spirit', equating it with Greek pneuma: life-breath belongs to and is lent by the high god.

src.l: Stephen Septimus Farrow, 1926, Faith, Fancies and Fetich, or Yoruba Paganism
src.loc: ch. III, The Supreme Deity; scan 51
src.q: Elemi.—"The Owner of Breath." Emi is "breath" or "spirit" (Greek πνεῦμα).

s: In an Ifa verse Farrow (1926) prints, Orunmila goes 'to receive àṣẹ from Olodumare' (gba ase l'owo Olodumare), and afterwards 'All that he said came to pass'; Farrow renders àṣẹ 'authority' and the closing formula A se! 'It will come to pass!', so the same word is both the power that makes speech effective and the 'amen'.

src.l: Stephen Septimus Farrow, 1926, Faith, Fancies and Fetich, or Yoruba Paganism
src.loc: ch. V, Ifa verse of Eji Ogbe; scan 64
src.q: Ada fun Orunmila nigbatijo nlo gba ase l'owo Olodumare

src.l: Stephen Septimus Farrow, 1926, Faith, Fancies and Fetich, or Yoruba Paganism
src.q: Ifa was consulted for Orunmila once, going to receive authority from the Almighty. He sacrificed. And the Almighty gave him authority. When all the world heard that he had received authority from the Almighty they came to him. All that he said came to pass. Ever since then we say, "It will come to pass!"

s: The Song of the White Buffalo Maiden, sung by the Teton singer Charging Thunder and recorded by Densmore (1918), opens niya' tanin'yan mawa'ni ye, 'with visible breath I am walking', as she brings the sacred pipe to the Buffalo nation; it is sung in the Spirit-keeping ceremony.

src.l: Frances Densmore, 1918, Teton Sioux Music
src.q: niya' tanin'yan with visible breath ¹ mawa'ni ye I am walking

src.l: Frances Densmore, 1918, Teton Sioux Music
src.q: This song is sung in the Spirit-keeping ceremony when the man who is keeping the spirit of his child can afford to have a white buffalo robe used in the ceremony.

s: Eastman (Ohiyesa, 1902) recalls his grandmother teaching him before his first offering that the Great Mystery 'looks at you from every creation', whispers in the wind, gives his war-whoop in the thunder, and watches by the sun and moon: the sacred power is met in and through living nature.

src.l: Charles A. Eastman (Ohiyesa), 1902, Indian Boyhood
src.q: you will call upon him who looks at you from every creation. In the wind you hear him whisper to you. He gives his war-whoop in the thunder. He watches you by day with his eye, the sun; at night, he gazes upon your sleeping countenance through the moon.

s: Skeat (Malay Magic, 1900) says the meaning of the Malay sěmangat 'covers both "soul" and "life"', not the state of being alive but its cause, the 'vital principle'; the soul-mannikin is 'the cause of life and thought in the individual it animates'.

src.l: Walter William Skeat, 1900, Malay Magic: Being an Introduction to the Folklore and Popular Religion of the Malay Peninsula
src.loc: ch. II (c) The Soul, n. 1; scan 77
src.q: The meaning covers both “soul” and “life” (i.e. not the state of being alive, but the cause thereof or “vital principle”).

src.l: Walter William Skeat, 1900, Malay Magic: Being an Introduction to the Folklore and Popular Religion of the Malay Peninsula
src.q: is “the cause of life and thought in the individual it animates,”

s: The Motul dictionary illustrates vayaz ('what passes quickly, like a dream') with a sentence that wealth, being and life (cuxtal) in this world pass like a dream — a contemptus-mundi example sentence put into Maya.

src.qo: Vayaz ayikalil. vuinicilil, cuxtal yokolcab: de presto passa como sueño la riqueza, el ser, y la vida, en este mundo.

s: Inca Garcilaso (1609) explains the Quechua verb cama as 'to give soul, life, being and substance', and Pacha Cámac as 'he who does with the universe what the soul does with the body', rendering the hymn's Pacha camac as 'the God who animates it' and camasunqui as 'and gave you a soul'.

src.l: Inca Garcilaso de la Vega, 1609, Comentarios reales de los Incas
src.loc: Part I, Book II, ch. 27; scan 121
src.q: Pacha Cámac quiere decir el que hace con el universo lo que el alma con el cuerpo. … cama es dar alma, vida, ser y sustancia.

s: Tregear (The Maori Race, 1904) says the mauri of a forest or river is a talisman that, kept in its place, holds the hau of forest, stream or land so that birds multiply and trees flourish; it is hidden, and a priest who seized an enemy's mauri 'held the heart of the enemy's country in his hand'.

src.l: Edward Tregear, 1904, The Maori Race
src.q: So too the mauri of a forest or a river is a talisman, and whilst it is in its proper place it keeps the hau of the forest, stream, or land, so that birds multiply and trees flourish.

s: Best (Spiritual Concepts of the Maori, 1900) sets three things apart at death: the wairua lives on, but the mauri, 'spark of life', is extinct, and the manawa ora, 'breath of life', has departed for all time.

src.l: Elsdon Best, 1900, Spiritual Concepts of the Maori (Journal of the Polynesian Society, Vol. 9, 1900)
src.q: The wairua lives on afte death of a person, but the mauri or spark of life is extinct, and thi manawa ora or breath of life has departed for all time.

s: Best (1900) says hau is held by animate and inanimate things alike: 'the hau of the land, of a forest, of a tree, of the kumara'; whoever takes the hau of land or its mauri can render the land infertile by incantation.

src.l: Elsdon Best, 1900, Spiritual Concepts of the Maori (Journal of the Polynesian Society, Vol. 9, 1900)
src.q: Thus we hear of the hau of the land, of a forest, of a tree, of the kumara, &c.

src.l: Elsdon Best, 1900, Spiritual Concepts of the Maori (Journal of the Polynesian Society, Vol. 9, 1900)
src.q: For, mark you, land may be bewitche as well as man, and should the haw of land, or its maurt, fall int hostile hands, that land will be rendered infertile by potent incantation:

s: Best (1900) describes the rites that keep a forest alive: the right wing of a kākā parrot (kira) is 'the mauri of the forest birds', kept hidden so it keeps the forest stocked, and at the ahi taitai fire a priest roasts and eats part of the first bird, burying or hanging the rest for Tāne; Tregear (1904) adds that the first bird snared was torn from the spit with the priest's teeth.

src.l: Elsdon Best, 1900, Spiritual Concepts of the Maori (Journal of the Polynesian Society, Vol. 9, 1900)
src.q: This kira is the mauri of the forest birds. It preserves them and keeps the forests well stocked. It is, of course, carefully concealed.

src.l: Elsdon Best, 1900, Spiritual Concepts of the Maori (Journal of the Polynesian Society, Vol. 9, 1900)
src.q: The ahi taitai is a sacred fire at which rites are performed th: have for their purpose the protection of the life principle and frui fulness of man, the land, forests, birds, &c.

src.l: Edward Tregear, 1904, The Maori Race
src.q: The first bird snared was roasted on a stick before the fire and when cooked was torn off the spit by the priest's teeth, he being careful not to use his hands, but gnawing the bird as a dog would do.

s: A Māori karakia for all food in Grey's collection (1853) urges the crop to grow from its mauri: 'Koi to mauri ka tupu, Tupu koe e to mauri … Ka te tupu koe i to mauri ora', then feeds the gods and Rongo.

src.l: George Grey (collector), 1853, Ko Nga Moteatea me Nga Hakirara o Nga Maori (Maori Songs)
src.q: Kia korikori koe, Koi to mauri ka tupu, Tupu koe e to mauri, Ka rau huihui koe i to mauri, Ka rau matomato koe i to mauri, Ka te tupu koe i to mauri ora hai, Whangaia nga atua kia anga mai e,

s: Best (The Maori School of Learning, 1923) reports the formula said over a stone before learning tapu lore, 'Here is my mauri, thy mauri, O Io the Parent!', and that such 'mana-possessing stones' protect the scholars' mauri and make their knowledge permanent.

src.l: Elsdon Best, 1923, The Maori School of Learning (Dominion Museum Monograph No. 6)
src.q: Here is my mauri, thy mauri, O lo the Parent ! ... the point ever stressed is the ability of such mana-possessing stones to protect the life-principle of the scholars and to render their acquired knowledge permanent.

s: Emerson (Unwritten Literature of Hawaii, 1909), annotating 'I kua i Mauli-ola' in a prayer to Pele, says Mauli-ola is a god of health and the word was 'applied to the breath of life, or to the physician's power of healing', the cognate of Māori mauri, 'life, the seat of life'.

src.l: Nathaniel B. Emerson, 1909, Unwritten Literature of Hawaii: The Sacred Songs of the Hula
src.q: The same word also was applied to the breath of life, or to the physician's power of healing. In the Maori tongue the word mauri, corresponding to mauli, means life, the seat of life.
